\section{Ordered arithmetic computation\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:model}

\subsection{States, rules, and operational semantics}
Throughout, $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and vector inequalities are coordinatewise.
All polynomial unknowns are natural numbers; polynomial coefficients may be
negative integers. We assume $m,d\geq1$.

\begin{definition}[Ordered multiset program]
An ordered multiset program is a list
$\mathcal P=((A_1,B_1),\ldots,(A_m,B_m))$ with $A_i,B_i\in\N^d$.
At state $x\in\N^d$, rule $i$ is enabled when $x\geq B_i$.
If an enabled rule exists, let $j$ be the smallest enabled index and perform
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:step}
 x\xrightarrow{j}_{\mathcal P}x-B_j+A_j.
\end{equation}
Otherwise the program halts. The instruction trace records the chosen indices.
\end{definition}

The term ``ordered'' is essential. A later enabled rule is not a legal
choice when an earlier rule is also enabled. The model can be viewed as
multiset rewriting with a deterministic priority policy: $B_i$ is consumed
and $A_i$ is produced. No stochastic or parallel scheduling semantics are
being imposed. In particular, the results below do not silently extend to
arbitrary chemical-reaction semantics.

\subsection{The exact FRACTRAN embedding}
Let $(a_i/b_i)_{i=1}^m$ be positive fractions in lowest terms. Let
$p_1,\ldots,p_d$ contain every prime dividing any numerator or denominator,
and set
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:valuation}
 A_{ip}=v_{p_p}(a_i),\qquad B_{ip}=v_{p_p}(b_i).
\end{equation}
Every positive integer has a unique decomposition
\[
 N=c\prod_{p=1}^d p_p^{x_p},\qquad
 \gcd\!\left(c,\prod_{p=1}^d p_p\right)=1.
\]
Because the fractions are reduced, $a_iN/b_i$ is an integer exactly when
$x\geq B_i$. Its valuation vector is $x-B_i+A_i$, and the coprime factor
$c$ stays unchanged. Thus \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:step} is an exact conjugate of FRACTRAN
on each fixed inert-factor component.

\begin{remark}[Reduction is not optional]
In the FRACTRAN subcase, $A_{ip}B_{ip}=0$ for every $i,p$.
For a general multiset rule, a coordinate may be both consumed and produced.
One must not replace such a rule by the fraction
$\prod p_p^{A_{ip}}/\prod p_p^{B_{ip}}$ and cancel it: cancellation can remove
a genuine enabling condition. The general multiset model and reduced
FRACTRAN are related but not identical syntactic classes.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Why priority permits universal computation}
For orientation, the conventional counter-machine simulation can be made
explicit. Give counter $r$ a prime $p_r$ and control state $s$ a distinct
prime $q_s$. A well-formed machine configuration is encoded by
$q_s\prod_r p_r^{x_r}$, with exactly one control prime present.
An increment transition $s\to t$ on counter $r$ is represented by
$p_rq_t/q_s$. A positive decrement transition uses
$q_t/(q_sp_r)$; place it before the default zero branch $q_u/q_s$.
All rules belonging to another control state are disabled. A halting state
has no outgoing fraction. Direct self-targets can first be split through
fresh control states, so cancellation does not destroy the control test.
This preserves the selected branch and produces a finite, effective
simulation. The universality conclusion is classical \cite{conway1987,lf2022};
we use it later only for a computability reduction.

\subsection{The compression interface}
Fix a nonempty word
\[
 w=(j_0,\ldots,j_{\ell-1})\in\{1,\ldots,m\}^{\ell}.
\]
Let $\Bvalid_{\mathcal P,w}(x,k,y)$ mean that the actual deterministic
execution from $x$ begins with $w^k$ and reaches $y$ immediately after those
$k\ell$ steps. Here $k=0$ is allowed, in which case the relation is exactly
$y=x$. No halting condition at $y$ is implicit.

The word is part of the compiled schema, not an unbounded input hidden in a
fixed polynomial. The program entries, $x,k,y$, will all be free inputs of
one polynomial for that schema. This distinction prevents a false inference
from the later unique-witness theorem to a universal single-fold theorem.

\section{Exact finite-block acceleration\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:interval}

\subsection{Affine phase trajectories}
Put
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:prefix}
 d_i=A_i-B_i,\qquad
 \beta_r=\sum_{s<r}d_{j_s},\qquad
 D=\sum_{s<\ell}d_{j_s}.
\end{equation}
Before phase $r$ of the $h$th copy, the only possible state consistent with
the prescribed word is
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:phase}
 z_{h,r}=x+\beta_r+hD.
\end{equation}
These are hypothetical integer vectors until validity has been proved.
It would be circular to assume in advance that every such vector is a
legal state.

\begin{lemma}[Exact local criterion]\label{cdc:pf:lem:local}
For $k\in\N$, the relation $\Bvalid_{\mathcal P,w}(x,k,y)$ holds if and only if
$y=x+kD$ and, for every $0\leq h<k$ and $0\leq r<\ell$,
\begin{align}
 x+\beta_r+hD&\geq B_{j_r},\label{cdc:pf:eq:chosen}\\
 x+\beta_r+hD&\not\geq B_i\quad(1\leq i<j_r).\label{cdc:pf:eq:prior}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Necessity follows by summing the updates of the actual run. Conversely,
induct on the lexicographically ordered pairs $(h,r)$. The initial state is
$x$. At the next prescribed phase, \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:chosen} makes $j_r$ enabled and
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:prior} disables every earlier rule. Hence the deterministic
semantics chooses $j_r$, and the resulting state is the next vector in
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:phase}. It is nonnegative because it is obtained from a state at
least $B_{j_r}$ by subtracting $B_{j_r}$ and adding $A_{j_r}$. The last state
is $x+kD$. For $k=0$ the phase conditions are empty and the same conclusion
reduces to $y=x$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A single coordinate contributes an interval}
For $a,s\in\Z$ and $k\in\N$, define
\[
 I(a,s,k)=\{h\in\Z:0\leq h<k,\ a+sh\geq0\}.
\]
We represent this as a half-open integer interval $[L,U)$; $L\geq U$
represents the empty set. The following formulas choose canonical endpoints:
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:scalarinterval}
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 \text{condition}&L&U\\ \hline
 s>0&\min\{k,\max\{0,\ceil{-a/s}\}\}&k\\
 s<0,\ a\geq0&0&\min\{k,\floor{a/(-s)}+1\}\\
 s<0,\ a<0&0&0\\
 s=0,\ a\geq0&0&k\\
 s=0,\ a<0&0&0
\end{array}
\end{equation}
Each row follows by solving a linear inequality and clipping to $[0,k)$.
In particular, all returned endpoints are natural numbers at most $k$.

At phase $r$, rule $i$ is enabled on the intersection of the $d$ intervals
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:ruleinterval}
 I(x_p+\beta_{r,p}-B_{ip},D_p,k),\qquad 1\leq p\leq d.
\end{equation}
Its lower endpoint is the maximum of the coordinate lower endpoints; its
upper endpoint is the minimum of their upper endpoints.

\begin{theorem}[Priority-sensitive interval checker]\label{cdc:pf:thm:interval}
The relation $\Bvalid_{\mathcal P,w}(x,k,y)$ can be decided without unrolling
$k$ copies. At every phase, require the chosen rule's interval to be $[0,k)$
and every earlier rule's interval to be empty, and finally check $y=x+kD$.
The number of coordinate interval calculations is $S$ from \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:RS}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A rule is enabled exactly when all its coordinate inequalities hold, so its
enabling times are precisely the intersection \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:ruleinterval}.
An earlier rule is disabled at every prescribed time exactly when the
intersection is empty, equivalently $L\geq U$. Since each coordinate
endpoint lies in $[0,k]$, the chosen rule is enabled throughout exactly when
$L=0$ and $U=k$. Apply Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:local}. Phase $r$ checks the $j_r$
rules with index at most $j_r$, giving $d\sum_r j_r=S$ calculations.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[An interior-only priority collision]\label{cdc:pf:ex:interior}
Consider
\[
 \mathcal F=(1/72,\ 3/2),\qquad N_0=32,
 \qquad w=(2).
\]
In the $(2,3)$ valuation coordinates, $x=(5,0)$, $D=(-1,1)$, and the earlier
rule consumes $(3,2)$. A proposed five-copy block has pre-states
\[
 (5,0),\ (4,1),\ (3,2),\ (2,3),\ (1,4).
\]
The second rule is enabled at all five pre-states. The first rule is
disabled at both ends but enabled at the middle state $(3,2)$. Its enabling
interval is exactly $[2,3)$. Consequently the proposed block is invalid;
the actual raw-integer run starts $32\to48\to72\to1$, with labels $2,2,1$.
An endpoint-only priority test accepts a false computation here.
\end{example}

\subsection{Maximal repetition from a given seed}
Let $M_w(x)$ be the largest number of complete copies of $w$ executable from
$x$, or $\infty$ if all numbers of copies are executable. Block validity is
prefix-closed in $k$. Thus, once infinitude has been excluded by
Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:infinite} below, doubling followed by binary search computes
$M_w(x)$ using the interval checker. No intermediate trace of length
$M_w(x)\ell$ has to be generated.

The phrase ``complete copies'' is important. If $M_w(x)=k$, the next copy may
execute some proper prefix before it fails. The certificate is not claiming
that the very next instruction already differs.

\section{Least seeds and the exact repetition capacity\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:capacity}

The interval theorem handles a supplied seed. A stronger structural result
emerges when the seed is existentially quantified. There is no search over
all starting vectors: one canonical vector suffices.

\subsection{The resource-minimal seed}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:lambda}
 \lambda_p=\max_{0\leq r<\ell}
       \bigl(B_{j_r,p}-\beta_{r,p}\bigr),\qquad
 D_p^- =\max\{0,-D_p\}.
\end{equation}
The term $r=0$ is $B_{j_0,p}\geq0$, so $\lambda\in\N^d$.
For $k\geq1$ put
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:lambda-k}
 \lambda(k)=\lambda+(k-1)D^-.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Resource lower bound]\label{cdc:pf:lem:resource}
All selected-rule inequalities \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:chosen} hold for $w^k$ if and only if
$x\geq\lambda(k)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed coordinate, all the selected inequalities are equivalent to
\[
 x_p\geq\max_{r,h}\bigl(B_{j_r,p}-\beta_{r,p}-hD_p\bigr).
\]
The two indices vary independently. The maximum over $r$ is $\lambda_p$;
the maximum of $-hD_p$ over $0\leq h<k$ is $(k-1)D_p^-$. This is exactly
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:lambda-k}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Lowering cannot create a priority conflict]\label{cdc:pf:lem:lower}
Suppose $x$ executes $w^k$ and $\lambda(k)\leq x'\leq x$. Then $x'$ executes
$w^k$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:minimal-equivalence}
 \exists x\in\N^d\ \exists y\ \Bvalid_{\mathcal P,w}(x,k,y)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \lambda(k)\text{ executes }w^k.
\end{equation}
Whenever the set of valid seeds is nonempty, $\lambda(k)$ is its unique least element.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The resource lower bound preserves all selected-rule inequalities at $x'$.
At any fixed phase and repetition index, an earlier rule's enabling
predicate is upward closed in the seed. If that rule were enabled at $x'$,
it would also be enabled at $x$, a contradiction. Thus all prior rules
remain disabled and Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:local} applies. Every valid seed is at
least $\lambda(k)$ by Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:resource}, proving the last assertions.
\end{proof}

This monotonicity is deliberately restricted. The entire deterministic
transition system is not monotone in the sense that raising a seed preserves
its selected trace. Raising a seed can enable an earlier instruction and
change the computation. The lemma uses lowering within a resource-safe box.

\subsection{The collision window at the least seed}
For every phase $r$ and earlier rule $i<j_r$, set
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:c}
 c_{ri,p}=\lambda_p+\beta_{r,p}-B_{ip}.
\end{equation}
Call $(r,i)$ \emph{permanently blocked} if some coordinate satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:blocker}
 D_p=0\quad\hbox{and}\quad c_{ri,p}<0.
\end{equation}
For a pair that is not permanently blocked, define two nonnegative integers
\begin{align}
 L_{ri}&=\max\left(\{0\}\cup
 \left\{\ceil{\frac{\pos{-c_{ri,p}}}{D_p}}:D_p>0\right\}\right),
 \label{cdc:pf:eq:L}\\
 R_{ri}&=\max\left(\{0\}\cup
 \left\{\ceil{\frac{\pos{-c_{ri,p}}}{-D_p}}:D_p<0\right\}\right).
 \label{cdc:pf:eq:R}
\end{align}
Here $\pos{u}=\max\{u,0\}$, and an empty family contributes only the displayed
zero. The use of $R_{ri}$ as a right-margin quantity is distinct from the
aggregate count $R$ in \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:RS}.

\begin{lemma}[Two-sided collision window]\label{cdc:pf:lem:window}
At seed $\lambda(k)$, a non-permanently-blocked earlier rule $i$ is enabled
before phase $r$ precisely at the integers
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:window}
 L_{ri}\leq h\leq k-1-R_{ri}.
\end{equation}
A permanently blocked pair is never enabled there. Consequently the first
repetition count for which this pair creates a conflict is $L_{ri}+R_{ri}+1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At the least seed, its coordinate enabling inequality is
\[
 c_{ri,p}+(k-1)D_p^-+hD_p\geq0.
\]
If $D_p>0$, this says $h\geq\ceil{\pos{-c_{ri,p}}/D_p}$, once $h\geq0$ is
included. If $D_p<0$, it says
$k-1-h\geq\ceil{\pos{-c_{ri,p}}/(-D_p)}$.
If $D_p=0$, it is either identically true or identically false; the latter
is exactly a permanent blocker. Taking the strongest left and right bounds
gives \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:window}. This interval contains an integer exactly when
$k\geq L_{ri}+R_{ri}+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Closed repetition-capacity formula]\label{cdc:pf:thm:capacity}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:capacity}
 \Capacity(w)=\min_{\substack{0\leq r<\ell,\ 1\leq i<j_r\\
                        (r,i)\text{ not permanently blocked}}}
                  (L_{ri}+R_{ri}),
 \qquad\min\varnothing=\infty.
\end{equation}
Then for every $k\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:capacity-equivalence}
 \exists x,y\in\N^d\ \Bvalid_{\mathcal P,w}(x,k,y)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k\leq\Capacity(w).
\end{equation}
The capacity and the least valid seed for any permitted $k$ are computable
by the formulas above, using $O(d\ell+d\sum_r(j_r-1))$ elementary integer
operations, including divisions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At seed $\lambda(k)$, every selected-rule inequality already holds. By
Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:window}, a non-permanently-blocked earlier rule remains
inactive for the whole block exactly when $k\leq L_{ri}+R_{ri}$. All
permanently blocked pairs impose no further restriction. Intersect these
conditions and use Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:lower}. The computation forms prefixes and
coordinatewise maxima, then processes one $d$-tuple for every earlier-rule
pair. The stated operation bound follows. Integer bit costs depend on the
sizes of the input entries and the word, not on an enumeration of $k$ steps.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Structure of the seed region]\label{cdc:pf:cor:seedregion}
For each $k\geq1$, the valid seeds form either the empty set or a set with
least element $\lambda(k)$ that is downward closed relative to the orthant
$\lambda(k)+\N^d$. For fixed program and word, this set is Presburger-definable.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The order assertion is Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:lower}. For fixed program and word,
Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:local} is a Presburger formula: the coefficients $D_p$ and
$\beta_{r,p}$ are constants, and the quantifier over $h$ is a bounded
first-order quantifier over a linear formula. Fixing $k$ gives the claimed
seed region. This observation does not require quantifier elimination to
compute the least seed or capacity.
\end{proof}

\section{A sharp pumping bound\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:pumping}

\begin{theorem}[Threshold $2H+1$]\label{cdc:pf:thm:pumping}
Let $H=\max_{i,p}B_{ip}$. For every nonempty instruction word $w$,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:capbound}
 \Capacity(w)<\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Capacity(w)\leq2H.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, if some seed executes $w^{2H+1}$, then for every $k\in\N$
there is a seed executing $w^k$.
The threshold is independent of the word length, the number of rules, the
number of coordinates, and the sizes of the production entries.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By definition of $\lambda$, for every phase and coordinate,
$\lambda_p+\beta_{r,p}\geq B_{j_r,p}\geq0$. Thus
\[
 \pos{-c_{ri,p}}
 =\max\{B_{ip}-\lambda_p-\beta_{r,p},0\}\leq B_{ip}\leq H.
\]
Every nonzero $|D_p|$ is a positive integer. Therefore every ceiling in
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:L} or \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:R} is at most $H$, whence
$L_{ri}+R_{ri}\leq2H$. If the capacity is finite, it is a minimum of such
numbers by Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:capacity}. The equivalent pumping statement
follows immediately. For $k=0$, every seed works.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the parameter measures]
For FRACTRAN, $H$ is the largest prime exponent in a reduced denominator,
not the largest denominator itself, its numerical value, or its bit length.
For a squarefree-denominator program, $H=1$, so any word executable three
times from some seed is executable arbitrarily many times from suitable seeds.
If $H=0$, the same theorem allows only capacities $0$ and $\infty$.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness within reduced FRACTRAN]\label{cdc:pf:thm:sharp}
For every $H\geq1$, the reduced three-fraction program
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:sharp-family}
 \mathcal F_H=\left(\frac{1}{7\,6^H},\ \frac{7}{10},\ \frac{15}{7}\right)
\end{equation}
and word $w=(2,3)$ have $\Capacity(w)=2H$. Hence $2H+1$ is the smallest universal
pumping threshold as a function of $H$ alone.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use coordinates for primes $2,3,5,7$. The two selected rules transport
one unit from the $2$-counter to the $3$-counter, using $5$ and $7$ as
alternating control tokens. The one-copy least seed and drift are
\[
 \lambda=(1,0,1,0),\qquad D=(-1,1,0,0).
\]
Thus the least seed for $k$ copies is $(k,0,1,0)$, corresponding to the raw
integer $5\,2^k$. Before the second fraction in copy $h$ the state is
\[
 (k-h,h,1,0),
\]
and before the third it is
\[
 (k-1-h,h,0,1).
\]
The first fraction is disabled at the former state by the missing $7$.
At the latter it is enabled exactly when
\[
 h\geq H\quad\hbox{and}\quad k-1-h\geq H.
\]
The earlier second fraction is disabled at the latter state by the missing
$5$. All selected rules themselves are enabled for $0\leq h<k$.
Consequently the prescribed word works at the least seed precisely when
$k\leq2H$. Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:lower} excludes rescuing a larger $k$ by choosing
a different seed. The largest denominator exponent in \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:sharp-family}
is indeed $H$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The quantifier distinction}
The pumping theorem proves
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:quantifier-finite}
 \forall k\ \exists x\quad w^k\text{ is executable from }x,
\end{equation}
not necessarily
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:quantifier-infinite}
 \exists x\ \forall k\quad w^k\text{ is executable from }x.
\end{equation}
For the one-fraction program $(3/2)$ and word $(1)$, the first statement
holds by choosing a seed divisible by $2^k$. Every fixed seed has only
finitely many factors of $2$, so the second statement is false. This
example is also why the least seed grows with $k$ in negative-drift
coordinates. Section~\ref{cdc:pf:sec:infinite} gives the exact condition under
which the quantifiers can be exchanged.

\subsection{A refined, program-dependent bound}
The proof also gives more detailed bounds. For any nonblocked pair, retain
its actual coordinate deficits and drift magnitudes in \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:L}--\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:R}
instead of replacing them by $H$. Large drift magnitudes reduce the waiting
margins, and one-sided drift can remove one margin altogether. For example,
if $D\geq0$, every $R_{ri}=0$ and a finite capacity is at most $H$.
These refinements follow directly from the exact formula; they need not be
approximated by a universal threshold in an implementation.

\section{A canonical quartic Diophantine compiler\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:compiler}

This section replaces the interval algorithm by an explicit polynomial
construction. The central issue is not merely expressing the required
inequalities. It is doing so with a \emph{unique} tuple of auxiliary values,
including values associated with cases that do not apply.

\subsection{Single-fold representations and total gates}
\begin{definition}[Single-fold relative to the free inputs]
A polynomial $P(u,z)\in\Z[u,z]$ is a single-fold Diophantine representation
of a relation $\mathcal R(u)$ over $\N$ when
\[
 \mathcal R(u)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\N^n\ P(u,z)=0,
\]
and for every $u$ there is at most one such $z$.
\end{definition}

The ambient domain matters. Replacing natural auxiliary variables by four
squares to quantify over all integers can introduce many choices and does
not preserve this uniqueness assertion. We work directly over $\N$.

\begin{lemma}[Canonical comparison gate]\label{cdc:pf:lem:cmp}
For $u,v\in\N$, the equations
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:cmp}
 b(b-1)=0,\qquad
 b(v-u-1-s)=0,\qquad
 (1-b)(u-v-s)=0
\end{equation}
have a unique solution $(b,s)\in\N^2$. It is
\[
 (b,s)=\begin{cases}(1,v-u-1),&u<v,\\(0,u-v),&u\geq v.\end{cases}
\]
In particular, $b=\ip{u<v}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first equation forces $b\in\{0,1\}$. If $b=1$, the second equation
forces $s=v-u-1$, which is natural exactly when $u<v$. If $b=0$, the third
forces $s=u-v$, which is natural exactly when $u\geq v$. These alternatives
partition all input pairs and determine the slack uniquely, including the tie case.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Canonical division gate]\label{cdc:pf:lem:division}
For $a\in\N$ and $d\geq1$, the equations
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:division}
 a-dq-r=0,\qquad d-r-1-t=0
\end{equation}
have a unique solution $(q,r,t)\in\N^3$. Here
$q=\floor{a/d}$, $r$ is the Euclidean remainder, and $t=d-r-1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The second equation is equivalent to $0\leq r<d$ together with the uniquely
determined slack $t$. The first is Euclidean division, whose quotient and
remainder are unique under that bound.
\end{proof}

A straight-line assignment $z=E$ contributes one auxiliary and one residual
$z-E$. We use it only when $E$ has degree at most two in already available
variables and is nonnegative on the uniquely determined earlier values.
Comparison followed by one assignment gives
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:minmax}
 \min(u,v)=v-b(v-u),\qquad
 \max(u,v)=u+b(v-u),\qquad b=\ip{u<v}.
\end{equation}
Thus each min or max uses three auxiliaries and four residuals. We keep
separate comparison gates in the stated count even when sharing them could
save variables.

\subsection{Removing signed data without hiding arithmetic}
The mathematical interval formulas use signed drifts and intercepts. For
the natural-number circuit, form separate nonnegative prefix sums
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:PQ}
 P_{r,p}=\sum_{s<r}A_{j_s,p},\qquad
 Q_{r,p}=\sum_{s<r}B_{j_s,p}.
\end{equation}
Then $\beta_r=P_r-Q_r$. Write $P=P_\ell$ and $Q=Q_\ell$.
For each coordinate, compute
\[
 e^-_p=\ip{P_p<Q_p},\qquad e^+_p=\ip{Q_p<P_p},\qquad
 e^0_p=1-e^-_p-e^+_p.
\]
The comparison of $P_p,Q_p$ supplies a slack $s_p$. Define
\begin{align}
 D_p^+&=(1-e^-_p)s_p,& D_p^-&=e^-_p(s_p+1),\label{cdc:pf:eq:slopeparts}\\
 d_p^+&=D_p^++1-e^+_p,& d_p^-&=D_p^-+1-e^-_p.\label{cdc:pf:eq:safedenom}
\end{align}
The first two values are $\max(D_p,0)$ and $\max(-D_p,0)$. Both denominators
in \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:safedenom} are at least one: on the relevant nonzero-sign
branch they equal the true drift magnitude, and otherwise they equal one.
Also materialize $g_p=e^+_p k$ and $f_p=e^0_p k$.

The safe denominators are not a cosmetic detail. If a division gate were
introduced only under a conditional multiplier, its inactive branch could
leave quotient or remainder variables unconstrained. Here all gates are
always evaluated and all their outputs are uniquely fixed.

\subsection{A natural-number interval circuit}
For one phase-rule-coordinate triple, set
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:uv}
 u=x_p+P_{r,p},\qquad v=B_{ip}+Q_{r,p}.
\end{equation}
Thus $u-v=x_p+\beta_{r,p}-B_{ip}$. Apply the comparison gate to $u,v$,
obtaining $b=\ip{u<v}$ and slack $s$. In the following display, every
assignment to a named output is materialized as a gate; min and division
have the implementations just given:
\begin{align}
 a^-&=b(s+1),&a^+&=(1-b)s,\label{cdc:pf:eq:intervalcircuit1}\\
 n^+&=a^-+d_p^+-1,&q^+&=\floor{n^+/d_p^+},\nonumber\\
 \ell_p&=e^+_p\min(k,q^+),&q^-&=\floor{a^+/d_p^-},\nonumber\\
 t_p&=(1-b)\min(k,q^-+1),&u_p^-&=e^-_p t_p,\nonumber\\
 u_p^0&=f_p(1-b),&u_p&=g_p+u_p^-+u_p^0.\label{cdc:pf:eq:intervalcircuit2}
\end{align}
No product of three auxiliary variables is used: the intermediate outputs
$t_p,u_p^-,u_p^0,g_p,f_p$ are materialized separately.

\begin{lemma}[Correctness and totality of the interval circuit]\label{cdc:pf:lem:icircuit}
The circuit \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:intervalcircuit1}--\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:intervalcircuit2} has unique
natural outputs for every natural input tuple. Its pair $(\ell_p,u_p)$ is
exactly the canonical interval in \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:scalarinterval} with
$a=u-v$, $s=D_p$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The comparison gives $a^-=\max(v-u,0)$ and $a^+=\max(u-v,0)$.
All dividend and denominator values are natural, and both denominators are
positive. All remaining products and sums are nonnegative.

When $D_p>0$, $d_p^+=D_p$ and
$q^+=\ceil{a^-/D_p}$. The upper endpoint is $k$ because $g_p=k$ and the
other sign contributions vanish. This is the first row of
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:scalarinterval}. When $D_p<0$, the lower endpoint is zero,
$d_p^-=-D_p$, and the upper endpoint is
$\min(k,\floor{a^+/(-D_p)}+1)$ if $u\geq v$, and zero otherwise.
When $D_p=0$, only $u_p^0=k(1-b)$ survives. These are exactly the remaining
rows. Uniqueness follows successively from the comparison, assignments,
and division lemmas.
\end{proof}

\subsection{From coordinate intervals to one Boolean}
For each phase and each $i\leq j_r$, initialize $L=0,U=k$ and fold
\[
 L\leftarrow\max(L,\ell_p),\qquad
 U\leftarrow\min(U,u_p)
\]
over the coordinates. For an earlier rule use the Boolean
$1-\ip{L<U}$. For the selected rule use
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:selectedflag}
 \ip{L<1}\bigl(1-\ip{U<k}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Since $L,U\in[0,k]$, this selected flag is one exactly when $L=0$ and $U=k$.
Multiply the row flags in a materialized chain, starting at one, to produce
an acceptance bit $a_w$. This product is a conjunction of already
canonical Boolean values; it does not choose which failed guard to witness.

\begin{proposition}[Canonical accelerated decision circuit]\label{cdc:pf:prop:decision}
For every fixed $m,d,w$, the preceding circuit has exactly one natural
auxiliary evaluation on every natural input $(A,B,x,k)$. Its output satisfies
\[
 a_w=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists y\ \Bvalid_{\mathcal P,w}(x,k,y).
\]
All circuit residuals have total degree at most two, even when the entries
of $A$ and $B$ are treated as variables rather than constants.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The prefix sums and nonnegative input sums have canonical values. The slope
and interval constructions are total by the preceding lemmas. Min, max,
comparison, and product assignments are also canonical. Induction over the
finite gate order gives totality and uniqueness. The acceptance conditions
are those of Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:interval}. Every residual is an assignment of
a linear or quadratic expression, one of \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:cmp}, or one of
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:division}; the materialization of intermediate products ensures
that no residual exceeds degree two.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The polynomial and its proof}
Adjoin the obligation $a_w-1=0$. For each coordinate, materialize
$q_p^{\mathrm{out}}=kQ_p$ and $p_p^{\mathrm{out}}=kP_p$, and add
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:endpoint}
 x_p+p_p^{\mathrm{out}}-y_p-q_p^{\mathrm{out}}=0.
\end{equation}
Let $F_1,\ldots,F_{n_f}$ be all gate residuals and obligations, and set
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:quartic}
 \mathscr P_{m,d,w}(A,B,x,k,y,z)=\sum_{a=1}^{n_f}F_a(A,B,x,k,y,z)^2.
\end{equation}
Equation \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:quartic}, together with the displayed gate rules and their
finite ordering, is an explicit polynomial construction. Expanding its
monomials is optional and gives the same integer polynomial. The supplied
JSON represents the residuals exactly, so there is no unimplemented MRDP
oracle inside this definition.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform canonical quartic representation]\label{cdc:pf:thm:quartic}
For fixed $m,d\geq1$ and nonempty $w\in\{1,\ldots,m\}^\ell$, the polynomial
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:quartic} has integer coefficients and degree at most four. For every
$A,B\in\N^{m\times d}$, $x,y\in\N^d$, and $k\in\N$,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:singlefold}
 \Bvalid_{\mathcal P,w}(x,k,y)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists!z\in\N^{n_z}\ \mathscr P_{m,d,w}(A,B,x,k,y,z)=0.
\end{equation}
When the block relation is false, the polynomial has no natural auxiliary
zero. The construction has the exact counts \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:nz-intro} and
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:nf-intro}, with $2md+2d+1$ free input coordinates.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A sum of squares of integers is zero if and only if each summand is zero.
Thus a zero of \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:quartic} satisfies every gate and final obligation.
Proposition~\ref{cdc:pf:prop:decision} forces the unique canonical evaluation of
all decision auxiliaries. The acceptance obligation says precisely that
the word is executable, and \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:endpoint} says that its endpoint is
$y=x+k(P-Q)$. Conversely, if the block relation holds, the canonical gate
evaluation is natural and satisfies both kinds of obligations, giving a
zero. Endpoint multiplication outputs are also unique, establishing the
single-fold claim. Each $F_a$ has degree at most two, so their squared sum
has degree at most four. The count is verified in the next subsection.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Audited size accounting}
Table~\ref{cdc:pf:tab:counts} specifies the count at the level of the actual compiler.
Prefix sums are not optimized away, initial max/min folds are not simplified,
and duplicate comparisons are not shared.
\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Exact contributions to the endpoint compiler.}\label{cdc:pf:tab:counts}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
Component & Auxiliaries & Residuals\\
\midrule
Separate $P,Q$ prefix sums & $2d\ell$ & $2d\ell$\\
Shared $u=x+P_r$ per phase & $d\ell$ & $d\ell$\\
Slope signs, magnitudes, safe denominators & $10d$ & $12d$\\
Coordinate row, including $v$ and interval folds & $29S$ & $32S$\\
Row flags and conjunction chain & $3R+3\ell$ & $4R+4\ell$\\
Endpoint products and equations & $2d$ & $3d$\\
Acceptance obligation & $0$ & $1$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Here is a finer check of the largest row. One coordinate interval uses
22 auxiliaries and 23 residuals. Constructing $v$ costs one of each.
Folding its lower and upper endpoint into $L,U$ uses two min/max gates,
costing six auxiliaries and eight residuals. The total is 29 and 32.
An earlier-rule row uses a comparison and one acceptance-product assignment,
costing three and four. A selected-rule row uses two comparisons, one
selected-flag assignment, and one acceptance-product assignment, costing
six and eight. There are $R-\ell$ earlier rows and $\ell$ selected rows.
Summing the table yields \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:nz-intro}--\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:nf-intro}.

For a polynomial whose inputs must themselves encode reduced FRACTRAN
fractions, append $md$ residuals $A_{ip}B_{ip}=0$. This changes neither the
auxiliary count nor the degree bound. Alternatively, reduction can remain
a stated input promise, as in the sample endpoint compiler.

\subsection{Magnitude and bit complexity}
\begin{proposition}[Small canonical witnesses]\label{cdc:pf:prop:height}
Suppose all free input entries other than $k$ are at most $M$, with $M\geq1$.
Every auxiliary in the endpoint compiler's canonical evaluation is at most
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:height}
 16(k+1)(\ell+1)(M+1).
\end{equation}
In particular, the witness bit length per coordinate is
$O(\log(k+1)+\log(\ell+1)+\log(M+1))$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The prefix sums are at most $\ell M$, and $u,v$ are at most $(\ell+1)M$.
Slope magnitudes are at most $\ell M$, while the safe denominators are at
most $\ell M+1$. The signed-intercept deficit and surplus are at most
$(\ell+1)M$. The ceiling dividend is at most $(2\ell+1)M+1$.
A nonnegative quotient with denominator at least one is bounded by its
dividend; its remainder and division slack are bounded by the denominator.
Clipped endpoints lie in $[0,k]$, and all their comparison slacks are bounded
by the largest compared value. Sign bits, row flags, and acceptance products
are at most one. Finally, endpoint products are at most $k\ell M$.
These bounds, including the harmless additions of one in the gate definitions,
are all smaller than \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:height}.
\end{proof}

For a fixed schema, computing the canonical witness and checking the
residuals therefore take time polynomial in the bit lengths of the natural
inputs. A repetition count with a thousand decimal digits does not require
a thousand-digit number of simulation steps. This claim is about the
valuation-vector interface, not about expanding a raw integer such as $2^k$.

\section{Variants, composition, and what is not free\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:variants}

\subsection{Failure and exact maximality}
Because the decision circuit is total, changing only its final obligation
from $a_w=1$ to $a_w=0$ gives a single-fold quartic representation of failure
of the prescribed block. This version has inputs $(A,B,x,k)$ and no endpoint
obligation. Merely retaining a guessed endpoint while switching the bit
would not represent the complement of the full endpoint relation; failure
of the word and failure of a proposed endpoint are different predicates.

For exact maximality of complete copies, make two decision circuits with
inputs $k$ and $k+1$ sharing only the free inputs. Require their outputs to
be one and zero respectively, and append the endpoint equations for $k$.
The result represents
\[
 M_w(x)=k\quad\hbox{and}\quad y=x+kD
\]
with exactly one witness whenever true. In terms of the counts for the
ordinary endpoint compiler, the duplicated construction uses
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:maxcounts}
 n_z^{\max}=2n_z-2d,\qquad n_f^{\max}=2n_f-3d.
\end{equation}
Indeed, each ordinary circuit consists of a decision core, $2d$ endpoint
product auxiliaries, $3d$ endpoint residuals, and one acceptance obligation.
Two cores, one endpoint, and two acceptance obligations give \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:maxcounts}.

\subsection{Fixed concatenations of repeated words}
Let $w_1,\ldots,w_s$ be fixed nonempty words and $k_1,\ldots,k_s$ supplied
repetition counts. Compile each block, giving it a fresh set of internal
auxiliaries. Introduce boundary states $x_1,\ldots,x_{s-1}$, with $x_0=x$
and $x_s=y$, and add all block residuals to one sum of squares.

\begin{corollary}[Single-fold flat-schema composition]\label{cdc:pf:cor:flat}
For fixed $w_1,\ldots,w_s$, the relation that the actual trace begins with
$w_1^{k_1}\cdots w_s^{k_s}$ and ends at $y$ has a single-fold quartic
representation relative to the free tuple $(A,B,x,k_1,\ldots,k_s,y)$.
Its auxiliary count is the sum of the block auxiliary counts plus $d(s-1)$
for the internal boundaries.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A zero is exactly a sequence of valid block certificates with matching
boundaries. If all blocks are valid, their endpoints are forced recursively
by the previous boundary and the known update $k_iD_i$. Thus every internal
boundary is unique, and each block's auxiliary tuple is unique by
Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:quartic}. The sum of all squared residuals remains quartic.
\end{proof}

Making the counts $k_i$ existential may yield multiple witnesses: distinct
factorizations can describe the same overall endpoint, especially when a
word has zero drift. The corollary's single-fold property fixes the count
tuple as part of the free input. This is a schema-relative statement.

\subsection{Raw integers and variable prime powers}
For a reduced FRACTRAN program, the compiler currently accepts exponent
vectors. The relation between a raw initial integer and these vectors is
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:raw}
 N=c\prod_{p=1}^d p_p^{x_p},\qquad
 \gcd\!\left(c,\prod_{p=1}^d p_p\right)=1.
\end{equation}
For a given concrete input, this can be computed externally; the supplied
small examples use exact integer factorization. Uniformly adjoining
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:raw} as an existential polynomial relation requires a genuine
representation of variable exponentiation and the inert-factor condition.
The repository already treats exponential input encodings in its FRACTRAN
Diophantine development \cite{repo-coq}, but its witness costs and uniqueness
are not inherited for free by the present compiler.

The same caution applies to the raw output integer. An endpoint of the form
$2^{10^{1000}}$ cannot be explicitly printed using a certificate whose
entire bit size is only thousands of bits. The succinct exponent interface
is an explicit part of the theorem, not an output-size miracle.

\subsection{Why this is not a universal single-fold result}
A fixed word schema describes a restricted, efficiently checkable relation.
A universal computation may require unboundedly many distinct macro words
or boundaries. Encoding an arbitrary word into one natural-number input
and verifying all its phases with a fixed number of polynomial variables is
an additional problem. Our size grows with $\ell$, and the compiler does
not remove that dependence.

Furthermore, one equation is not the same as one auxiliary solution. The
vendored name \code{FRACTRAN_HALTING_dio_single} refers to a single equation
representation, not automatically to a single-fold witness fiber.
The general single-fold problem belongs to a much broader research program
\cite{cco-history}; no conclusion about it follows from a family of
schema-indexed canonical verifiers.

\subsection{Why this is not a new universal operation record}
The numbers $n_z,n_f$ count witnesses and residual constraints for a specified
macro. They are not counts of additions and multiplications in a complete
universal halting certificate. Priority checks have been included in this
macro compiler, but arbitrary history structure, input conversion, terminal
conditions, and universal control remain separate. The repository's
reported 75-operation certificate and its older 90-operation research
baseline concern a different complete task \cite{repo-h10,repo-variants}.
No numerical comparison that omits these differences is justified.

\section{Infinite periodic instruction tails\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:infinite}

\subsection{An exact finite criterion}
An infinite repetition of labels need not return to the same numerical
state. A word with positive drift can repeat forever while its state grows.
Accordingly, periodicity below always refers to the \emph{instruction trace},
not to equality of consecutive block-boundary states.

\begin{theorem}[Infinite repetition criterion]\label{cdc:pf:thm:infinite}
The execution from a supplied state $x$ begins with $w^\omega$ if and only if
all three conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $D_p\geq0$ for every coordinate $p$;
\item $x+\beta_r\geq B_{j_r}$ for every phase $r$;
\item for every phase $r$ and earlier rule $i<j_r$, there is a coordinate $p$
with $D_p=0$ and $x_p+\beta_{r,p}<B_{ip}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If the infinite repetition occurs, the boundary states $x+hD$ are natural
for every $h$. A negative coordinate of $D$ would eventually make one of
them negative, proving (i). The first copy proves (ii).
If (iii) failed for a pair $(r,i)$, every zero-drift coordinate would already
meet that earlier rule's threshold. Every positive-drift coordinate would
meet its threshold for all sufficiently large $h$. There are finitely many
coordinates, so some common $h$ would enable rule $i$ at phase $r$, contrary
to the selected trace.

Conversely, by (i) and (ii), every chosen rule is enabled at every vector
$x+\beta_r+hD$. For each earlier rule, the coordinate provided by (iii)
stays below its consumption threshold forever. Thus all earlier rules are
disabled at every phase. Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:local} gives every finite prefix
$w^k$, and determinism makes these prefixes one infinite execution.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Existence of a periodic seed]\label{cdc:pf:cor:infinite-seed}
There exists a state executing $w^\omega$ exactly when $D\geq0$ and
$\Capacity(w)=\infty$. When such a state exists, $\lambda$ is the least one.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If an infinite seed exists, all finite capacities are possible and the drift
is nonnegative. Conversely, when $D\geq0$, formula \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:lambda-k}
gives $\lambda(k)=\lambda$ for all $k\geq1$. Infinite capacity therefore
makes the same seed execute every finite prefix. Leastness follows from the
one-copy resource lower bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sharp one-sided pumping]\label{cdc:pf:cor:onesided}
When $D\geq0$, existence of a seed executing $w^{H+1}$ implies existence of
a seed executing $w^\omega$. The threshold $H+1$ is sharp for $H\geq1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
With no negative drift, every right margin in \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:R} is zero. A finite
capacity is therefore at most $H$, and the preceding corollary applies.
For sharpness use the reduced FRACTRAN list $(1/2^H,2)$ and word $(2)$.
Its least seed has $2$-valuation zero, its drift is $+1$, and the earlier
rule first becomes enabled at valuation $H$. Hence its capacity is exactly $H$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A canonical polynomial for a supplied infinite tail}
For fixed $m,d,w$, the three conditions in Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:infinite} can
also be compiled into a single-fold quartic polynomial, with natural inputs
$A,B,x$. This requires no unbounded search: compare $P_p$ and $Q_p$ for the
drift sign and zero tests; use $x_p+P_{r,p}$ versus $B_{ip}+Q_{r,p}$ for the
phase inequalities; and combine the resulting Boolean values.

For completeness, a conjunction of Boolean values uses the gate $z=ab$.
A disjunction uses $z=a+b-ab$, which is again Boolean and nonnegative.
Each stationary-blocker flag is the product of the zero-drift flag and a
strict-deficit flag. Fold disjunction over coordinates and conjunction over
phase-rule pairs. Every flag is computed, so the polynomial does not guess
one of several possible blocking coordinates. The proofs of totality,
uniqueness, and quartic degree are the same gate induction as before, and
the size is $O(d\ell+d\sum_r j_r)$. This extension is a proved construction;
the delivered code implements its decision criterion, not a separate
infinite-tail polynomial exporter.

\section{Discovering periodic tails is still undecidable\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:ep}

Define $\EP$ to be the set of finite encodings $(\mathcal F,N)$ of positive
reduced FRACTRAN programs and positive initial integers whose actual run
has an eventually periodic infinite instruction trace. A halted finite
trace is not in $\EP$.

\begin{theorem}[Computably enumerable completeness]\label{cdc:pf:thm:ep}
The set $\EP$ is computably enumerable and is complete for computably
enumerable sets under computable many-one reductions. Hardness persists on
a computably constructed family of inputs whose runs are all nonhalting.
Consequently, some finite descriptions certify nontermination effectively,
but discovering a periodic-tail certificate is not decidable in general.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For membership, enumerate a finite prefix length $t$ and a nonempty word
$w$. Simulate exactly $t$ steps; discard the pair if the run halts earlier.
Factor the finitely many program numerators, denominators, and the reached
state to obtain its relevant valuation vector. Apply
Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:infinite}. This is a finite decision for each pair. Dovetailing
all pairs accepts precisely the inputs in $\EP$.

For hardness, start with a deterministic counter-machine halting instance
$(M,c)$. Its halting problem is computably enumerable complete, and the
control-prime compilation in Section~\ref{cdc:pf:sec:model} is effective. We describe
an effective counter-machine transformation before applying that compilation.

Add two fresh clock counters $C,E$, initially zero. At the beginning of
 each round, test whether the simulated control is halting; if so, enter a
fresh two-control-state loop forever. Otherwise simulate one instruction
of $M$ and then run a delay routine: emit
one distinguished marker, increment $C$, transfer all units of $C$ to $E$,
and then transfer all units of $E$ back to $C$. The clock is thus restored,
$E$ is again zero, and the next simulation round begins. A transfer is
implemented with the usual positive-decrement/zero-test branches and an
increment on the other counter. Every delay terminates because each of its
two transfer loops decreases its source counter at every iteration.

The continuation after a delay can be handled by finitely many copies of
the routine, one for each simulated control state. In that implementation
there is a finite set of distinguished marker labels, exactly one of which
occurs per nonhalting simulation round, and none occurs inside a delay or
the final two-state loop. This avoids assuming an implicit return stack.
The state-splitting convention removes any self-target that could cause
cancellation in the FRACTRAN compilation.

If $M$ halts, the transformed run eventually enters the fresh two-state
loop, so its instruction trace is eventually periodic. If $M$ never halts,
markers occur infinitely often, but their successive gaps are unbounded:
the clock grows by one per round and each delay performs at least $C$
ordinary steps. Compilation replaces each instruction by a bounded finite
number of labeled arithmetic steps and preserves designated marker
occurrences. Hence the gaps between the finite set of marker labels remain
unbounded in the FRACTRAN trace.

In any eventually periodic infinite word, a finite set of labels that occurs
infinitely often has bounded gaps after the periodic prefix: some such label
occurs in the period, so every sufficiently long interval of the period
length contains one. Thus the nonhalting simulation case cannot have an
eventually periodic label trace. The transformed program itself never halts
in either case: it either keeps simulating with finite delays or reaches the
fresh loop. We have an effective reduction
\[
 M\text{ halts on }c\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 (\mathcal F_{M,c},N_{M,c})\in\EP,
\]
with the announced nonhalting promise, proving completeness.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[One fixed squarefree-denominator program]\label{cdc:pf:cor:fixed}
There is a fixed reduced FRACTRAN program $\mathcal F_*$, all of whose
denominators are squarefree, such that
\[
 \{N\geq1:(\mathcal F_*,N)\in\EP\}
\]
is computably enumerable complete. The hardness reduction maps every input
to a nonhalting run of this same program.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose a fixed universal deterministic counter machine $U$. Encoding a
machine and its input into an initial configuration of $U$ is an effective
reduction of the general halting problem to halting of $U$ on its encoded
configurations. Apply the clock transformation in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:ep} to $U$ once. The transformed control graph and its
FRACTRAN fraction list depend on $U$, not on its initial counter values.
Only the encoded initial integer varies. Therefore the same proof gives
the claimed fixed-program reduction.

Use the increment and decrement/zero-test instruction basis for $U$ and
for the clock. After splitting self-targets through fresh states, the
control-prime compilation uses denominators $q_s$ or $q_sp_r$, where a
control prime and a counter prime are distinct. Each denominator is
squarefree, and numerators do not cancel the control or decrement test.
Thus the resulting program has $H=1$. All constructed inputs still follow
either the infinite simulation-with-delays or the final two-state loop.
Membership is semidecidable by the same prefix-and-word enumeration as
before. This is an effective existence construction, not a claim that a
minimal or literal fraction list has been printed here.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An existential arithmetic class of divergent runs]\label{cdc:pf:cor:ep-dioph}
For any effective natural-number encoding of FRACTRAN instances, $\EP$ has
a Diophantine representation and is undecidable.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply MRDP to Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:ep}; the required equivalence between
computable enumerability and Diophantine representability is established
in the sources discussed in Section~\ref{cdc:pf:sec:context} \cite{lf2022,repo-h10}.
\end{proof}
This corollary is qualitative. No variable bound, canonical witness, or
single-fold claim is supplied for the existential choice of an arbitrary
prefix and arbitrary word. The constructive quartic theorem concerns the
verification of a \emph{supplied fixed schema}, not this global search problem.

\begin{proposition}[No complete existential divergence certificates]\label{cdc:pf:prop:nocomplete}
There is no effective certificate relation, decidable on each finite
certificate, that is both sound and complete for nontermination of all
FRACTRAN inputs. In particular, no single existential Diophantine relation
represents their full nontermination set under an effective encoding.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If such certificates existed, enumerate them to semidecide nontermination.
Halting is already semidecidable by simulation. Running the two procedures
in parallel would decide halting on every input, contradicting universality
and halting undecidability. The zero relation of a fixed integer polynomial
is decidable on each natural tuple, so a purported Diophantine representation
would provide just such finite certificates.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} Eventual periodicity and the affine macro certificates below are finite certificates of nontermination: the $\Sigma^0_1$ fragment of the recurrence and liveness hierarchy of the neighbouring report \emph{liveness-beyond-halting} of this category.

\section{Beyond periodic instruction words\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:nonperiodic}

\subsection{An explicit six-fraction counterexample to completeness}
Consider the program
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:doubling}
 \mathcal D=\left(\frac{33}{10},\frac5{11},\frac75,
                  \frac{52}{21},\frac7{13},\frac57\right).
\end{equation}
Use primes $2,3$ as data counters and $5,7,11,13$ as control tokens.
All reduced denominators are squarefree, so this example already lies in
the threshold-$H=1$ class.

\begin{proposition}[Exact doubling macro]\label{cdc:pf:prop:doubling}
For every $a\geq1$, the actual execution of \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:doubling} from
$5\,2^a$ begins with the word
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:doublingword}
 (1,2)^a\ (3)\ (4,5)^a\ (6)
\end{equation}
and reaches $5\,2^{2a}$. Starting at $10$, the program never halts and its
instruction trace is not eventually periodic.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
At a state $5\,2^u3^v$ with $u>0$, fraction 1 consumes one factor of $2$
and the control $5$, producing one factor of $3$ and the control $11$.
Fraction 2 then restores the control $5$. No earlier rule is enabled at the
intermediate control-$11$ state. Hence $(1,2)^a$ transports all $a$ units
from the $2$-counter to the $3$-counter and reaches $5\,3^a$.
Here fraction 1 is disabled and fraction 3 changes control $5$ to $7$.

At a state $7\,2^u3^v$ with $v>0$, fraction 4 consumes one factor of $3$
and the control $7$, producing two factors of $2$ and control $13$.
Fraction 5 restores control $7$. Earlier fractions are disabled by their
missing control primes. Thus $(4,5)^a$ reaches $7\,2^{2a}$. Fraction 4 is
now disabled by the absence of $3$, and fraction 6 changes the control back
to $5$. This proves the macro, including all priority choices.

Iterate with $a=1,2,4,8,\ldots$. Every round is finite and has $4a+2$ steps,
so the actual run is infinite. Label 3 occurs exactly once in each round.
The gap between its occurrence in the $a$ round and its next occurrence in
the $2a$ round is $6a+2$. These gaps are unbounded. An eventually periodic
word in which label 3 occurs infinitely often has bounded gaps, so this
instruction trace is not eventually periodic.
\end{proof}

The example shows concretely that even correct fixed-period certificates
miss some transparent arithmetic nontermination. It also shows why the
sharp finite-word pumping theorem does not imply eventual periodicity of
all runs, even at the smallest positive threshold.

\subsection{Finite affine macro certificates}
A modest extension captures this example and many similar nested schedules.
Fix a program, words $w_1,\ldots,w_s$, and a parameter dimension $q$.
Specify integer-affine maps
\[
 g:\Z^q\to\Z^d,\qquad T:\Z^q\to\Z^q,
 \qquad \rho_i:\Z^q\to\Z,
\]
and a Presburger-definable invariant $V\subseteq\N^q$.
The intended macro starts at $g(v)$, executes
$w_1^{\rho_1(v)}\cdots w_s^{\rho_s(v)}$, and ends at $g(T(v))$.
The word drifts $D_i$ are fixed integer vectors.

Define intermediate affine boundaries
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:affineboundaries}
 b_0(v)=g(v),\qquad
 b_i(v)=g(v)+\sum_{t=1}^{i}\rho_t(v)D_t.
\end{equation}
They are affine because the $D_t$ are constants, not variable parameters.
A certificate asserts, for every $v\in V$, that all $\rho_i(v)$ and $b_i(v)$
are natural, every block $(b_{i-1}(v),\rho_i(v),b_i(v))$ is valid,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:pf:eq:affineclosure}
 T(v)\in V,\qquad b_s(v)=g(T(v)),\qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^s |w_i|\rho_i(v)\geq1.
\end{equation}
It also supplies $v_0\in V$ and an actual finite prefix reaching $g(v_0)$.

\begin{theorem}[Soundness and decidable checking of affine macro certificates]
\label{cdc:pf:thm:affine}
Every such certificate proves nontermination of its supplied initial
configuration. For a fixed finitely described program and proposed affine
certificate data, all universal obligations just listed are decidable by
Presburger arithmetic. Restricted to FRACTRAN instances, the resulting class of finitely
certifiable nontermination strictly contains $\EP$, but is not all
nontermination instances.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By induction, $v_n=T^n(v_0)$ stays in $V$. The certified macro at $v_n$
is an actual finite execution from $g(v_n)$ to $g(v_{n+1})$ and contains at
least one step. Concatenating these macros after the supplied reachable
prefix gives arbitrarily long prefixes of one deterministic run, hence
nontermination.

For decidability, insert the local criterion of Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:local}
for each block. The program and the words are fixed. Every prefix vector
and every drift is therefore constant, and the expressions in $v$ and the
bounded repetition index $h$ are linear. Conditions
\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:affineboundaries}--\eqref{cdc:pf:eq:affineclosure}, naturalness, and the
Presburger invariant add only Presburger formulas. Their universal closure
is a sentence in decidable Presburger arithmetic. No product of two
independently varying parameters is introduced.

To include $\EP$, take a supplied reachable periodic seed $x$, its valid
word $w$, parameter $n\in\N$, invariant $V=\N$, embedding $g(n)=x+nD$,
update $T(n)=n+1$, and repetition count one. The infinite-tail theorem
ensures these obligations. The example in Proposition~\ref{cdc:pf:prop:doubling}
lies outside $\EP$ but has an affine certificate as displayed below,
proving strictness. Finally, these finite certificate descriptions can be
enumerated and their correctness decided. If they covered every
nonterminating input, they would contradict Proposition~\ref{cdc:pf:prop:nocomplete}.
\end{proof}

For \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:doubling}, in coordinate order $(2,3,5,7,11,13)$, use
\[
 V=\{a\in\N:a\geq1\},\qquad
 g(a)=(a,0,1,0,0,0),\qquad T(a)=2a.
\]
Take words $(1,2),(3),(4,5),(6)$ with respective counts $a,1,a,1$.
Their successive boundaries are
\begin{align*}
 &(a,0,1,0,0,0),&&(0,a,1,0,0,0),&&(0,a,0,1,0,0),\\
 &(2a,0,0,1,0,0),&&(2a,0,1,0,0,0).
\end{align*}
Proposition~\ref{cdc:pf:prop:doubling} proves the block obligations for all $a\geq1$;
closure and positivity are immediate. Starting at the raw integer $10$, which encodes $g(1)$,
requires no initial prefix.

\begin{remark}[Scope of the affine extension]
Fixed-path and invariant-based verification are established methods, not
novel in themselves \cite{bdd,dp}. The contribution here is their precise
connection to the priority interval compiler and the explicit strict
separation example. The delivered executable includes the six-fraction
example and the fixed-word checkers; it is not a general Presburger solver
or an implemented synthesis engine for affine invariants.
\end{remark}

\section{Reproducible artifacts and finite validation\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:validation}

\subsection{What the implementation actually contains}
The archive includes a standard-library Python implementation requiring
Python 3.10 or later. Its central object is a finite directed acyclic circuit
of assignment, comparison, and division gates. Each residual is stored as
an exact sparse integer polynomial, with monomials represented by tuples
of variable indices. No floating-point arithmetic, symbolic simplification
oracle, or external theorem prover is used.

The principal entry point is
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small]
compile_block(m, d, word, endpoint=True,
              reject=False, maximal=False, reduced=False)
\end{Verbatim}
\end{minipage}\par
In code, instruction indices are \emph{zero-based}. Thus the mathematical
word $(2,3)$ is supplied as \code{[1, 2]}. The dimensions and the word are
compile-time data; all program entries are free inputs. The exporter writes
the exact list of quadratic residuals defining their sum-of-squares
polynomial. The witness method executes the canonical gates and the value
method evaluates the polynomial exactly.

Separate functions implement direct one-step simulation, direct finite
unrolling, the interval checker, infinite-tail recognition, exact
repetition capacity, least seeds, and maximal full-copy counts. Keeping
both the unrolled interpreter and interval checker makes it possible to
cross-check different implementations on small instances.

\subsection{What was tested}
The delivered run used pseudorandom seed \code{20260930} and recorded
\textbf{114,875 counted finite checks}. The word ``counted'' is literal:
the total includes program instances, elementary gate cases, corrupted
witness checks, and individual steps in the native-integer comparison.
It is not a count of independent theorems or an exhaustive enumeration of
all program inputs.

\section{A formalization roadmap for ProveIt\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:formal}

A clean implementation should separate a semantic development from
certificate generation. The recommended first target is the pumping
argument, because it uses finite maxima, integer linear arithmetic, and
coordinatewise order, without invoking the full MRDP machinery.

\subsection{Semantic layer}
Define an ordered rule as two vectors in $\N^d$ and selection as the least
enabled list index. Prove determinism, nonnegativity of successors, and the
prefix-state identity. Then formalize Lemma~\ref{cdc:pf:lem:local}. This layer
should not mention fraction factorization or Diophantine polynomials.

For the FRACTRAN bridge, add a separate theorem connecting reduced positive
fractions to prime valuations, explicitly retaining the inert coprime
factor. A proof must not use unreduced numerator and denominator exponent
vectors as if cancellation were harmless.

\subsection{Capacity and pumping layer}
The core milestones are the resource maximum \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:lambda-k}, lowering
within the safe orthant, the two-sided interval \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:window}, and the
finite-or-infinite capacity formula. The bound on each deficit by $H$ then
makes Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:pumping} short. The sharp family requires only checking
four-coordinate rules and the two inequalities $h\geq H$ and
$k-1-h\geq H$. This proof order keeps the genuinely important monotonicity
claim visible and avoids proving the wrong global monotonicity property.

\subsection{Verified arithmetic circuit layer}
Give gates a syntax and an evaluation relation over naturals. Prove the
comparison and Euclidean-division uniqueness lemmas first. A gate-DAG
induction should establish a generic theorem: a total canonical circuit
with quadratic residuals has exactly one auxiliary tuple satisfying its
gate equations. A second theorem appends an output obligation and forms
a sum of squares in an integer multivariate polynomial ring.

The interval circuit then needs a sign-case proof, including $k=0$ and
$D_p=0$. Next prove its acceptance bit equivalent to the semantic block
predicate. Finally, make variable and residual counts functions of the
syntax and prove the accounting formulas structurally. The certificate
producer should return both a sparse polynomial and a theorem connecting
its evaluation to that syntax, rather than trusting an external JSON file.

\subsection{Where existing repository results can be reused}
The inspected Rocq file already exposes
\code{dio_rel_fractran_step}, \code{dio_rel_fractran_rt},
\code{dio_rel_fractran_stop}, and \code{dio_rel_fractran_eval}
\cite{repo-coq}. These are useful targets for an extensional correctness
bridge from the accelerated semantics. The new compiler should not be
advertised as replacing their unbounded reachability theorem: it verifies
one prescribed macro family.

For the qualitative $\EP$ corollary, the existing MRDP interface is an
appropriate endpoint after formalizing the effective semidecider and the
clocked reduction. For quantitative canonical certificates, however,
invoking a generic Diophantine closure theorem may erase the witness count
and uniqueness information. Those properties need their own strengthened
interface and proof.

No Lean or Rocq source is included as a purported checked implementation.
The roadmap names proof obligations rather than inventing successful
builds or unverified theorem APIs.

\section{Further research questions\srctag{10}}
\label{cdc:pf:sec:questions}

The following are concrete next questions arising from this manuscript.
They are research proposals, not claims that each is an independently
established longstanding open problem. The first priorities are an external
novelty audit and formal verification of the exact statements proved here.

\begin{question}[A sharp structural hierarchy beyond $H$; source 10]
Can the exact capacity be bounded sharply by a smaller invariant combining
which coordinates occur in earlier guards, the signs of $D$, and the
priority dependency graph? The formula $\min(L_{ri}+R_{ri})$ provides a
starting point. A useful result would characterize the programs in which
all finite capacities are at most $H$, even when mixed drift is permitted.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Presburger guards instead of consumption orthants; source 10]
Which extensions of the enabling predicates preserve a word-length-independent
pumping threshold? The least-seed argument depends on upward-closed
consumption guards. Arbitrary Boolean combinations of linear inequalities
need not have a least resource-safe seed. A sharp positive theorem for a
specific guard class, or a small counterexample showing unbounded finite
capacity with bounded guard constants, would locate the boundary precisely.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A substantially smaller canonical interval circuit; source 10]
How much can the constants 29 and 32 per coordinate row be reduced while
retaining totality and unique witnesses? Natural opportunities are shared
min/max comparisons, elimination of initially trivial folds, constant
propagation for fixed programs, and shared sign tests. The target should
be a proved count for a complete macro verifier, including priority and
endpoint obligations, rather than a transport-only operation estimate.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Direct raw-integer interfaces; source 10]
Can useful classes of FRACTRAN macros be certified directly on $N$ and its
raw endpoint without first exposing all valuations, and with a controlled
single-fold witness cost? Factoring externally is an implementation choice,
not a uniform polynomial interface. Any proposed improvement must account
for variable powers and output size explicitly.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Canonical macro decompositions; source 10]
For which deterministic priority programs is there a computable normal form
for finite traces as concatenations of repeated words, with uniqueness of
the repetition counts and a bounded number of boundaries? This would extend
Corollary~\ref{cdc:pf:cor:flat} from fixed counts to canonical existential counts.
A general affirmative answer cannot simply be assumed from deterministic
small-step execution, because the same trace can admit many macro factorizations.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:acceleration}.

\wtag{} Batch~78, 2 October 2026: for one deterministic substrate other than priority programs, Part~III of the neighbouring report \emph{quadratic-orthant-certificates} (its source~14, batch-78 manuscript~14) proves such a normal form. For Iijil's fixed universal Waterfall program, the run of each simulated source step is a fixed concatenation of eleven blocks, five of them repeated words with forced repetition counts (its Theorem \texttt{qoc:wf:thm:macro}), proved for all tape values by a finite affine certificate, and the witnesses of its quadratic certificate are exactly these counts, uniquely (\texttt{qoc:wf:thm:certificate}). The number of boundaries is bounded per source step, not over a run, and the number of source steps is compiler data; the question for priority programs is not addressed.

\begin{question}[Certificate synthesis with completeness on a subclass; source 10]
Can periodic-tail or affine-macro certificates be synthesized completely
for a natural syntactic class of ordered programs? Possibilities include
bounded control alternation, a fixed number of phase changes, or a
well-founded priority dependency graph. A useful theorem would combine
sound synthesis with an explicit completeness hypothesis, avoiding the
impossibility of a complete method for all nontermination.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:restricted}.

\begin{question}[Nonlinear parameter updates with linear phase checking; source 10]
The doubling example uses the affine update $a\mapsto2a$. Can a broader
certificate class handle nonlinear updates while keeping phase-validity
obligations decidable or directly Diophantine with manageable witness growth?
The point where a variable repetition count multiplies a variable drift
should be isolated: it is exactly where the elementary Presburger argument
in Theorem~\ref{cdc:pf:thm:affine} no longer applies.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:compression}.

\begin{question}[A small explicit fixed interpreter; source 10]
Corollary~\ref{cdc:pf:cor:fixed} establishes fixed-program completeness already at
$H=1$, but does not print an optimized fraction list. What quantitative
tradeoffs between fraction count, number of primes, and input encoding can
be achieved by an explicit clocked universal interpreter? The reduction
must preserve its unbounded-gap marker invariant at the level of actual
selected fraction labels, and any claimed small certificate must include
that control machinery rather than count only the simulation instructions.
\end{question}

The input contract is explicit (both half tapes as raw integers, four binary operations to load), every source step costs exactly $6+3Q+r+3Y$ nonhalting firings, and $k$ source steps have a degree-two certificate with $35k$ natural witnesses. The matrix and its compiler are Iijil's prior work, and the FRACTRAN tradeoffs and the marker invariant of this question are not addressed.

\begin{question}[Proof-carrying sparse polynomial export; source 10]
Can the Python exporter be replaced by a verified Lean or Rocq exporter
whose output carries a checkable coefficient certificate, a semantics
proof, and a structural proof of the variable count? The modest size of
individual gates makes a small independent residual checker attractive.
The trust boundary should include the exact polynomial, not merely its
high-level circuit specification.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:verified}.

\begin{question}[Use inside the universal arithmetic-certificate project; source 10]
Can priority-exact macro compression remove enough repeated history
structure from a fixed universal interpreter to improve a \emph{complete}
universal certificate? This would require measuring input conversion,
macro decomposition, all control obligations, halting, and arithmetic
operations together. The present results supply a sound local component,
not a numerical answer to that global optimization problem.
\end{question}

\section{Conclusion\srctag{10}}
The most useful additional structure in this problem is not merely that
FRACTRAN computes arbitrary partial recursive functions. It is the geometry
of one prescribed priority trace. At a phase of a repeated word, every
coordinate evolves affinely. Earlier-rule enabling therefore occupies an
exact interval of repetition indices, and the least resource-safe seed
turns that interval into a left waiting margin and a right waiting margin.
Their sum is the exact repetition capacity. Bounding each margin by the
largest consumption threshold gives a sharp $2H+1$ pumping theorem.

The same interval geometry admits a completely explicit quartic polynomial
with a unique natural auxiliary solution, provided the word schema is fixed.
This answers the priority obligation for a meaningful compressed class
without pretending to solve arbitrary history compression. Infinite periodic
tails have an equally exact finite criterion, while clocked universality
and the doubling example show why certificate verification, certificate
discovery, and full nontermination must remain distinct.

The next decisive steps are independent scrutiny of the claimed contribution
boundary, machine verification of the capacity and gate theorems, and
experiments that integrate the macro checker into a complete interpreter
certificate while preserving honest end-to-end cost accounting.

\section{An executable specification of the interval algorithm\srctag{10}}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~A of manuscript~10.}
The following pseudocode uses signed integers for clarity. Its canonical
natural-number implementation is the gate circuit in Section~\ref{cdc:pf:sec:compiler}.
It returns only word validity; an endpoint check is then appended.
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small]
valid_block(A, B, x, word, k):
    drift := sum(A[j] - B[j] for j in word)
    phase := x
    for selected in word:
        for i in 1 .. selected:
            low, high := 0, k
            for coordinate p:
                l, u := affine_interval(phase[p] - B[i,p],
                                         drift[p], k)
                low  := max(low, l)
                high := min(high, u)
            if i < selected and low < high:
                return false
            if i = selected and (low != 0 or high != k):
                return false
        phase := phase + A[selected] - B[selected]
    return true
\end{Verbatim}
\end{minipage}\par
A hypothetical phase may have a negative coordinate before validity is
established; this is allowed in the mathematical pseudocode. The actual
polynomial circuit does not introduce negative natural variables: it keeps
production and consumption prefixes separate as in \eqref{cdc:pf:eq:PQ}.

\section{An executable specification of the capacity formula\srctag{10}}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~B of manuscript~10.}
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small]
capacity(A, B, word):
    prefixes := cumulative sums of A[j] - B[j] along word
    drift := final prefix
    least[p] := max(B[word[r],p] - prefixes[r,p] for r)
    cap := infinity
    for phase r, selected := word[r]:
        for i in 1 .. selected-1:
            c[p] := least[p] + prefixes[r,p] - B[i,p]
            if exists p: drift[p] = 0 and c[p] < 0:
                continue
            left := max(0, ceil(max(0,-c[p])/drift[p])
                           for p with drift[p] > 0)
            right := max(0, ceil(max(0,-c[p])/(-drift[p]))
                            for p with drift[p] < 0)
            cap := min(cap, left + right)
    return cap, least, drift
\end{Verbatim}
\end{minipage}\par
For $k\geq1$, the candidate seed is
$\texttt{least}+(k-1)\max(0,-\texttt{drift})$ coordinatewise.
The value $\infty$ returned by this algorithm means arbitrary \emph{finite}
repetition from suitable seeds. For infinite repetition from one seed,
the additional nonnegative-drift condition must be checked.

\part{Conservative priority reaction networks and a canonical-fuel form of the finite-fold problem}\label{cdc:part:reactions}

\paragraph{Source and scope.} \wtag{} This Part is manuscript~11, ``One Shared Fallback: Conservative Reaction Computation, Unique Quartic Certificates, and a Canonical Fuel Form of the Finite-Fold Problem'' (batch~62, manuscript~05; archive \path{one_shared_fallback_research.zip}, inner directory \path{one_shared_fallback}; shipped files prefixed \path{11-reaction-fallback-}; labels \texttt{cdc:rx:}). It prints the manuscript's Sections 2--14 in their own order: models and multiplicity; the one-fallback conservative compiler (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:compiler}); reservoir thresholds and the fixed universal instance with 61 species and 62 reactions (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:threshold,cdc:rx:cor:universality}); why priority cannot be erased (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:nopriority,cdc:rx:prop:rates}); decidable bounded resources (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:logspace,cdc:rx:thm:nobound}); single-fold trace quartics (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:quartic}); bounded minimum-fuel quartics (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:QL}); the canonical-fuel form of the finite-fold problem (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:FF}); Pareto-minimal resources (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:pareto}); the worked example and executed tests; the integration plan; the seven research questions; and the conclusion. Its two appendices follow: the universal source machine with a discrepancy in the source literature, and the manifest. Its title, abstract and introduction are in \cref{cdc:sec:ms11}; the conventions of this Part are \cref{cdc:conv:b62-11}.

\paragraph{Relation to the other Parts.} \wtag{} Manuscript~11 inspected ProveIt at \texttt{4e128356d} (and names a later commit \texttt{ccfb084ad}, at which the cited files are unchanged), before this report existed, and does not cite it. It adds a substrate to Part~VIII: Part~VIII already treats counter and register programs with zero tests, and discrete reaction networks as instances of multiset firing \emph{without} priority; here a conservative two-to-two network with one shared low-priority fallback implements every zero test, with an exact reservoir threshold and a proof that one priority level does not suffice. Its trace quartic is the priority analogue of Part~II's raw-run certificates, without a commutation quotient (the compiled networks are deterministic). Its arithmetic content is Part~IX's reduction pattern with a smaller canonical witness: \cref{cdc:rx:thm:FF} is the one-parameter refinement of \cref{cdc:bd:thm:universal}(c), with the least reservoir, a single number decidable in unary logarithmic space, in place of the first-halting history; and \cref{cdc:rx:thm:nobound} is the reservoir case of \cref{cdc:bd:prop:nobound}. The canonical-fuel theorem re-scopes the question on finite-fold arithmetic primitives (\cref{cdc:q:ffprimitives}); see the note there. The finite-rate obstruction (\cref{cdc:rx:prop:rates}) concerns the physical semantics asked about in the neighbouring report \emph{probabilistic-quantum-and-continuous-computation}; no probabilistic law is computed here.

\paragraph{Setting and hypotheses.} \wtag{} Deterministic increment/decrement register machines are compiled to priority reaction systems with two priority levels and two-to-two reactions with distinct unit reactants. Closed finite-reservoir instances are finite-state and decidable; universality holds only after existentially quantifying the reservoir, or in the open-reservoir semantics. Priority is an ideal execution rule, not a claim about physical reaction rates. The quartic certificates are families indexed by the horizon $T$ or the resource cutoff $L$.
