\section{A history-free characterization of exact routing\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:balance}

\subsection{The zero-retention stack model}
Fix disjoint finite sets $V$ of active vertices and $S$ of absorbing sinks,
with $|V|=n$ and $|S|=s$. Each active vertex has an infinite destination stack
\[
 \rho_v:\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\longrightarrow V\sqcup S.
\]
An initial configuration is $\mathbf x=(x_v)_{v\in V}\in\N^V$.
Sinks initially contain no chips, except in the explicitly stated trap-collapse
construction later. Each active vertex also has a firing counter, initially
zero. A legal firing at $v$ is allowed when $v$ contains at least one chip. It
removes one chip, increments the counter to $j$, and sends that chip to
$\rho_v(j)$. A sink never fires. The rule retains no chip permanently at an
active vertex.

A finite execution is \emph{complete} when all active vertices are empty.
The number of firings at each active vertex is its \emph{odometer}
$\mathbf u\in\N^V$. We say the input terminates when a finite complete legal
execution exists. We will prove that in that case every maximal legal
execution is finite and has the same odometer. No fairness hypothesis is
needed for this statement.

For $t\in\N$, define the prefix-routing counts
\begin{equation}
 R_{vw}(t)=\#\{j:1\le j\le t,\ \rho_v(j)=w\},
 \qquad w\in V\sqcup S.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:prefix}
\end{equation}
They are nondecreasing in $t$, vanish at zero, and satisfy
$\sum_w R_{vw}(t)=t$. A candidate odometer $\mathbf u$ is \emph{balanced} when
\begin{equation}
 u_v=x_v+\sum_{a\in V}R_{av}(u_a)\qquad(v\in V).
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:balance}
\end{equation}
This is conservation of chips with final active occupancy zero. The associated
sink count is
\begin{equation}
 y_s=\sum_{v\in V}R_{vs}(u_v),\qquad s\in S.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:sink}
\end{equation}
When $u_v>0$, define the last exit $L_{\mathbf u}(v)=\rho_v(u_v)$.
The selected last-exit graph has one outgoing edge at every vertex in
$\supp(\mathbf u)$ and no outgoing edge at the other active vertices or sinks.
Acyclicity means that this selected graph contains no directed cycle.

\subsection{Least action, existence, and uniqueness}
\begin{lemma}[Least action for balanced candidates]
\label{cdc:rt:lem:least}
If $\mathbf u$ satisfies \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:balance}, the firing-count vector of every
finite legal execution prefix is componentwise at most $\mathbf u$.
Consequently a finite complete legal execution exists and has odometer at
most $\mathbf u$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose a legal sequence is about to exceed $\mathbf u$ for the first time,
at vertex $v$. Just before that firing its count vector $\mathbf a$ satisfies
$a_v=u_v$ and $a_w\le u_w$ for all $w$. The number of chips currently at $v$
is
\[
 x_v+\sum_w R_{wv}(a_w)-a_v
 \le x_v+\sum_w R_{wv}(u_w)-u_v=0.
\]
But a legal firing needs a positive number of chips there, a contradiction.
Thus no legal sequence can exceed $\sum_v u_v$ firings. Repeatedly choose
any occupied active vertex, for example the least one in a fixed order.
The procedure must stop after finitely many firings and can stop only when
all active vertices are empty.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Order independence]
\label{cdc:rt:cor:abelian}
If there is a complete legal execution, its odometer $\mathbf U$ and all
sink outputs are independent of the legal firing order. Every maximal legal
execution is finite.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A complete execution gives a balanced vector. Lemma~\ref{cdc:rt:lem:least} bounds
all legal executions by that vector. If $\mathbf U$ and $\mathbf U'$ are two
complete odometers, applying the lemma in both directions gives
$\mathbf U\le\mathbf U'$ and $\mathbf U'\le\mathbf U$. The sink formula then
fixes every output. The same finite bound excludes an infinite execution.
\end{proof}

Balance alone proves the existence of \emph{some} termination, but need not
make a proposed count vector exact. This distinction is crucial: a balanced
flow may add an artificial circulation to the genuine odometer.

\begin{theorem}[Exact odometer from balance and last exits]
\label{cdc:rt:thm:last}
For arbitrary stacks on a finite active set, a vector $\mathbf u\in\N^V$ is
the odometer of a complete legal execution if and only if it is balanced and
its selected last-exit graph is acyclic.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First suppose $\mathbf u$ comes from a complete execution. Balance is
conservation. If the last departure from $v$ sends a chip to an active vertex
$w$, there must be a departure from $w$ strictly later: otherwise that newly
arrived chip would remain when the execution ends. Hence the times of last
departures strictly increase along selected active edges. They cannot
strictly increase around a directed cycle.

Conversely, suppose $\mathbf u$ is balanced with acyclic last exits.
Lemma~\ref{cdc:rt:lem:least} produces the genuine odometer $\mathbf U\le\mathbf u$.
Write $d_v=u_v-U_v$ and $W=\{v:d_v>0\}$. Define residual routing counts
\[
 E_{vw}=R_{vw}(u_v)-R_{vw}(U_v)\ge0.
\]
Subtracting the two balance equations gives
\begin{equation}
 d_w=\sum_{v\in V}E_{vw}\quad(w\in V),\qquad
 \sum_{w\in V\sqcup S}E_{vw}=d_v.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:residualflow}
\end{equation}
If $w\notin W$, its incoming residual sum is zero, so every $E_{vw}$ into it
is zero. Summing \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:residualflow} over the active vertices shows also
that the total residual flow to sinks is zero. Finally, when $v\in W$, the
last symbol $\rho_v(u_v)$ belongs to the nonempty residual suffix
$U_v+1,\ldots,u_v$. It therefore cannot point to a sink or outside $W$.
If $W$ were nonempty, every vertex of the finite set $W$ would have its selected
successor inside $W$. Iterating successors would produce a directed cycle.
Acyclicity excludes this possibility, so $W$ is empty and $\mathbf u=\mathbf U$.
\end{proof}

This proof is a sink-routing version of the classical least-action and
last-exit methods \cite{friedrich-levine,arrival,switching}. Its advantage for compilation
is that it refers to neither a schedule nor a temporal tableau.

\subsection{Canonical heights rather than arbitrary rankings}
An acyclic graph can be certified by a topological ordering, but that ordering
usually has many valid choices. To preserve single-foldness we instead use
exact distances along the selected functional graph.

\begin{lemma}[Canonical forest certificate]
\label{cdc:rt:lem:height}
For a candidate $\mathbf u$, its last-exit graph is acyclic if and only if
there exist natural heights $h_v$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 h_v=\begin{cases}
 0,&u_v=0,\\
 1,&u_v>0,\ L_{\mathbf u}(v)\in S,\\
 1+h_w,&u_v>0,\ L_{\mathbf u}(v)=w\in V.
 \end{cases}
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:height}
\end{equation}
When they exist, the heights are unique and at most $n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Adding the height differences around a cycle of length $r>0$ would give
$0=r$, which is impossible. Conversely, an acyclic selected graph has a
unique finite path from each active vertex until it reaches either a sink or
a vertex with no selected outgoing edge. Set its height to that path length.
This satisfies the equations and is forced by following the path backwards.
A path visits at most $n$ active vertices.
\end{proof}
For balanced vectors, a selected edge cannot end at an inactive active vertex:
such an arrival would give that vertex strictly positive incoming flow but
zero odometer. Hence the nonempty paths of a valid complete certificate
actually end at sinks.

\section{A parametric single-fold quartic for run-length routing\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:rle}

\subsection{Topology, parameters, and the nonzero remainder convention}
Fix the destination lists of a finite routing topology. At vertex $v$, let
its period consist of $m_v\ge1$ blocks
\begin{equation}
 W_v=w_{v1}^{\ell_{v1}}w_{v2}^{\ell_{v2}}\cdots
      w_{vm_v}^{\ell_{vm_v}},\qquad \ell_{vj}\ge1.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:rle}
\end{equation}
Adjacent blocks are allowed to have the same destination; the supplied block
boundaries are part of the description. Set $m=\sum_v m_v$. The stack is the
infinite repetition of $W_v$, starting with the first symbol.

To make every parameter natural, write
$\ell_{vj}=\lambda_{vj}+1$ with $\lambda_{vj}\in\N$. The initial loads
$\mathbf x$ and the $m$ values $\boldsymbol\lambda$ will be \emph{free
parameters}, not witnesses. Define
\begin{align}
 D_v&=\sum_j\ell_{vj},&
 P_{vj}&=\sum_{i<j}\ell_{vi},\label{cdc:rt:eq:perioddata}\\
 C_{vw}&=\sum_{j:w_{vj}=w}\ell_{vj},&
 B_{vjw}&=\sum_{i<j:w_{vi}=w}\ell_{vi}.\nonumber
\end{align}
These are linear polynomials in the run-length parameters. When lengths are
fixed, they are simply nonnegative integer coefficients.

For $u_v>0$ we use the unique decomposition
\begin{equation}
 u_v=D_vq_v+r_v,\qquad q_v\ge0,\quad 1\le r_v\le D_v.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:positive-remainder}
\end{equation}
Thus $q_v=\lfloor(u_v-1)/D_v\rfloor$. In particular, at a period boundary
$r_v=D_v$, not zero. This convention identifies the actual last symbol
without a special wraparound case.

\subsection{The complete residual system}
The natural witness variables are
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 u_v,q_v,z_v,h_v\quad(v\in V),\\
 b_{vj},t_{vj},\alpha_{vj},\beta_{vj}\quad(1\le j\le m_v),\\
 y_s\quad(s\in S).
 \end{gathered}
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:witnesses}
\end{equation}
Here $z_v$ marks a nonzero odometer, $b_{vj}$ selects the block containing
the last symbol, and $t_{vj}$ is the one-based position within that selected
block. Unselected blocks have all four coordinates zero.

Impose the following equations at every vertex:
\begin{align}
 z_v(z_v-1)&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:r1}\\
 \sum_j b_{vj}-z_v&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:r2}\\
 q_v(1-z_v)&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:r3}\\
 u_v-D_vq_v-\sum_j(P_{vj}b_{vj}+t_{vj})&=0.\label{cdc:rt:eq:r4}
\end{align}
At each block impose
\begin{align}
 t_{vj}-b_{vj}-\alpha_{vj}&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:r5}\\
 t_{vj}+\beta_{vj}-\ell_{vj}b_{vj}&=0.\label{cdc:rt:eq:r6}
\end{align}
Because all witnesses are natural, \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r1}--\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r2} force
$b_{vj}\in\{0,1\}$ without separate Boolean equations. If $b_{vj}=0$,
\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r5}--\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r6} force $t_{vj}=\alpha_{vj}=\beta_{vj}=0$.
If $b_{vj}=1$, they give exactly
\[
 1\le t_{vj}\le\ell_{vj},\qquad
 \alpha_{vj}=t_{vj}-1,\quad\beta_{vj}=\ell_{vj}-t_{vj}.
\]
The slacks are uniquely determined, including in the inactive case.

Define, without adding new witness variables, the routing expressions
\begin{equation}
 F_{vw}=C_{vw}q_v+\sum_j B_{vjw}b_{vj}
                +\sum_{j:w_{vj}=w}t_{vj}.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:flowformula}
\end{equation}
They count complete periods, complete blocks before the selected block, and
the selected partial block. These expressions have degree at most two when
run lengths are parameters, and are linear when lengths are fixed.
The remaining equations are
\begin{align}
 h_v-z_v-\sum_{j:w_{vj}\in V} b_{vj}h_{w_{vj}}&=0
    &&(v\in V),\label{cdc:rt:eq:r7}\\
 u_v-x_v-\sum_{a\in V}F_{av}&=0
    &&(v\in V),\label{cdc:rt:eq:r8}\\
 y_s-\sum_{v\in V}F_{vs}&=0
    &&(s\in S).\label{cdc:rt:eq:r9}
\end{align}
Let $\mathcal R$ be the list of all left-hand sides in
\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r1}--\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r9}, with their stated multiplicities. Define
\begin{equation}
 Q_{\mathcal T}(\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\lambda;\mathbf w)
       =\sum_{R\in\mathcal R}R^2.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:quartic}
\end{equation}
The subscript $\mathcal T$ denotes the fixed destination-list topology. No
floor, divisibility predicate, quantifier, or machine simulator remains in
this definition: it is an ordinary integer polynomial.

\begin{theorem}[Parametric canonical RLE quartic]
\label{cdc:rt:thm:rle}
For every finite destination-list topology with $n$ active vertices,
$s$ sinks, and $m$ blocks, the polynomial \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:quartic} has the following
properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Its total degree in both parameters and witnesses is at most four.
There are exactly $4n+4m+s$ natural witness coordinates, $n+m$ natural
parameters, and $6n+2m+s$ residuals of degree at most two.
\item For every initial load $\mathbf x$ and every run-length tuple
$\boldsymbol\ell=\boldsymbol\lambda+\mathbf1$, the natural zero set of
$Q_{\mathcal T}$ in all witness coordinates is empty if the input does not
terminate, and is a singleton if it terminates.
\item In that unique root, $\mathbf u$ is the exact odometer and $\mathbf y$
is the complete vector of sink outputs.
\item The residual list, and also the expanded polynomial, have descriptions
of size polynomial in the finite topology description. Specializing binary
run lengths preserves polynomial description size in the specialized input
length.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every residual displayed above has total degree at most two. The quantities
$D,P,C,B$ are linear in the free $\lambda$ parameters, and every product
involving them has only one further witness factor. Squaring establishes the
degree bound. There are four coordinates per active vertex, four per block,
and one per sink. There are six residuals per vertex, two per block, and one
per sink, giving the stated counts.

A sum of integer squares is zero exactly when every summand is zero.
Suppose first that all residuals vanish. If $z_v=0$, the nonnegative sum of
selectors in \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r2} is zero. The block equations force their offsets
and slacks to vanish, the gate \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r3} forces $q_v=0$, and
\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r4} forces $u_v=0$. Equation~\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r7} then forces $h_v=0$.
If $z_v=1$, exactly one selector is one. Its offset lies in
$[1,\ell_{vj}]$, so \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r4} gives precisely the positive-remainder
decomposition \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:positive-remainder}. In particular $u_v>0$.
The selected block and its offset are unique for that remainder, since the
block intervals partition $\{1,\ldots,D_v\}$.

Consequently $F_{vw}=R_{vw}(u_v)$ and the selected destination is exactly
$\rho_v(u_v)$. Equation~\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r8} is genuine balance, while
\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r7} is the canonical height condition of Lemma~\ref{cdc:rt:lem:height}.
Theorem~\ref{cdc:rt:thm:last} therefore identifies $\mathbf u$ with the true
complete odometer. The sink equations identify $\mathbf y$.

Conversely, a terminating execution has a unique odometer. Use its positive
remainders to set $q,z,b,t$, set the two slacks to their forced differences,
and take the unique forest heights. The exact prefix formula and
conservation make every residual zero. For fixed parameters, every coordinate
has now been shown to be uniquely forced by the odometer. This proves both
existence and single-foldness.

Finally, the expressions in \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:perioddata} and \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:flowformula}
are finite sums with at most polynomially many terms in the topology size.
Squaring an explicitly listed polynomial-size residual multiplies its term
count by at most a polynomial factor. Substitution of binary lengths only
requires additions and multiplications of integers of polynomial bit length.
There is no expansion of a word of length $D_v$, and no unrolling of
$\sum_v u_v$ firing steps.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What is and is not linear in the description]
The exact variable and residual counts are linear in $n+m+s$. The number
of terms inside a residual need not be bounded by a constant, and the
expanded quartic need not have only $O(n+m+s)$ monomials. The polynomial-size
claim is deliberately weaker and is the one proved above.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Why natural witnesses and canonical gates are essential}
The construction uses nonnegativity, not just equations over a field.
For example, $\sum_j b_{vj}=0$ forces every selector to vanish only because
the selectors are natural. Similarly, two linear slack equations express an
interval only with nonnegative slack variables. The sum of squared residuals
can be evaluated over $\Z$, but its intended witness domain is $\N$.
A routine replacement of natural variables by sums of four integer squares
preserves existence and generally destroys uniqueness: the same natural
number can have several square decompositions. We make no corresponding
single-fold claim over unrestricted integer witnesses.

The inactivity gate $q_v(1-z_v)=0$ is indispensable. Without it, take an
initially empty one-vertex self-routing network with period length $D$.
The values $z=b=t=h=0$, $q=1$, and $u=D$ satisfy the other displayed local
conditions and balance, inventing a complete cycle of firings without a
chip. The gate eliminates this fake execution. Likewise, replacing the exact
height equation by the inequality $h_v>h_w$ would typically admit infinitely
many rankings for the same true odometer, defeating single-foldness.

\subsection{A large exact example with thirteen unknowns}
\begin{example}
\label{cdc:rt:ex:huge}
Take one active vertex $v$, one sink $s$, and period $v^L s$ with $L\ge1$.
Put $M$ chips at $v$. Each chip is absorbed after $L+1$ firings, so
\[
 U=M(L+1),\qquad y=M.
\]
For $M>0$ the unique witness is
\[
 q=M-1,\quad z=h=1,\quad
 (b_1,b_2)=(0,1),\quad(t_1,t_2)=(0,1),
\]
with all four block slacks zero. For $M=0$, every witness coordinate is zero.
There are $4+8+1=13$ witness variables and $6+4+1=11$ residuals.

The supplied checker evaluates this certificate with
\[
 L=M=2^{4096},\qquad U=2^{8192}+2^{4096}.
\]
It obtains exactly zero for the sum of the eleven squared residuals, using
ordinary arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic. It does not simulate the
$U$ firings. The integer $U$ has $8193$ binary digits, which is a manageable
certificate size despite the infeasible execution length.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[A spurious balanced circulation]
Let $a$ have period $(b,s)$ and $b$ have period $(a,s)$, with no initial
chips. Both active vertices have paths to the sink. The proposed odometer
$(u_a,u_b)=(1,1)$ is balanced: each alleged firing supplies the other one.
Its last-exit graph is the cycle $a\to b\to a$, so no heights can satisfy
$h_a=1+h_b$ and $h_b=1+h_a$. The genuine odometer is $(0,0)$.
Thus even global accessibility of a sink does not make balance alone an
exact execution certificate.
\end{example}

\section{Shared grammar periods without word expansion\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:grammar}

\subsection{The representation and its useful statistics}
Run lengths compress long constant blocks. A straight-line grammar can
compress a different kind of repetition, such as a word obtained by repeated
doubling of a nonconstant pattern. For each active vertex $v$, let its period
be specified by a finite acyclic grammar whose nodes have one of two forms:
\[
 A\longrightarrow w\quad(w\in V\sqcup S),\qquad
 A\longrightarrow BC.
\]
Every node defines exactly one nonempty word. Children occur before parents
in a topological order, and one distinguished root $A_v$ defines the period.
Nodes may be shared within the grammar: the same subword can occur as a child
of many different concatenations, including twice in the same concatenation.
We count $g_v$ nodes and $c_v$ concatenation nodes at $v$, and set
$g=\sum_v g_v$, $c=\sum_v c_v$. Thus the accounting includes a separate
certificate coordinate system for each active vertex's grammar. It does not
claim that several independent prefix queries can share the same witness
coordinates for a globally shared grammar.

Precompute the length $L_A$ and symbol-count vector $(C_{Aw})_w$ by
\[
 L_w=1,\quad C_{wz}=[w=z],\qquad
 L_A=L_B+L_C,\quad C_{Az}=C_{Bz}+C_{Cz}\quad(A\to BC).
\]
These calculations are polynomial in the grammar size and alphabet size.
In a grammar with $g_v$ nodes, every word has length at most $2^{g_v}$;
therefore its lengths and counts have $O(g_v)$ bits. No word expansion is
needed. Let $D_v=L_{A_v}$.
\wtag{} [The bound can be halved: a terminal defines a word of length one, a concatenation defines a word at most twice as long as the longer of its children's, and a descending path meets at most $c_v\le g_v-1$ concatenation nodes, so every word has length at most $2^{g_v-1}$. The doubling example below, with $k+3$ nodes and period $2^{k+1}$, is within this bound.]

The key observation is that a positive prefix of one grammar word needs only
one root-to-terminal descent path. Every right turn contributes the whole
left subword to the prefix count. A prefix certificate should describe this
path, not a derivation tree containing all repeated copies of the word.

\subsection{Canonical path variables and equations}
For each grammar node $A$, introduce natural variables
\[
 a_A,k_A,\eta_A,\theta_A.
\]
Here $a_A$ records whether the selected descent visits that node and $k_A$
is its one-based local position. Impose
\begin{align}
 a_A(a_A-1)&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:g1}\\
 k_A-a_A-\eta_A&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:g2}\\
 k_A+\theta_A-L_Aa_A&=0.\label{cdc:rt:eq:g3}
\end{align}
An inactive node therefore has all four coordinates zero; an active node
has $1\le k_A\le L_A$ and unique interval slacks.

At a concatenation $A\to BC$, introduce four additional natural variables
$l_A,r_A,\sigma_A,\tau_A$, and impose
\begin{align}
 l_A+r_A-a_A&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:g4}\\
 \sigma_A-l_A(L_B-k_A)&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:g5}\\
 \tau_A-r_A(k_A-L_B-1)&=0.\label{cdc:rt:eq:g6}
\end{align}
Thus $l_A,r_A$ are automatically Boolean. At an active node the left branch
is possible exactly when $k_A\le L_B$, and the right branch exactly when
$k_A\ge L_B+1$. Only one is possible, and the corresponding slack is its
forced nonnegative difference. Every unused comparison slack is zero.

For every node $X$ other than the root of its grammar, impose the incoming
activation and position equations
\begin{align}
 a_X&=\sum_{A\to XC}l_A+\sum_{A\to BX}r_A,\label{cdc:rt:eq:g7}\\
 k_X&=\sum_{A\to XC}l_Ak_A
           +\sum_{A\to BX}r_A(k_A-L_B).\label{cdc:rt:eq:g8}
\end{align}
Each occurrence of $X$ as a left or right child contributes in the appropriate
sum. In particular, if a rule is $A\to XX$, the two occurrences are handled
separately and only the selected occurrence is active.

At each active routing vertex retain the four variables $u_v,q_v,z_v,h_v$
and impose
\begin{align}
 z_v(z_v-1)&=0,&q_v(1-z_v)&=0,\label{cdc:rt:eq:g9}\\
 a_{A_v}-z_v&=0,&u_v-D_vq_v-k_{A_v}&=0.\label{cdc:rt:eq:g10}
\end{align}
The root offset is again the positive remainder; it is zero exactly for an
inactive vertex. These equations do not impose a freely chosen path at each
shared occurrence. The single activated root, unique branching, and acyclic
node order force one path, with all other nodes inactive.

\subsection{Prefix counts, last symbols, and global balance}
Define
\begin{equation}
 F_{vw}=q_vC_{A_vw}
       +\sum_{A\to BC}r_AC_{Bw}
       +\sum_{A\to w}a_A,
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:gflow}
\end{equation}
where both sums range over the grammar at $v$. A selected right turn adds
the whole left word; the final selected terminal adds the last symbol.
This accounts exactly for the selected prefix, in addition to the complete
periods. The selected terminal is also the last-exit destination, so impose
\begin{equation}
 h_v-z_v-\sum_{\substack{A\to w\\ w\in V}}a_Ah_w=0.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:gheight}
\end{equation}
The active balance equations and sink equations are the same as
\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r8}--\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:r9}, using \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:gflow}. Once again, the final
polynomial is the sum of the squares of all residuals.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical grammar quartic]
\label{cdc:rt:thm:grammar}
For a network whose nonempty periodic words are specified by the grammars
above, there is an explicitly constructible integer polynomial of total
degree at most four, with
\[
 4n+4g+4c+s\quad\text{natural witness coordinates}
\]
and
\[
 4n+5g+3c+s\quad\text{residuals of degree at most two}.
\]
For every natural initial load, the polynomial has exactly one natural root
if the execution terminates and no natural root otherwise. Its root contains
the exact odometer and every sink output. Construction time and polynomial
description size are polynomial in the grammar description and alphabet size,
not in the lengths of the expanded periods.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Start with the local path system. When the root is inactive, an induction
from parents to children shows that every incoming activation sum is zero;
all nodes are inactive and all their coordinates vanish. When the root is
active, \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:g1}--\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:g6} force exactly one child at each active
concatenation, with the uniquely appropriate translated offset. Acyclicity of
the grammar ensures this process reaches a terminal without revisiting a
node. All activations outside this path are zero: process the nodes from
parents to children, noting that no node can become active without an active
incoming selected edge. Sharing therefore causes no ambiguity.

Conversely, the usual descent to a position in the root word gives a solution
to all local equations, and the same argument proves that this solution is
unique. At a left descent the prefix lies entirely in the left child. At a
right descent it consists of the entire left word followed by the selected
prefix in the right child. Induction along the descent proves
\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:gflow}. Exactly one selected terminal supplies the final symbol.

The global equations now give genuine balance and the canonical last-exit
heights. Theorem~\ref{cdc:rt:thm:last} proves soundness and identifies the odometer.
Conversely, the true odometer determines a unique positive remainder at every
active vertex, a unique grammar path, and all its unique slacks. This proves
completeness and single-foldness.

There are four variables per routing vertex, four per grammar node, four per
concatenation, and one per sink. For the residual count, the node equations
contribute $3g$, the concatenation equations contribute $3c$, and the
nonroot incoming equations contribute $2(g-n)$. Root activation contributes
$n$; Boolean $z$, the quotient gate, the odometer decomposition, the height,
and the balance contribute another $5n$; sinks contribute $s$. Their sum is
$4n+5g+3c+s$. Every product contains at most two variables. The metadata have
polynomial bit length, which also proves the description-size and construction
bounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Shared repeated doubling]
Start with a terminal $a$, a terminal $b$, and the word $A_0\to ab$.
Define $A_{i+1}\to A_iA_i$. The final period has length $2^{k+1}$ after $k$
doublings, but the grammar has only $k+3$ nodes. For a prefix of length $t$,
its counts are $\lceil t/2\rceil$ copies of $a$ and $\lfloor t/2\rfloor$
copies of $b$. The supplied checker uses $1024$ doublings, giving a period
of length $2^{1025}$, and checks six prefix certificates without expanding
that word. This tests the case where both children of every doubling node
are the very same grammar node.
\end{example}

\section{Certificate height, both outcomes, and fixed-period structure\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:complexity}

\subsection{A binary height bound}
Assume first that every active vertex has a directed path to a sink in the
underlying graph of destinations that occur in its period. Put
$M=\sum_v x_v$.

\begin{lemma}[Absorption and a finite-state bound]
\label{cdc:rt:lem:bound}
Under this accessibility assumption, every maximal legal execution
terminates. For a deterministic rule that always chooses the least occupied
active vertex, the total number $T$ of firings satisfies
\begin{equation}
 T<(M+1)^n\prod_{v\in V}D_v.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:timebound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If a legal execution were infinite, some vertex would fire infinitely often.
Let $I$ be the nonempty set of such vertices. A periodic stack used infinitely
often sends infinitely many chips to every destination occurring in its
period. No sink can receive infinitely many chips, since the total number of
chips is the fixed finite number $M$. Likewise, an active vertex receiving
infinitely many chips must fire infinitely often; otherwise it would eventually
hold more than $M$ chips. Therefore $I$ is closed under all underlying
destination edges and has no path to a sink, a contradiction.

For the quantitative bound, a state relevant to future behavior consists of
the active chip vector and each counter modulo $D_v$. There are at most
$(M+1)^n\prod_vD_v$ such states. Accumulated sink counts are not needed to
determine future active dynamics. A deterministic run reaching termination
cannot repeat a nonterminal state, or its future would repeat forever.
Including the final state yields \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:timebound}.
\end{proof}

The bound can be crude in numerical value and still be useful for
certificates. Taking binary logarithms gives
\begin{equation}
 \log_2(T+1)=O\!\left(1+n\log_2(M+1)+\sum_v\log_2D_v\right).
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:bitbound}
\end{equation}
Every odometer coordinate and quotient is at most $T$. RLE offsets and
slacks are at most the corresponding period length; grammar offsets and
slacks are at most a node-word length. Heights are at most $n$ and sink
outputs at most $M$. Thus the complete natural root has polynomial binary
length in a binary RLE or grammar input. This is a bound on the length of a
certificate, not a polynomial bound on execution time or a polynomial-time
method for finding it.

\subsection{Canonical nontermination certificates by trap collapse}
For a general finite periodic network, let $R\subseteq V$ be the set of active
vertices that can reach a sink in the underlying destination graph. Let
$Z=V\setminus R$. No destination from $Z$ can be in $R$ or in a real sink;
otherwise that source would itself reach a sink.

Construct a modified network with active set $R$ and a new sink $\bot$.
Every edge from $R$ into $Z$ is redirected to $\bot$. Retain the original
sinks, and add the fixed initial quantity $\sum_{v\in Z}x_v$ to the final
output at $\bot$. Every remaining active vertex reaches a real sink, so the
modified system always terminates. Its output equation at the new sink is
\begin{equation}
 y_\bot=\sum_{v\in Z}x_v+\sum_{a\in R}F_{a\bot}.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:trapoutput}
\end{equation}
The case $R=\varnothing$ has no routing variables and is handled directly
by these fixed output counts.

\begin{theorem}[A unique finite certificate for either answer]
\label{cdc:rt:thm:classify}
For RLE or grammar-period networks, the modified instance has exactly one
natural certificate. The original input terminates if and only if
$y_\bot=0$. Consequently the binary-input decision problem ``are all chips
eventually absorbed at real sinks?'' is in $\UP\cap\coUP$ for both
representations.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The existence, uniqueness, and polynomial bit length of the modified
certificate follow from the previous theorems and Lemma~\ref{cdc:rt:lem:bound}.
Firing inside $Z$ never affects $R$. Projecting an original execution to its
firings in $R$ therefore preserves exactly the chip dynamics of the modified
network until the corresponding chips have been absorbed or entered $Z$.
A chip initially in $Z$, or entering $Z$, can never reach a real sink and can
never disappear; hence a positive value of $y_\bot$ excludes a complete
original execution. If $y_\bot=0$, there were no initial chips in $Z$ and the
modified execution sends none there. That complete execution in $R$ is then
also a complete original execution.

For the complexity assertion, construct the modified instance deterministically
and guess its unique certificate in a fixed coordinate order with prescribed
polynomial-width binary fields. Verify the residual equations and require
$y_\bot=0$ for the yes verifier, or $y_\bot\ge1$ for the no verifier. Integer
arithmetic on the established bit bounds is polynomial time. There is at most
one accepting certificate string for either verifier, since every integer
coordinate is unique and the binary encoding is fixed. There is one for
exactly the correct answer. This is the defining certificate condition for
$\UP\cap\coUP$.
\end{proof}

The one-token explicit-switching upper bound and related succinct
certificates are established in the ARRIVAL literature
\cite{arrival,switching}. The theorem above supplies a direct proof for the
present multi-chip, grammar-aware, fully canonical algebraic formulation;
it is not asserted as a new upper bound for ordinary ARRIVAL.

\subsection{Fixed periods give an existential Presburger description}
\begin{proposition}
\label{cdc:rt:prop:presburger}
Fix all periods, not only the destination topology. The graph of the partial
map taking initial loads to complete odometers and sink outputs is definable
by an existential Presburger formula: a finite disjunction of existential
systems of integer-linear equalities and inequalities over natural variables.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In the RLE residual system, first split into the finitely many possibilities
for $z_v$ and the one-hot block selectors. All products of two witness
variables are then either a variable times zero or a variable times one.
The periods and their metadata are constants. What remains is a linear
system with nonnegative unknowns. The finite disjunction over selectors,
with the auxiliary coordinates existentially quantified, defines exactly
the desired graph by Theorem~\ref{cdc:rt:thm:rle}. For the grammar compiler, similarly
split over the Boolean node activations and branch choices; all remaining
products become linear.
\end{proof}

This observation helps prevent a false universality conclusion from the
unbounded chip counts. With periods fixed, even the nonlinear-looking height
conditions have only a finite number of selector cases. With run lengths
left as parameters, products such as $\ell q$ remain and this particular
Presburger argument does not apply. Nevertheless, the whole class of finite
explicitly described periodic networks remains decidable by finite-state
analysis, with an effectively computable bound for each instance.

\subsection{A phase-preserving transport identity}
The positive-remainder convention also yields a useful exact relation between
different inputs. Fix the periods and form the diagonal matrix
$D=\operatorname{diag}(D_v)$ and the active routing-count matrix
$C=(C_{vw})_{v,w\in V}$, with source vertices indexing rows. Put
$\mathcal L=D-C^{\mathsf T}$.

\begin{proposition}[Full-period input transport]
\label{cdc:rt:prop:transport}
Suppose the input $\mathbf x$ terminates with $U_v>0$ for every active vertex.
Let $\mathbf k\in\N^V$ and assume
$\mathbf x'=\mathbf x+\mathcal L\mathbf k\in\N^V$. Then $\mathbf x'$
terminates and
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf U(\mathbf x')=\mathbf U(\mathbf x)+D\mathbf k.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:transport}
\end{equation}
The sink-output increase at $s$ is $\sum_vC_{vs}k_v$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Adding $D_vk_v$ firings at vertex $v$ adds $k_v$ whole periods. It changes
its routing count to $w$ by $C_{vw}k_v$ and leaves its nonzero last phase,
last destination, and support unchanged. The new candidate is balanced
because its extra departure vector is $D\mathbf k$, its extra active
arrival vector is $C^{\mathsf T}\mathbf k$, and the input change is their
difference. Its last-exit graph remains acyclic. Theorem~\ref{cdc:rt:thm:last}
therefore proves \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:transport}, and the sink formula gives the output
change. The strict positivity hypothesis avoids activating previously unused
vertices, whose new last exits would require a separate analysis.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} [The positivity hypothesis is used only at vertices with $k_v>0$. At a vertex with $k_v=0$ the candidate count and last exit are unchanged, and a vertex with $U_v=0$ and $k_v=0$ keeps count zero and has no selected edge; adding $k_a$ whole periods at a vertex $a$ with $U_a=0$ also adds exactly $C_{aw}k_a$ to each routing count, so balance holds, but its new last exit $\rho_a(D_ak_a)$ may close a cycle. Hence the proposition holds whenever $U_v>0$ at every $v$ with $k_v>0$.]

\section{A circuit-defined period already hides a counting problem\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:circuit}
The preceding compilers exploit particular representations of prefix counts.
It is not enough that the destination at a given position can be computed
quickly. Random access and prefix counting can have very different costs.

Let $C$ be a Boolean circuit on $k$ input bits. Use one active vertex $v$ and
two sinks $s_0,s_1$. Its period has length $2^k$, with the destinations
specified in lexicographic assignment order:
\begin{equation}
 \rho_v(j)=s_{C(\operatorname{bin}_k(j-1))},
 \qquad 1\le j\le2^k,
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:circuitperiod}
\end{equation}
and the period repeats. Give $v$ exactly $2^k$ chips. Every firing goes
directly to a sink, so the execution is particularly simple.

\begin{proposition}[Counting in a one-vertex acyclic routing system]
\label{cdc:rt:prop:counting}
For \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:circuitperiod}, the odometer and sink outputs are
\[
 U_v=2^k,\qquad
 y_{s_1}=\#\{a\in\{0,1\}^k:C(a)=1\},\qquad
 y_{s_0}=2^k-y_{s_1}.
\]
Thus computing the exact output on these succinct instances computes the
number of satisfying assignments of an arbitrary Boolean circuit.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Each of the $2^k$ input chips causes exactly one firing, and the first full
period queries each assignment once. The displayed counts follow directly.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Obstruction to uniformly small bounded-height certificates]
\label{cdc:rt:thm:countbarrier}
Suppose a polynomial-time procedure, on a circuit $C$, produces a
polynomial-size bounded-degree integer polynomial $Q_C(\mathbf w)$ with the
following properties: it has a natural root exactly when the routing output
$y_{s_1}$ above is zero, and whenever it has a root it has one whose total
binary encoding length is polynomial in $|C|+k$. Then $\NP=\coNP$.
The same conclusion holds for polynomial-size systems of quadratic residuals.
Uniqueness of their witnesses is not needed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{cdc:rt:prop:counting}, zero output is exactly circuit
unsatisfiability. Guess a root of the guaranteed polynomial bit length and
evaluate $Q_C$ using exact integer arithmetic. Bounded degree, polynomial
coefficient bit length, and polynomially many explicitly described monomials
make this a polynomial-time check. Thus circuit unsatisfiability has
polynomially verifiable existential certificates.

For completeness, the usual complexity consequence follows directly from
verifier circuits. If $A\in\coNP$, membership in its complement is expressed
by some polynomial-time verifier $V(x,z)$ with a polynomial-length guessed
string $z$. On fixed input $x$, unrolling that bounded deterministic verifier
gives a Boolean circuit $C_x$ whose satisfying assignments are precisely its
accepting guesses. Therefore $x\in A$ exactly when $C_x$ is unsatisfiable.
The assumed certificates put every such $A$ in $\NP$, so
$\coNP\subseteq\NP$. Taking complements gives the reverse inclusion.
\end{proof}

This theorem does not rule out Diophantine representations of circuit-defined
routing. It isolates a conjunction of requirements: a uniform polynomial-time
compiler, polynomial description size, bounded degree, and short witnesses.
Allowing much larger witnesses removes the stated complexity consequence.
Nor does the obstruction concern firing-order ambiguity: the example has no
active-to-active edges at all. The difficulty is the prefix-count information
compressed into a circuit.

\section{A universal one-router system with easy prefix ranks\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:universal}
There is a second, logically independent boundary. Even a polynomial-time
\emph{prefix-rank} function does not guarantee that a finite semantic
certificate has any computable size bound in the input length. An
exponentially dilated universal clock makes the distinction explicit.

\subsection{One fixed interpreter and one total rank routine}
Fix a deterministic universal Turing machine $\mathcal U$ taking a natural
input code $c$ in binary. Choose its interpreter convention so that for every
computably enumerable set $A\subseteq\N$ there is a program code $e$ with
\begin{equation}
 n\in A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal U(\pi_{\mathrm C}(e,n))\text{ halts},\qquad
 \pi_{\mathrm C}(e,n)=\frac{(e+n)(e+n+1)}2+n.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:pairing}
\end{equation}
This is ordinary effective universality with an explicit polynomial pairing
of the program and its input. Let $T(c)$ be the first halting time, when it
exists; time zero is allowed.

Define one total Boolean function on natural arguments:
\begin{equation}
 \rankf(c,0)=0,\qquad
 \rankf(c,k)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\mathcal U(c)\text{ halts within }\lfloor\log_2 k\rfloor\text{ steps},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}
 \quad k\ge1.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:rankclock}
\end{equation}
This definition is an executable bounded simulation, not a halting oracle.
Given binary $c,k$, compute the bit length of $k$, simulate the fixed machine
for that many steps minus one, and return the indicated bit. A standard direct
simulation uses time polynomial in $\bits(c)+\bits(k)$: only
$O(\bits(k))$ transitions and a polynomial-size portion of the input and tape
can be involved. Initial halting is checked before the first transition.

The function is nondecreasing in $k$. More precisely,
\begin{equation}
 \rankf(c,k)=
 \begin{cases}
 [k\ge2^{T(c)}],&\mathcal U(c)\text{ halts},\\
 0,&\mathcal U(c)\text{ does not halt}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:stepfunction}
\end{equation}
Thus it is an especially simple function pointwise: either identically zero
or a single threshold step.

\subsection{The routing rule and its universality}
Use one active vertex $v$, one absorbing sink $s$, one initial chip, and a
read-only input code $c$. The destination of firing $j\ge1$ is determined by
\begin{equation}
 \rho_{c}(j)=
 \begin{cases}
 s,&\rankf(c,j)-\rankf(c,j-1)=1,\\
 v,&\rankf(c,j)-\rankf(c,j-1)=0.
 \end{cases}
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:clockstack}
\end{equation}
The difference is always zero or one because of monotonicity. The full sink
prefix rank is exactly $R_{vs}(k)=\rankf(c,k)$, by telescoping, and the self
prefix rank is $R_{vv}(k)=k-\rankf(c,k)$.

\begin{theorem}[Universal halting with polynomial-time ranks]
\label{cdc:rt:thm:universal}
The family \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:clockstack} has all the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The graph has one active vertex and one sink, independently of $c$.
A single fixed total algorithm computes both random access to its stack and
all prefix counts in time polynomial in the binary input lengths.
\item For every $c$, the stack is eventually constant. It contains at most one
sink symbol. If $\mathcal U(c)$ first halts at time $T$, that symbol occurs
exactly at position $2^T$; otherwise every symbol is $v$.
\item The router terminates if and only if $\mathcal U(c)$ halts, and in that
case its exact odometer is $u=2^{T(c)}$. Its halting set is computably enumerable
complete. With the terminal counter as an observable output, arbitrary
partial-computable outputs can be recovered effectively.
\item There is no computable function of $\bits(c)$ bounding the bit length
of the terminating odometer on all halting inputs. There is likewise no
computable uniform bound on the position of the last exceptional stack symbol.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The bounded-simulation algorithm above proves the rank bound; two rank
queries decide \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:clockstack}. Equation~\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:stepfunction} says
that the rank changes only at $2^T$ when a first halt exists. This proves the
stack description. The lone chip returns to $v$ until that unique position
and then leaves for $s$, or returns forever when no such position exists.
The reduction \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:pairing} proves computably enumerable completeness;
simulation of the router proves its halting set is computably enumerable.
After observing a terminal counter $u$, compute $T=\log_2u$ and run
$\mathcal U(c)$ for $T$ transitions to recover its final output. This is a
computable decoding of any simulated partial function's output.

Finally, suppose a computable function $f(a)$ bounded $\bits(u)$ on every
halting input $c$ of bit length $a$. Since $\bits(2^T)=T+1$, simulating
$\mathcal U(c)$ for $f(a)$ transitions would decide whether it ever halts.
This contradicts universal undecidability. A computable bound on the
exceptional position would yield a computable bound on its bit length and
hence the same contradiction.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} Item~(iv) is the routing form of \cref{cdc:bd:prop:nobound}, with the same finite-search proof: a computable bound on the odometer, or on some witness of any Diophantine representation of this undecidable halting set, would decide halting.

\begin{remark}[Where the computational power resides]
The theorem is not a claim that a one-state finite automaton has become
universal. The routing apparatus has an unbounded firing counter, a read-only
input, and a fixed polynomial-time algorithm allowed to inspect the counter's
binary digits. That algorithm performs bounded universal simulation. There is
no oracle, but the model is algorithmic rather than a finite-state rotor with
a supplied finite period. Universality here is a precise time-dilated
simulation, not an assertion of a new physically minimal universal device.
\end{remark}

If the input halts, its stack has the finite semantic description
\[
 v^{2^{T(c)}-1}\,s\,v^\omega;
\]
if it does not, it has description $v^\omega$. These descriptions exist
pointwise, but no effective procedure can always produce a correct finite
preperiod-plus-period description from $c$. Such a procedure would make the
existence of a sink symbol decidable by examining the finite prefix and
period. Thus \emph{being} eventually periodic and \emph{being supplied with}
an effective finite periodic description are different hypotheses.

For comparison, universality in an abelian physical-style substrate is not
merely a hypothetical possibility: Cairns constructs universal behavior and
undecidable halting questions for three-dimensional sandpiles with suitable
infinite backgrounds \cite{cairns}. That model is not the finite conservative
routing model of Sections~\ref{cdc:rt:sec:rle}--\ref{cdc:rt:sec:complexity}. We do not transfer
its universality to finite periodic rotors.

\wtag{} Batch~78, 2 October 2026: Part~XVI (manuscript~16) attaches cubic certificates with unique natural witnesses to finite spatial restrictions of Cairns's sandpiles, with a one-layer exterior collar that certifies global halting exactly, and shows that no computable function of the input description bounds the radius that must be certified (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:collar,cdc:sp:thm:nobound}). The universality remains Cairns's there too, and is not transferred to rotors.

\subsection{Its unique semantic certificate}
Apply the general balance theorem to the one-router system. With one input
chip, balance reads
\[
 u=1+u-\rankf(c,u),
\]
so it requires $\rankf(c,u)=1$. Exactness also requires that the last exit
be a sink; otherwise it is a selected self-loop. Equivalently, the exact
semantic certificate is
\begin{equation}
 u=v'+1,\qquad
 \rankf(c,u)=1,\qquad \rankf(c,v')=0,
 \qquad u,v'\in\N.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:clockcertificate}
\end{equation}
When it exists, this pair is uniquely $u=2^{T(c)}$, $v'=u-1$.
Checking it takes time polynomial in its binary length and the input length.
Its length, however, has no computable input-only upper bound. Uniqueness
plus efficient verification in the certificate length therefore does not
place this universal halting problem in $\UP$; the missing hypothesis is a
polynomial \emph{input-length} certificate bound.

\section{An exact finite-fold and single-fold bottleneck\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:bottleneck}
The previous construction lets us turn a caution about witnesses into a
precise equivalence theorem. It singles out one fixed, total, monotone,
polynomial-time Boolean function whose multiplicity-preserving Diophantine
representation already captures the full general problem.
\wtag{} [Compare \cref{cdc:pt:prop:exponential-boundary}, where the graph of $2^n$ plays the same role through the single-fold exponential normal form, which ProveIt formalizes (\cref{cdc:bd:rem:sfu}), and \cref{cdc:rx:thm:FF}, where the least-reservoir relation of one reaction network does.]

\subsection{The two representation principles}
Let $\SF$ be the principle that every computably enumerable subset
of $\N$ has a single-fold Diophantine representation over natural witnesses.
Let $\FF$ be the analogous finite-fold principle. We use these names
as mathematical statements; no assertion that either is proved is being made.
The corresponding statements for relations of finitely many natural variables
are equivalent, since iterated Cantor pairing has unique natural values and
is expressed by integer polynomial equations after clearing the factor two.
\wtag{} [$\SF$ and $\FF$ are statement~(a) of \cref{cdc:bd:thm:universal} in its single-fold and finite-fold versions, and the remark on relations of finitely many variables is (a)$\Leftrightarrow$(a$'$) there; Part~XIII uses the same names (\cref{cdc:conv:b62-11}).]

The graph of the fixed rank function is
\[
 \Gamma_{\rankf}=\{(c,k,b)\in\N^3:b=\rankf(c,k)\}.
\]
It is a recursive relation, indeed decidable in polynomial time on binary
inputs. Ordinary MRDP supplies a polynomial representation of this graph,
but its auxiliary multiplicity is not controlled by that theorem
\cite{repo-mrdp}. The distinction is exactly what matters next.

\begin{theorem}[One monotone rank function is a complete multiplicity bottleneck]
\label{cdc:rt:thm:bottleneck}
For the fixed function $\rankf$ in \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:rankclock}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\Gamma_{\rankf}$ has a single-fold Diophantine representation if and
only if $\SF$ holds.
\item $\Gamma_{\rankf}$ has a finite-fold Diophantine representation if and
only if $\FF$ holds.
\item More quantitatively, suppose a polynomial
$G(c,k,b,\mathbf z)$ of degree $d$, with $r$ natural auxiliary coordinates,
represents $\Gamma_{\rankf}$ with either of these multiplicity properties.
Then every computably enumerable subset of $\N$ has a representation with
the same property, at most $2r+3$ natural witnesses, and degree at most
$\max\{4,2d\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The forward implications require a construction. Fix a computably enumerable
set $A$ and choose its interpreter code $e$ from \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:pairing}.
Use disjoint $r$-tuples $\mathbf a,\mathbf b$ and three additional natural
witnesses $c,u,v'$. Define the explicit polynomial schema
\begin{align}
 H_e(n;c,u,v',\mathbf a,\mathbf b)
 ={}&\bigl(2c-(e+n)(e+n+1)-2n\bigr)^2\nonumber\\
   &+(u-v'-1)^2\nonumber\\
   &+G(c,u,1,\mathbf a)^2
     +G(c,v',0,\mathbf b)^2.
 \label{cdc:rt:eq:bottleneckpoly}
\end{align}
At a natural zero, the first squared residual forces the unique value
$c=\pi_{\mathrm C}(e,n)$. The remaining residuals say exactly
\eqref{cdc:rt:eq:clockcertificate}, with witnesses for its two rank queries.
Thus a root exists exactly when $\mathcal U(\pi_{\mathrm C}(e,n))$ halts, equivalently
when $n\in A$.

For a fixed $n\in A$, the triple $(c,u,v')$ is unique. If $G$ is single-fold,
there is also exactly one $\mathbf a$ and one $\mathbf b$, so the complete
witness tuple for $H_e$ is unique. If $G$ is finite-fold, there are finitely
many choices of each of these two tuples, and their Cartesian product is
finite. Hence $H_e$ has the corresponding multiplicity property.
There are $2r+3$ witnesses. Its first residual is quadratic, its second is
linear, and substituting constants for the third argument of $G$ does not
increase its degree. Squaring therefore gives the bound $\max\{4,2d\}$.
The use of the extra variable $c$, rather than substituting the quadratic
pairing polynomial directly inside $G$, is what preserves this degree bound.

For the reverse implications, $\Gamma_{\rankf}$ is computably enumerable,
so the asserted general principle supplies its representation after a unique
triple encoding. More explicitly, encode $(c,k,b)$ by
$\pi_{\mathrm C}(\pi_{\mathrm C}(c,k),b)$. Apply the unary principle to the set of such codes in the
graph, and adjoin the two unique polynomial pairing equations. A sum of
squares combines the equations without creating choices in the pairing
coordinates. This preserves single-foldness or finite-foldness, respectively.
\end{proof}

The theorem is an equivalence, not a solution of either representation
principle. Its content is that even a very benign-looking local arithmetic
routine cannot be assumed to admit a fixed-arity multiplicity-preserving
polynomial graph for free. The routine is total, monotone in its second
argument, Boolean-valued, and polynomial time on binary inputs; those
properties do not remove the global representation issue.

There is also an unconditional statement: if one chooses any ordinary MRDP
polynomial $G$ for the graph, \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:bottleneckpoly} is an ordinary
Diophantine representation of every $A$. What is missing in that
unconditional construction is precisely control of the $G$-witnesses.
The paper does not supply the coefficients of such a global rank polynomial;
its explicit coefficient-level compilers are the finite RLE and grammar
constructions, not a claimed new constructive proof of MRDP.

\paragraph{\wtag{} Relation to Part~IX and Part~XIII.} \Cref{cdc:rt:thm:bottleneck} is the history-free form of~(c) in \cref{cdc:bd:thm:universal}. There the decidable relation is the first-halting trace verifier $\operatorname{Trace}_U(e,x,h)$, whose history argument $h$ is unbounded; here it is the graph of one total, monotone, Boolean function of two arguments, computable in polynomial time on binary inputs, and the proof follows the same cycle through a canonical witness, here the pair $(u,v')$ of \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:clockcertificate}. \Cref{cdc:rx:thm:FF} (Part~XIII) proves the same pattern for the least-reservoir relation of a fixed reaction network, and \cref{cdc:pt:prop:exponential-boundary} for the graph of $2^n$, in the single-fold direction, through the single-fold exponential normal form that ProveIt formalizes (\cref{cdc:bd:rem:sfu}). New in \cref{cdc:rt:thm:bottleneck}: a Boolean threshold function, an elementary proof that does not use the exponential normal form, the finite-fold version beside the single-fold one, and the explicit accounting of~(iii), $2r+3$ witnesses and degree at most $\max\{4,2d\}$.

\subsection{Why bounded circuit quartics do not close the gap}
\begin{proposition}[Canonical quartics at every external bit budget]
\label{cdc:rt:prop:boundedclock}
For every pair of positive integers $a,b$, there is an effectively
constructible quartic polynomial $Q_{a,b}(c;\mathbf w)$, with a number of
natural witness coordinates polynomial in $a+b$, such that it has a unique
natural root exactly when
\[
 0\le c<2^a\quad\text{and}\quad T(c)=b-1.
\]
The root may include the uniquely forced routing odometer $u=2^{b-1}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use $a$ Boolean witness bits to encode $c$, with the linear equality
$c=\sum_{i=0}^{a-1}2^i c_i$. They give a unique encoding exactly in the
specified range. Construct a Boolean circuit that simulates the fixed machine
on this input for $b-1$ transitions and tests that its first halting time is
exactly $b-1$. This is a deterministic bounded computation on a tape segment
of polynomial size in $a+b$, so the circuit has polynomially many gates.
It also handles $b=1$ by checking the initial configuration.

Take gates of types AND and NOT, introducing one variable for each wire.
Impose Boolean equations $t(t-1)=0$ on the wire values, equations $z-xy=0$
for AND gates, and $z+x-1=0$ for NOT gates. Fix the initial input and constant
wires, require the final acceptance wire to equal one, and add
$u-2^{b-1}=0$. All equations have degree at most two. Their squared sum is
quartic. The circuit is deterministic and acyclic, so for fixed input bits
all wire values are uniquely determined. The input bits and $u$ are also
unique. This proves the claim.
\end{proof}

A different $b$ produces a different polynomial with potentially a different
number of coordinates. The assertion
\[
 \exists b\;\bigl(Q_{a,b}(c;\mathbf w_b)=0\text{ for some }\mathbf w_b\bigr)
\]
is not yet one ordinary fixed-arity Diophantine equation. Turning this
externally indexed family into a fixed polynomial while preserving all
auxiliary uniqueness is exactly the issue that must not be skipped. The
one-router example makes the gap visible even though there is only one
semantic exit count and one accepting time.

\section{Executable artifacts and the formalization boundary\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:artifacts}

\subsection{What the supplied programs actually do}
The archive contains two dependency-free Python programs. The file
\path{code/12-rle-routing-verify_certificates.py} supplies direct legal execution, analytic prefix
counts, canonical RLE witnesses, residual evaluation, canonical grammar-path
witnesses, and deterministic regression tests. Its integer arithmetic is
exact. The test instantiation of the universal-clock routine uses small
countdown and looping transition systems; it tests the rank mechanism, not
the universality of a particular encoded Turing machine.

The file \path{code/12-rle-routing-compile_quartic.py} is a sparse integer-polynomial compiler
for the RLE residual system. It supports both fixed numeric run lengths and
free natural parameters $\lambda_{vj}$ with $\ell_{vj}=\lambda_{vj}+1$.
It constructs and expands the sum of squared residuals. Its output is a
coefficient-and-monomial representation of an actual polynomial, not a call
to an MRDP oracle or a numerical equation solver.

For the one-vertex period $v^3s$, the expanded fixed-length polynomial has
$50$ nonzero monomials, total degree four, and thirteen witness variables.
The same destination topology with both block lengths left free produces
$81$ nonzero monomials and still has degree four and thirteen witnesses.
These are illustrative counts for the supplied compiler, not minimality
claims. Both versions have eleven quadratic-or-linear residuals.

The human-readable residuals and expanded polynomials are included as
\path{data/12-rle-routing-example_quartic.txt} and \path{data/12-rle-routing-parametric_quartic.txt}; their JSON
counterparts list every integer coefficient and monomial exponent. The sample
root uses two input chips, giving eight firings and two sink arrivals.
This small example makes the coefficient-level construction inspectable
without printing a very long multivariate polynomial in the main text.

\subsection{Exact test results and their scope}
The following results were obtained from the supplied suite. The detailed
machine-readable receipt is \path{data/12-rle-routing-test_results.json}.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}Xr@{}}
\toprule
Check & Count or value\\
\midrule
Two-active-vertex, one-sink, length-two networks & $81$\\
Network/input pairs, with each initial count in $\{0,1,2\}$ & $729$\\
Candidate odometers in $\{0,\ldots,12\}^2$ examined & $123{,}201$\\
Balanced candidates among these & $2{,}037$\\
Accepted exact odometers among these & $535$\\
Single-coordinate $+1$ mutations of true RLE roots rejected & $13{,}375$\\
Additional random halting RLE networks & $200$\\
Analytic-versus-expanded RLE prefix comparisons & $13{,}236$\\
Small shared grammars / prefix comparisons & $150\;/\;712$\\
Single-coordinate $+1$ grammar-witness mutations rejected & $35{,}952$\\
Large unexpanded grammar period length & $2^{1025}$\\
Universal-clock mechanism checks on toy systems & $205$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The bounded odometer enumeration is not an enumeration of every auxiliary
tuple of every polynomial. Arithmetic uniqueness of the local fields reduces
the comparison to candidate odometers; the general completeness and
single-foldness claims rest on the proofs. Likewise, mutation tests are good
at finding missing constraints but cannot establish a universal theorem.

For every tested halting finite network, the suite compares smallest-index and
largest-index legal scheduling and obtains the same full odometer and sink
outputs. The largest observed total firing count in the exhaustive tiny
network experiment is $20$. The enormous example of
Example~\ref{cdc:rt:ex:huge} is a separate direct certificate evaluation and does
not involve a simulation of those firings.

Each illustrative symbolic polynomial is additionally compared with the
independent residual evaluator at $500$ arbitrary natural assignments, not
only at its true root. At those assignments, the expanded polynomial exactly
equals the sum of the directly evaluated squared residuals. These checks
exercise coefficient aggregation and cancellation in the sparse compiler.

\subsection{A concrete Lean integration plan}
The repository snapshot used for this paper is
\code{e18718e837d43e162252f9a314e8cb797fbd1a1f}. Its documented MRDP endpoint
works with one free natural input and a finite tuple of natural witnesses,
with integer polynomial evaluation. The guide also identifies
\code{MRDP.boundedForall_dioph}, \code{MRDP.primrec_diophFn}, and the older
\code{DiophantineTrace.lean} reachability interfaces \cite{repo-mrdp}.
\wtag{} [The two declarations are in \path{Computability/HilbertTenthProblem/Lean/Diophantine/Common/MRDPCore.lean}, namespace \code{MRDP}; this report elsewhere cites the separate \code{Diophantine.boundedForall_dioph} of \path{DiophantineTrace.lean} \cite{repo-trace}.]
These are relevant integration points, but none of them supplies the new
single-fold routing theorem merely by being imported.

A suitable new formal development would separate five layers.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item \textbf{Operational semantics.} Use finite active and sink types, natural
chip vectors and firing counters, arbitrary stack functions, and finite legal
execution lists. Prove the conservation formula first. The least-action proof
then needs only prefix monotonicity and a first attempted excess, not an
external theorem about infinite abelian networks.
\item \textbf{Exactness.} Define the selected last-exit function on positive
odometer support. Prove that complete legal executions induce strictly
increasing last-departure times along selected active edges. For the reverse
direction, formalize the residual-flow argument of
Theorem~\ref{cdc:rt:thm:last}, including the finite functional-graph cycle lemma.
\item \textbf{Canonical local arithmetic.} Prove the unique positive-remainder
and block-selection theorem, with inactive coordinates forced to zero. For
grammars, prove the one-path theorem by induction through the acyclic node
order. Keep the unique-witness statements explicit in these interfaces.
\item \textbf{Polynomial extraction.} Build a finite list of multivariate
integer polynomials, one per residual. Prove that evaluating their squared sum
at natural assignments gives zero exactly when every residual vanishes.
Then establish a bijection between roots and complete odometers, rather than
only an existence equivalence. Variable-count and degree bounds are separate
syntactic obligations.
\item \textbf{Effective universality and reductions.} Formalize the bounded
rank evaluator and the time-dilation lemma for the chosen universal machine.
Only the ordinary unbounded rank-graph representation needs MRDP. The
single-fold and finite-fold implications should remain explicitly conditional
on the corresponding local rank-graph hypothesis.
\end{enumerate}

The integer/natural interface merits particular care. Polynomial residuals
use signed subtraction in $\Z$; semantic chip counts and all witnesses are
natural. One should not translate a signed residual such as $u-x-F$ into
truncated subtraction on $\N$. The most convenient semantic invariant is
usually an equality of natural sums, followed by an explicit coercion into
$\Z$ when connecting it to the polynomial.

None of these new layers has been kernel-checked in this package. The
repository's existing audit reports concern its existing declarations, not
this manuscript. This distinction is consistent with the broader practice of
developing mathematical constructions and their formalization in parallel,
as discussed in recent work on universal Diophantine bounds \cite{bayer}.

\section{Further research questions and concrete targets\srctag{12}}
\label{cdc:rt:sec:research}
The following is a proposed research program. Items described as questions are
questions for this construction or project; the list is not a claim that every
formulation is an established open problem in the literature.

\srcnote{\wtag{} Manuscript~12 posed its eight items under numbered headings of unnumbered subsections; the headings, without their numbers, are the titles here, and the text is unchanged. A \wtag{} line after an item names the question of \cref{cdc:sec:questions} it overlaps; the items are not merged with them.}

\begin{question}[A kernel-checked single-fold compiler, end to end; source 12]
The first target is the exact statement of Theorem~\ref{cdc:rt:thm:rle}, including
free run-length parameters, complete witness uniqueness, degree four, and the
precise coordinate count. A useful deliverable would be a Lean function
returning the residual polynomials together with proofs of its semantic
correctness and of a unique-root theorem. The residual-flow converse is a
natural independent mathematical milestone. A successful compiler should emit
a checkable theorem about its output polynomial, not only validate examples.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:verified}, and Part~XIII's question on a verified compiler with a solution-set bijection.

\begin{question}[Smaller canonical certificates without hidden multiplicity; source 12]
Can the $4n+4m+s$ coordinate count be reduced while retaining an explicit
quadratic-residual presentation and natural single-foldness? Some equations
are deliberately redundant or chosen for clarity. Savings should be measured
against coefficient size and polynomial sparsity, not only variable count.
Eliminating a height coordinate by substituting a long path expression, for
example, may raise degree or expression size. A rigorous lower-bound question
would first fix a compiler model and an allowed local gadget vocabulary;
there is no unrestricted minimality assertion in this paper.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:degree}.

\begin{question}[Multiple prefix queries on a globally shared grammar; source 12]
The grammar theorem shares subwords within each local period but gives each
independent prefix query its own activation and position coordinates. Networks
with many roots in one enormous shared grammar may waste these duplicated
certificates. Can several paths be certified canonically using a compressed
query structure whose size follows the actual overlap of the paths? A useful
result would specify a sharp parameter, such as the number of distinct
selected node/offset pairs, and prove both degree control and uniqueness.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:locality}, which asks for canonical DAG codings with polynomial bit height; here the DAG is given and the descent path is canonical (\cref{cdc:rt:thm:grammar}).

\begin{question}[Algorithms exploiting the forest certificate; source 12]
The polynomial certificate describes an answer without efficiently finding it.
Can its canonical last-exit forest guide a practical solver on networks with
small feedback vertex sets, bounded treewidth, or few distinct period blocks?
The phase-transport identity in Proposition~\ref{cdc:rt:prop:transport} suggests
reusing solutions for related loads. A meaningful algorithmic result must
bound the number of selector or forest changes rather than simply invoke
uniqueness of the final certificate. Comparisons with existing ARRIVAL methods
should be made on the same representation and output task.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The intermediate territory between grammars and circuits; source 12]
Theorem~\ref{cdc:rt:thm:countbarrier} shows why arbitrary circuit random access is too
broad for the same short-certificate guarantee without a major complexity
consequence. Which intermediate descriptions admit efficient prefix counting
and compact canonical algebraic certificates? Candidates include restricted
branching programs, decomposable circuit descriptions, and descriptions with
an explicit small dynamic-programming interface. The task is to prove a
representation-sensitive theorem, with the rank routine and its certificate
size exposed, rather than to call every description merely ``succinct.''
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The monotone rank bottleneck as a test for general claims; source 12]
Theorem~\ref{cdc:rt:thm:bottleneck} gives a specific stress test for any proposed
single-fold or finite-fold compilation theorem for total polynomial-time
functions. Does the proposed theorem apply to \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:rankclock}? If it
does, the explicit polynomial \eqref{cdc:rt:eq:bottleneckpoly} must be included in
the claimed consequences. A constructive attack could look for special
arithmetic structure in the threshold-time relation, while a limitation
result could identify exactly which local-certificate hypotheses exclude it.
This is a substantial global target, not a consequence already delivered by
bounded Boolean-circuit encodings.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:compression,cdc:q:ffprimitives}, and the notes added to them in batch~63.

\begin{question}[Infinite-background abelian computation; source 12]
Cairns's universal sandpile construction \cite{cairns} offers a physically
more local setting in which to seek arithmetic certificates. For a specified
finite toppling event, what finite causal region can be certified without
unrolling every toppling? Which global halting questions require information
outside every effectively bounded region? The functional last-exit proof here
uses one outgoing chip per firing; sandpile topplings send several chips and
need a different residual-flow or causal-forest invariant. Establishing that
invariant, or proving an obstruction to a proposed one, would be a meaningful
extension rather than a black-box application of MRDP.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Batch~78, 2 October 2026: answered by Part~XVI (manuscript~16) for finite undirected sink graphs and for finite global stabilization on $\Z^d$. The invariant is support burning: a stable endpoint $z=\eta-Lu$ certifies the odometer $u$ exactly when it is burnable on the support of $u$ (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:support}), and canonical parallel burning ranks, characterized by two local comparisons per ordered adjacency (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:ranks}), make the cubic certificate unique (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:compiler,cdc:sp:thm:compact}). The certified finite region is a box with a one-layer exterior collar, which certifies global halting exactly and has a unique canonical radius (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:collar,cdc:sp:cor:radius}); inside a box every witness has polynomial height (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:height}). On Cairns's input class, no total computable function of the input description bounds the radius that must be certified (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:nobound}). Directed dissipative graphs stay open: a two-vertex example shows that burning alone is unsound there (\cref{cdc:sp:sec:directed}, \cref{cdc:sp:q:digraphs}).

\wtag{} Batch~79, 2 October 2026: manuscript~19, written independently of manuscript~16 and printed inside Part~XVI as a second route, gives the same answer by the same invariant (\cref{cdc:nb:thm:burning,cdc:nb:thm:ranks}) with a system of quadratic residuals instead of a cubic (\cref{cdc:nb:thm:finitecompiler}), a no-firing halo in place of the collar (\cref{cdc:nb:thm:halo}), and a fixed-field normal form on $\Z^3$ with 47 finite-deviation fields that removes the choice of radius (\cref{cdc:nb:thm:fields}).


\begin{question}[Explicit preperiods and more general abelian processors; source 12]
There is a useful gap between explicitly supplied ultimately periodic stacks
and the non-effectively bounded eventual constancy of the universal clock.
A next compiler can handle supplied finite prefixes followed by RLE or grammar
periods, with a canonical selector for whether the odometer ends before or
after the cutoff. Beyond routing, one can ask which finite-state abelian
processors retain a canonical completion certificate when firings consume or
produce several messages. The conservation and minimality hypotheses should
be stated first; replacing the functional last-exit forest by an unjustified
ranking condition would risk accepting false circulations.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:beyond}.

\wtag{} Batch~78, 2 October 2026: answered in part by Part~XVI (manuscript~16) for one class of processors whose firings send several messages, undirected sandpiles. Its canonical completion certificate is support burning with canonical burning ranks, both proved exact (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:support,cdc:sp:thm:ranks}), and the conservation-only false odometer after \cref{cdc:sp:thm:support} is exactly the false circulation that a bare balance condition accepts. Along an input ray it also gives the exact eventual period (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:period}). Supplied finite prefixes before periodic stacks, and processors beyond undirected sandpiles (directed dissipative toppling matrices among them, \cref{cdc:sp:q:digraphs}), stay open.

\section{Conclusion\srctag{12}}
The paper develops two complementary conclusions. For explicitly compressed
finite routing, the entire execution history can be replaced by a canonical
spatial object: prefix counts together with exact last-exit distances. This
produces a genuine fixed-arity, parametric, single-fold quartic for each
routing topology, and extends to shared grammar descriptions of periods.
Its size follows the description of the local instructions, not the number
of firings.

For universally generated instructions, even strikingly simple pointwise
stacks do not provide the same guarantee. The universal clock has one chip,
one active vertex, at most one sink event, eventual constancy, and
polynomial-time prefix ranks. Nevertheless its exact exit count has no
computable input-length bound. Its local rank graph carries the entire
single-fold and finite-fold representation issue, as witnessed by an explicit
conditional polynomial construction with $2r+3$ auxiliaries.

The useful frontier is therefore not simply ``classical machine versus
unconventional substrate.'' It is the interaction between effective instruction
descriptions, exact local prefix arithmetic, canonical global causality, and
control of every arithmetic witness. The constructions and reductions here
make those requirements separate, testable, and suitable for a formal
continuation in ProveIt.

each actual length in the returned polynomial is a free natural parameter
plus one.

The archive includes the PDF and \LaTeX{} source, both Python programs,

a README, a build file, and a provenance note. These exported polynomials are

schema and executable local-path checks, not by a separately exported global

\part{Interaction combinators: exact wiring, loop-exact gluing and bounded quartic frontends}\label{cdc:part:wiring}

\paragraph{Source and scope.} \wtag{} This Part merges three manuscripts delivered together in batch~78 of ProveIt's incoming reports (arrival commit \texttt{1977e6ea6}), all dated 2 October 2026 and all written in answer to the research note \emph{A finite wiring obstruction for interaction combinators} \cite{repo-icobs}.
