Manuscript~14 is ``Topology Is Not Free: Loop-Sensitive Diophantine Certificates for Interaction Nets'' (batch~78, manuscript~04; \path{Topology_Is_Not_Free_Interaction_Nets.zip}; \path{14-net-topology-}; \texttt{cdc:nt:}). Manuscript~15 is ``No Ghost Wires: Loop-Exact Quartic Certificates for Interaction Combinators'' (batch~78, manuscript~05; \path{no_ghost_wires.zip}; \path{15-no-ghost-wires-}; \texttt{cdc:ng:}). Unlike Parts~X--XIV, which print one manuscript each in its own order, this Part is arranged by subject, because the three share their target, the rule table, the gluing theorem and the bounded compiler: port-labelled nets and the six rules (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:nets}); exact gluing and loop accounting (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:gluing}); contextual information, with the sharp $2/5$--$2/3$ loop-parity theorem (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:context}); the local annihilation kernel (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:kernel}); memory logs, as second routes to Part~V (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:memory}); the bounded six-rule compiler (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:compiler}); the permutation-orbit route and its implemented scheduled compiler (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:orbits}); the boundaries and the MRDP interface (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:boundaries}); implementation, validation and formalization proposals (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:validation}); the twenty-five research questions and the three conclusions (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:questions}); and, as the last seven sections of the Part, the manuscripts' appendices. Every section or subsection taken from a manuscript carries its number in brackets. The title pages, abstracts, status statements and introductions are \cref{cdc:sec:ms13,cdc:sec:ms14,cdc:sec:ms15}; the source audits of manuscripts~13 and~14 are in the provenance appendix (\cref{cdc:sec:provenance}). The conventions of this Part are \cref{cdc:conv:b78-wiring}.

\paragraph{What is printed once.} \wtag{} The three manuscripts were written independently, at three pins of the same morning, without knowledge of one another. A result proved by two or three of them is printed once and credits all; a genuinely different proof or construction is kept as a marked second route. The six-rule table and the repository's witness pair are printed once (\cref{cdc:ew:tab:rules}; \cref{cdc:ic:sec:example}), with the other manuscripts' definitions and readings beside them. The storage and loop bounds are \cref{cdc:ew:cor:storage}. Order-independent gluing is \cref{cdc:ew:thm:glue}; manuscript~15's division-free matrix form (\cref{cdc:ng:thm:suppress,cdc:ng:cor:order}) and manuscript~14's locality lemma and suppression proposition (\cref{cdc:nt:lem:local,cdc:nt:prop:suppress}) follow it as the further statements they are. Manuscript~15's contextual completeness (\cref{cdc:ng:thm:context}) is the loop-count form of manuscript~13's injectivity consequence (\cref{cdc:ew:cor:injective}) and is kept with its own two-closure proof, which also proves sufficiency. The bounded six-rule compiler is stated once, as manuscript~14's \cref{cdc:nt:thm:main} with its explicit ledger; manuscript~13's statement follows as a remark (\cref{cdc:ew:thm:compiler}) with its proof as a second presentation, and likewise its transfer corollary after manuscript~14's \cref{cdc:nt:thm:general}. The carry-free product lemma of manuscripts~13 and~14 is Part~V's (see below). Manuscript~15 reaches the scheduled relation by a different route, a canonical permutation-orbit certificate, and is printed whole in \cref{cdc:ic:sec:orbits}.

\paragraph{Relation to the other Parts.} \wtag{} Manuscripts 13, 14 and~15 inspected ProveIt at \texttt{439c0a2d9}, \texttt{6914ccca6} and \texttt{928ea9701}, on the morning of 2 October 2026, when Parts~I--XIV had been written. Manuscript~14 read this report's README and cites it for the memory and heap compilers of manuscripts~03 and~08 \cite{repo-cdc}; manuscripts~13 and~15 do not cite the report. Four relations matter.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Part~X.} The Part answers, for bounded scheduled histories, Part~X's question on a complete interaction-combinator frontend (\cref{cdc:nh:q:frontend}): rule interpreters and semantic simulation (all three manuscripts); reciprocal ports, self-connections, parallel temporary edges, interface splicing and creation slots (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:nets,cdc:ic:sec:gluing}); polynomial compilers (\cref{cdc:nt:thm:main}, on paper, and \cref{cdc:ng:thm:compiler}, implemented for fixed schedules); and tests (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:validation}). The transfer theorem \cref{cdc:nt:thm:general} supplies, for port graphs with reciprocal links and bare loops, the adapter that Part~X's subsection on interaction systems asks for before its graph-transfer theorem (\cref{cdc:nh:thm:graph}) can be applied. It is proved directly, through this Part's memory certificates, and no novelty is claimed for it beside \cref{cdc:nh:thm:graph}. Manuscript~15's finite schedule disjunction gates inactive branches as Part~X's guarded quadratization does (\cref{cdc:nh:thm:gating}). The commutation quotient of independent schedules, fixed arity and an ordinary-integer universal loader stay open (\cref{cdc:q:graphfront} and Part~X's question on quotienting independent schedules, \cref{cdc:nh:sec:research}).
\item \emph{Part~V.} The carry-free product lemma of manuscripts~13 and~14 (\cref{cdc:ew:lem:product,cdc:nt:lem:product}) is Part~V's \cref{cdc:mem:lem:fingerprint}, proved there first; manuscripts~13 and~15 were written without knowledge of this report, and manuscript~14 cites only its README. No novelty is claimed for the lemma. The memory theorems \cref{cdc:ew:thm:memory,cdc:nt:thm:memory} are variants of \cref{cdc:mem:thm:linear-memory} for different relations. Manuscript~14's count $17L-4$ assumes external address and value caps and zero-initialized memory, and is not an improvement on Part~V's $24L$; manuscript~13 audits initial and final arrays. The comparison is at the end of \cref{cdc:ic:sec:memory}.
\item \emph{Part~II.} The bijections of this Part are with \emph{scheduled} executions: choosing a different active pair gives a different zero, even when the two reductions commute (\cref{cdc:nt:thm:main} and the paragraphs after it). Part~II's quotient of executions by a commutation relation has no counterpart here.
\item \emph{Parts~XII and~XIV, and the neighbouring reports.} Manuscript~15's lasso up to renaming (\cref{cdc:ng:prop:lasso}) is a finite certificate of nontermination for another substrate; it is related to Part~XII's infinite periodic tails (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:infinite}), not a case of them. Infinite behaviour is the subject of the neighbouring report \emph{liveness-beyond-halting}; its question on clock-faithful translations into interaction nets is not answered here: the Part supplies a local polynomial compiler for the target's own finite steps, not the clock-faithful simulation theorem. Part~XIV's history-free certificates have no analogue here: every compiler of this Part certifies a history.
\end{itemize}
Two notes of ProveIt's Hilbert's-tenth-problem research tree, maintained elsewhere, bear on the Part. The ten-pattern loop formula of manuscript~14 (\cref{cdc:nt:thm:glue}) was derived independently in \cite{repo-icqt}, which was written after manuscript~14's pin; and the tree's review of the three archives \cite{repo-icrev} finds no mathematical error in them and derives three natural-domain reductions of their exported systems. Dated notes after \cref{cdc:nt:thm:glue}, \cref{cdc:nt:thm:kernel}, \cref{cdc:ew:thm:memory} and manuscript~15's worked example say what these are. Neither note is a source of this Part, and priority is claimed for neither the manuscripts nor the notes.

\paragraph{Setting and hypotheses.} \wtag{} All witnesses and parameters range over $\N$; no uniqueness statement is claimed over $\Z$ (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:boundaries}). Nets are explicitly labelled: cells carry identifiers, auxiliary ports are ordered by Lafont's numbering ($\delta\delta$ keeps the auxiliary labels, $\gamma\gamma$ exchanges them), free ports are labelled, and port-free cyclic wires are counted by a separate natural number. Every construction is a family indexed by an external horizon~$T$ and the input dimensions; none is one polynomial of fixed arity. In manuscripts~13 and~14 the schedule of active pairs is a tuple of source coordinates of the polynomial, and the auxiliary witness is unique for each legal schedule; in manuscript~15 the lifetime schedule is structural data of the compiler, and the endpoint matchings and loop counts are parameters. Fresh cells are named by a fixed allocation rule; there is no quotient by schedule, graph isomorphism or observational equivalence. Manuscript~13's contextual theorems concern bare perfect matchings, without agents. The six-rule compilers of manuscripts~13 and~14 are paper constructions; manuscript~15's fixed-schedule compiler and the memory and kernel components of manuscripts~13 and~14 are implemented (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:validation}). Nothing in this Part is formalized in Lean or Rocq.

\section{Port-labelled nets and the six interaction rules}\label{cdc:ic:sec:nets}
\srcnote{\wtag{} All three manuscripts define port-labelled nets, the six rules of Lafont's interaction combinators in numbered-port form, and the repository's witness pair. The definitions are printed from each, because each fixes conventions that its later sections use (manuscript~14's predicates ``normal'', ``agent-free'' and ``completely empty'', and its fresh-name rule; manuscript~15's treatment of the removed principal edge and its gluing data). The rule table is printed once, from manuscript~13; manuscript~14's equations \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:2.1}--\eqref{cdc:nt:eq:2.2} and manuscript~15's \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:mixed} state the same rules, and all three agree with each other, with Lafont's numbered figures \cite{lafont} and with the research note \cite{repo-icobs}. The witness pair is printed from manuscript~13, with manuscript~15's table and argument after it and manuscript~14's reading through its kernel in \cref{cdc:ic:sec:kernel}.}

% ---- manuscript 13, lines 633-686 ----
\subsection{All six interaction-combinator rules as literal wiring\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:rules}

\subsubsection{Representation and ordered ports}

An agent has type $\epsilon$, $\delta$ or $\gamma$, with respective arities
$0,2,2$. It has one principal port, numbered $0$, and its auxiliary ports
are ordered $1,2$. A finite net consists of a finite typed cell set, a finite
labelled set of free ports, a matching of all these ports, and a natural
number of isolated cyclic wires. Self-wires between different ports of one
cell are permitted. A principal--principal wire between two cells is an
\emph{active pair}.

The numerical rules below follow Lafont's clockwise convention. In
particular, $\gamma\gamma$ exchanges numbered auxiliaries, whereas
$\delta\delta$ does not. This can look reversed when an unnumbered picture
is read as if both cells had the same orientation; the numbered picture on
journal page 82 removes the ambiguity \cite{lafont}.

\subsubsection{The complete right-hand-side table}

The principal wire of the selected pair is removed as part of the
interaction. It is \emph{not} counted as an isolated cyclic wire. The rule
then reconnects the old auxiliary interface as follows.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{22mm}p{118mm}@{}}
\toprule
Pair & Replacement, in numbered-port notation \\
\midrule
$\epsilon\epsilon$ & No agents and no interface. \\
$\delta\delta$ & For old cells $u,v$, join $u1$ to $v1$ and $u2$ to $v2$. \\
$\gamma\gamma$ & Join $u1$ to $v2$ and $u2$ to $v1$. \\
$\epsilon\delta$ & Two fresh $\epsilon$ agents; connect their principal ports to
the old $\delta$ auxiliary ports $1,2$, respectively. \\
$\epsilon\gamma$ & Two fresh $\epsilon$ agents; connect their principal ports to
the old $\gamma$ auxiliary ports $1,2$, respectively. \\
$\delta\gamma$ & Fresh $\gamma$ cells $G_1,G_2$ and $\delta$ cells $D_1,D_2$.
Old $\delta i$ attaches to $G_i0$, old $\gamma j$ to $D_j0$, and
$G_i j$ attaches to $D_j i$ for every $i,j\in\{1,2\}$. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The literal six-rule controller. The last rule specifies all eight
right-hand-side wires: four boundary wires and four internal wires.}
\label{cdc:ew:tab:rules}
\end{table}

To use a single gluing algorithm, create a fresh temporary boundary port
$\beta_a$ for every old auxiliary port $a$. In the right-hand side, use
$\beta_a$ wherever the table mentions the old interface port $a$. This gives
a matching on fresh agents and fresh boundary ports, disjoint from the old
matching after removal of the principal wire. Finally splice every
$a$ with $\beta_a$. There are at most four such splices.

% ---- manuscript 13, lines 688-705 ----
\begin{proposition}[Exact constant-size interaction macro]\label{cdc:ew:prop:macro}
The boundary-port construction implements every rule of
Table~\ref{cdc:ew:tab:rules} in every valid surrounding net. Its number of memory
accesses is bounded by an absolute constant. It preserves existing cyclic
wires and creates exactly the cyclic wires of the rule's contextual gluing.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The right-hand side is a finite literal matching with at most four new
agents and four boundary ports. Removing the active principal edge removes
both its endpoints, so it has no incident surviving wire. Adding the
right-hand-side matching is a disjoint union. Each remaining interface
connection is a splice, and Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:glue} proves that their
composition is exactly the contextual rule application. Each splice uses
boundedly many accesses, as do the bounded lists of type updates, port
initializations and retirements. The bound is uniform over all input nets
and all six rules.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} The storage bounds $C_t\le C_0+2t$ and ``at most $C_0+4t$ allocated identifiers'' are those of the research note \cite{repo-icobs}, which derives them from the rule shapes; the loop bound $\ell_0\le\ell_t\le\ell_0+2t$ is new to the repository. All three manuscripts prove them: \cref{cdc:ew:cor:storage} below; manuscript~14's \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.4} in \cref{cdc:nt:prop:resources}, which adds the fixed log length of its machine; and manuscript~15's \cref{cdc:ng:prop:growth}, which adds port and temporary-vertex bounds. They are printed once, here; the other two statements keep their additions.

% ---- manuscript 13, lines 707-730 ----
\begin{corollary}[Storage and loop bounds]\label{cdc:ew:cor:storage}
After $t$ interactions from a net with $C_0$ cells and $\ell_0$ cyclic wires,
\begin{equation}
 C_t\le C_0+2t,\qquad
 \ell_0\le\ell_t\le\ell_0+2t.
\end{equation}
A fresh-identifier implementation needs at most $C_0+4t$ allocated cell
identifiers.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Every interaction deletes two agents and creates at most four. Only the
mixed binary rule creates four; either erasing rule creates two; the
annihilation rules create none. At most four new identifiers are allocated
per step.

Existing isolated wires never participate in a rule. Only the binary
annihilation rules can create new isolated wires: their four interface
ports can make at most two closed components. In the mixed and erasing
rules, every boundary wire reaches a principal port of a fresh surviving
agent, so its gluing component is a path, not a port-free cycle. The
$\epsilon\epsilon$ rule has no boundary. Thus each step adds at most two
loops and removes none.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} Manuscript~14's definitions, rule templates and fresh-name convention. Its templates \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:2.1}--\eqref{cdc:nt:eq:2.2} are the rules of \cref{cdc:ew:tab:rules}; its three terminal predicates are used again in \cref{cdc:nt:sec:terminal}.

% ---- manuscript 14, lines 180-240 ----
\subsection{Exact nets and a fully specified rule convention\srctag{14}}\label{cdc:nt:sec:nets}
\subsubsection{Data and equality}
We use $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A net has a finite set of cells, each labelled
$\eps$, $\gamma$, or $\delta$; a fixed finite ordered set of free ports;
a fixed-point-free involution on its incident ports; and a natural number
$\ell$ of agent-free cyclic wires. The arities are $0,2,2$. A cell $c$ has
principal port $c0$ and, when binary, ordered auxiliary ports $c1,c2$.
A self-wire may join two \emph{different} ports of one cell. There is no edge
from a port to itself. An agent-free cycle is represented separately by $\ell$,
not by a fictitious self-pair of an incident port.

Two cells form an active pair exactly when their principal ports are matched.
Distinct active pairs have disjoint cell sets. Port ordering is structural:
forgetting it changes the semantics. We follow Lafont's numbered-port
convention, including the different $\gamma\gamma$ and $\delta\delta$
annihilations \cite[pp.~71,81--82]{lafont}.

A \emph{normal} net has no active pair. An \emph{agent-free} net has no cells;
it may still have free-port wires and bare loops. A \emph{completely empty}
closed net has no cells and $\ell=0$. These are different predicates.

\subsubsection{The six local templates}
The following is the literal convention used by the implementation.
For a pair of like binary cells $u,v$, write
\begin{equation}
B=(u1,u2,v1,v2),\qquad
J_\delta=\{13,24\},\quad J_\gamma=\{14,23\},                 \label{cdc:nt:eq:2.1}
\end{equation}
where $ij$ denotes an unordered pair of positions in $B$. Delete the two
cells and their principal wire; insert the two joins specified by $J$;
then suppress the old auxiliary ports, counting every closed component.
An $\eps\eps$ interaction simply removes its two cells and principal wire.

An $\eps\alpha$ interaction, with $\alpha$ binary, creates two fresh erasers,
whose principal ports replace the two old auxiliary endpoints of $\alpha$.
For a mixed pair $\gamma(u),\delta(v)$, create
\[
D_1,D_2:\delta,\qquad G_1,G_2:\gamma.
\]
Replace old endpoint $ui$ by $D_i0$ and $vj$ by $G_j0$, and add the four
internal wires
\begin{equation}
                        D_i j\;---\;G_j i\quad (i,j\in\{1,2\}). \label{cdc:nt:eq:2.2}
\end{equation}
These equations specify the numbered rule table; they are not schematic
instructions to exchange arbitrary auxiliary ports. The new roles are
ordered as $D_1,D_2,G_1,G_2$, or as the two erasers in auxiliary-port order.
No template creates a bare loop on its own.

\subsubsection{Fresh names and executions}
Initially the cells are labelled $0,\ldots,C_0-1$. The next unused identifier
is $h=C_0$. New agents receive $h,h+1,\ldots$ in template-role order and $h$
is increased accordingly. Identifiers are never reused, and deleted cells
are not renumbered. At step $t$ the scheduler supplies the unordered active
pair, represented uniquely as $u_t<v_t$.

An execution records these choices and the successive exact nets. Fixing the
choices fixes every state. The fresh-name convention is equivalently a
normalization of role-labelled executions under consistent renaming of newly
created agents, fixing the original cells and free ports. It does not
identify independent reduction schedules or solve graph isomorphism.

\wtag{} Manuscript~15's definition and ordered-port conventions. Its rule table is \cref{cdc:ew:tab:rules} and is not printed again; its mixed rule \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:mixed} and its gluing data \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:alphabeta} (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:gluing}) are used by its orbit compiler (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:orbits}).

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 183-248 ----
\subsection{Port-labelled nets and the complete rule table\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:nets}

\begin{definition}
A finite net consists of a finite set of labelled agents, a type
$\gamma,\delta$, or $\varepsilon$ for each agent, a finite set of labelled free
ports, a perfect matching of all agent and free ports, and a number
$\ell\in\N$ of cyclic wires that have no ports. A $\gamma$ or $\delta$ agent
has ports $0,1,2$; an $\varepsilon$ agent has port $0$. Port $0$ is principal.
A pair of agents is active precisely when their principal ports are matched.
\end{definition}

This is the convention of Lafont's original definition, which permits both
self-wires between different ports of an agent and cyclic wires with no ports
\cite[pp.~71--72]{lafont}. A wire from a port to itself is not permitted:
a matching always pairs two distinct ports. Parallel edges in an intermediate
gluing graph, on the other hand, are essential.

The principal--principal edge of an active pair belongs to the redex and is
removed with that redex. It is \emph{not} automatically converted into a cyclic
wire. Thus an isolated $\varepsilon\varepsilon$ pair disappears without creating
a loop.

\subsubsection{Literal ordered-port conventions}
Suppose agents $a,b$ are active. Write $a_i,b_i$ for auxiliary ports before
removal. The boundary positions in the following table denote those former
auxiliary incidences. Each new agent gets a distinct fresh identity, in a fixed
order chosen by the compiler.


The annihilation conventions are different. Lafont explicitly warns that it is
$\gamma\gamma$, not $\delta\delta$, that exchanges the numbered auxiliary
ports \cite[p.~82]{lafont}. Looking only at whether the two strands cross
in an unnumbered drawing is unsafe because rotating an agent reverses their
left-to-right placement.

For a mixed pair, orient the notation so that $a$ is the $\gamma$ agent and $b$
is the $\delta$ agent. Create $\delta$ agents $D_1,D_2$ and $\gamma$ agents
$G_1,G_2$. The replacement has
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:mixed}
\begin{aligned}
a_i&\longleftrightarrow (D_i)_0 &&(i=1,2),\\
b_j&\longleftrightarrow (G_j)_0 &&(j=1,2),\\
(D_i)_j&\longleftrightarrow (G_j)_i &&(i,j=1,2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This is the numbered-port form of the commutation picture in
\cite[Fig.~2]{lafont}. It makes the template independently implementable
without inferring port identities from a drawing.

All three manuscripts replay it; manuscript~13's text comes first, manuscript~15's table and complete argument follow, and manuscript~14 derives the successors from its kernel formulas (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:kernel}).

\subsection{The repository obstruction, now with exact successors\srctag{13}}\label{cdc:ic:sec:example}

For comparison with the repository, this example uses its zero-based port

The two original matchings are
\begin{align}
 M_A={}&\{\{0,3\},\{1,7\},\{2,9\},\{4,10\},\{5,6\},\{8,11\}\},\\
 M_B={}&\{\{0,3\},\{1,7\},\{2,9\},\{4,10\},\{5,8\},\{6,11\}\}.
\end{align}
Both have no isolated cycles. Their common unique initial active pair is
$AB$. Annihilation gives
\begin{align}
 M_A'&=\{\{C0,D0\},\{C1,D1\},\{C2,D2\}\},\\
 M_B'&=\{\{C0,D2\},\{C1,D1\},\{C2,D0\}\}.
\end{align}
The first successor has active pair $CD$; its annihilation leaves no cells
and two cyclic wires. The second has no active pair and retains two cells.
The original nets have the same labelled $K_4$ graph and port-pair histogram
$(1,0,2,2,0,1)$ in the order $(00,01,02,11,12,22)$
\cite{repo-icobs}. Our replay recovers these successors by both gluing
algorithms. It does not identify the two-loop target with the empty net.

The code uses positive live-port identifiers $3c+p+1$, reserving zero for
inactive memory. Its saved example traces therefore add one to the original
port codes. Both inputs normalize; the distinguishing predicate is
\emph{agent-free reachability}, not the existence of a normal form.

\subsection{Matching closure and exact local splicing\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:splice}

\subsubsection{Matchings and cyclic components}

Let $X$ be a finite set of even cardinality. A perfect matching $M$ on $X$
is equivalently a fixed-point-free involution $m:X\to X$. Write
$\M_n$ for the matchings on $[2n]=\{0,\ldots,2n-1\}$ and
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:Dn}
 D_n=|\M_n|=(2n-1)!!=\frac{(2n)!}{2^n n!},\qquad D_0=1.
\end{equation}
The recurrence $D_n=(2n-1)D_{n-1}$ follows by choosing the partner of one
specified port and then matching the rest.

For two matchings $M,Q$ on the same set, form the \emph{edge-coloured
multigraph} $M\cup Q$. It is a disjoint union of alternating even cycles.
An edge common to $M$ and $Q$ occurs twice and is a two-edge cycle, not a
single edge. Let
\begin{equation}
 c(M,Q)=\text{the number of components of this doubled multigraph}.
\end{equation}
Closing the ports of the wiring $M$ by the wiring $Q$ produces exactly
$c(M,Q)$ agent-free cyclic wires.

More generally, a state of a wiring evaluator is a matching on live ports,
together with a natural number $\ell$ of already isolated cyclic wires.
Those cycles have no incident ports and cannot be rediscovered by traversing
the live matching. Consequently, $\ell$ is essential state data whenever
exact loop counts matter.

\subsubsection{The splice operation}

Suppose $a,b$ are distinct live ports and a new join is to identify their
wire ends, after which $a,b$ disappear. Read
\begin{equation}
 p=m(a),\qquad q=m(b).
\end{equation}
There are exactly two cases.

If $p=b$, involutivity gives $q=a$. The old wire and the new join form a
two-edge cycle. Delete $a,b$ and increment $\ell$ by one.

If $p\ne b$, the four ports $a,b,p,q$ are distinct. Delete $a,b$ and replace
the two old wires by $p\leftrightarrow q$. The loop count does not change.

\begin{lemma}[Exact splice]\label{cdc:ew:lem:splice}
The preceding operation produces precisely the matching and cyclic-wire
count obtained by adding the join $a$--$b$ and suppressing its two endpoints.
It requires two mate reads and at most four mate writes when deletion is
represented by writing zero.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $a,b$ were matched, the component is the pair of parallel edges just
described. Otherwise the affected component is the path
$p$--$a$--$b$--$q$. Suppressing the two internal vertices leaves the wire
$p$--$q$. All other edges and all previously isolated cycles are unchanged.
There is no third case because $m$ is a fixed-point-free involution.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sequential gluing is order independent]\label{cdc:ew:thm:glue}
Let $J$ be a set of pairwise disjoint joins on live ports. Add these joins to
the old matching, and declare all their endpoints to be suppressed. The
result is a matching on the unsuppressed ports plus one isolated wire for
each component with no unsuppressed endpoint. Performing the splices in
\emph{any} order gives this same result.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In the temporary multigraph, every suppressed port has degree two and every
unsuppressed port has degree one. A connected component is therefore a path
with two unsuppressed endpoints, or an alternating cycle with none.

At any intermediate stage, maintain the following invariant: each live wire
represents the unsuppressed remainder of a path in the original temporary
graph; each completed component with no remaining endpoint has been
recorded once in the loop counter. Lemma~\ref{cdc:ew:lem:splice} contracts one such
path or completes one such cycle. It neither merges two original components
nor changes their surviving endpoints. At the end, every path has become
its endpoint wire and every cycle has been counted exactly once. This
description is independent of the splice order.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Two easy but consequential implementation errors]
Parallel edges must not be deduplicated: doing so destroys the first case
of Lemma~\ref{cdc:ew:lem:splice}. Also, the reads for a later splice must use the
\emph{updated} mate table. Reading all incident wires once and then applying
several stale updates is not equivalent to the theorem. The attached two
evaluators intentionally use different algorithms: local pointer splicing
and connected components of a multigraph.
\end{remark}

\wtag{} Manuscript~15's gluing data and its division-free form of the splice. Its $\alpha$ is the temporary matching of old and replacement wires and its $\beta$ the involution of the new joins; \cref{cdc:ng:thm:suppress} is \cref{cdc:ew:lem:splice} written as an identity of natural matching matrices, and \cref{cdc:ng:cor:order} is \cref{cdc:ew:thm:glue}.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 250-269 ----
\subsection{Gluing a replacement into its context\srctag{15}}
For a uniform implementation, do not immediately redirect the old auxiliary
wires. Instead, remove just the two principal ports and their common edge. Keep
the old auxiliary ports temporarily. Take a disjoint copy of the replacement,
with one new interface port for every old auxiliary port. Match the replacement
ports according to its rule template. Finally, join each old auxiliary port to
its corresponding interface port and suppress these joined ports.

All old and replacement wires together form a perfect matching $\alpha$ of a
temporary vertex set $V$. The new joins form a second matching on a subset
$I\subseteq V$. Let $B=V\setminus I$ be the surviving ports. Extending the
second matching by the identity on $B$ gives an involution $\beta$ with
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:alphabeta}
\alpha^2=\id,\quad \alpha(v)\ne v,\qquad
\beta^2=\id,\quad \operatorname{Fix}(\beta)=B.
\end{equation}
An internal vertex has degree two, one edge of each kind. A boundary vertex has
one actual edge; a fixed point of $\beta$ is bookkeeping, not an additional
self-loop. Every component of the temporary multigraph is therefore a path
between two boundary vertices or a cycle with no boundary vertex.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 271-378 ----
\subsection{Division-free elimination and locality\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:elimination}

\subsubsection{An exact quadratic update}
Encode a perfect matching by a symmetric matrix $W$ with zero diagonal and
entries in $\N$, subject to
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:matching}
\sum_{v}W_{uv}=1\qquad\text{for every }u.
\end{equation}
These equations already force every entry to be $0$ or $1$. Explicit Boolean
constraints on the off-diagonal entries are unnecessary.

\begin{theorem}[Pair-suppression identity]\label{cdc:ng:thm:suppress}
Let $x\ne y$ be ports that are to be joined and suppressed. For remaining
ports $u\ne v$, the resulting matching matrix and cyclic-wire count satisfy
\begin{align}
W'_{uv}&=W_{uv}+W_{ux}W_{yv}+W_{uy}W_{xv},\label{cdc:ng:eq:suppress}\\
\ell'&=\ell+W_{xy}.\label{cdc:ng:eq:suppress-loop}
\end{align}
The diagonal of $W'$ is zero. These formulas are exact over natural matching
matrices and use neither division nor a case-selection witness.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $W_{xy}=1$, $x,y$ are already matched. The old edge and the newly added join
form a two-edge cycle. Every other entry in the $x$ and $y$ rows is zero, so
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:suppress} leaves the surviving matching unchanged and
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:suppress-loop} adds exactly one loop.

Otherwise let $u_0$ be the partner of $x$ and $v_0$ the partner of $y$. They are
distinct surviving ports. The old edges $u_0x$ and $yv_0$, together with the
join $xy$, become a single edge $u_0v_0$. The two product terms in
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:suppress} add exactly the symmetric entries for this edge. No
surviving edge incident with $u_0$ or $v_0$ was already present because their
old partners were $x,y$. All other edges are unchanged. No closed component
is created in this case.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Order-independent loop accounting]\label{cdc:ng:cor:order}
Suppress the pairs of the internal matching in any order. The final boundary
matching and the total increment of $\ell$ are independent of the order.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Within a path component, each suppression shortens the same path and never
closes a component. Its two surviving endpoints are unchanged. Within a cycle
component, successive suppressions shorten that cycle until its last join
meets an already present edge; that final suppression contributes exactly
one to $\ell$. Different connected components do not interact. Consequently
the result consists of one edge per original path and one loop per original
cycle, independently of the suppression order.
\end{proof}

This provides one direct quartic implementation: introduce the intermediate
matching matrices and impose \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:suppress}--\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:suppress-loop} for
each internal join. The compiler in \cref{cdc:ng:sec:compiler} instead uses a single
orbit certificate for the whole gluing. It avoids these additional dense
intermediate matrices.

\subsubsection{Only sixteen ports can participate in nontrivial surgery}
\begin{proposition}[Support-local gluing]\label{cdc:ng:prop:support}
Let $I=\supp(\beta)$ and $S=I\cup\alpha(I)$. Then $S$ is invariant under
both $\alpha$ and $\beta$. On $V\setminus S$, the gluing does nothing:
its components are already surviving matching edges. In particular,
$|S|\le 2|I|$.

For one interaction-combinator step, $|I|\le8$ and therefore $|S|\le16$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The identity $\alpha^2=\id$ gives
$\alpha(S)=\alpha(I)\cup I=S$. The involution $\beta$ permutes $I$ and fixes
every point outside $I$, so it preserves $S$ as well. Outside $S$, both
endpoints of an $\alpha$ edge are outside $I$, hence are boundary ports, and
$\beta$ fixes them. Each consumed agent has at most two auxiliary ports.
There are at most four old auxiliaries and four interface copies, which
are precisely the moved points of $\beta$.
\end{proof}

The bound does not mean that the current dense arithmetic exporter has
constant-size memory access. Locating $\alpha(I)$ inside an unknown global
matching still costs something. It identifies a sharp place for future sparse
memory work: the actual topological surgery is of bounded size; global
addressing and untouched-memory preservation are the remaining expenses.

\subsection{The local gluing theorem\srctag{14}}\label{cdc:nt:sec:glue}
\subsubsection{Why no global path search is necessary}
Suppose a rewrite removes two cells. Delete their principal wire, keep every
other old wire, and add the right-hand-side template, identifying its boundary
ports with the former auxiliary ports of the removed cells. In the resulting
temporary multigraph each such auxiliary port has degree two. Every surviving
incident port has degree one. Thus every nonempty component is either a path
with two surviving endpoints or a cycle with none.

\begin{lemma}[Locality of suppression]\label{cdc:nt:lem:local}
Every temporary component changed by a fixed interaction rule has all of its
internal vertices in that rule's auxiliary boundary. Suppressing these
vertices replaces each path by its endpoint wire and each cycle by one bare
loop. In particular, for the binary rules all changed paths have at most four
internal vertices, independently of the size and topology of the surrounding
net.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An old wire ends at an incident port. It does not continue through the agent
owning that port. Only a boundary port receives a second temporary edge from
the replacement. A surviving port therefore terminates a path rather than
passing it into the rest of its agent. Degree two gives continuation without
branching at an internal vertex; degree one gives a unique endpoint.
Finite components with no degree-one vertex are cycles. These statements
also hold when two vertices are joined by two parallel edges. Such a
component is a two-edge cycle and must not be simplified to one edge.
\end{proof}

The lemma is compatible with the established execution-formula account of
port fusion \cite{defalco}; its purpose here is to expose the bounded
arithmetic workload. In particular, an arbitrary graph-connectivity
subroutine is unnecessary.

% ---- manuscript 14, lines 384-400 ----
\subsubsection{Composition and loop accounting}
\begin{proposition}[Suppression is order-independent]\label{cdc:nt:prop:suppress}
For a finite temporary wiring with designated degree-two internal vertices,
suppressing those vertices in any order gives the same boundary matching
and the same total number of newly closed components. The loop count is
additive over intermediate suppression stages.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A path component retains its two boundary endpoints until it becomes one
wire. It cannot produce a closed component during suppression. A cycle
component never acquires a boundary endpoint, and its last suppression
produces exactly one bare loop. Distinct original components never merge.
Classifying components before suppression therefore determines both the
final matching and the sum of all loop increments, independent of order.
\end{proof}
This elementary proof is included to make the loop invariant explicit, not
to claim a new associativity theorem for interaction-net gluing.

\wtag{} Manuscript~14's ``at most four internal vertices'' (\cref{cdc:nt:lem:local}) and manuscript~15's ``at most sixteen ports'' (\cref{cdc:ng:prop:support}) are one locality statement with two bookkeepings: the internal vertices of the changed paths are the at most four old auxiliary ports of one step, and manuscript~15's support adds the at most four interface copies and the old partners of these eight vertices. Neither bound is a constant-cost global lookup; both manuscripts say so.

\subsection{A sharp theorem for one-bit wiring observations\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:parity}

\subsubsection{Statement}

For a closing context $Q$, define its one-bit observation on $M$ by
\begin{equation}
 b_Q(M)=c(M,Q)\bmod2.
\end{equation}
Although this observable forgets almost the entire closed net, its family
over all contexts is unexpectedly discriminating.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp loop-parity separation]\label{cdc:ew:thm:sharp}
Let $n\ge2$ and $M,N\in\M_n$ with $M\ne N$. If $Q$ is uniform on $\M_n$,
then
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:sharp}
 \boxed{\quad\frac25\ \le\
 \PP\bigl(b_Q(M)\ne b_Q(N)\bigr)\ \le\ \frac23.\quad}
\end{equation}
The upper equality holds exactly when $M\cup N$ consists of one alternating
four-cycle and any number of common-edge two-cycles. The lower equality
holds exactly when it consists of one alternating six-cycle and any number
of common-edge two-cycles. In particular the lower bound is attained for
every $n\ge3$, and the upper bound for every $n\ge2$.
\end{theorem}

The proof will be elementary. It uses neither an asymptotic estimate nor a
spectral assertion about an uncomputed matrix.

\subsubsection{Cycle type and signed correlation}

The \emph{cycle half-length partition} of $M\cup N$ is the partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ whose parts are half the component lengths. Thus a common
edge contributes a part $1$. Simultaneous relabelling acts transitively on
pairs $(M,N)$ of the same cycle type: enumerate the vertices alternately
around each component to construct the relabelling. It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:F}
 F(\lambda)=\sum_{Q\in\M_n}(-1)^{c(M,Q)+c(N,Q)}
\end{equation}
depends only on $\lambda$. Set
\begin{equation}
 h(\lambda)=\frac{F(\lambda)}{D_n}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:prob-corr}
 \PP\bigl(b_Q(M)\ne b_Q(N)\bigr)=\frac{1-h(\lambda)}2.
\end{equation}
The identity case $M=N$ is $\lambda=(1^n)$ and has $h=1$.

\subsubsection{The contraction recurrence}

For a partition $\mu$, notation such as $(k,\mu)$ means the multiset of its
parts together with $k$, with order immaterial. Repeated parts in a sum over
$\ell\in\mu$ are counted repeatedly. Set $F(\varnothing)=1$.

\begin{lemma}[Signed closure recurrence]\label{cdc:ew:lem:recurrence}
If $|\mu|=n-1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:common}
 F(1,\mu)=(2n-1)F(\mu).
\end{equation}
If $k\ge2$ and $k+|\mu|=n$, then
\begin{align}
 F(k,\mu)={}&(k-3)F(k-1,\mu)\notag\\
 &+\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}F(i,k-1-i,\mu)\label{cdc:ew:eq:recurrence}\\
 &+\sum_{\ell\in\mu}2\ell\,
    F(k+\ell-1,\mu\setminus\{\ell\}).\notag
\end{align}
Every term on the right has total weight $n-1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose a port $a$ and condition on its partner $x$ in $Q$. Remove the edge
$\{a,x\}$ from $Q$. Separately in $M$ and $N$, suppress $a,x$ by
Lemma~\ref{cdc:ew:lem:splice}. A matching containing $\{a,x\}$ contributes one
closed component and hence a factor $-1$ to its signed loop count; otherwise
its two incident edges are contracted without this factor. The remaining
$Q$ is an arbitrary matching on the remaining $2n-2$ ports.

First suppose $\{a,b\}$ is common to $M,N$. If $x=b$, the two signs cancel
and the common component disappears. If $x\ne b$, both signs are positive,
and the old port $b$ takes the place of $x$ in the residual pair of
matchings. In all $2n-1$ cases the residual type is $\mu$. This proves
\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:common}.

For a nontrivial component, label its ports
$a_0,b_0,\ldots,a_{k-1},b_{k-1}$ so that
\begin{equation}
 M:\ \{a_i,b_i\},\qquad
 N:\ \{b_i,a_{i+1}\},
 \qquad i\pmod k.
\end{equation}
Choose $a=a_0$. The complete case distinction for its $Q$-partner is given
in Table~\ref{cdc:ew:tab:contraction}. The two partners $b_0,b_{k-1}$ give the two
negative terms; the $k-1$ partners $a_i$ give positive terms of the same
residual type. Their combined coefficient is $k-3$.

For $x=b_i$ with $1\le i\le k-2$, removing the selected ports cuts the
alternating cycle into components of half-lengths $i$ and $k-1-i$. For a
partner in a different component of half-length $\ell$, the two components
merge into one of half-length $k+\ell-1$. None of these cases closes an
$M$- or $N$-edge, so all their signs are positive. They exhaust the
$2n-1$ choices of $x$, proving \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:recurrence}.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{48mm}c p{57mm}@{}}
\toprule
Partner of $a_0$ & Sign & Residual cycle half-lengths \\
\midrule
$b_0$ or $b_{k-1}$ & $-$ & $(k-1,\mu)$ in each case \\
$a_i$, $1\le i\le k-1$ & $+$ & $(k-1,\mu)$ in each case \\
$b_i$, $1\le i\le k-2$ & $+$ & $(i,k-1-i,\mu)$ \\
A port in another component of half-length $\ell$ & $+$ &
$(k+\ell-1,\mu\setminus\{\ell\})$, with $2\ell$ choices \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Exhaustive local contraction underlying the signed recurrence.}
\label{cdc:ew:tab:contraction}
\end{table}

Dividing \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:common} by $D_n$ yields the particularly useful identity
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:ones}
 h(1,\mu)=h(\mu).
\end{equation}
Adding common wires changes the number of closing contexts but does not
change the signed correlation.

\subsubsection{Proof of the sharp bounds and equality cases}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:sharp}]
By \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:prob-corr}, it suffices to show
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:hbound}
 -\frac13\le h(\lambda)\le\frac15
\end{equation}
for every nonidentity cycle type, and to characterize equality. Remove all
parts $1$ using \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:ones}. Induct on the remaining total weight.

The first two cases follow directly from the recurrence:
\begin{equation}
 F(2)=-1,\quad D_2=3,\qquad
 F(3)=F(1,1)=3,\quad D_3=15.
\end{equation}
Thus $h(2)=-1/3$ and $h(3)=1/5$.

Suppose the partition has a part $k\ge3$ and total weight $n>3$. Use that
part as the distinguished $k$ in \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:recurrence}. Every coefficient
is nonnegative, and their sum is
\begin{equation}
 (k-3)+(k-2)+2(n-k)=2n-5.
\end{equation}
Every term with positive coefficient has a nonidentity residual partition.
Indeed, the merged part is at least $4$; for $k\ge4$ the split parts have
sum at least $3$; and for $k=3$ the other nontrivial parts prevent the split
term from becoming the identity. The sole exception to this reasoning is
$(3)$ itself, already treated.

Divide the recurrence by $D_n=(2n-1)D_{n-1}$ and apply the induction
hypothesis to every residual correlation. This gives
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:strict-inner}
 -\frac{2n-5}{3(2n-1)}
 \le h(\lambda)\le
 \frac{2n-5}{5(2n-1)}.
\end{equation}
Both endpoints are strictly inside the interval in \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:hbound}.

It remains to handle $\lambda=(2^r)$ with $r\ge2$. The recurrence and
\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:ones} give
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:alltwos}
 h(2^r)=
 \frac{-h(2^{r-1})+4(r-1)h(3,2^{r-2})}{4r-1}.
\end{equation}
Both correlations on the right have smaller active weight. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \frac{-1/5-4(r-1)/3}{4r-1}
 \le h(2^r)\le
 \frac{1/3+4(r-1)/5}{4r-1}.
\end{equation}
The left endpoint exceeds $-1/3$, since the numerator after moving
$-(4r-1)/3$ across is $4/5>0$. The right endpoint is less than $1/5$,
since $1/3<3/5$. Thus these cases are also strict.

The only equality cases after removing parts $1$ are therefore $(2)$ and
$(3)$. Equation~\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:prob-corr} gives exactly the asserted constants
and classification.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Small values and an independent finite check}

Table~\ref{cdc:ew:tab:correlations} illustrates that the probability is not a
function of the number of differing edges alone. The exact recurrence is
implemented in \path{code/13-exact-wiring-parity.py}. The verification script independently
enumerates closing matchings and counts multigraph components for every
partition of weight at most six: 29 partition cases and 121,537 closures.
It also checks the bounds and equality cases on all 28,598 nonidentity
partitions of weight at most thirty. These finite calculations detect
implementation and transcription errors; the induction above, not the
finite range, proves the theorem.

\subsection{Consequences for abstraction, information, and tomography\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:tomography}

\subsubsection{A lossless-information obstruction}

\begin{corollary}[One-bit contextual observations force injectivity]
\label{cdc:ew:cor:injective}
Suppose $s:\M_n\to\Sigma$ is a summary map and a function $g$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 g(s(M),Q)=b_Q(M)\qquad(M,Q\in\M_n).
\end{equation}
Then $s$ is injective. In particular, $|\Sigma|\ge D_n$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If $s(M)=s(N)$ for distinct matchings, the displayed equality gives
$b_Q(M)=b_Q(N)$ for every $Q$. This contradicts the positive lower bound in
Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:sharp}.
\end{proof}

This is stronger than an isolated pair of indistinguishable summaries: it
applies to \emph{every} identification of two distinct matchings, and only
requires parity of the final loop count. Its assumptions are nevertheless
specific. The contexts range over all labelled bare wirings. A summary for
one restricted family of contexts, or an overapproximating reachability
analysis, is not ruled out.

\begin{corollary}[State-bit lower bound]\label{cdc:ew:cor:bits}
A fixed-width binary summary satisfying Corollary~\ref{cdc:ew:cor:injective} requires
at least $\lceil\log_2D_n\rceil$ bits. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:entropy}
 \log_2D_n
 =n\log_2n+(1-\log_2e)n+\frac12
   -\frac{1}{24n\log 2}+O(n^{-3}).
\end{equation}
Thus a mate table using $O(n\log n)$ bits has the correct asymptotic order
for contextually exact state information.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
There are at most $2^b$ states of a $b$-bit register, so injectivity implies
$2^b\ge D_n$. Subtracting the Stirling expansions of $\log(2n)!$ and
$\log n!$ in \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:Dn}, and dividing by $\log2$, gives
\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:entropy}. The $1/n$ coefficient is
$1/24-1/12=-1/24$ in natural logarithms. A table of $2n$ partner identifiers
uses $2n\lceil\log_2(2n)\rceil$ bits, up to a constant convention for labels.
\end{proof}

This is an information lower bound, not a Diophantine variable lower bound.
A single unbounded natural number can encode arbitrarily much finite
information. Nor does it prove the bit optimality of the large-height
history certificate constructed later.

\subsubsection{A short distinguishing context for every modulus}

The following result supplies a deterministic, very local witness to
contextual separation, without the random theorem.

\begin{proposition}[Two-edge contextual separation]\label{cdc:ew:prop:modular}
For distinct $M,N\in\M_n$ and every integer $r\ge2$, there is a matching
$Q$, equal to $M$ or differing from it in exactly two edges, such that
\begin{equation}
 c(M,Q)\not\equiv c(N,Q)\pmod r.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $d=n-c(M,N)>0$. If $d\not\equiv0\pmod r$, use $Q=M$, since
$c(M,M)=n$.

Otherwise choose two $M$-edges in one nontrivial alternating component of
$M\cup N$. Removing those edges cuts the component into two paths. Of the
two nonoriginal pairings of their four endpoints, one closes the paths
separately and one reconnects them into a single cycle. Choose the latter
and leave every other $M$-edge unchanged; call the result $Q$.
Then $c(N,Q)=c(N,M)$, whereas $c(M,Q)=n-1$: the two changed edges form one
four-cycle in $M\cup Q$, and all other edges are common. The difference is
$d-1$, which is nonzero modulo $r$.
\end{proof}

The attached code checks this construction on every pair of matchings of at
most eight ports, for moduli $2,3,4,5$, giving 22,272 tests. The proposition
also clarifies the role of the random theorem: existence of a separator is
much easier than a sharp lower bound on the density of separators.

\subsubsection{An order-optimal number of nonadaptive one-bit probes}

A \emph{probe family} is a list $Q_1,\ldots,Q_K$ fixed before the unknown
matching is seen. Its observation vector is
\begin{equation}
 \Phi(M)=\bigl(b_{Q_1}(M),\ldots,b_{Q_K}(M)\bigr)\in\{0,1\}^{K}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Random simultaneous tomography]\label{cdc:ew:thm:probes}
For $n\ge2$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$, choose the probes independently and
uniformly from $\M_n$. If
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:K}
 K\ge\left\lceil
 \frac{\log\binom{D_n}{2}+\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log(5/3)}
 \right\rceil,
\end{equation}
then $\Phi$ is injective with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$.
Consequently a separating family of $O(n\log n)$ one-bit probes exists.
Every separating one-bit family has $K\ge\lceil\log_2D_n\rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a fixed pair $M\ne N$, a single probe fails to distinguish them with
probability at most $3/5$. Independence makes the probability of agreement
on all probes at most $(3/5)^K$. A union bound over the
$\binom{D_n}{2}$ pairs gives failure probability at most
$\binom{D_n}{2}(3/5)^K\le\varepsilon$. The asymptotic statement follows
from \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:entropy}. Finally an injective map to $\{0,1\}^{K}$ has
at most $2^K$ distinct inputs.
\end{proof}

This is an existence and sampling theorem, not an efficient decoding
algorithm. Exhaustively testing injectivity over $D_n$ matchings is not a
polynomial-time construction in $n$. Random probes are also not used in the
Diophantine compiler: its soundness will be exact for every witness tuple.

Its sufficiency half, that $(M,\ell)$ determines the result of every further matching gluing, is not stated by manuscript~13. Both proofs are kept.

\subsection{A complete summary for matching contexts\srctag{15}}
The following statement concerns wire diagrams, with agents treated as external
boundary attachments. It does not say that arbitrary interaction nets are
determined by a boundary matching independently of their internal agents.

\begin{theorem}[Contextual completeness of the wire summary]
\label{cdc:ng:thm:context}
A finite wire-only diagram with labelled boundary $B$, all nonboundary vertices
of degree two, and any pre-existing cyclic wires is completely described for
future matching gluings by its suppressed boundary matching $M$ and its total
loop count $\ell$.

Conversely, two such summaries $(M,\ell)$ and $(M',\ell')$ give the same
closed-loop count in every perfect-matching closure of $B$ if and only if
$M=M'$ and $\ell=\ell'$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Sufficiency follows from \cref{cdc:ng:cor:order}: suppressing the internal vertices
before or after any further gluing gives the same result.

For necessity put $|B|=2m$. For boundary matchings $M,Q$, let $c(M,Q)$ be
the number of components in the union of the two matchings, retaining parallel
edges. Every component contains at least one edge of $M$, so $c(M,Q)\le m$.
Equality holds exactly when all components have two edges, equivalently
$M=Q$.

Suppose $M\ne M'$ and write $c=c(M,M')<m$. Closure by $M$ would force
$\ell+m=\ell'+c$ if the observed counts agreed. Closure by $M'$ would force
$\ell+c=\ell'+m$. Subtracting these equalities gives $2(m-c)=0$, a
contradiction. If $M=M'$, any closure distinguishes unequal $\ell,\ell'$.
For $B=\varnothing$, the unique empty closure directly reads the loop count.
\end{proof}

This places the repository's obstruction in a positive framework. Counts and
histograms are not sufficient, but the exact matching and closed-loop scalar
are sufficient for all purely wiring contexts. This is consonant with classical
Brauer-diagram composition \cite{lehrer-zhang}; the arithmetic certificate below
makes the summary available to a polynomial verifier.

\wtag{} The local analogue is manuscript~14's ten-state theorem \cref{cdc:nt:thm:minimal} (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:kernel}): on the four boundary positions of one annihilation, a summary from which the external positions and both annihilation loop counts can be read must be injective on the ten partial matchings.

\subsection{The ten boundary patterns\srctag{14}}
For binary annihilation let $M$ be the matching formed by old wires whose
\emph{both} endpoints lie in $B$. It is a partial matching on four labelled
positions. The remaining positions have distinct external mates $q_i$.
There are
\begin{equation}
            1+\binom42+3=10                                           \label{cdc:nt:eq:3.1}
\end{equation}
possible $M$: the empty matching, six single-edge matchings, and three
perfect matchings. A position unmatched by $M$ is called external.
Let $m_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ be the six edge indicators and put
\begin{equation}
                 e_i=1-\sum_{j\ne i}m_{ij}.                            \label{cdc:nt:eq:3.2}
\end{equation}
For a legal pattern $e_i$ is exactly the external-position indicator.
We use $m_{ij}=m_{ji}$ in formulas.

Write
\[
\mathcal P=\{\{12,34\},\{13,24\},\{14,23\}\}
\]
for the three perfect matchings. Fix an annihilation matching $J\in\mathcal P$.
Its involution sends $i$ to $J(i)$.

\begin{theorem}[Closed formulas for exact gluing]\label{cdc:nt:thm:glue}
The number of newly created bare loops is
\begin{equation}
 c_J(M)=\sum_{ij\in J}m_{ij}
      +\sum_{K\in\mathcal P\setminus\{J\}}\prod_{ij\in K}m_{ij}.        \label{cdc:nt:eq:3.3}
\end{equation}
For $i<j$, the surviving endpoints $q_i,q_j$ are joined exactly when
\begin{equation}
 g_{ij}=e_i e_j
 \begin{cases}
  1,&ij\in J,\\
  m_{J(i),J(j)},&ij\notin J.
 \end{cases}                                                         \label{cdc:nt:eq:3.4}
\end{equation}
The indicators $g_{ij}$ form a perfect matching of the external positions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $M$ is empty, each of the two $J$ edges makes a path between two external
mates, and no cycle is created. If $M$ has a single edge, that edge and a
coincident $J$ edge form a two-edge cycle precisely when the edge belongs to
$J$. Otherwise the old edge links the two $J$ edges into one longer path
between the two external positions. If $M$ is perfect and equals $J$, there
are two two-edge cycles. If $M$ is perfect and differs from $J$, their union
is one alternating four-cycle. These cases give \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:3.3}.

For \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:3.4}, an external position $i$ first follows its $J$ edge. If this
immediately reaches external position $j$, then $ij\in J$. Otherwise both
$J(i)$ and $J(j)$ must be the remaining internal positions, and the only
possible path uses the old edge between them. Conversely that edge gives
exactly the required path. All components are disjoint paths or cycles by
Lemma~\ref{cdc:nt:lem:local}, so each external position has one and only one partner.
\end{proof}

In particular,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 c_\delta&=m_{13}+m_{24}+m_{12}m_{34}+m_{14}m_{23},\\
 c_\gamma&=m_{14}+m_{23}+m_{12}m_{34}+m_{13}m_{24}.
\end{aligned}\label{cdc:nt:eq:3.5}
\end{equation}
These are genuine quadratic expressions, including the all-internal case.
Counting only coincident old and new edges would miss the alternating
four-cycle.

\caption{Every local pattern for a fixed annihilation matching $J$.}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}\toprule
Pattern & Number & External positions & New loops\\\midrule
$M=\varnothing$ & 1 & 4 & 0\\
One edge belonging to $J$ & 2 & 2 & 1\\
One edge not belonging to $J$ & 4 & 2 & 0\\
$M=J$ & 1 & 0 & 2\\
Perfect $M\ne J$ & 2 & 0 & 1\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{A sharp local abstraction result\srctag{14}}
The previous obstruction concerns summaries of whole nets. There is also a
small, exact lower bound at a single boundary.

\begin{theorem}[Ten distinguishable boundary states]\label{cdc:nt:thm:minimal}
Let $\sigma$ be a summary of partial matchings on the four labelled boundary
positions. Suppose the external-position set and both numbers
$c_\delta(M),c_\gamma(M)$ can be recovered from $\sigma(M)$. Then $\sigma$ is
injective on the ten partial matchings. Consequently such a summary needs
at least ten states, or at least four bits in a fixed-width binary encoding.
Conversely the partial matching itself is a sufficient ten-state summary
for both annihilation rules, provided the ordered external addresses are
retained separately.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Four external positions force $M=\varnothing$. Two external positions
identify their complementary pair, which must be the unique internal edge.
With no external positions, $M$ is perfect. For the three possibilities
$\{12,34\},J_\delta,J_\gamma$, the observed cycle-count pairs are respectively
$(1,1),(2,1),(1,2)$. They are distinct. Sufficiency follows from
Theorem~\ref{cdc:nt:thm:glue}.
\end{proof}

The observation class is essential. For one fixed annihilation rule and no
external positions, the two nonmatching perfect patterns both produce one
loop; that weaker observation does not distinguish them. Nor does the theorem
say that ten states can encode arbitrary external port identifiers.

\subsection{A 23-residual quartic topology kernel\srctag{14}}\label{cdc:nt:sec:kernel}
\subsubsection{All equations and all witnesses}
Take the six natural numbers $m_{ij}$ as source coordinates. Introduce the
four $e_i$, six $h_{ij}$, six $g_{ij}$, and one $c$ as auxiliary coordinates:
17 in total. Impose
\begin{align}
 m_{ij}(m_{ij}-1)&=0 &&(i<j),                                           \label{cdc:nt:eq:4.1}\\
 e_i+\sum_{j\ne i}m_{ij}-1&=0 &&(1\leq i\leq4),                        \label{cdc:nt:eq:4.2}\\
 h_{ij}-e_i e_j&=0 &&(i<j),                                            \label{cdc:nt:eq:4.3}\\
 g_{ij}-h_{ij} f_{ij}&=0 &&(i<j),                                      \label{cdc:nt:eq:4.4}\\
 c-\sum_{ij\in J}m_{ij}
   -\sum_{K\in\mathcal P\setminus\{J\}}\prod_{ij\in K}m_{ij}&=0,       \label{cdc:nt:eq:4.5}
\end{align}
where $f_{ij}=1$ for $ij\in J$ and $f_{ij}=m_{J(i),J(j)}$ otherwise.
These are $6+4+6+6+1=23$ residuals, all of degree at most two.
Let $K_J$ be the sum of their squares.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical quartic gluing]\label{cdc:nt:thm:kernel}
For source tuple $\mathbf m\in\N^6$, the equation $K_J=0$ has a natural
solution exactly when $\mathbf m$ is the indicator of a partial matching.
In that case its 17-coordinate extension is unique and its outputs are
precisely \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:3.3}--\eqref{cdc:nt:eq:3.4}. The polynomial has degree at most four.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A sum of integer squares is zero exactly when every summand is zero.
Equation \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:4.1} forces the six indicators to be Boolean. Nonnegativity of
$e_i$ in \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:4.2} forces each position to meet at most one internal edge; it also
uniquely determines $e_i$. The remaining equations determine successively
$h_{ij}$, $g_{ij}$, and $c$. Theorem~\ref{cdc:nt:thm:glue} proves their semantic
meaning and nonnegativity. Every legal partial matching supplies this
extension. Squaring quadratic residuals gives the degree bound.
\end{proof}

Thus the scalar cycle output is not an existentially guessed component
count. It is forced. The supplied expanded $\delta$ and $\gamma$ quartics
each have 104 nonzero monomials. This is an executable count for the stated
presentation, not an optimality claim.
