\subsection{An exact large-integer multiset certificate\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:product}

\subsubsection{Why a single product can be exact}

The memory proof will compare two lists of packed access records. A random
fingerprint would be inappropriate for an exact Diophantine zero-set
statement. A sufficiently large, \emph{computed} base avoids collisions
without any probability.

\begin{lemma}[Collision-free product identity]\label{cdc:ew:lem:product}
Let $L\ge1$, $U\ge2$, and let $0\le x_i,y_i<U$ for $1\le i\le L$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:base}
 B=U^L+1.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:product}
 \prod_{i=1}^{L}(B+x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^{L}(B+y_i)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \multiset(x_1,\ldots,x_L)=\multiset(y_1,\ldots,y_L).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}


\begin{proof}[Pointer]
\wtag{} This is \cref{cdc:mem:lem:fingerprint} with $(U,B,x_i,y_i)$ for $(C,\beta,c_i,d_i)$, indexed from $1$; manuscript~13's proof is that proof: $f(1)=\prod_i(1+x_i)\le U^L<B$, so the coefficients of $f(X)=\prod_i(X+x_i)$ and of $g$ are base-$B$ digits, $f(B)=g(B)$ forces $f=g$, and evaluation at $X=-x_1$ with cancellation of the common monic factor recovers the multiset.
\end{proof}

The argument is the positive-coefficient form of large-base coefficient
packing, often called Kronecker substitution; see, for example,
\cite{sutherland}. The exact scale and the bounds on \emph{both} lists are
part of the proof, not optional implementation hints.

\begin{example}[An arbitrary small base is unsound]
For every positive integer $b$,
\begin{equation}
 (b+0)(b+(b+2))=(b+1)(b+b),
\end{equation}
although the multisets $\{0,b+2\}$ and $\{1,b\}$ differ. Consequently one
cannot replace \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:base} by an unconstrained existential base and
retain the equivalence. Nor can the prover be allowed to invent unbounded
``sorted records'' outside the packing range.
\end{example}

% ---- manuscript 13, lines 814-848 ----
\subsubsection{Quadratic implementation and honest bit costs}

The exponent $L$ in \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:base} is an external size parameter. Compute
$U^L$ by its binary addition chain: each squaring uses a variable $z$ and
equation $z-x^2=0$, and multiplication by $U$ uses $z-Ux=0$. This requires
$O(\log(L+1))$ gates. Define $B$ by one further linear equation.

Compute each product in \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:product} by a balanced binary tree of
multiplication gates. Leaves are the affine expressions $B+x_i$ or
$B+y_i$. Each gate residual is quadratic and has a constant number of
monomials. Each tree uses $L-1$ multiplication gates; the final comparison
is linear. Coefficients need only $O(\log U)$ bits: the huge integer $B$ is
a computed witness, not a huge printed coefficient.

\begin{proposition}[Height of the product certificate]\label{cdc:ew:prop:height}
The construction uses $O(L+\log(L+1))$ auxiliary variables. Its largest
product has $O(L^2\log U)$ bits. With balanced product trees, the total bit
length of the product-tree witnesses is
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:height}
 O\bigl(L^2\log U\log(L+1)\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Since $B=U^L+1$, each factor has $O(L\log U)$ bits. A product of $s$ factors
therefore has $O(sL\log U)$ bits. At one level of a balanced tree, the
blocks partition at most $L$ leaves, so their total bit length is
$O(L^2\log U)$. There are $O(\log(L+1))$ levels. The binary powering
witnesses have smaller total order and do not alter the stated bound.
\end{proof}

A linear number of arithmetic coordinates is therefore obtained at a
substantial height cost. Replacing a balanced tree by a long product chain
would keep the coordinate count linear but give a weaker total-bit bound.
No constant-time big-integer multiplication assumption is used here.

% ---- manuscript 13, lines 850-1017 ----
\subsection{A canonical quadratic certificate for bounded memory\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:memory}

\subsubsection{The relation to be represented}

Fix $A\ge1$, $m\ge0$ and $V\ge2$. Memory addresses are $0,\ldots,A-1$ and
values are $0,\ldots,V-1$. The proposed input consists of initial contents
$I_a$, final contents $O_a$, and chronological access events
\begin{equation}
 (a_j,r_j,w_j),\qquad 1\le j\le m.
\end{equation}
An event must read the current value $r_j$ at address $a_j$ and then replace
it by $w_j$. A read-only event has $w_j=r_j$. The \emph{memory consistency
relation} says that all these reads are correct and the final array is $O$.

This relation includes untouched addresses. Omitting initial or final
records for such addresses would weaken the intended assertion.

\subsubsection{Initial, ordinary and final records}

Use four-field records $(a,t,r,w)$ and form the chronological list
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:raw}
 \underbrace{(a,0,0,I_a)}_{a=0,\ldots,A-1},\qquad
 \underbrace{(a_j,j,r_j,w_j)}_{j=1,\ldots,m},\qquad
 \underbrace{(a,m+1,O_a,O_a)}_{a=0,\ldots,A-1}.
\end{equation}
Its length is $L=2A+m$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:pack-params}
 H=m+2,\qquad U=AHV^2,\qquad B=U^L+1.
\end{equation}
The initial record initializes an address; its artificial read value zero
has no preceding record at that address. The final record audits the last
value without changing it.

Pack a record injectively by
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:pack}
 x(a,t,r,w)=HV^2a+V^2t+Vr+w.
\end{equation}
The bounds
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:field-bounds}
 0\le a<A,\quad0\le t<H,\quad0\le r,w<V
\end{equation}
imply $0\le x<U$. Uniqueness is ordinary mixed-radix uniqueness: successively
reduce modulo $V$, divide by $V$, and then reduce modulo $H$.

Introduce $L$ proposed sorted records
$(\bar a_i,\bar t_i,\bar r_i,\bar w_i)$, all satisfying the same bounds.
Require the product identity of Lemma~\ref{cdc:ew:lem:product} between the packed
raw records and these packed proposed records. Thus the sorted rows must
be a permutation of the entire raw list, including all four fields.

\subsubsection{Sorting and adjacent consistency without a sorting network}

Define the key $K_i=H\bar a_i+\bar t_i$. For each $1\le i<L$, introduce
natural witnesses $s_i,z_i,d_i$ and impose
\begin{align}
 K_i+1+s_i&=K_{i+1},\label{cdc:ew:eq:sort}\\
 z_i(z_i-1)&=0,\label{cdc:ew:eq:bool}\\
 \bar a_{i+1}-\bar a_i&=(1-z_i)(d_i+1),\label{cdc:ew:eq:addr}\\
 z_id_i&=0,\label{cdc:ew:eq:gapzero}\\
 z_i(\bar r_{i+1}-\bar w_i)&=0.\label{cdc:ew:eq:link}
\end{align}
Every equation is quadratic or linear. Equation~\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:sort} makes keys
strictly increasing. If addresses agree, \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:addr} forces $z_i=1$
and \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:gapzero} forces $d_i=0$. If they differ, $z_i=0$ and $d_i$ is
the address difference minus one. Thus \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:link} is exactly the
consecutive-read consistency condition within an address block.

A bound $0\le x<R$ is encoded by the natural slack equation
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:bound}
 x+u=R-1,\qquad u\in\N.
\end{equation}
The raw event fields, initial and final values, and every sorted field
receive these bounds. The timestamps in the raw list are literal constants.
No bounded universal quantifier remains: the equations are instantiated
once for each external index.

\begin{theorem}[Exact canonical bounded-memory certificate]
\label{cdc:ew:thm:memory}
For the fixed parameters $A,m,V$, the equations
\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:raw}--\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:bound}, together with the quadratic product-tree
implementation, have a natural solution exactly when the proposed memory
history is consistent. For fixed raw event data and initial/final arrays,
the extension to sorted records, comparison bits, slacks and product-gate
variables is unique whenever it exists.

There are $O(A+m)$ auxiliary variables and equations, each of degree at
most two and with a bounded number of monomials. All coefficients have
$O(\log(A+m+V))$ bits. Replacing the equations by their sum of squares gives
a polynomial of degree at most four with $O(A+m)$ sparse monomials.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Soundness]
Lemma~\ref{cdc:ew:lem:product} and the field bounds show that the proposed sorted
records are precisely a permutation of the raw records. Raw keys are all
distinct: ordinary event times are globally distinct, initial records have
time zero and distinct addresses, and final records have time $m+1$ and
distinct addresses. Thus \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:sort} forces the unique increasing
ordering of those keys.

Because $0\le t<H$, increasing $Ha+t$ sorts first by address and then by
time. Every address block begins with its initial record and ends with its
final record. Within the block, \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:addr} forces $z_i=1$, so
\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:link} makes the next read equal the preceding write. Induction
along the block shows that every ordinary read has the current memory
value and that the final audit equals the final content. A block containing
only its initial and final records forces $O_a=I_a$, as required.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Completeness and uniqueness]
For a consistent history, sort the actual raw records by their keys. Assign
$s_i=K_{i+1}-K_i-1$, set $z_i$ to the equal-address indicator, and set $d_i$
to zero for equal addresses or to the address difference minus one
otherwise. All these numbers are natural, and every equation holds. Use
actual computed products for the arithmetic gates and the unique range
slacks in \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:bound}.

Conversely, soundness fixed the sorted rows uniquely. Equations
\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:sort}--\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:gapzero} then determine $s_i,z_i,d_i$ uniquely.
All range slacks and all gates are definitional and hence unique. The
condition $z_id_i=0$ is important: without it, the inactive address-gap
witness could vary arbitrarily when $z_i=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Size and degree]
There are $L=2A+m$ sorted records, a constant number of range equations per
record, five equations per adjacent pair, $O(\log L)$ powering gates and
two product trees with $L-1$ gates each. All packed expressions have four
fields. Thus the counts and the monomial bound are linear. The constants
$H,V,HV^2,U$ have logarithmic bit length in $A+m+V$. Squaring a residual
with a bounded number of monomials introduces only a bounded number more;
summing the squares preserves the linear sparse-description bound.
\end{proof}

The theorem certifies a proposed sort rather than computing a sort inside
the polynomial. Soundness is supplied by exact multiset equality and strict
key order; there is no appeal to a sorting-network size estimate.

\subsubsection{A fully exported example}

The distributed example has $A=3$, $m=5$, $V=8$, initial memory $(1,2,0)$,
final memory $(3,1,0)$, and events
\begin{equation}
 (0,1,3),\ (2,0,4),\ (0,3,3),\ (1,2,1),\ (2,4,0).
\end{equation}
The five reads agree with the evolving memory. Here $L=11$, $H=7$,
$U=1344$, and $B=1344^{11}+1$. The file
\path{data/13-exact-wiring-example_memory_certificate.json} contains every parameter,
every witness value, every quadratic residual, and the expanded quartic
sum of squares. Its exact counts are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Parameters & 21 \\
Natural witnesses & 167 \\
Quadratic/linear residuals & 144 \\
Monomials in the expanded quartic & 2,496 \\
Largest witness bit length & 1,258 \\
Total witness bit length & 9,874 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
These are counts for the memory example only. They are neither interaction
macro counts nor universal-polynomial records. Every designated residual
and the quartic evaluate to zero. Increasing any one of the 167 witness
coordinates by one, while keeping the others fixed, makes the quartic
strictly positive. This mutation test checks local sensitivity, not the
all-tuples uniqueness theorem, which was proved above.

\wtag{} Batch~78, 2 October 2026. The review \cite{repo-icrev} shows, for the exported example above, that the Boolean equations \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:bool} are redundant on the natural domain: the strict keys and the time bounds force adjacent addresses to be nondecreasing, so \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:addr} with natural $z_i,d_i$ forces $z_i\in\{0,1\}$; keeping \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:gapzero}, the address equation can be replaced by the linear $\bar a_{i+1}-\bar a_i-d_i-1+z_i=0$. One residual per adjacent pair is removed, $144\to134$ in the example, with the same natural zero set. The review notes that the deletion needs the key and time bounds, and that it does not transfer to manuscript~14's different encoding $\alpha_j-\alpha_{j-1}=b_j(1+h_j)$, which does not force $b_j$ to be Boolean. It is the review's result; the shipped certificate is unchanged.

% ---- manuscript 14, lines 465-506 ----
\subsection{Canonical bounded-memory certificates\srctag{14}}
\subsubsection{Source relation and the role of external caps}
Fix positive integers $L,A,V$. A source log is
\[
            (a_i,w_i,v_i)\quad (0\leq i<L),
\]
where $0\leq a_i<A$, $0\leq v_i<V$, and $w_i\in\{0,1\}$. A record with
$w_i=1$ writes $v_i$ at address $a_i$; a record with $w_i=0$ reads that address
and asserts that its current value is $v_i$. Memory starts at zero.
The three coordinates per record are source coordinates, not included in
the auxiliary count below.

Here $L,A,V$ are \emph{fixed parameters of the polynomial family}. In
particular, products such as $AL$ in coefficients do not increase its degree.
Allowing those caps themselves to be free arithmetic inputs requires additional
product gates and changes the exact ledger. This qualification matters in
comparisons with unrestricted memory-log compilers.

\subsubsection{One deterministic product test for multiset equality}
\begin{lemma}[Carry-free multiset certificate]\label{cdc:nt:lem:product}
Let $0\leq x_i,y_i<M$ for $0\leq i<L$, and set
$B=(M+1)^L$. Then
\begin{equation}
                  \prod_{i=0}^{L-1}(B+x_i)
                  =\prod_{i=0}^{L-1}(B+y_i)                           \label{cdc:nt:eq:5.1}
\end{equation}
holds if and only if the two lists have the same multiset of entries.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Pointer]
\wtag{} Manuscript~14's proof is that of \cref{cdc:mem:lem:fingerprint}, with entries below $M$ and the base $B=(M+1)^L$ instead of $C^L+1$: the coefficient sum is $F(1)=\prod_i(1+x_i)\le M^L<B$, every coefficient is a base-$B$ digit with no carries, $F(B)=G(B)$ forces $F=G$, and evaluation at $-x_0$ with cancellation recovers the multiset.
\end{proof}

The large base is doing genuine work. Equality of products at an arbitrary
small base is not a reliable multiset test. No probability, finite field,
random challenge, or unproved collision assumption occurs in \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.1}.

% ---- manuscript 14, lines 508-674 ----
\subsubsection{Records, bounds, and sorted order}
Introduce a putatively sorted list $(\alpha_j,\tau_j,\omega_j,\nu_j)$ for
$0\leq j<L$. It carries address, original time, write bit, and value. Define
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 x_i&=a_i+A i+ALw_i+2ALv_i,\\
 y_j&=\alpha_j+A\tau_j+AL\omega_j+2AL\nu_j,\\
 M&=2ALV,\qquad B=(M+1)^L.
\end{aligned}\label{cdc:nt:eq:5.2}
\end{equation}
All source and sorted fields have their indicated bounds:
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
 a_i,\alpha_j<A,\quad v_i,\nu_j<V,\quad \tau_j<L,\\
 w_i,\omega_j\in\{0,1\}.
\end{gathered}                                                       \label{cdc:nt:eq:5.3}
\end{equation}
Each strict bound $z<D$ is imposed by one natural complement $\bar z$ and
one equation $z+\bar z=D-1$; each bit satisfies $b(b-1)=0$.
The packing in \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.2} is injective on these fields. Its maximum is $M-1$.
The time field ensures that complete records are distinct, even when two
accesses otherwise coincide.

Sort by the key
\[
                           k_j=L\alpha_j+\tau_j.
\]
For $1\leq j<L$, introduce $d_j\in\N$ and require
\begin{equation}
                   k_j-k_{j-1}-1-d_j=0.                              \label{cdc:nt:eq:5.4}
\end{equation}
Once the product test verifies the multiset, \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.4} selects its unique strictly
increasing arrangement.

\subsubsection{Quadratic product chains}
Do not put an exponentiation symbol in the final Diophantine equation.
Instead use $q_0=1$ as a constant and introduce $q_1,\ldots,q_L$ with
\begin{equation}
                      q_i=(M+1)q_{i-1}\quad(1\leq i\leq L).           \label{cdc:nt:eq:5.5}
\end{equation}
Use $q_L$ as $B$. Likewise take $R_0=S_0=1$ as constants, and introduce
\begin{equation}
 R_{i+1}=R_i(B+x_i),\qquad S_{i+1}=S_i(B+y_i)
                      \quad(0\leq i<L),                              \label{cdc:nt:eq:5.6}
\end{equation}
followed by $R_L=S_L$. Each residual in \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.5}--\eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.6} is at most quadratic.
All chain values are uniquely determined and nonnegative.

\subsubsection{Local read/write consistency in sorted order}
Let $z_j$ be the value at the sorted address after record $j$, and let $r_j$
be the value before it. Set $r_0=0$ as a constant. For $1\leq j<L$, introduce
$b_j,h_j\in\N$ with
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 b_j(b_j-1)&=0,\\
 \alpha_j-\alpha_{j-1}&=b_j(1+h_j),\\
 (1-b_j)h_j&=0,\\
 r_j&=(1-b_j)z_{j-1}.
\end{aligned}\label{cdc:nt:eq:5.7}
\end{equation}
The bit $b_j$ indicates a change of address. It and $h_j$ are unique: if the
address stays the same they are both zero; otherwise $b_j=1$ and
$h_j=\alpha_j-\alpha_{j-1}-1$.
For every $j$, require
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
            (1-\omega_j)(\nu_j-r_j)&=0,\\
            z_j-\omega_j\nu_j-(1-\omega_j)r_j&=0.
\end{aligned}\label{cdc:nt:eq:5.8}
\end{equation}
A read must equal the prior value and preserves it. A write supplies the
new value. The key order guarantees that records of the same address are
processed in their original chronological order.

\begin{theorem}[A $17L-4$ canonical memory system]\label{cdc:nt:thm:memory}
For fixed $L,A,V\geq1$, equations \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.3}--\eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.8}, with the product equality,
form a quadratic system having exactly $17L-4$ auxiliary variables and
$17L-4$ residuals. A source log has a natural solution if and only if it
lies within the caps and is a valid zero-initialized memory log. When it has
a solution, the entire auxiliary tuple is unique. The sum of the residual
squares is an integer polynomial of degree at most four.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The range equations and bit equations enforce well-typed records. By
Lemma~\ref{cdc:nt:lem:product}, the product chains and final equality force equality
of the packed-record multisets. Injectivity of the packing recovers the full
records. Their time fields distinguish all records, so the strict key order
forces the unique sorted list.

Because $0\leq\tau_j<L$, increasing keys imply nondecreasing addresses.
Equations \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.7} therefore have their asserted unique natural values. Within
each address block, \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.8} inductively enforces precisely its chronological
read/write history starting from zero. Since operations at different
addresses do not affect one another, this is equivalent to validity of the
original log. This proves soundness.

Conversely sort a valid log, set all complements and key gaps to their
unique differences, evaluate the product chains, and replay the sorted
address blocks. This produces a natural solution. The preceding soundness
argument forces the same sorted rows in every solution, and each remaining
variable is then forced successively. The exact count is in
Table~\ref{cdc:nt:tab:memory}; the degree statement follows from the displayed
quadratic equations.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\caption{Complete memory ledger. Source coordinates: $3L$, not included in the auxiliary column.}\label{cdc:nt:tab:memory}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}\toprule
Component & Auxiliaries & Residuals\\\midrule
Sorted four-field records & $4L$ & $0$\\
Source range complements and bits & $2L$ & $3L$\\
Sorted range complements and bits & $3L$ & $4L$\\
Base chain & $L$ & $L$\\
Two product chains and equality & $2L$ & $2L+1$\\
Strict sorted-key gaps & $L-1$ & $L-1$\\
New-address bits and normalized gaps & $2L-2$ & $3L-3$\\
Pre-values except $r_0$ & $L-1$ & $L-1$\\
Read checks & $0$ & $L$\\
Post-values & $L$ & $L$\\\midrule
Total & $17L-4$ & $17L-4$\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{corollary}[Precomputed-base variant]\label{cdc:nt:cor:precomputed}
If the coefficient $B=(M+1)^L$ is precomputed by the compiler, the base-chain
variables and residuals may be omitted. The count becomes $16L-4$ in both
columns, at the price of a coefficient with $O(L\log(M+1))$ bits.
\end{corollary}
The main theorem uses \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:5.5} to keep coefficient bit lengths small and expose
all arithmetic. Neither variant is claimed optimal.

\subsubsection{Height, bit complexity, and comparison with earlier memory work}\label{cdc:nt:sec:memhist}
\begin{proposition}[Height bound]\label{cdc:nt:prop:height}
Every solution of the system in Theorem~\ref{cdc:nt:thm:memory} satisfies
\[
       R_L,S_L\leq (B+M-1)^L,
\]
and every auxiliary has bit length
\begin{equation}
                         O\!\left(L^2\log(M+1)\right).                \label{cdc:nt:eq:5.9}
\end{equation}
The residual coefficients have $O(\log(M+1))$ bits. The expanded sum of
squares has $O(L)$ monomials before possible cancellations and merging.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Each factor of either product is at most $B+M-1$. Since $B=(M+1)^L\geq M$,
$\log_2(B+M-1)\leq1+L\log_2(M+1)$. All product prefixes satisfy the same
bound. Other coordinates are capped fields, gaps, post-values below $V$,
or base powers no larger than $B$. Every residual has a bounded number of
terms, with coefficients built from $A,L,V$ and their fixed products.
Squaring each residual therefore contributes only a bounded number of
monomials.
\end{proof}

This is linear \emph{arithmetic description size}, not linear total witness
bit volume. A crude total-volume bound is $O(L^3\log(M+1))$. The large products
are an explicit size--height trade-off, not a hidden unit-cost claim about
binary arithmetic. Sorting-network arithmetization gives an alternative
with $O(L\log^2 L)$ fixed comparators and small intermediate words; the
network ingredient is classical \cite{batcher}.

The repository's existing memory and heap compilers have different interfaces
and published ledgers \cite{repo-cdc}. A smaller auxiliary count here
must not be advertised as an unconditional improvement of every prior bound:
our $A,V$ are external caps, and we use large carry-free product witnesses.
What is established is the exact count for this explicitly stated relation.

Manuscript~14 says itself that its smaller auxiliary count ``must not be advertised as an unconditional improvement of every prior bound'' (\cref{cdc:nt:sec:memhist}); here the prior bound is Part~V's, for a relation without caps. Manuscript~13's binary powering of $U^L$ is the suggestion of Part~V's question on the scalar constant (\cref{cdc:q:scalar}), and manuscript~14's $17L-4$ answers that question in part for its capped relation; see the dated note there. Both keep Part~V's height cost: a largest witness of $O(L^2\log U)$ or $O(L^2\log(M+1))$ bits (\cref{cdc:ew:prop:height,cdc:nt:prop:height}; compare \cref{cdc:mem:thm:linear-height}), so Part~V's size--height question (\cref{cdc:q:sizeheight}) is not answered; manuscript~14 names sorting networks as the alternative, as Part~V does.

\section{The bounded six-rule compiler}\label{cdc:ic:sec:compiler}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Manuscripts~13 and~14 prove the same theorem by the same method: exact length-$T$ scheduled reductions of all six rules from an explicit net with $C_0$ cells and $F$ (or $f$) free ports have a quartic certificate with $O(C_0+F+T)$ coordinates, residuals and monomials and exactly one auxiliary witness per legal schedule, built from a constant-size per-step controller and \emph{one} large-integer sorted-memory certificate for the whole access log. \subsection{A loop-aware memory machine for the six rules\srctag{14}}\label{cdc:nt:sec:machine}
\subsubsection{Fixed storage layout}
Fix a valid explicit input net with $C_0$ cells, $f$ free ports, and $\ell_0$
bare loops, and fix an external horizon $T$. Set
\begin{equation}
 C=C_0+4T,\qquad A=4C+f+1,\qquad V=3C+f+4.                            \label{cdc:nt:eq:6.1}
\end{equation}
The completely empty zero-horizon case is handled separately without a
memory log. When $C=0$ and $f>0$ the same layout works for free ports alone.
For cell $c<C$, use port identifiers
\[
                         p(c,j)=3c+j+1.
\]
Free port $i$, for $0\leq i<f$, has identifier $3C+i+1$. Address zero is a
read-only dummy initialized to zero. The four cell slots are
\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{ll}
4c+1 &: \text{type code }0,1,2,3\text{ for dead},\eps,\gamma,\delta,\\
4c+2+j &: \text{mate identifier of port }cj\quad (j=0,1,2).
\end{array}                                                          \label{cdc:nt:eq:6.2}
\end{equation}
The mate slot of free port $i$ is $4C+i+1$. For an eraser the unused auxiliary
slots are zero. Every slot of a deleted cell is reset to zero. All actual
values lie below $V$ and all addresses below $A$.

Besides memory we carry scalar registers $h_t,n_t,\ell_t$: next fresh cell
identifier, live-cell count, and bare-loop count. They start at
$C_0,C_0,\ell_0$. These are circuit registers, not additional memory accesses.

\subsubsection{A fixed 36-access rewrite schedule}
Initialize the $4C_0+f$ occupied cell/free-port slots by writes in their fixed
layout order; untouched memory is zero. One rewrite uses the following fixed
36 log positions.
\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Literal per-step memory budget. Unused positions are dummy reads $(0,0,0)$.}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrp{86mm}@{}}\toprule
Stage & Accesses & Purpose\\\midrule
Read & 8 & Two type codes and all six mate slots of the selected cells.\\
Delete & 8 & Reset both selected four-slot records to zero.\\
Allocate & 16 & Write up to four complete fresh records; inactive record positions are dummy reads.\\
Patch & 4 & Update the mates of the external old auxiliary endpoints, at most one per boundary position.\\\midrule
Total & 36 & No global graph scan and no hidden path-following accesses.\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The fixed read stage includes the zero auxiliary slots of any selected
eraser. All old mates are read before any deletion or patch. For every
dummy position the address, read flag, and value are fixed to zero; there
is no unconstrained inactive log data.

Check $u_t<v_t<h_t$, nonzero type codes, and the principal pairing using the
read values. Derive the unique rule from the two type codes. For binary
annihilation, compute the six comparisons
\[
          m_{ij}=\boldsymbol{1}\{\text{old mate of }B_i\text{ is }B_j\}
\]
and apply \cref{cdc:nt:sec:kernel}. Each $g_{ij}=1$ determines the two reciprocal external
patches. For the other rules use the relocation operation below. Compute
complete new records locally before the allocation stage.

The scalar updates are
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
 h_{t+1}&=h_t+b_t,\\
 n_{t+1}+2&=n_t+b_t,\\
 \ell_{t+1}&=\ell_t+c_t.
\end{split}\label{cdc:nt:eq:6.3}
\end{equation}
where $b_t\in\{0,2,4\}$ is the number of new cells. The only nonzero $c_t$
comes from a binary annihilation and is the forced kernel output.

\subsubsection{Endpoint relocation for creation rules}
For a mixed interaction or a binary erasure, the replacement sends each old
auxiliary position $i$ to a distinct new principal port $\rho(i)$. If its old
mate is another old boundary position $j$, set the new mate to $\rho(j)$.
If its old mate is external endpoint $q_i$, join $\rho(i)$ to $q_i$ and patch
$q_i$ reciprocally. Add the fixed internal auxiliary wiring \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:2.2} for the
mixed rule. This produces no bare loops: every component touching the old
boundary now reaches at least one new incident port. An internally matched
pair of old boundary positions becomes a wire between two distinct new
principals, not a disappearing wire.

\begin{lemma}[One-step representation invariant]\label{cdc:nt:lem:machine}
Starting from the valid storage representation of a net, the preceding
36-access procedure succeeds for a supplied pair exactly when that pair is
active. Its output is the storage representation of the literal interaction
rule applied to the net, including the exact loop count. All unmentioned
memory cells are preserved.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The initial checks enforce distinct live cells and their principal wire, so
they characterize an active pair. The old matching invariant implies that
the external boundary mates are distinct, are not removed principal ports,
and do not belong to any newly allocated record. Freshness follows from $h$.

For annihilation, Theorem~\ref{cdc:nt:thm:glue} gives exactly the surviving endpoint
matching and new loops. The reciprocal patches restore the involution at
every affected surviving endpoint. For a creation rule, endpoint relocation
preserves every old boundary incidence with its endpoint renamed to the
specified new principal. Equation \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:2.2} matches the remaining new ports
exactly once. Unused eraser auxiliaries are zero. The old records are cleared;
new records use fresh addresses; unrelated records are neither read for
path-search nor modified. These facts prove the storage invariant and the
claimed literal result. Equation \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.3} gives the correct scalar registers.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Resource bounds]\label{cdc:nt:prop:resources}
After $t$ successful steps,
\begin{equation}
 h_t\leq C_0+4t,\qquad n_t\leq C_0+2t,\qquad
                 \ell_t\leq\ell_0+2t.                               \label{cdc:nt:eq:6.4}
\end{equation}
For a length-$T$ trace with no final scan, the fixed log length is
\begin{equation}
                         L=4C_0+f+36T.                               \label{cdc:nt:eq:6.5}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
No rule creates more than four cells or increases the live count by more
than two. Equation \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:3.3} gives at most two new loops; the other rules give
none. Induction proves \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.4}. Initialization and the fixed access schedule
prove \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.5}. The loop increment bound is attained by a like-binary active
pair whose auxiliary matching equals its annihilation matching.
\end{proof}
The exact 36 is a deliberately uncomplicated memory-access upper bound. It
is not the number of arithmetic operations, residuals, or quantified
coordinates per interaction.

\wtag{} The bounds \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.4} are \cref{cdc:ew:cor:storage} (\cref{cdc:ic:sec:nets}); \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.5} is manuscript~14's own.

\subsection{The loop-sensitive quartic compilation theorem\srctag{14}}\label{cdc:nt:sec:main}
\subsubsection{Functional arithmetic circuits}
A \emph{functional quadratic circuit} is a system of degree-at-most-two
integer equations whose auxiliary tuple is unique for every permitted
source tuple. Straight-line addition and multiplication, Boolean gates,
normalized comparisons, fixed-divisor quotient/remainder, and selection
have such presentations. Appendix~\ref{cdc:nt:app:gadgets} supplies literal gadgets.

A finite branch is compiled by total deterministic computations on its branch
inputs and by selecting its outputs. Inactive branches receive fixed dummy
inputs when necessary. Their auxiliaries are then uniquely determined;
merely multiplying an arbitrary equation by an inactive flag is insufficient.
The per-step controller of \cref{cdc:nt:sec:machine} has only a fixed number of boundary
positions, type cases, and template slots, so it is such a circuit of constant
size, with constants independent of $C_0,f,T$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact quartic family for interaction combinators]\label{cdc:nt:thm:main}
Fix a valid explicitly labelled input net $N$, an external horizon $T$, and
one of the terminal conditions described in Section~\ref{cdc:nt:sec:terminal}.
There is an effective construction of a polynomial
\begin{equation}
                    P_{N,T}(\mathbf s,\mathbf z)\in\Z[\mathbf s,\mathbf z]
                    \quad\text{of degree at most }4                 \label{cdc:nt:eq:7.1}
\end{equation}
with these properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For a supplied ordered-pair schedule
$\mathbf s=(u_0,v_0,\ldots,u_{T-1},v_{T-1})$, there is a natural zero in
$\mathbf z$ if and only if it is a legal length-$T$ execution satisfying the
terminal condition.
\item Such an auxiliary zero is unique. Thus, when schedules are also
quantified, natural zeros are in bijection with the accepted scheduled
executions in the fresh-name convention.
\item The total number of coordinates, number of quadratic residuals, and
number of monomials in the sum-of-squares presentation are
$O(C_0+f+T)$ for the fixed six-rule system and fixed terminal-query type.
\item Every witness coordinate has bit length
\begin{equation}
 O\!\left((C_0+f+T+1)^2\log(C_0+f+T+2)
                     +\log(\ell_0+2)\right).                         \label{cdc:nt:eq:7.2}
\end{equation}
The constants do not depend on the particular input matching.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Unroll the fixed controller $T$ times and link its access triples into one
log. Initialize the fixed input layout by its prescribed writes. Add the
memory system of Theorem~\ref{cdc:nt:thm:memory} with caps \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.1}, and add the
scalar and terminal equations. All circuit nodes are separately named, so
no high-degree substitution is made. Let $R_1,\ldots,R_m$ be the resulting
quadratic residuals and set
\begin{equation}
                         P_{N,T}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}R_j^2.                 \label{cdc:nt:eq:7.3}
\end{equation}
This is an effective finite prescription, not an appeal to an unspecified
universal polynomial.

For soundness, a natural zero satisfies every residual. The memory theorem
makes every log read agree with the latest prior write to its address. The
input writes therefore establish the valid starting representation. Apply
Lemma~\ref{cdc:nt:lem:machine} successively. At each step the supplied pair is an
actual active pair, the controller performs the exact rule, and the stored
matching and loop count remain valid. The final checks give the required
terminal condition.

For completeness, execute any legal supplied schedule, write down its fixed
log and scalar registers, evaluate every functional circuit, and extend the
log by its canonical memory witness. Every residual vanishes.

For uniqueness, fix the input and schedule. Chronological induction forces
every read value, since all earlier writes and the initial memory are already
forced. The local deterministic controller forces the writes, scalars, and
its own auxiliary values. Hence the complete source log is forced. The
memory theorem then forces all its auxiliary coordinates. Fixed dummy
records and normalized branch gadgets remove any inactive choices.

The log length is \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.5}, plus a linear final scan when needed. The local
controller uses a constant number of circuit nodes per step; initialization
and terminal scanning use linearly many. The memory theorem is linear in
$L$, and each residual has a bounded number of terms. These facts give the
size claims. The largest arithmetic witnesses occur in the product chains;
apply Proposition~\ref{cdc:nt:prop:height} with the polynomial caps \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.1}.
Scalar loop values add only $O(\log(\ell_0+T+2))$ bits. Every other controller
register is a bounded pointer, a comparison gap, a small selector, or a
bounded number of arithmetic combinations of these. This proves \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:7.2}.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{A transparent, nonoptimized global ledger}
Let $G$ denote the number of private controller/scalar/gadget coordinates,
and $H$ the number of controller, initialization-link, and terminal residuals
in a chosen full assembler. Counting all $3L$ log fields as coordinates,
including those forced to constants, gives
\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{rcl}
\text{total coordinates, including schedules}&\leq&20L-4+2T+G,\\
\text{quadratic residuals}&=&17L-4+H.                                 
\end{array}\label{cdc:nt:eq:7.4}
\end{equation}
Here $G,H=O(C_0+f+T)$. The paper proves this and supplies the full finite
recipe, but does not report a measured numerical $G,H$ for an emitted
unknown-schedule interaction-net polynomial. Consequently \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:7.4} must not be
compared as a numerical universal-operation record with the repository's
separately audited fixed-universal polynomials.

\subsubsection{What the bijection does not quotient}
Choosing a different available active pair generally gives a different zero,
even if the computations commute or later reach isomorphic nets. The
bijection is with scheduled executions, not with normal forms, interleaving
classes, or observational equivalence classes. It removes artificial
auxiliary multiplicity and fresh-name choices; it does not remove semantic
scheduler choices. This limitation is especially important in a strongly
confluent substrate: confluence alone does not canonically identify the
arithmetic witnesses of different schedules.

\srcnote{\wtag{} Second presentation (source 13). Manuscript~13 compiles the same controller through its bounded-fanin controller lemma (\cref{cdc:ew:lem:controller}), with its own three-way comparison gadget \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:compare} (manuscript~14's is in \cref{cdc:nt:app:gadgets}), and a splice performed as a fixed access schedule. Its allocation reserves $C_0+4T$ cell slots and four transient boundary ports per step, as manuscript~14's layout \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.1} reserves $C_0+4T$ cell records. It adds a paid validation scan of a public dense input, coefficients of $O(\log S)$ bits by binary powering, a total witness-length bound, and the treatment of ``at most $T$'' steps.}

\subsection{Quadratic compilation of the finite controller\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:quadratic}

\subsubsection{Definitional gates and canonical branches}

The memory theorem certifies that reads and writes agree globally. It must
be combined with local equations saying that the proposed accesses really
come from the chosen interaction rule. This section makes explicit why
this can be done without increasing the degree or hiding a large circuit.

For natural values, addition and multiplication are represented by
$z-x-y=0$ and $z-xy=0$. Fixed affine address calculations are linear. A
finite list of alternatives uses natural selectors $b_1,\ldots,b_s$ with
$\sum b_i=1$; each is automatically zero or one. If desired, individual
Boolean equations can also be included. For a fixed alphabet and fixed
macro, $s$ is an absolute constant.

A useful total comparison gadget for $x,y\in\N$ has natural variables
$l,e,g,d_l,d_g$ and equations
\begin{align}
 l+e+g&=1,& e(x-y)&=0,\label{cdc:ew:eq:compare}\\
 l(y-x-1-d_l)&=0,& g(x-y-1-d_g)&=0,\notag\\
 (1-l)d_l&=0,&(1-g)d_g&=0.\notag
\end{align}
Exactly one of $x<y$, $x=y$, $x>y$ is possible, forcing the corresponding
selector and its unique gap. Inactive gaps are zero. Thus this is a
quadratic, uniquely extending comparison certificate. It can test pointer
equality, validity ranges, or the ordering $u<v$ of a scheduled pair.

A conditional linear equation $E=0$ is imposed as $bE=0$. One must not
blindly multiply a quadratic residual by $b$, which would raise its degree.
Instead introduce a definitional product gate for each nonlinear term,
then guard the resulting \emph{linear} equality. For example, to impose
$x y=z$ only when $b=1$, first define $p=xy$ unconditionally and then impose
$b(p-z)=0$. All residuals remain quadratic. Dead branch inputs, unused
slacks, and unused outputs are set to fixed canonical values; unconditional
gate outputs remain their uniquely computed values.

\begin{lemma}[Bounded-fanin controller compilation]\label{cdc:ew:lem:controller}
A fixed finite macro using a bounded number of memory accesses, affine
address operations, additions, multiplications and comparisons can be
translated into a bounded number of quadratic equations with boundedly
many monomials. For a deterministic macro and fixed input registers and
read values, its ancillary extension can be made unique. Repeating the
macro $t$ times produces $O(t)$ equations and variables.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Translate arithmetic instructions to definitional gates and comparisons to
\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:compare}. Translate the finite control alternatives with
selectors; their conditions force the selected branch uniquely. Use the
flatten-before-guard construction for nonlinear branch equations and
canonical values for unused local fields. Each instruction introduces
boundedly many variables and equations because both the instruction set
and each expression's fanin are fixed. Induction through the instruction
sequence proves both semantic correctness and unique extension. Repeating
this finite construction adds its constant costs once per macro.
\end{proof}

This lemma does not grant arbitrary unbounded arithmetic predicates for
free. Only the displayed finite operations and fixed control are allowed.
All long sums or products must themselves be represented by gates.

\subsubsection{A splice as a fixed access schedule}

Represent an inactive port by a zero mate value, and reserve one dummy
memory address with constant value zero. For a legal splice, read $p=m(a)$
and $q=m(b)$ by read-only events. A comparison determines whether $p=b$.
Always retire $a,b$ by writing zero. In the nonclosing branch, write $q$ at
$p$ and $p$ at $q$; in the closing branch, replace these two writes by
zero-preserving accesses to the dummy address. Increment the separate loop
counter by the closing bit.

This has a fixed maximum number of access slots. Crucially the two later
writes are conditional: writing to $p=b$ after retiring $b$ would revive a
retired port and be wrong. Canonical dummy accesses avoid this error while
keeping the number and timestamps of memory events fixed.

The valid-matching invariant guarantees the distinctness conditions in
Lemma~\ref{cdc:ew:lem:splice}. They may also be checked locally, at constant cost,
but no scan of the full graph is needed after each interaction. A
right-hand-side initialization writes its literal mate pairs into fresh
slots; erasure and type updates are likewise finite lists of writes.
Thus Proposition~\ref{cdc:ew:prop:macro} meets every hypothesis of
Lemma~\ref{cdc:ew:lem:controller}.

\subsection{The linear-description quartic compiler\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:compiler}

\subsubsection{Explicit allocation}

Let the input have cell identifiers $0,\ldots,C_0-1$ and $F$ free ports.
Fix a horizon $T$. Reserve
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:capacity}
 C_* = C_0+4T
\end{equation}
cell slots, with three possible port slots per cell. At step $t$, the four
possible new cell identifiers are
\begin{equation}
 C_0+4t,\ C_0+4t+1,\ C_0+4t+2,\ C_0+4t+3.
\end{equation}
Unused slots stay zero; erased cell identifiers are never reused. Reserve
four transient boundary ports per step, also never reused. The total port
capacity is
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:portcapacity}
 P_*=3C_*+F+4T=3C_0+16T+F.
\end{equation}
Use positive live-port addresses, with zero reserved for inactivity. A type
array records inactive, $\epsilon$, $\delta$ or $\gamma$. The mate array
records zero or a live partner. Static arrays can mark principal-port
addresses and distinguish cell slots, free ports and transient ports.
All these arrays together have
\begin{equation}
 A=O(1+C_0+F+T)
\end{equation}
addresses, with value bound $V=O(1+C_0+F+T)$. The isolated-loop counter is
kept separately, so an arbitrarily large supplied $\ell_0$ need not inflate
the pointer radix.

The scheduled pair at a real interaction is ordered $u_t<v_t$. Checks read
the types and principal mates, verify that both cells are live and paired
through their principal ports, and then choose the appropriate one of the
six literal rules. Fresh identifiers are assigned by the displayed formula,
not existentially selected from an unbounded supply.

\subsubsection{Input validation is paid for}

The public input is a dense typed-port representation, not a single encoded
natural number. Its types must be in the stated alphabet. Its live-port
domain must match those types and the designated free interface; every
inactive slot has zero mate value. For each live port $p$, read $q=m(p)$,
check that $q$ is a live, distinct port in range, and read $m(q)$ to verify
$m(q)=p$. Free-port and transient-slot conventions are checked as well.

This takes a constant number of local checks and accesses per allocated
slot, hence $O(1+C_0+F+T)$ in total. Input cells occupy the first $C_0$
slots; the remaining type slots and all future boundary slots are zero.
One may instead state a theorem on promised-valid inputs, but the bound
here includes validation, and malformed inputs have no certificate.

Once this invariant is established, Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:glue} proves its
preservation. A repeated graph-wide validity tableau is unnecessary.

\subsubsection{Exact terminal predicates}

The following predicates have distinct meanings and distinct encodings.

\paragraph{Agent-free.}
Maintain a live-cell counter initialized to $C_0$ and changed by the known
number created minus two at each real interaction. Require its final value
to be zero. Free-interface wires and isolated cycles may still be present.

\paragraph{Normal.}
All unordered pairs of agent types have a rule. Thus normality means there
is no principal--principal wire. Scan allocated cell slots once. For each
live cell, read its principal mate and a static principal-address flag;
require that flag to be zero. Validity ensures that a flagged mate really
is the principal port of a live cell. Inactive slots use dummy accesses.
The scan costs $O(C_*)$ accesses, not $O(C_*T)$.

\paragraph{Exact loop target.}
Require
\begin{equation}
 \ell_T=\ell_0+\sum_{\text{splice slots }j} b_j=\ell_{\mathrm{target}},
\end{equation}
where $b_j$ is the uniquely determined closing bit, and encode the sum by
prefix additions. It is often more economical to store just the accumulated
new-loop count, bounded by $2T$, and make the single final comparison with
$\ell_0$.

\paragraph{Exact labelled target.}
Compare final type and mate arrays to the supplied target arrays, one slot
at a time, together with the loop count. The target uses the same canonical
allocation convention. No uncharged isomorphism search is included.

These predicates may be combined, for example ``agent-free with exactly
two cyclic wires''. In the closed domain, ``agent-free with zero cycles''
is the completely empty net, whereas ``normal'' is substantially weaker.

\subsubsection{The compiler theorem}

\begin{remark}[Cycle-preserving bounded Diophantine compiler; manuscript~13's statement of \cref{cdc:nt:thm:main}]
\label{cdc:ew:thm:compiler}
Fix $C_0,F,T\in\N$ and one of the terminal predicates above, or a fixed
conjunction of them. Put $S=1+C_0+F+T$. There is an effectively constructed
integer polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ew:eq:compiler}
 P_{C_0,F,T}(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)
\end{equation}
with the following properties.

For every public dense input $\mathbf x$, including any supplied target
parameters, $P_{C_0,F,T}(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)=0$ has a solution
$\mathbf z\in\N^{k}$ exactly when the input is valid and has a sequence of
exactly $T$ legal interaction-combinator reductions satisfying the terminal
predicate. The polynomial has degree at most four, $k=O(S)$, $O(S)$ sparse
monomials and coefficients of $O(\log S)$ bits. It can be presented as the
sum of $O(S)$ squares of bounded-fanin quadratic residuals.

For each fixed legal ordered schedule $(u_t,v_t)_{t<T}$, the remaining
witnesses can be chosen canonically so that exactly one complete certificate
lies over that schedule. All isolated cyclic-wire counts are exact.

The largest noninput arithmetic witness can be bounded by $O(S^2\log S)$
bits and the total such witness length by $O(S^2\log^2(S+1))$. Supplied
unbounded loop counts remain parameters and are compared by a final linear
equation, rather than copied into every memory record.
\end{remark}

\wtag{} Manuscript~13's statement differs from \cref{cdc:nt:thm:main} in three respects, none of which makes either statement stronger in every respect. (i) Its input net is a tuple of public parameters of fixed dimensions $C_0,F$, validated inside the polynomial at linear cost; manuscript~14 fixes the input net in the compiler, $P_{N,T}$, and gives an ordinary-integer loader for fixed dimensions as a variant (\cref{cdc:nt:sec:terminal}). (ii) Its schedule is part of the witness $\mathbf z$ and uniqueness holds above each legal schedule; manuscript~14 makes the schedule a source tuple $\mathbf s$ with a unique zero above each legal one, and quantifies it to obtain the same bijection. (iii) It bounds coefficient lengths by $O(\log S)$ bits and the total witness length by $O(S^2\log^2(S+1))$; manuscript~14 bounds every coordinate by \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:7.2}. Both are paper constructions.

\begin{proof}[Second presentation (source 13): construction and completeness]
Allocate memory as in \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:capacity}--\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:portcapacity}, including
a dummy zero address and static metadata. Perform the input-validation
scan, $T$ copies of the interaction macro, and any final scan required by
the terminal predicate. Each interaction macro has a fixed maximum number
of access slots, using canonical dummy accesses in inactive branches.
Thus the complete chronological memory log has $m=O(S)$ events, with
$A=O(S)$ and $V=O(S)$.

Translate each local instruction and branch by
Lemma~\ref{cdc:ew:lem:controller}, and connect consecutive local registers by
linear equalities. Use Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:memory} once for the \emph{whole}
chronological access log. Its event fields, which were public parameters
in the standalone memory theorem, are now witnesses constrained by the
controller. Final contents used in the memory audit are witnesses unless
the chosen target supplies them; either way the actual deterministic
history fixes them. Add the terminal equations and sum all residual squares.

Given a valid reducing history with the chosen schedule, execute the exact
pointer macros. Proposition~\ref{cdc:ew:prop:macro} supplies precisely its true
successive nets and loop increments. Fill in the true access records,
local registers, branch selectors and final arrays. The memory theorem
supplies the unique sorted record list and gate values. All residuals
vanish, so the polynomial vanishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second presentation (source 13): soundness and canonicality]
Suppose the polynomial vanishes on natural witnesses. Every residual is
zero. The memory theorem implies that every certified read obtains the
latest certified write to that address, starting with the designated input
array. Input-validation residuals therefore establish a genuine initial
net. Local controller residuals select a live principal pair and implement
the appropriate literal rule. By induction over interaction macros and
Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:glue}, the certified arrays are the actual arrays after
exactly the chosen reductions, including every closed wire. The final
residuals impose the stated predicate on that actual final net.

For fixed input and schedule, execution is deterministic. Fresh allocation,
branch selectors, dummy records, comparison gaps and local gates use the
canonical conventions of Section~\ref{cdc:ew:sec:quadratic}. Thus the chronological
log, final arrays and loop increments are forced. The unique-extension
part of Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:memory} forces all remaining witnesses. This proves
uniqueness over a fixed schedule, not uniqueness of the schedule itself.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second presentation (source 13): size, coefficient length and height]
There are $O(S)$ accesses and local instructions. Each produces only a
bounded number of variables and bounded-fanin quadratic residuals. Input
and final scans also cost $O(S)$. The global memory certificate has
$L=2A+m=O(S)$ and $U=AHV^2=S^{O(1)}$. Its powering gates avoid printing
$U^L$ as a coefficient. The resulting constants are bounded by fixed powers
of $S$, so their bit lengths are $O(\log S)$.

Every quadratic residual has a constant number of monomials; its square
therefore has a constant number as well. Summing $O(S)$ such squares gives
the asserted sparse polynomial, including the bound on its joint degree
in public inputs and witnesses. Prefix gates are used for all long sums.
Finally Proposition~\ref{cdc:ew:prop:height}, with $L=O(S)$ and $\log U=O(\log S)$,
gives the witness-height bounds. Pointer values, local registers and
range slacks are smaller. Store new-loop counts rather than repeated
copies of a potentially huge $\ell_0$, as specified above.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exactly versus at most $T$]
The theorem counts exactly $T$ real interactions. To represent ``at most
$T$'', add a forced monotone stopped flag. Before stopping, slots execute
real interactions; after stopping, every slot is a canonical no-op. Require
the terminal predicate at the stopping boundary. This is still a linear
bounded family. Its canonicality statement is relative to the selected
stopping time as well as the real schedule, unless stopping is required at
the first occurrence of a locally decidable terminal predicate.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Terminal predicates and bounded native input\srctag{14}}\label{cdc:nt:sec:terminal}
\subsubsection{Queries with no final graph scan}
The terminal conditions $n_T=0$ and $\ell_T=k$ express agent-free execution
with exactly $k$ bare loops. Either equality may be used alone. For a closed
net, the conjunction $n_T=0$, $\ell_T=0$ expresses the completely empty
result. For an open net, $n_T=0$ still permits a matching of free ports; that
matching is present in memory and has not been erased.

For $T>0$, an execution ending agent-free cannot have become agent-free at
an earlier step, because an agent-free net has no active pair. Thus exact
length-$T$ agent-free traces already have the appropriate first-hit property.
No extra halting-padding witnesses are needed for this query.

\subsubsection{Normality and exact labelled targets}
To check normality, scan the reserved cell records at the final memory
state. At every live principal port, determine whether its mate is the
principal port of another live cell. Reject precisely that case. Unused
slots and free-port identifiers are distinguished by their fixed ranges.
Range comparisons and quotient/remainder modulo three are functional
constant-size gadgets. A scan of $O(C_0+T)$ records is therefore sufficient.

An exact labelled target is checked by scanning all reserved cell and
free-port mate slots and comparing them with the specified target layout,
and by checking the scalar loop count. This costs $O(C_0+f+T)$ accesses.
Equality is literal in the declared naming convention. An unlabelled target
requires a different interface; guessing a graph isomorphism can introduce
multiple witnesses, so it is not silently substituted for this comparison.

An at-most-$T$ family can also use an explicitly selected stopping time and
fixed dummy steps thereafter. The selected time is part of the represented
finite execution. To avoid duplicate encodings, its activity mask and every
padded slot must be determined by that time, not chosen independently.
The exact-horizon theorem does not need this extension.

\subsubsection{An ordinary integer can load a bounded explicit net}
The main theorem takes a valid explicit net as fixed input to the compiler.
This is not a paid loader for an arbitrary integer into one fixed universal
net. There is, however, a straightforward bounded native-input variant.

Fix $C_0,f$ and use an initial port layout with $C_0$ reserved cells. Let
$K=4C_0+f$ and $D=3C_0+f+4$. Pack the type and mate entries as digits
$d_0,\ldots,d_{K-1}<D$ of an ordinary input integer $x$. With $x_0=x$, use
\begin{equation}
 x_i=Dx_{i+1}+d_i,\qquad d_i+\bar d_i=D-1,
 \qquad x_K=0.                                                       \label{cdc:nt:eq:8.1}
\end{equation}
Every digit, suffix, and complement is unique. This costs $O(K)$ variables
and equations; the bit cost of the suffixes is bounded by the supplied input
length. If $K=0$, the only empty-table code is $x=0$.

Validate the type codes, zero unused eraser slots, and the involutive,
fixed-point-free pairing on exactly the live and free ports. The reciprocal
pairing check can be performed by reads of the initialized mate array:
for each actual port $p$, read its supplied mate $q$, verify that $q$ is an
actual distinct port, and read the mate at $q$ to check that it equals $p$.
These tests cost linearly many accesses. An invalid encoding is rejected,
not repaired. Remap initial free-port identifiers from $3C_0+i+1$ to
$3(C_0+4T)+i+1$ by a range-controlled affine operation before using the
horizon-dependent layout.

This gives a uniform arithmetic interface for fixed input dimensions and
external horizon, with unique decoding. It does not make the dimensions,
horizon, universal interpreter, or arbitrary source-language translator
free of arithmetic cost.

\wtag{} The transfer to other fixed interaction systems is proved by both manuscripts: manuscript~14's \cref{cdc:nt:thm:general}, printed first, with the count \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:9.1} of partial matchings on $r$ positions, and manuscript~13's \cref{cdc:ew:cor:general}, printed after it as a remark with its proof. For port graphs with reciprocal links and bare loops it is the adapter that Part~X's bounded-local graph transfer (\cref{cdc:nh:thm:graph}) leaves to be proved (the subsection on interaction systems in \cref{cdc:nh:sec:graphs}); it is proved here directly and is not claimed as new beside \cref{cdc:nh:thm:graph}.

\subsection{Extension to other fixed interaction systems\srctag{14}}
\begin{theorem}[Fixed-rule finite-interface transfer]\label{cdc:nt:thm:general}
Consider a fixed finite interaction-net signature and finite rule table.
Assume a rule removes an active pair, has a fixed finite auxiliary interface,
and replaces it with a fixed finite net having the same interface, possibly
including a fixed number of bare loops. Then bounded scheduled reductions
of explicit inputs have witness-faithful quartic families of size linear in
the explicit input and external horizon. Bare loops are preserved exactly.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $r$ be the maximum number of old auxiliary boundary positions, and $b$
the maximum number of newly created cells. These are constants of the fixed
system. On $r$ positions the number of partial matchings is
\begin{equation}
 I_r=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}
                   \frac{r!}{2^k k!(r-2k)!}.                          \label{cdc:nt:eq:9.1}
\end{equation}
For each rule and each pattern, precompute the suppression of the finite
temporary wiring. Lemma~\ref{cdc:nt:lem:local} applies with $r$ in place of four:
the only internal vertices are boundary positions. The output is a fixed
routing of the ordered external mates and newly created ports, together with
a fixed loop increment plus any loops already in the template.

A finite selector circuit chooses this precomputed case from exact partner
comparisons. Retain arbitrary external identifiers as data, rather than
including their values in the finite table. The number of reads, writes,
comparisons, and arithmetic gates per interaction is constant for the fixed
system. The storage layout generalizes \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:6.2} with a fixed number of slots
per cell, fresh allocation uses at most $bT$ new identifiers, and the memory
certificate and chronological uniqueness proof apply unchanged.
\end{proof}

The dependence on the rule signature is not claimed small: enumeration of
$I_r$ can be expensive when arity varies. The transfer theorem is uniform
in inputs and horizons for a \emph{fixed} rule table, not a linear-time theorem
for arbitrarily large rules supplied as data.

This is a route to arithmetic certificates for esoteric graph-rewriting
languages that compile into bounded-interface interaction systems. It still
requires an exact source-to-net translation and a statement of which source
observations that translation preserves. The substrate name alone is not a
proof of that interface.

\subsection{Other finite local graph-rewriting substrates\srctag{13}}

\begin{remark}[Bounded local interaction systems; manuscript~13's statement of \cref{cdc:nt:thm:general}]\label{cdc:ew:cor:general}
Fix a finite interaction-system signature of bounded arity and a finite
rule table whose right-hand sides have boundedly many cells, boundary ports
and isolated cyclic wires. A history of $T$ rule applications from input
size $N_0$ has a cycle-preserving quadratic certificate with
$O(N_0+T)$ variables and residuals, and hence a quartic sum-of-squares
certificate of that size. For a fixed schedule and fixed rule choice, the
ancillary witnesses can be canonical.
\end{remark}

\begin{proof}[Second presentation (source 13)]
The maximum arity and right-hand-side sizes are constants because the rule
table is fixed. Replace the constants four and three in the allocation by
those maxima. Each application is still a bounded literal right-hand side
followed by boundedly many boundary splices. Any intrinsic right-hand-side
cyclic wires contribute a fixed known increment to the loop counter. The
same input scan, local compilation and global memory theorem apply.
\end{proof}

This corollary concerns local port-matching rewrites. It does not automatically
cover a rule that tests global graph connectivity, identifies arbitrarily
large subgraphs, or performs an unbounded graph search in one ``step''.
Such operations require their own paid certificates. An esoteric syntax
alone is not a source of arithmetic savings; the sizes of its controller,
mutable memory and input interface are the relevant quantities.

\section{A second route: permutation orbits and an implemented scheduled compiler}\label{cdc:ic:sec:orbits}
