\subsection{From wire components to permutation orbits\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:permutation}
Define the permutation
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:sigma}
\sigma=\alpha\circ\beta,\qquad \sigma(v)=\alpha(\beta(v)).
\end{equation}
Let $\cyc(\sigma)$ denote its number of orbits, including fixed points.

\begin{theorem}[Path--cycle dictionary]\label{cdc:ng:thm:dictionary}
For the gluing data \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:alphabeta}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Each path component gives one $\sigma$-orbit. That orbit contains its
      two boundary endpoints and no other boundary vertices.
\item Each boundary-free cycle component gives two $\sigma$-orbits.
\item Two boundary ports are paired after suppression if and only if they
      belong to the same $\sigma$-orbit.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, if $L$ is the number of newly created cyclic wires, then
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:loopformula}
\boxed{\quad \cyc(\sigma)=\frac{|B|}{2}+2L,\qquad
L=\frac{\cyc(\sigma)-|B|/2}{2}.\quad}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A boundary-free component is an alternating cycle of $\alpha$ edges and
$\beta$ edges. On it, $\sigma$ moves two edges at a time. The vertices in
each of the two parity classes form one orbit, so there are exactly two.
This remains true for a two-edge cycle: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the same
transposition, and their product has two fixed points.

For a path, label its consecutive vertices $v_0,\ldots,v_{2q+1}$ so that
$v_0,v_{2q+1}$ are the boundary points. Its first and last edges are
$\alpha$ edges; its intervening edges alternate. Applying $\sigma$ travels
along one parity class toward an endpoint, uses the fixed-point action of
$\beta$ there to reverse to the other parity class, and returns along it.
Thus all vertices of the path belong to one orbit. In the shortest case,
the path is just one $\alpha$ edge between two boundary points, and
$\sigma$ is their transposition.

All components are of these two forms. Their vertex sets are invariant under
$\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\sigma$. There are $|B|/2$ path components; each
contributes one orbit, and each of the $L$ cyclic components contributes two.
This proves the formula and the endpoint criterion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Neither $\cyc(\sigma)$ alone nor an unweighted connected-component count
has the required meaning. Boundary paths count once, while closed alternating
cycles count twice. Omitting the factor of two in \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:loopformula}
already miscounts a single two-edge cycle.
\end{remark}

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 472-587 ----
\subsection{Canonical, single-fold certificates for permutation cycles\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:orbit}

\subsubsection{Fixed successor indices}
Fix a permutation $\sigma$ of $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. For each $i$, introduce
natural variables $r_i,d_i,h_i,e_i$ and impose
\begin{align}
e_i(e_i-1)&=0,\label{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-bit}\\
r_i+(1-e_i)(h_i+1)&=i,\label{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-min}\\
e_i h_i&=0,\label{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-h}\\
r_i&=r_{\sigma(i)},\label{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-r}\\
d_i&=(1-e_i)(d_{\sigma(i)}+1).\label{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-d}
\end{align}
There are $4n$ variables and $5n$ quadratic equations.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical orbit witness]\label{cdc:ng:thm:orbit}
For every $\sigma$, equations \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-bit}--\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-d}
have exactly one solution in $\N^{4n}$. In that solution, on every orbit $C$,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:canonical}
\begin{aligned}
r_i&=\min C,\\
e_i&=\mathbf 1_{\{i=\min C\}},\\
h_i&=\begin{cases}0,&i=\min C,\\i-\min C-1,&i\ne\min C,\end{cases}\\
d_i&=\min\{k\ge0:\sigma^k(i)=\min C\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In particular $\sum_i e_i=\cyc(\sigma)$, and all coordinates are at most $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The Boolean equation gives $e_i\in\{0,1\}$. The $r$ equations make $r_i$
constant on each orbit. Suppose an orbit had $e_i=0$ at all its vertices.
Its distance equations would give $d_i=d_{\sigma(i)}+1$. Summing around
that orbit yields $0=|C|$, an impossibility. Thus each orbit has a vertex
$j$ with $e_j=1$.

At such a vertex, \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-min} gives $r_j=j$. A second vertex $k$
in the same orbit with $e_k=1$ would give $k=r_k=r_j=j$, so the root is
unique. At every other vertex $i$ the same equation gives $r_i<h_i+r_i+1=i$.
Since $r_i=j$, this proves $j<i$ for every $i\ne j$ in the orbit. Hence
$j=\min C$.

Equation \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-h} forces $h_j=0$ at the root. At the nonroots,
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-min} determines $h_i=i-j-1$. The root distance is zero by
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-d}; working backwards along the orbit uniquely determines
every other distance and gives exactly the forward distance to $j$.
Thus every solution must be \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:canonical}. Direct substitution verifies
that these values do form a natural solution. The bounds follow from the
orbit length and the range of labels.
\end{proof}

The proof establishes uniqueness over the entire unbounded natural orthant,
not just inside a bounded search box. The distance variables prevent a fictitious
root label outside the orbit. The strict-gap equation selects the minimum root,
and the reset equation $e_i h_i=0$ prevents a free slack at that root.

\begin{example}
For $\sigma=(1\,3\,2)(4\,5)$ the unique coordinates are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$i$&$\sigma(i)$&$r_i$&$d_i$&$h_i$&$e_i$\\
\midrule
1&3&1&0&0&1\\
2&1&1&1&0&0\\
3&2&1&2&1&0\\
4&5&4&0&0&1\\
5&4&4&1&0&0\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The sum of the root bits is two, as required.
\end{example}

\subsubsection{Successor selection without raising the degree}
In a compiler the wiring is not a fixed coefficient table: it may be unknown
intermediate data. Let $S$ be the permutation matrix of $\sigma$ in row-successor
convention, so $S_{ij}=1$ exactly when $j=\sigma(i)$. Then
$r_{\sigma(i)}=\sum_jS_{ij}r_j$, a quadratic expression in input entries and
witnesses. Directly substituting $\sum_jS_{ij}d_j$ into
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-d} would produce a cubic expression. Introduce one additional
natural variable $s_i$ per vertex and replace the last two equations by
\begin{align}
r_i&=\sum_j S_{ij}r_j,\label{cdc:ng:eq:selector-r}\\
s_i&=\sum_j S_{ij}d_j,\label{cdc:ng:eq:selector-s}\\
d_i&=(1-e_i)(s_i+1).\label{cdc:ng:eq:selector-d}
\end{align}

\begin{corollary}[Selector form]\label{cdc:ng:cor:selector}
For every natural permutation matrix $S$, equations
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-bit}--\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-h} and
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:selector-r}--\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:selector-d} have exactly one solution.
They use $5n$ natural witnesses and $6n$ residuals, each of total degree at
most two in $S$ and the witnesses. The coordinates are those of
\cref{cdc:ng:thm:orbit}, together with $s_i=d_{\sigma(i)}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Since $S$ is a permutation matrix, its selected sums equal the corresponding
successor coordinates. The new $s_i$ values are uniquely determined, and the
remaining system is exactly that of \cref{cdc:ng:thm:orbit}.
\end{proof}

If $S$ is an arbitrary natural input matrix rather than already known to be a
permutation matrix, add its $n$ row-sum and $n$ column-sum equations. They
force $S$ to be a permutation matrix without further witnesses. In our
interaction compiler, that fact is instead inherited from a perfect matching
and a fixed interface involution.

\subsubsection{Why these equations are not merely a guessed spanning forest}
An existential spanning forest normally admits many choices of root, parent,
and traversal order. Those choices create extra polynomial zeros even when
the underlying computation is deterministic. Here the directed orbit is
already given, its root is forced to be its least label, and every distance
is forced by the orbit. There is no residual choice of a tree or traversal.
The construction is therefore suitable for witness-faithful compilation rather
than only for existential correctness.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 589-654 ----
\subsection{Loop-exact gluing as a quartic relation\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:gluing}
Let $B$ be the surviving boundary and let $M'$ be a proposed perfect matching
on it. With fixed successor indices, impose \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-bit}--\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-d},
then impose
\begin{align}
r_u-r_v&=0 &&\text{for every }\{u,v\}\in M',\label{cdc:ng:eq:target-fixed}\\
\sum_i e_i+2\ell_0-2\ell_1-|B|/2&=0.\label{cdc:ng:eq:target-loops}
\end{align}
All vertex names in the orbit equations are their fixed positions in the
ordered temporary vertex set; they need not coincide with global port identities.

\begin{theorem}[Single-fold gluing certificate]\label{cdc:ng:thm:gluing}
Fix valid gluing data $(V,\alpha,\beta,B)$ and a target boundary matching $M'$.
The sum of squares of the residuals in
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-bit}--\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:orbit-d},
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:target-fixed}, and \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:target-loops} has degree at most four
and uses $4|V|$ witnesses and
\[
5|V|+|B|/2+1
\]
residuals. For given natural $\ell_0,\ell_1$, it has exactly one natural zero
if gluing produces $M'$ and changes the loop count from $\ell_0$ to $\ell_1$;
otherwise it has none.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A sum of squares of integers vanishes exactly when every summand vanishes.
By \cref{cdc:ng:thm:orbit}, the orbit coordinates are unique and identify actual
orbits. By \cref{cdc:ng:thm:dictionary}, every boundary orbit contains exactly two
boundary vertices. Thus the equal-root constraints for the proposed perfect
matching force precisely the real output matching. Equation
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:target-loops} is exactly \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:loopformula}, with the old loop
count carried through. Conversely, the actual output and the canonical orbit
coordinates satisfy all these equations.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Both endpoint matchings may be arithmetic data}
Let $A$ be a symmetric natural matching matrix for $\alpha$, and suppose
$\beta$ is fixed. The successor-selector matrix requires no new matrix
multiplication:
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:rowpermute}
S_{ij}=A_{\beta(i),j}.
\end{equation}
This is just a permutation of rows. Use the selector certificate of
\cref{cdc:ng:cor:selector}. For an unknown or parameter-valued output matching
$W'$ on $B$, replace \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:target-fixed} by
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:target-variable}
W'_{uv}(r_u-r_v)=0\qquad (u<v,\ u,v\in B),
\end{equation}
and enforce the row-sum matching constraints on $W'$.

All equations remain quadratic. There are $5|V|$ orbit witnesses and
$6|V|+\binom{|B|}{2}+1$ gluing residuals, in addition to matching validation.
The natural zeros are still unique for fixed valid endpoint matchings.
This is the form used by the implementation.

\subsubsection{A separately quadratic alternative}
The Boolean residual $e_i(e_i-1)$ contains a repeated variable. An optional
variant replaces it by $e_i+f_i-1=0$, with $e_i,f_i\in\N$, and replaces
$1-e_i$ in the other equations by $f_i$. Every residual is then multiaffine:
no variable appears with exponent greater than one within an individual
residual. There is one extra uniquely determined witness per vertex.
Consequently the resulting quartic is of degree at most two in each individual
coordinate and is convex in each coordinate separately, with the others fixed.
This is a structural refinement, not a claim of joint convexity or an
implemented optimization of the exported example.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 656-821 ----
\subsection{The all-six-rule trace compiler\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:compiler}

\subsubsection{Static lifetime data and dynamic matching data}
Fix an initial type-labelled set of agents, a fixed free-port set, and a
positive-length schedule
\[
\mathcal S=((a_0,b_0),\ldots,(a_{T-1},b_{T-1})).
\]
Require $a_t<b_t$ and require both identities to be live at the corresponding
stage. Their types determine the unique rule template. The allocator starts
above the largest initial identity and assigns consecutive fresh identities
in a prescribed template order. It never reuses an identity.

This produces the successive agent sets and their types without examining any
wire. A schedule that consumes a nonexistent or already deleted agent is
rejected syntactically. A schedule that selects two live but unconnected
principal ports is \emph{not} rejected syntactically; the polynomial must rule
it out.

Write $P_t$ for the number of ports of configuration $t$, including free ports.
For $1\le t<T$, introduce one natural variable $W^{(t)}_{uv}$ for every
unordered pair of distinct live ports, and a natural loop-count variable
$\ell_t$. Use the same scalar for the symmetric matrix entries and set the
diagonal to zero. The full matrices $W^{(0)}$ and $W^{(T)}$, and loop counts
$\ell_0,\ell_T$, are endpoint parameters. Validate every state by the row-sum
equations \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:matching}.

\subsubsection{One step, without arithmetic indirection}
For step $t$, impose the active-pair residual
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:active}
W^{(t)}_{(a_t,0),(b_t,0)}-1=0.
\end{equation}
Remove these two principal ports. The remaining old matching is disjointly
united with the fixed replacement matching; call its matrix $A^{(t)}$.
Every entry of $A^{(t)}$ is either an entry of $W^{(t)}$ or a constant $0$ or
$1$. The row-sum constraints and \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:active} ensure that this really is
a perfect matching after the principal row and column removal.

Create the fixed interface involution $\beta_t$ described in
\cref{cdc:ng:sec:nets}. Let $N_t$ be the size of this temporary vertex set. Impose
its $5N_t$-variable selector certificate using
$S^{(t)}_{ij}=A^{(t)}_{\beta_t(i),j}$. Finally impose
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:target-variable} for $W^{(t+1)}$ and
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:target-loops} for $\ell_t,\ell_{t+1}$.

This explicitly pays for dynamic wire selection: the sums selecting $r$ and
$d$ contain matching variables multiplied by orbit variables. There is no
unaccounted-for ``array lookup'' in the proof. Its cost is dense rather than
asymptotically optimal, but it is fully present.

\begin{theorem}[Loop-exact scheduled compilation]\label{cdc:ng:thm:compiler}
For every syntactically valid positive-length lifetime schedule $\mathcal S$,
the construction above effectively produces an integer polynomial
\[
Q_{\mathcal S}(W^{(0)},\ell_0,W^{(T)},\ell_T;\mathbf z)
   =\sum_{j=1}^{R} f_j^2
\]
with each $f_j$ of total degree at most two. For fixed natural endpoint data:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item a natural zero exists exactly when the endpoint matrices are valid
matchings and the specified sequence of $T$ interaction-combinator steps
transforms the initial net into the exact target net, including cyclic wires;
\item whenever a zero exists, the complete natural witness tuple $\mathbf z$
is unique.
\end{enumerate}
The compiler treats all six rules and does not use MRDP as a compilation step.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose first that the endpoint nets and the scheduled trace are valid.
Supply each actual intermediate matching and actual intermediate loop count.
For every step, supply the unique canonical orbit certificate of its temporary
matching. The rule construction, active-pair equation, output matching
constraints, and loop equation all hold. Thus every residual vanishes.

Conversely suppose all residuals vanish. The natural row-sum equations force
all displayed matrices to be perfect matchings. Equation \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:active}
forces the selected principal pair to be an actual redex. Because the template
was constructed from the actual types in the lifetime ledger, the temporary
matching and interface involution describe exactly the correct rule in exactly
that context. The selector certificate is therefore a certificate for a true
permutation. By \cref{cdc:ng:thm:gluing} and its selector extension, the next matching
and loop count are exactly the true result. Induction over $t$ gives the entire
scheduled computation and its stated target.

For uniqueness, fix the initial data and schedule. A rule at a specified active
pair has a unique result with the chosen allocator. Inductively, every
intermediate matching and loop count is forced. Every step's orbit coordinates
are then forced by \cref{cdc:ng:cor:selector}. These are all the existential variables,
so the complete tuple is unique.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Exact resource ledger}
No witnesses are used for agent types, principal-port identities, or template
selection because the lifetime schedule and its type ledger are structural
inputs to this compiler. No witnesses are hidden in the matrix notation:
only upper-triangular matching entries are stored.

\begin{corollary}[Literal counts]\label{cdc:ng:cor:counts}
For $T\ge1$, the compiler uses exactly
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:variables}
\boxed{\quad V=5\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}N_t
       +\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\binom{P_t}{2}+(T-1)\quad}
\end{equation}
existential variables, and exactly
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ng:eq:residuals}
\boxed{\quad R=\sum_{t=0}^{T}P_t+2T+6\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}N_t
       +\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\binom{P_{t+1}}{2}\quad}
\end{equation}
residuals in its literal, unpruned construction. The number of endpoint scalar
parameters is $\binom{P_0}{2}+\binom{P_T}{2}+2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first term of \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:variables} counts the five orbit coordinates per
temporary vertex. The second counts intermediate matching matrices; the last
counts intermediate loop scalars. Equation \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:residuals} counts,
respectively, state row sums, one active-pair and one loop equation per step,
six orbit equations per temporary vertex, and every output-pair implication.
Endpoint loop scalars are parameters, not witnesses. Some residuals can become
identically zero or duplicate after specialization, but the displayed ledger
is the literal exporter count before such pruning.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Rule & New agents & $P_{t+1}-P_t$ & $N_t-P_t$ & New loops\\
\midrule
$\varepsilon\varepsilon$ &0&$-2$&$-2$&0\\
$\gamma\varepsilon$, $\delta\varepsilon$ &2&$-2$&$2$&0\\
$\gamma\gamma$, $\delta\delta$ &0&$-6$&$2$&0, 1, or 2\\
$\gamma\delta$ &4&$6$&$14$&0\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\wtag{} The bounds on $C_t$, on the number of allocated identities and on $\ell_t$ are \cref{cdc:ew:cor:storage}; the bounds on $P_t$ and $N_t$ and the size estimate are manuscript~15's own.

\begin{proposition}[Growth and witness-height bounds]\label{cdc:ng:prop:growth}
For an initial net with $C_0$ agents and $F$ free ports,
\[
C_t\le C_0+2t,\qquad P_t\le3C_0+6t+F,\qquad N_t\le P_t+14.
\]
At most $C_0+4T$ distinct agent identities are allocated through $T$ steps.
Moreover,
\[
\ell_0\le\ell_t\le\ell_0+2t.
\]
Thus the witness and residual counts are $O(T(C_0+T+F)^2)$. Every intermediate
matching entry is a bit, every orbit coordinate is at most $N_t$, and every
intermediate loop coordinate is at most $\ell_0+2T$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The rule table gives the agent and port increments and the maximum of four
fresh agents per step. A mixed or erasing rule joins every old auxiliary
through a replacement interface to a surviving new principal port. Therefore
no internal component can close in these rules. The eraser--eraser rule has
no internal joins. Only binary annihilation can produce closed components;
there are just two replacement wires, and every such component uses at least
one of them. Hence at most two loops are added. The remaining claims follow
from the explicit ledger and \cref{cdc:ng:thm:orbit}.
\end{proof}

These estimates count witnesses and residuals, not a minimal arithmetic circuit
for their evaluation. The selector sums can have $O(N_t^2)$ monomials across
a stage. We make no comparison with the repository's optimized fixed universal
operation counts: these are different objects and different resource measures.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 823-865 ----
\subsection{Unknown schedules, multiplicity, and the fixed-arity boundary\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:boundary}

\subsubsection{A finite disjunction can remain quartic and witness-faithful}
For a fixed horizon and initial type ledger, there are finitely many lifetime
schedules. For a fixed labelled target shape, discard schedules ending in the
wrong agent ledger. The remaining branches use common endpoint parameters
$x$, with disjoint witness vectors $z^{(s)}$.

Each residual in the compiler has the form
\[
f_{s,j}(x,z)=c_{s,j}(x)+g_{s,j}(x,z),
\]
where $c_{s,j}$ is affine in the endpoint parameters, $g_{s,j}(x,0)=0$, and
$f_{s,j}$ has total degree at most two. The absence of a pure quadratic
parameter term follows by inspection: the nonlinear terms are parameter--witness
products or products of witness coordinates.

\wtag{} Setting the witnesses of inactive branches to fixed values, so that the gated residuals vanish and the active branch is unchanged, is the mechanism of Part~X's guarded quadratization (\cref{cdc:nh:thm:gating}); manuscript~15 applies it to retained schedules and claims no novelty for it.

\begin{proposition}[One zero per successful schedule]\label{cdc:ng:prop:disjunction}
Introduce a natural branch bit $b_s$ for every retained schedule and impose
\begin{align*}
b_s(b_s-1)&=0,&\sum_s b_s&=1,\\
(1-b_s)z^{(s)}_i&=0,&
b_s c_{s,j}(x)+g_{s,j}(x,z^{(s)})&=0.
\end{align*}
The sum of squares of these residuals is quartic. For fixed endpoints its
natural zeros are in bijection with successful retained schedules.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Exactly one branch bit is one. All witnesses in inactive branches are zero,
so their gated residuals vanish automatically. The active branch reduces to
its original equations and has one witness exactly when its scheduled trace
is valid, by \cref{cdc:ng:thm:compiler}. The branch bit itself distinguishes different
successful schedules. Every displayed residual is quadratic because $c$ is
affine and $g$ already has total degree at most two.
\end{proof}

This is an existence construction, not an efficient schedule selector. The
number of branches can be exponential in the horizon. The archive implements
the practical fixed-schedule compiler, not an all-schedules disjunction
exporter. The zero-step case is simply endpoint equality and can be handled
separately; a length-at-most-$T$ construction includes the finite family of
lengths $0,\ldots,T$ with the same gating method.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 887-907 ----
\subsubsection{A finite certificate can nevertheless prove an infinite execution}
\begin{proposition}[Explicit lasso up to renaming]\label{cdc:ng:prop:lasso}
Suppose a nonempty scheduled trace takes a net $N$ to a net $N'$ with the same
loop count and an explicitly given type- and port-order-preserving isomorphism
$N'\cong N$ that fixes free-port labels. Then there is an infinite reduction
from $N$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Interaction rules depend on types, ordered port incidences, and freshness, not
on the numerical values of agent names. Transport the given finite trace
through the isomorphism, choosing fresh identities above all those already
used. This yields another copy of the trace from $N'$. Repeat inductively.
The positive trace length makes the concatenation infinite.
\end{proof}

An explicit endpoint renaming can be imposed by linear equalities between the
corresponding endpoint matching entries and loop counts. Combining these with
our quartic compiler certifies this sufficient condition for nontermination.
It is not claimed that every infinite computation admits such a finite lasso,
nor that the existence of one infinite execution decides every normalization
question.

\wtag{} The lasso is a finite certificate of nontermination for interaction nets. It is related to, not a case of, Part~XII's criterion for infinite periodic instruction tails (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:infinite}), which concerns priority programs; and it is a sufficient condition only, as manuscript~15 says. Infinite behaviour is the subject of the neighbouring report \emph{liveness-beyond-halting}.

\subsection{Worked examples: the exported quartic and a repeatable net\srctag{15}}
\subsubsection{The exported parametric quartic}
Give the agents identities $0,1,2,3$ and choose schedule
$((0,1),(2,3))$. The endpoint target has no agents and two cyclic wires.
The compiler is generated from the agent types and schedule \emph{before}
any input wire values are supplied. It therefore produces the same polynomial
for both initial matchings.

The configuration port counts are $(12,6,0)$, and the two temporary vertex
counts are $(14,8)$. Equations \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:variables}--\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:residuals} give
\begin{align*}
V&=5(14+8)+\binom62+1=126,\\
R&=(12+6+0)+4+6(14+8)+\binom62+\binom02=169.
\end{align*}
There are $\binom{12}{2}+2=68$ endpoint parameters: 66 initial matching
entries and the initial and final loop counts. The empty target has no
matching-entry parameters.

The archive contains all 169 residual polynomials and all coordinates of the
unique witness for $\mathcal A$. Its sum of squares evaluates to exactly zero.
For $\mathcal B$, the second scheduled pair is not active, so the theorem
implies that no natural witness exists. Merely changing the initial parameters
of the saved $\mathcal A$ witness to those of $\mathcal B$ produces the positive
value $332$; this is a useful implementation check, not the proof of
nonexistence of every alternative witness.

\subsubsection{A four-step repeatable net}
Consider agents $0:\delta$, $1:\gamma$, $2:\varepsilon$, $3:\varepsilon$
with wires
\[
(0,0)(1,0),\quad(0,1)(2,0),\quad
(0,2)(1,1),\quad(1,2)(3,0).
\]
This is the numbered-port version of the familiar repeating interaction pattern
illustrated by Lafont \cite[Fig.~3]{lafont}. With our fresh-name convention,
a checked four-step schedule is
\[
(0,1),\quad(2,6),\quad(3,5),\quad(9,10).
\]
The resulting ordered-port net is isomorphic to the input, with no cyclic
wires. Its four-step certificate has 505 existential variables and 650
quadratic residuals. The exact initial and terminal wires and the schedule
are in the receipt. By \cref{cdc:ng:prop:lasso}, the finite calculation establishes
an infinite reduction after repeating the renaming pattern.

\srcnote{\wtag{} The limitations stated by the three manuscripts, each in its own words: a fixed horizon is not fixed arity, the bijections do not quotient schedules, and none of the three gives an ordinary-integer universal loader, a single-fold or finite-fold MRDP theorem, or an operation-count record. Manuscript~13 adds that its construction does not improve the project's 75- and 87-operation figures. \subsection{Why this does not improve a fixed universal-polynomial record\srctag{13}}

The family \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:compiler} grows with the horizon. The single product
comparison compresses a \emph{permutation check}, not an unbounded list into
finitely many scalar coordinates independent of its length. In particular,
there are still $O(T)$ chronological access records, controller witnesses
and product-tree gates.

The audited repository README reports 75 arithmetic operations for a
complete certificate and 87 for a separate fixed universal polynomial
\cite{repo-h10}. Those are different resources and a different target.
The present construction does not lower either number, supply their
ordinary-integer input loader, or prove a global arithmetic-circuit optimum.
An explicit counted fixed-arity interaction-net history compiler remains a
further project.

\wtag{} The figures quoted are those of the project README at manuscript~13's pin \cite{repo-h10}: 75 operations for a complete certificate and 87 for one universal polynomial. They are unchanged at this write. Manuscript~14's ledger \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:7.4} and manuscript~15's counts \cref{cdc:ng:cor:counts} make the same disclaimer.

\subsection{Generalization and the MRDP interface\srctag{13}}\label{cdc:ew:sec:mrdp}
\subsubsection{Qualitative unbounded Diophantineness}

For finite encoded nets, the exact successor relation is computable: verify
the finite input, perform the finite table lookup, and execute the splice
algorithm. A finite history and any of the stated terminal predicates are
therefore decidably checkable. Enumerating finite schedules semidecides
unbounded reachability of such a target.

Consequently, after choosing an ordinary effective coding of all public
finite data by natural numbers, the unbounded target-reachability relation
is computably enumerable and hence Diophantine by MRDP. This last
consequence is classical, not a new universality theorem. The repository's
\code{Diophantine/MRDP.lean} explicitly exposes the finite-polynomial
statement \code{Diophantine.mrdp_iff}: the polynomial and witness dimension
are selected before the input natural number \cite{repo-mrdp-lean}.

The logical interface is therefore clean:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \text{exact finite-net semantics}
 &\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{computable history checker}\\
 &\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{c.e. target set}\\
 &\ \xRightarrow{\mathrm{MRDP}}\ \text{fixed finite polynomial}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Only the first two arrows have the local topology and bounded size analysis
of this report. The last arrow does not preserve the displayed linear
family, its explicit operation count, its height bound, or its
schedule-relative unique-extension property.

\subsubsection{No illicit single-fold conclusion}

It is tempting to argue that a deterministic evaluator plus unique memory
witnesses yields a single-fold Diophantine representation of every
computably enumerable set. That inference is not justified. The bounded
construction fixes $T$ externally, can have several legal schedules, and
still uses a number of witnesses growing with $T$. Applying MRDP to the
unbounded relation may introduce new witnesses with uncontrolled
multiplicity. Neither eliminating the horizon nor preserving witness
uniqueness through MRDP has been proved here.

Similarly, universality of the six-rule formalism does not by itself prove
that a particular closed-net agent-free predicate, under one particular
ordinary-integer loader, is complete for all computably enumerable sets.
An explicit simulation and output interface would be required for that
stronger statement. We do not infer it from the four-$\delta$ example.

% ---- manuscript 14, lines 1027-1067 ----
\subsection{Boundaries: what has not been compressed\srctag{14}}\label{cdc:nt:sec:boundaries}
\subsubsection{Fixed horizon is not fixed arity}
The schema $P_{N,T}$ has linearly many coordinates in $T$. It is a family of
ordinary integer polynomials, not one polynomial with a fixed number of
variables that uniquely represents every unbounded run. Quantifying a code
of a variable-length sequence introduces a new problem: the decoding and
verification of that code must itself be represented, and its witness fibers
must be controlled.

The MRDP theorem provides an ordinary Diophantine representation for any
computably enumerable relation, including effectively coded finite
reachability \cite{mat-scholarpedia}. Applying it to a verifier does not preserve
the verifier's unique witness automatically. General finite-fold and
single-fold representations are a distinct question, discussed explicitly by
Matiyasevich \cite{mat2010}. No step in this paper resolves that question.

\subsubsection{Degree, domain, and integer-size claims}
All witnesses range over $\N$. Simply allowing arbitrary integers would
invalidate range-complement arguments and their uniqueness. Replacing
nonnegative coordinates by sums of four squares would add representation
multiplicity, so it cannot be done while retaining the same bijection.
The quartic bound comes from a sum of squares of residuals; it is not a
claim about a least possible degree for every semantic relation.

The large integer-product witnesses are bounded in bit length, not small
in numerical magnitude. A sparse quartic can be cheap to describe and still
have large coordinates. No fast general algorithm for finding its zeros is
claimed. In particular, verification complexity, witness construction from
a supplied execution, and existential search are different tasks.

\subsubsection{No unproved universality interface}
Interaction combinators are a classical universal system \cite{lafont}.
The exact six-rule reducer here uses that system, rather than a universal
claim about the terminating all-$\delta$ fragment. The four-cell counterexample
and its exhaustive search lie in that fragment and serve as wiring tests.

We do not infer, just from universality, that every particular terminal
predicate used here is c.e.-complete under a paid ordinary-integer loader.
Nor do we infer that the existence of a fixed universal net supplies a
short arithmetic circuit for its input map. Those would be additional
constructions and are recorded as research directions below.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 867-885 ----
\subsection{Why this does not prove finite-fold MRDP\srctag{15}}
The schedule length and its wire universes determine the syntax and number of
variables of the polynomial. They are \emph{not} ordinary numeric parameters
in one fixed polynomial. Quantifying over $T$ in a metatheoretic statement
therefore gives a family of polynomial formulas, not a single formula with a
fixed tuple of existential variables.

Unbounded interaction-combinator reachability is computably enumerable: enumerate
finite schedules and simulate them. A fixed-arity Diophantine representation
then follows abstractly from MRDP \cite{mat1970,repo-mrdp-lean}. That
existence theorem does not preserve the unique witnesses, explicit degree and
size ledger, or wire-level semantics of the present compiler. The distinction
between arbitrary Diophantine representations and single-fold or finite-fold
representations is substantive \cite{mat2010}.

Accordingly, the present result does not resolve the finite-fold or single-fold
Diophantine representation problem. It also does not instantiate one fixed
universal interaction net with a paid ordinary-integer input loader. These are
separate research tasks, not costs silently absorbed into a universality claim.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 1138-1149 ----
\subsection{Statements not established here\srctag{15}}
We do not establish a fixed-arity, fixed-degree, explicitly instantiated
universal interaction-net polynomial with a paid ordinary-natural input
interface. We do not provide a sparse near-linear-memory exporter, a canonical
quotient of all concurrent schedules, a minimal witness count, or a globally
optimal arithmetic circuit. We also do not establish priority for the specific
canonical certificate or claim an externally refereed breakthrough.

What is established by the supplied proofs is narrower and concrete: exact
arithmetic wire composition, exact closed-loop accounting, unique natural
witnesses for each finite schedule, and a complete six-rule executable
implementation with a literal resource ledger.

\wtag{} The formal interface named by manuscripts~13 and~15 is \code{Diophantine.mrdp} and \code{Diophantine.mrdp_iff} in \path{Computability/HilbertTenthProblem/Lean/Diophantine/MRDP.lean} (lines~33 and~42; the file is the same blob, \texttt{74aea8c5e}, at the two pins and at this write) \cite{repo-mrdp-lean}. These declarations assert existence of a Diophantine representation and say nothing about its number of witnesses. No theorem of Part~XV is formalized in Lean or Rocq; the project's formalized single-fold exponential representation (\cref{cdc:bd:rem:sfu}) is not an input to this Part.

\subsection{A proposed formalization path\srctag{13}}

A useful formalization can be divided into four theorem layers rather than
starting with a very large expanded polynomial. First formalize finite
matchings, doubled components, and the splice invariant. Next formalize
the contraction recurrence and the induction proving
Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:sharp}. Independently formalize the exact product lemma,
the mixed-radix record injection and Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:memory}. Finally prove
that the finite six-rule controller realizes the semantic reduction relation
and compose it with the memory certificate.

These are proposed proof obligations, not claims that new Lean files have
been checked. The source text of the repository's MRDP interface was read,
but its dependency closure and axioms were not rebuilt during this work.
A later integration should run the project's compiler and its explicit
axiom checks on every newly added declaration.

\subsection{Reproducibility and finite validation\srctag{14}}
\subsubsection{Two reducers, not two calls to one algorithm}
The reference component reducer builds the temporary multigraph, explicitly
retaining parallel edges, and suppresses connected components. The local
reducer instead uses the four-port formulas for annihilation and endpoint
relocation for creation rules. They share the declared numbered rule
\emph{templates} but not the gluing algorithm. Thus agreement tests the
arithmetic topology construction against the component semantics; it does
not independently derive Lafont's rule table. The original numbered diagrams
were separately inspected on journal pages 81--82.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\caption{Actual results of \code{code/14-net-topology-verify.py}. All checks passed.}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{99mm}r@{}}\toprule
Check & Count\\\midrule
Boolean boundary patterns checked, per annihilation rule & 64\\
Legal / impossible boundary patterns, per rule & 10 / 54\\
Capped source logs, $A=V=2$, $L=1,2,3$ & 584\\
Valid logs among those source logs & 258\\
One-auxiliary-coordinate $+1$ mutations rejected & 11,310\\
Closed two-cell inputs across all ordered type assignments & 73\\
Enabled rewrites on those two-cell inputs compared & 17\\
All perfect matchings on four labelled $\delta$ cells & 10,395\\
Enabled first rewrites on those four-cell inputs compared & 5,670\\
Seeded full-system random inputs & 1,000\\
Full-system rewrite steps compared & 2,762\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All six rules occur in the random tests: 194 $\delta\delta$, 435
$\delta\eps$, 1,011 $\delta\gamma$, 509 $\eps\eps$, 409 $\eps\gamma$, and
204 $\gamma\gamma$ steps. The seed is 20261002; each random input is followed
for at most eight steps. Free ports, pre-existing bare loops, self-wires,
and allocation growth are included. The largest observed live net has 22
cells. These numbers describe the actual finite workload, not an asymptotic
proof or an exhaustive search of the full universal system.

Every four-$\delta$ input is also normalized along all available choices;
its resulting literal terminal set has cardinality one. That finite
observation is consistent with the classical confluence theory but is not
used as a substitute for the correctness proofs above.

\subsubsection{What the exported equations establish}
An independent JSON checker reconstructs the sum of squares from the
serialized residuals, compares it coefficient-by-coefficient with the
exported quartic, checks the supplied natural witness, and rejects a
single-coordinate increment of every private coordinate in each export.
It does not import the compiler or witness constructor.

The two loop-kernel JSON files each contain six source fields, 17 auxiliaries,
23 quadratic residuals, and an expanded degree-four polynomial with 104
monomials. A supplied valid witness realizes the two-loop case.
The memory example has $L=4,A=4,V=10$ and log
\begin{equation}
             (1,1,7),\ (2,0,0),\ (1,0,7),\ (1,1,3).                  \label{cdc:nt:eq:11.1}
\end{equation}
It exports 12 source fields, 64 auxiliaries, 64 residuals, and a degree-four
polynomial with 402 nonzero monomials. Its source execution is a write of 7,
a zero read elsewhere, a read of 7, and a final write of 3.

For all short logs in the exhaustive test, the constructed sorted witness
satisfies the equations exactly when direct chronological replay says the
log is valid. The mutation test changes each private coordinate of each
valid short witness individually by $+1$ and confirms rejection. It is a
useful implementation check, not an exhaustive search over all natural
auxiliary assignments. Uniqueness over \emph{all} such assignments is proved
in Theorem~\ref{cdc:nt:thm:memory}.

The package does not contain a kernel-checked proof. Its confidence boundary
is the written mathematical argument plus exact Python integer tests.

\subsection{Implementation, tests, and reproducibility\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:implementation}

\subsubsection{What the code actually does}
The implementation uses Python's standard library and exact integers only.
\path{code/15-no-ghost-wires-loop_exact.py} defines typed nets, the complete rule templates, two
gluing algorithms, the canonical orbit witness, a sparse polynomial data type,
the parametric scheduled compiler, and a witness generator. The compiler
\code{compile_schedule} receives initial types, free-port labels, and a
lifetime schedule; it does not receive the initial or terminal matching.

Every intermediate matching scalar and orbit coordinate has a name. Each
residual is stored as an exact sparse integer polynomial. The exporter rejects
any residual whose total degree exceeds two. The quartic is represented as
the sum of their squares, not as an unnecessarily expanded monomial list.
This is a complete polynomial specification: expanding it is mechanical and
does not change its mathematical meaning.

The witness generator is a separate procedure. It executes the actual input
net, constructs the canonical coordinates, checks the exact requested target,
and evaluates every residual. It cannot turn an invalid schedule into a
certificate by changing the polynomial.

\subsubsection{Three independent gluing algorithms}
The test suite compares three methods on the same finite gluing data:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the $\alpha\beta$ permutation, its orbit minima, and
      \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:loopformula};
\item an undirected multigraph component traversal, retaining the multiplicity
      of parallel edges;
\item sequential pair suppression, using direct partner rewiring and a loop
      increment when the two suppressed vertices are already matched.
\end{enumerate}
The second and third methods do not call the permutation algorithm. Agreement
therefore exercises the central topological claim more meaningfully than
checking an implementation against another wrapper around itself. These are
independent algorithms within the accompanying implementation effort, not an
external independent review.

\subsubsection{Exact finite test receipt}
The complete run produced the following results:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}Xr@{}}
\toprule
Test family & Count\\
\midrule
All permutations on sets of size $0$ through $8$ &46,234\\
Candidate assignments in bounded uniqueness checks through size $4$ &240,393\\
All matching/involution gluing instances on even sizes through $8$ &81,393\\
Local active-pair contexts spanning all six rules &412\\
Compiled zero-witness checks for those contexts &412\\
Single-coordinate witness mutations rejected in local tests &600\\
All perfect matchings on four $\delta$ agents &10,395\\
Enabled rewrites checked on those four-agent nets &5,670\\
Saved-example witness mutations rejected &203\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The gluing family ranges over every perfect matching $\alpha$ and every
involution $\beta$ on each even vertex set through size eight; its fixed
points determine the boundary. Thus it includes empty boundaries, no internal
joins, overlapping old and new matching pairs, and two-edge cycles. The
local-rule family takes the two chosen active agents, fixes their principal
edge, varies the number of external free ports over $0,2,4$, and enumerates
all remaining perfect matchings. Its rule counts are
\[
5\ (\varepsilon\varepsilon),\quad
19\ (\gamma\varepsilon),\quad19\ (\delta\varepsilon),\quad
123\ (\gamma\gamma),\quad123\ (\delta\delta),\quad123\ (\gamma\delta).
\]
Pre-existing loop count three is retained in these local tests.

The bounded uniqueness test deliberately includes the spurious root label
zero. It enumerates all tuples compatible with the local minimum/reset
conditions and distances through $n-1$, then checks orbit consistency and
distance equations. Exactly one remains for every tested permutation. This
finite test is not the unbounded uniqueness proof; that proof is
\cref{cdc:ng:thm:orbit}.

The complete recorded run took approximately four seconds in the authoring
container. That timing is an observation about this run, not a performance
guarantee. The receipt includes code hashes and a hash of the ordered gluing
records.

\subsection{Integration and formal verification boundaries\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:integration}

\subsubsection{A narrow repository audit}
The repository inspection was deliberately scoped. It read the
Hilbert's-tenth-problem README, the concrete wiring-obstruction note, and the
MRDP interface, in addition to the repository directory information. The
observed tree identifier was
\begin{center}\small\ttfamily
928ea97017a25ebe56d240c84f27d2275d818c75.
\end{center}
The obstruction note was returned with blob identifier
\begin{center}\small\ttfamily
764c982297342093307a0e831bc0d9ed5084c87f.
\end{center}
The MRDP interface was read at the recorded tree revision. This is not a
whole-repository correctness audit, and no Lean or Rocq build was run.

The present Python compiler is standalone: it neither imports a repository
proof as an axiom nor claims that its new theorems are already formalized.
A natural integration location would be alongside the existing
\code{native-stream-queue} wiring-obstruction report, but the archive does
not write to that location automatically.

\subsubsection{A feasible proof-assistant decomposition}
A formalization can keep the graph and arithmetic layers separate. Represent
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ as finite permutations with proofs of their involution
properties, and represent the boundary as the fixed-point set of $\beta$.
Prove the path--cycle dictionary and the pair-suppression identity first.
Neither theorem depends on interaction combinators.

Next formalize the orbit certificate over natural-valued finite functions.
The critical argument is a finite-orbit sum: absence of a root gives
$\sum d_i=\sum d_i+|C|$. The minimum, slack, and distance uniqueness proofs
then use only finite permutation reasoning and natural arithmetic. The selector
version is a matrix-row selection lemma.

Finally define the six finite templates and a reflected compiler producing
lists of multivariate-polynomial residuals. A correctness theorem for the
compiler should connect its zeros to the exact net semantics, including loop
counts. Testing the generated residuals alone is not a substitute for that
connection. The source and receipt are suitable inputs for such a development,
not an assertion that the development has already been completed.

\wtag{} The ``natural integration location'' that manuscript~15 names, beside the research note in the Hilbert's-tenth-problem tree, was not used: the three manuscripts are placed in this report, as Part~XV, and the research tree is maintained separately.

\section{Research questions and conclusions}\label{cdc:ic:sec:questions}

Each is one \texttt{question} environment titled by its heading and source, with its text unchanged. They are not merged with one another or with the questions of \cref{cdc:sec:questions} and Parts~X--XIV; a \wtag{} line after a question names the questions it overlaps. Four topics recur in all three manuscripts: a complete exporter for the six-rule compiler, a canonical quotient of concurrent schedules (Part~X's question on quotienting independent schedules and \cref{cdc:q:graphfront,cdc:q:dynamic}), fixed-arity compression with a paid ordinary-integer loader (\cref{cdc:q:compression,cdc:q:restricted}), and formalization (\cref{cdc:q:verified}). Manuscript~13's question on low-height memory certificates and manuscript~14's on the memory size--height cost are Part~V's size--height question (\cref{cdc:q:sizeheight}) for their relations. The three conclusions follow.}

\subsection{Further research questions and concrete next targets\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:sec:future}

The following are proposed research problems emerging from the proved
results. They are not all asserted to be previously named open problems in
the literature. A priority search should accompany work on each one.

\begin{question}[Deterministic, efficiently decodable one-bit tomography; source 13]

Theorem~\ref{cdc:ew:thm:probes} proves the existence of an $O(n\log n)$ separating
family, but does not construct or decode one in polynomial time. Find an
explicit family of that size and a polynomial-time algorithm reconstructing
$M$ from its loop-parity vector. Proposition~\ref{cdc:ew:prop:modular} provides
local separators once two candidate matchings are known; turning that
pairwise knowledge into a global nonadaptive decoder is a distinct problem.

A sharper numerical target is to minimize
\begin{equation}
 \tau(n)=\min\bigl\{K:\exists Q_1,\ldots,Q_K\text{ with }\Phi
 \text{ injective on }\M_n\bigr\}.
\end{equation}
We proved $\log_2D_n\le\tau(n)=O(\log D_n)$. Does
$\tau(n)/\log_2D_n\to1$, or is there a larger limiting obstruction imposed
by the restricted family of allowable probes?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Sharp separation probabilities modulo larger integers; source 13]

Proposition~\ref{cdc:ew:prop:modular} proves separation modulo every $r\ge2$,
but not a uniform sharp probability. Determine, for fixed $r$,
\begin{equation}
 \inf_{n,\,M\ne N}
 \PP\bigl(c(M,Q)\not\equiv c(N,Q)\pmod r\bigr).
\end{equation}
The signed recurrence can be generalized by replacing $-1$ with roots of
unity and tracking the pair of loop increments. The extremal cycle types
need not remain a single six-cycle. Small-rank exact enumeration provides
a direct way to formulate testable conjectures.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Error-correcting and restricted-context tomography; source 13]

The $2/5$ lower bound suggests sampling probe families with positive
relative Hamming distance between every two observation vectors. Quantify
the best tradeoff between probe count, minimum distance and efficient
reconstruction. Separately, determine what changes when contexts are planar,
geometrically local, bounded-depth, or generated by a restricted rule
system. Corollary~\ref{cdc:ew:cor:injective} cannot be transferred to such a family
without proving that its contexts still separate the relevant matchings.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Asymptotics and spectra of signed closure correlations; source 13]

The recurrence computes $F(\lambda)$ without enumerating all closing
matchings. Study the asymptotic behavior of $h(\lambda)$ along families such
as $(k)$, $(2^r)$ and $(k^r)$, including sharp decay estimates and sign
patterns. Relate the matrix
$\bigl((-1)^{c(M,Q)}\bigr)_{M,Q\in\M_n}$ and its row correlations to the
matching association scheme and Brauer-algebra specializations. A useful
outcome would be a closed spectral formula that recovers, and perhaps
strengthens, the elementary extremal theorem without obscuring its equality
cases.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Low-height exact memory certificates; source 13]

The present memory argument pays $O(S^2\log S)$ bits in its largest witness.
Can a deterministic, exact, uniquely extending memory certificate retain
$O(S)$ arithmetic coordinates while substantially reducing this height?
Possible approaches include structured multi-evaluation schemes or
coefficientwise certificates with carefully balanced costs. A finite-field
fingerprint with nonzero error is not a solution to the exact zero-set
problem, and an unconstrained base is ruled out by the explicit collision
example in Section~\ref{cdc:ew:sec:product}.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:sizeheight}, Part~V's size--height question, and manuscript~14's question on reducing the memory size--height cost below; each asks it for its own relation.


\begin{question}[A fully instrumented interaction-net polynomial exporter; source 13]

The next implementation task is to turn the controller construction into a
literal fixed instruction schedule, route every array access through the
existing memory generator, and export a complete polynomial for each
$(C_0,F,T)$. The important output is not just a degree bound: it should
include a register ledger, branch conventions, raw/sorted record layouts,
canonical witness generator, independent replay, and operation counts for
each macro. Compare degree, coordinate count, sparse monomial count,
arithmetic operations and witness height separately.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~14's question on finishing the full symbolic assembler and manuscript~15's on sparse certificates using the sixteen-port support bound, below. Manuscript~15's fixed-schedule exporter (\cref{cdc:ng:thm:compiler}) is implemented, but it is dense and does not route accesses through a memory certificate.


\begin{question}[A fixed-arity history encoding and an ordinary input loader; source 13]

An unbounded universal equation through the six-rule substrate requires a
new history-compression layer whose coordinate count is independent of
$T$. The exact memory certificate is a sound bounded starting point, not
that layer itself. A productive target is to combine it with the
repository's existing history arithmetic while preserving enough
port-incidence information to satisfy Corollary~\ref{cdc:ew:cor:injective}.

In parallel, specify one fixed universal net construction receiving an
ordinary natural-number input through an explicit loader. Prove the
simulation and its output predicate, including behavior on malformed
encodings. Only then can a counted comparison with the repository's
universal-polynomial constructions be made.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:compression,cdc:q:restricted}, and below manuscript~14's questions on a fully charged universal input interface and on restricted, genuinely uniform compression, and manuscript~15's on fixed-arity compression with a completely paid input loader.


\begin{question}[Schedule quotients and honest multiplicity statements; source 13]

The compiler is canonical over a fixed schedule, but distinct legal
schedules may represent the same concurrent computation. Investigate a
canonical representative of commuting reductions and the arithmetic cost
of checking it. Any resulting multiplicity theorem must distinguish the
bounded trace, the schedule quotient and the auxiliary witnesses introduced
by later unbounded Diophantine compilation. No conclusion about the general
single-fold representation problem follows solely from local confluence.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:dynamic,cdc:q:graphfront}, Part~X's question on quotienting independent schedules (\cref{cdc:nh:sec:research}), and below manuscript~14's question on canonicalizing genuine concurrency and manuscript~15's on witness-faithful quotienting by independent reductions.


\begin{question}[Formal proof and broader substrates; source 13]

Formalize the sharp theorem first: it has a compact finite combinatorial
core and an induction with explicit exceptional cases. The memory theorem
is an independent second milestone. A successful combination would provide
a reusable compiler for fixed bounded-arity port-rewriting systems,
including variants of interaction nets with additional finite agent types.
For substrates with priorities, global pattern tests or nonlocal rewrites,
identify the exact extra relation requiring arithmetic certification rather
than treating the entire ``esoteric instruction'' as a free primitive.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:verified}, and below manuscript~14's question on a formal verification boundary and manuscript~15's on formalizing the whole semantic bridge. For substrates with timing, the neighbouring report \emph{liveness-beyond-halting} asks for clock-faithful translations, among others into interaction nets; this Part does not supply one.

is preserved and why the restricted construction does not silently assume
a solution to the general finite-fold problem.
\end{question}

\subsection{Further research questions and proposed projects\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:sec:future}

\begin{question}[Sparse certificates using the sixteen-port support bound; source 15]
The dense compiler stores entire intermediate matching matrices. Replace them
by a canonical read/write log for partner pointers. Each elementary suppression
reads two partners and modifies at most two surviving pointers; every rule uses
at most four such suppressions. The support bound shows that topology itself
does not require scanning the whole net. The main task is a witness-faithful
memory-consistency checker, with every sorting, lookup, allocation, and
untouched-memory cost included. A useful target is quasi-linear certificate
size in the number of initial ports and interaction events, rather than in
history length times the square of the live graph size.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~13's question on a fully instrumented exporter and manuscript~14's on the full symbolic assembler, above: the sparse certificate asked for here is in substance the paper construction of \cref{cdc:nt:thm:main} and \cref{cdc:ew:thm:compiler}, whose exporter is what those two questions ask for.


\begin{question}[Can variable-topology orbit certification use fewer coordinates?; source 15]
The fixed-index certificate needs four coordinates per vertex; the selector
certificate uses five to prevent a cubic distance expression. Determine whether
an equally explicit unique-witness certificate can use four coordinates with
quadratic residuals when the successor matrix is arithmetic data. A meaningful
lower bound must specify the allowed equation schema and the input interface;
no unrestricted lower bound is suggested by our ledger.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Fixed-arity compression with a completely paid input loader; source 15]
Use the loop-exact gluing module as the semantic front end of a packed-history
construction. The target should state the full polynomial, the witness domain,
the input encoding, the allocated-name policy, and the treatment of loops.
A universality theorem for interaction combinators is not an input loader.
Before optimizing operation counts, prove that invalid packed port incidences
cannot masquerade as valid memory and that cycle counts remain exact.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:compression}, and manuscript~13's and manuscript~14's questions on loaders, above.


\begin{question}[Witness-faithful quotienting by independent reductions; source 15]
The current finite-disjunction construction has one zero per successful
schedule, not one zero per concurrent trace class. Independent active pairs
can be reduced in either order; their wiring suppressions commute by
\cref{cdc:ng:cor:order}, up to the fresh-name convention. Construct a canonical
representative of each appropriate concurrency class without deleting valid
resource or loop information. A useful intermediate goal is to prove a
precise local diamond with an explicit fresh-name bijection.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:dynamic,cdc:q:graphfront}, Part~X's question on quotienting independent schedules, and manuscript~13's and manuscript~14's questions on schedule quotients and concurrency, above.


\begin{question}[Canonical renaming without changing topology; source 15]
Our single-fold theorem fixes the agent names. To obtain one witness per
isomorphism class of traces, a canonical naming policy must account for ordered
ports, agent types, free-port labels, and cyclic wires. Birth-order naming is
natural once a schedule is fixed, but it is not automatically canonical across
all schedules. Establish the exact equivalence relation first, then decide
whether its normalization can be certified at low degree without introducing
multiple witnesses for automorphisms.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare Part~X's birth-order normalization (\cref{cdc:nh:thm:names}), a canonical naming of created objects once the schedule is fixed, and manuscript~14's question on observational targets, above.


\begin{question}[Loop-sensitive semantics for diagrammatic computation; source 15]
For ordinary matching contexts, \cref{cdc:ng:thm:context} identifies a complete

separately or evaluated in a target algebra. The distinction matters for

\end{question}

\subsection{Conclusion\srctag{13}}

The concrete wiring gap leads in two directions. On the negative side,
port incidence cannot be discarded by any summary that remains exact in
all closing contexts: even final cyclic-wire parity distinguishes any two
matchings in at least two fifths of contexts, and that constant is sharp.
On the positive side, preserving exact incidence need not force a complete
graph tableau at every moment. Constant-size splices and one exact global
memory argument yield a linear-description, degree-four bounded history
certificate, with canonical ancillary witnesses for each schedule.

The resulting boundary is precise. Exact topology, exact cyclic components
and a horizon-sensitive arithmetic construction are proved. A smaller
fixed universal polynomial, an ordinary-number loader with a paid ledger,
and uniqueness through an unbounded MRDP conversion are not. The package
supplies both the proofs and enough executable structure to make those
remaining tasks concrete.

% ---- manuscript 14, lines 1211-1227 ----
\subsection{Conclusion\srctag{14}}
The obstruction in the motivating repository note is not repaired by adding
more global graph statistics. It is repaired by retaining the actual port
involution and compiling its bounded local changes. A disappearing boundary
can create a two-edge or four-edge cycle, and both must remain visible to
arithmetic. The formulas \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:3.3}--\eqref{cdc:nt:eq:3.4} capture that distinction with a constant
kernel; Theorem~\ref{cdc:nt:thm:minimal} identifies an exact local distinguishability
threshold; and the capped-memory theorem controls all remaining access
witnesses without a probabilistic permutation test.

The resulting quartic family represents complete bounded scheduled
interaction-combinator computations, not just a coarse reachability shadow.
Its semantic proof and linear asymptotic ledger are complete within the
stated explicit-input, external-horizon scope. The next engineering task is
to turn the specified full assembler into an audited emitter with an exact
global constant ledger. The next mathematical tasks concern variable-arity
gluing, genuine concurrency quotients, and justified restricted compression.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 1223-1235 ----
\subsection{Conclusion\srctag{15}}
The arithmetic obstacle was not the number of combinator symbols. It was the
need to retain which port is connected to which, and to account for the closed
wire components created by suppression. We have supplied two exact solutions
to that local problem: a division-free quadratic elimination identity and a
canonical permutation-orbit certificate. The latter fits directly into a
single-fold quartic trace compiler with an explicit size ledger.

The construction preserves information lost by the repository's obstructed
summary, treats all six rules rather than only the terminating all-$\delta$
fragment, and distinguishes a port-free cyclic component from the absence of
a component. It supplies a finite-horizon topology-aware foundation on which
more ambitious memory and history compression can safely be built.

\section{A compact mathematical specification of the memory compiler\srctag{13}}
\label{cdc:ew:app:spec}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~A of manuscript~13. Its Appendix~B, the source audit, is in the provenance appendix.}


For implementation or formalization, the entire memory certificate can be
summarized without invoking the controller. The structural parameters are
$A,m,V$; the public fields are $(I_a),(O_a),(a_j,r_j,w_j)$. The construction
is the following finite schema, with every displayed range instantiated
externally.

First bound all public values and addresses by \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:bound}. Form the
$L=2A+m$ literal raw rows \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:raw}. Introduce four natural fields per
sorted row and bound each by \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:field-bounds}. For every adjacent
pair introduce $s_i,z_i,d_i$ and impose the five residuals
\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:sort}--\eqref{cdc:ew:eq:link}.

Next construct $B=U^L+1$, $U=AHV^2$, by binary powering. For each of the raw
and sorted row lists, form affine leaves $B+HV^2a+V^2t+Vr+w$, combine them
in a fixed balanced product tree, and equate the two roots. There is no
need to add a variable for a leaf. Every intermediate product receives
one natural variable and one defining residual.

All auxiliary choices have been specified: sort by the strictly ordered
key, use natural difference slacks, force inactive address gaps to zero,
and use the unique value of every gate. The sum of squared residuals is
the single exported polynomial. Parameters and witnesses are distinguished
in the JSON by a role field; monomials are sorted tuples of variable IDs,
with integer coefficients.

The implementation intentionally permits an in-range but inconsistent
proposed history to be passed to the constructor. It fills in the canonical
sort and gates and returns the list of failed residuals. For such a history
the adjacent memory-link equations expose the inconsistency. Values outside
the structural ranges are rejected before constructing an example tuple;
the polynomial equations themselves enforce those ranges for arbitrary
candidate tuples.

% ---- manuscript 14, lines 1230-1282 ----
\section{Literal functional gadgets\srctag{14}}\label{cdc:nt:app:gadgets}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~A of manuscript~14. Manuscript~13's comparison gadget is \eqref{cdc:ew:eq:compare}; the two gadgets differ in their equations and both have unique natural extensions.}

\subsection{Comparison with no unspecified witnesses}
For source $x,y\in\N$, introduce $E,L,G,h_L,h_G\in\N$ and require
\begin{align*}
 E+L+G&=1,\\
 x+L(1+h_L)&=y+G(1+h_G),\\
 (1-L)h_L&=0,\\
 (1-G)h_G&=0.
\end{align*}
The first equation makes $E,L,G$ one-hot because they are natural numbers.
If $x=y$, the unique solution has $E=1$ and all other fields zero. If $x<y$,
it has $L=1$, $h_L=y-x-1$, and the other fields zero. The $x>y$ case is
symmetric. Thus five auxiliaries and four quadratic residuals implement
an exact three-way comparison. Equality indicators and strict-order bits
are outputs of this total gadget, not free Boolean guesses.

\subsection{Range and division}
For fixed $D\geq1$, $x<D$ is represented by the unique natural complement
$x+s=D-1$. Division uses
\[
                     x=Dq+r,\qquad r+s=D-1.
\]
It has exactly one natural triple $(q,r,s)$ for every $x\in\N$. The same
uniqueness holds when $D$ is a positive source variable, with a quadratic
first residual. The interaction-net address decoder needs only fixed
division by three and affine range changes.

\subsection{Boolean circuits and selection}
Once $b,c$ are Boolean, $z=bc$ implements AND and $z=1-b$ implements NOT.
A selected scalar value is forced by
\[
                         z=b x+(1-b)y.
\]
Every product receives its own variable when substitution would exceed
degree two. A finite truth table is compiled into a Boolean circuit in the
usual explicit way: AND the literals of each input pattern and OR the
corresponding disjoint cases. Its gate values are all unique.

For the ten-state kernel one may instead directly use \eqref{cdc:nt:eq:4.1}--\eqref{cdc:nt:eq:4.5}. These
relations already enforce the legal input patterns and have a unique
extension. In a larger conditional controller, set an inactive kernel's
source to a fixed legal pattern before invoking it. Its outputs are then
fixed and may be ignored by deterministic selection.

\subsection{Why guarding alone is unsafe}
The equation $b\,R(\mathbf z)=0$ does not constrain $\mathbf z$ when $b=0$.
Moreover, multiplying a quadratic residual by $b$ creates a cubic residual,
whose square has degree six. Neither issue is solved by calling the branch
``inactive.'' Use total functional evaluation, fixed dummy inputs, or a
properly quadratized and normalized branch construction. Complements of
inactive zero inputs need not be zero: for instance the complement of zero
under $z+s=D-1$ is $D-1$. The requirement is uniqueness, not an unjustified
blanket zeroing rule.

\section{Assembler specification and trust boundaries\srctag{14}}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~B of manuscript~14. The pseudocode specifies the paper construction of \cref{cdc:nt:thm:main}; it is not a shipped program.}

The following pseudocode specifies the full mathematical compiler. It is
separate from the delivered executable kernel emitters.
\begin{lstlisting}
compile_exact_trace(valid_net N, external_horizon T, terminal_query Q):
    reserve C0 + 4*T cell records and f fixed free-port records
    choose A = 4*C + f + 1 and V = 3*C + f + 4
    create source variables for unordered schedule pairs u[t] < v[t]
    emit fixed initialization log records
    for t = 0, ..., T-1:
        emit eight read records for selected cell records
        compile active-pair checks and unique type/rule selection
        derive exact boundary comparisons from the read mate values
        compile annihilation kernel or deterministic endpoint relocation
        assign fresh identifiers in the declared template-role order
        emit eight zero writes, sixteen allocation slots, four patch slots
        replace each unused slot by the fixed dummy read (0,0,0)
        emit scalar fresh/live/loop updates
    emit terminal-query checks and any required final scan
    attach the capped-memory system to the entire fixed-length log
    retain every intermediate product as a separate functional node
    return the sum of squares of all quadratic residuals
\end{lstlisting}

The initial validity condition can either be checked by the effective
compiler, producing the constant polynomial $1$ for malformed fixed inputs,
or be arithmetized using \cref{cdc:nt:sec:terminal} when the input table is a source tuple.
The theorem does not assume a malformed input magically represents a net.
The numbered local templates are finite constants of the six-rule system.
The only dependence on surrounding graph topology enters through the actual
memory reads of port partners and their exact comparisons.

\section{The complete residual schema in one place\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:app:schema}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~A of manuscript~15.}

For clarity, here is the entire scheduled compiler as an equation list. All
indices, vertex sets, rule templates, and the row permutation $\beta_t$ are
fixed by the type/lifetime ledger. Symmetric matching entries share a variable;
diagonal entries are zero.

For configurations $0\le t\le T$:
\[
\sum_{v\ne u}W^{(t)}_{uv}-1=0\qquad(u\text{ a live or free port}).
\]
For steps $0\le t<T$:
\[
W^{(t)}_{(a_t,0),(b_t,0)}-1=0.
\]
For every temporary vertex $i\in[N_t]$:
\begin{align*}
e_{t,i}(e_{t,i}-1)&=0,\\
r_{t,i}+(1-e_{t,i})(h_{t,i}+1)-i&=0,\\
e_{t,i}h_{t,i}&=0,\\
r_{t,i}-\sum_j A^{(t)}_{\beta_t(i),j}r_{t,j}&=0,\\
s_{t,i}-\sum_j A^{(t)}_{\beta_t(i),j}d_{t,j}&=0,\\
d_{t,i}-(1-e_{t,i})(s_{t,i}+1)&=0.
\end{align*}
For every unordered pair of distinct surviving ports $u,v$:
\[
W^{(t+1)}_{uv}(r_{t,u}-r_{t,v})=0.
\]
Finally, for every step:
\[
\sum_i e_{t,i}+2\ell_t-2\ell_{t+1}-P_{t+1}/2=0.
\]
Here $r_{t,u}$ means the coordinate of the temporary index assigned to global
port $u$. The total certificate is the sum of the squares of every displayed
residual. No additional existential helper, divisibility condition, unbounded
quantifier, or implicit array operation is required.

% ---- manuscript 15, lines 1275-1309 ----
\section{Small omissions that would invalidate the result\srctag{15}}
\label{cdc:ng:app:pitfalls}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~B of manuscript~15.}

\paragraph{Omitting root-slack normalization.}
Without $e_i h_i=0$, the root's value of $h_i$ is completely free. The
representation remains existentially correct but loses uniqueness, with
infinitely many witnesses even for a one-vertex permutation.

\paragraph{Omitting the distance condition.}
Setting $e_i=0$, $r_i=0$, and $h_i=i-1$ satisfies the Boolean, minimum, slack,
and equal-root equations for any permutation. Thus component labels can all
be fictitious unless an equation forces the existence of an actual root.
The distance recurrence provides that forcing by contradiction around an orbit.

\paragraph{Treating the temporary graph as simple.}
An old edge that coincides with a join is not one edge: it is two parallel
edges belonging to different matchings. Replacing the multigraph by a simple
graph destroys precisely the elementary loop counted by
\eqref{cdc:ng:eq:suppress-loop}.

\paragraph{Dropping the output matching constraints.}
Equality of root labels for proposed output edges is insufficient if the
output is allowed to omit edges or use a port more than once. The natural
row-sum equations ensure a genuine perfect matching before the orbit criterion
is applied.

\paragraph{Confusing a removed principal edge with a suppressed wire cycle.}
The principal--principal edge is deleted as part of the interaction rule.
Only the separate interface gluing is normalized by $\alpha\beta$. Applying
the pair-suppression loop increment to the principal pair itself would already
misinterpret $\varepsilon\varepsilon$.

\paragraph{Claiming an unbounded single-fold theorem from finite schedules.}
The dimension in \eqref{cdc:ng:eq:variables} grows with the schedule. A collection
of uniquely witnessed equations, one for each length, is not a single
fixed-arity Diophantine equation with the same property.

\section{Data format and verification of the exported polynomial\srctag{15}}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~C of manuscript~15. The listing reads \path{data/quartic_A_schedule.json} and \path{data/witness_A.json} in the delivered layout; they are shipped as \path{data/15-no-ghost-wires-quartic_A_schedule.json} and \path{data/15-no-ghost-wires-witness_A.json}, and \path{code/15-no-ghost-wires-check_export.py} accepts \code{--data} for the directory but not the prefixed names, so it is run on a copy (this report's README).}

A residual is stored as a list of pairs consisting of an integer coefficient
and a list of variable names. Repeated names encode powers, and an empty name
list encodes the constant monomial. For example,
\begin{lstlisting}
[[1, ["t0.e[1]", "t0.e[1]"]],
 [-1, ["t0.e[1]"]]]
\end{lstlisting}
represents $e_{0,1}^2-e_{0,1}$. The file separately lists endpoint parameters
and existential witnesses. An assignment must provide exactly these names and
must assign every one a nonnegative Python integer. Booleans are not accepted
as integers by the assignment validator.

For the example, the following code independently evaluates the exported
residual list without using the compiler's polynomial class:
\begin{lstlisting}
import json
from pathlib import Path
root = Path("data")
spec = json.loads((root / "quartic_A_schedule.json").read_text())
values = json.loads((root / "witness_A.json").read_text())
assert set(values) == set(spec["parameters"] + spec["witnesses"])
assert all(type(v) is int and v >= 0 for v in values.values())
energy = 0
for residual in spec["residuals"]:
    total = 0
    for coefficient, monomial in residual["terms"]:
        term = coefficient
        for name in monomial:
            term *= values[name]
        total += term
    energy += total * total
assert energy == 0
print(len(spec["witnesses"]), len(spec["residuals"]), energy)
# 126 169 0
\end{lstlisting}
The archive also supplies this independent evaluation as
\path{code/15-no-ghost-wires-check_export.py}, with explicit input validation.
The article's soundness theorem explains what this zero means. The evaluation
alone certifies the arithmetic identity for the saved tuple, not the
correctness of an arbitrary compiler.
