\section{A concrete formalization route for ProveIt\srctag{16}}
\label{cdc:sp:sec:formalization}

A useful integration would separate the sandpile semantics from the generic
arithmetic compiler. It need not modify the existing MRDP proof. The following
are proposed module boundaries, not names of already implemented files.

\paragraph{Finite sink graphs.}
Represent a finite vertex type, symmetric adjacency in $\N$, sink
multiplicities, and a proof that each component reaches a sink edge. Prove
termination using a rational positive potential or a combinatorial
sink-distance potential. Establish the integer-valued balance identity and
the first-excess least-action lemma before introducing polynomial syntax.

\paragraph{Support burning.}
Define forbidden subsets and the synchronous burning sequence using finite
sets. Prove Theorem~\ref{cdc:sp:thm:support} with an integer maximum-level set.
This is the semantic core: integrality and the nonnegative sink multiplicity
must be explicit hypotheses. The directed example should be retained as a
regression test against an overgeneralized statement.

\paragraph{Canonical ranks.}
Prove the equivalence between the local success/failure predicates and the
parallel burning ranks. Derive the rank bound from the predicate rather than
assuming it. This keeps the final arithmetic polynomial free of redundant
rank-bound witnesses.

\paragraph{Polynomial gadgets.}
Implement the literal multivariate polynomial \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:compare}, with a
lemma characterizing its natural zero set and its unique witness tuple.
Prove nonnegativity of each displayed term under natural evaluation. The
shared support simplex requires its own small lemma because two comparisons
reuse the same selector pair.

\paragraph{Compiler and uniqueness.}
Use a disjoint finite index type for the thirteen vertex coordinates and six
ordered-edge coordinates. Define the complete polynomial and prove its
soundness, completeness, uniqueness, and degree bound. Keep certificate
coordinate counts separate from expression-size or circuit-cost metrics.
The finite-graph single-fold theorem should not depend on MRDP. Then
formalize the five-way edge gadget and the ten-coordinate vertex block,
prove Theorem~\ref{cdc:sp:thm:compact}, and verify the explicit maps on complete
natural zero sets. Do not assert an off-zero polynomial identity.

\paragraph{Spatial interface and imported universality.}
Formalize finite boxes, the exterior collar, and the equality between inner
heights in a sink computation and in the full lattice. The source-level
Cairns reduction should be a separately named assumption until an explicit
verified loader and simulation are available. A theorem whose proof uses
that assumption must not be presented as an unconditional machine-checked
universality result.

This separation would make the strongest new local theorem available early,
while making every remaining dependency visible. The first practical target
is the unique comparison gadget followed by the support criterion; neither
requires the substantial infinite-grid universality development.

\wtag{} None of these modules exists in ProveIt, which has no sandpile, chip-firing or burning material. The MRDP interface the plan names is \code{Diophantine.mrdp} in \path{Computability/HilbertTenthProblem/Lean/Diophantine/MRDP.lean}, documented by the guide \cite{repo-mrdp}. Nothing of this Part is formalized.

\section{Further research questions\srctag{16}}
\label{cdc:sp:sec:questions}

The following questions are proposed research targets. They are not assertions
that no related theorem exists in the literature. Where a question originates
in prior work, its source and the distinction from the present result are
stated.

\srcnote{\wtag{} Manuscript~16 posed its eight items as unnumbered subsections; their headings are the titles here, and the text is unchanged. A \wtag{} line after an item names the question of \cref{cdc:sec:questions} or of Part~XIV it overlaps; the items are not merged with them.}

\begin{question}[Canonical certificates for general dissipative digraphs; source 16]\label{cdc:sp:q:digraphs}
Can a directed burning script or a positive integral comparison vector replace
the uniform maximum-level-set argument while preserving a sparse canonical
certificate? The two-vertex counterexample in Section~\ref{cdc:sp:sec:directed}
shows that incoming-neighbor burning alone is insufficient. A first target is
a theorem for a precisely specified class of diagonally dominant toppling
matrices, followed by a characterization of which rescalings admit the same
cubic architecture. Any rescaling must preserve integrality, not merely the
real maximum principle.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare Part~XIV's question on more general abelian processors (\cref{cdc:rt:sec:research}), of which this one is the toppling-matrix case.

\begin{question}[Fewer witnesses without losing uniqueness; source 16]
The compact $10n+6E$ construction already exploits all four comparisons
across an undirected adjacency. Can its five-way edge gadget use fewer than
six natural coordinates while retaining cubic degree and unique complete
witness fibers? Can vertex and edge information share additional variables
without creating noncanonical inactive branches? Any further reduction should
be accompanied by explicit maps on complete zero sets, as in
Section~\ref{cdc:sp:sec:compact}, and should report expanded size separately from
structured size. These are concrete finite algebraic optimization problems.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare Part~XIV's question on smaller canonical certificates without hidden multiplicity (\cref{cdc:rt:sec:research}).

\begin{question}[Local certificates on adaptive support geometry; source 16]
A box can contain many sites that never topple. Can a finite support supplied
as a sparse lattice set be checked canonically with arithmetic size
proportional to the support and its boundary, including the cost of its
coordinate encoding and adjacency verification? The spatial compiler here
uses a fixed box geometry, so those geometric relations are coefficients.
Making the geometry a witness changes both the degree and the uniqueness
obligations. A claimed improvement must pay for sorting, distinctness, and
nearest-neighbor tests.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The exact transient to affine periodicity; source 16]
The bound $T_0$ in \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:perioddata} is elementary and often nonsharp.
Determine the first time at which $z(t+q)=z(t)$ holds forever, or an efficiently
checkable certificate for that time. Full support is sufficient but not
necessary. One possible route classifies the eventual active components and
uses support-restricted burning to avoid forcing vertices that do not matter
to the period. The exact minimal eventual period $q$ is already settled by
Theorem~\ref{cdc:sp:thm:period} under its stated hypothesis.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Coefficient height and arithmetic-operation ledgers; source 16]
The construction exposes degree, witness count, and structured summand count.
A repository-quality optimization should additionally specify a literal
arithmetic model and derive exact addition/multiplication counts, coefficient
heights, and expanded monomial counts for graph families. Sharing $A_v,B_v$
and balance sums is different from proving an identity between complete
polynomials; both should be documented separately. This is the natural point
of contact with ProveIt's existing operation-count program.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:repsize}.

\begin{question}[A verified universal periodic input loader; source 16]
Instantiate one precise version of the periodic-plus-finite Turing-machine
reduction, with a machine-readable background tile, defect table, orientation
conventions, and the exact global-halting predicate. Then compose it with the
spatial compiler. This would remove the largest imported semantic dependency
in the current universal application. It would not, by itself, remove the
variable-radius or variable-arity feature.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:verified}.

\begin{question}[Planar geometry and decidable radius bounds; source 16]
Cairns's paper asks about the corresponding nearest-neighbor two-dimensional
and periodic planar halting problems \cite{cairns}. We do not resolve those
questions or assert an exhaustive audit of their subsequent status. The
certificate suggests a sharp formulation: on a specified planar background
class, can one prove a computable radius bound for every globally halting
finite defect? Such a bound would give a decision procedure by the collar
test. Conversely a halting reduction would rule it out. Results for different
neighborhood shapes or graph classes should not be transferred to the
standard lattice without proof.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Fixed-arity compression with controlled multiplicity; source 16]
Develop a uniform encoding of the canonical spatial certificates whose
auxiliary multiplicity can be proved, rather than assumed. A fixed-arity
single-fold encoding for the complete relation would settle the principle
in Theorem~\ref{cdc:sp:thm:singlefold}; a finite-fold encoding has the corresponding
finite-fold consequence. More accessible intermediate targets include
restricted input classes, bounds on multiplicity in terms of spatial size,
and canonical encodings in exponential Diophantine languages. These are
separate from the already explicit finite-graph cubic construction.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:compression,cdc:q:ffprimitives}, and the note on Part~XI in \cref{cdc:sp:sec:mrdp}.

\section{Conclusion\srctag{16}}

For a finite undirected sink graph, the exact odometer can be certified by
its endpoint and a canonical support-burning structure. This produces the
literal cubic polynomials \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:fullpoly} and \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:compactpoly},
with unique natural witness fibers and explicit inverse zero-set maps. The
compact form has $10n+3m$ coordinates and no dependence of its arity on
execution length. A one-layer collar turns the same construction into an exact
finite-support global-halting certificate on the lattice. The canonical
radius condition removes redundant spatial choices, and the height estimate
shows that the universal obstruction is unbounded geometry rather than
uncontrolled coordinate sizes on a fixed box.

These results supply a concrete addition to a Diophantine compiler library.
They do not replace Cairns's universality theorem, improve a fixed universal
polynomial operation bound, or solve fixed-arity single-fold or cubic MRDP.
Their value is the explicit interface between a native abelian computational
substrate, a sparse canonical arithmetic certificate, and sharply identified
remaining compression problems.

\paragraph{\wtag{} Editorial note: priority.} Manuscripts~16 and~19 were written independently on 2 October 2026, at the pins \texttt{928ea9701} and \texttt{e58b724c2}; when manuscript~19 was pinned, manuscript~16's archive had arrived but was not placed, and manuscript~19's repository search for ``sandpile'' found only manuscript~12's source ledger. The support criterion, the canonical parallel burning ranks with the same two comparisons per ordered adjacency, the directed counterexample, the collar (here a halo), the height bound $u\le\frac M2((R+1)^2-x_1^2)$ and the absence of a computable radius bound are proved in both. Priority is claimed for neither. New in manuscript~19 are the degree-two residual system with its integral gap (\cref{cdc:nb:thm:finitecompiler,cdc:nb:cor:gap}), the fixed-field normal form (\cref{cdc:nb:thm:fields}) with its completeness statement (\cref{cdc:nb:thm:complete}), the unique field codes (\cref{cdc:nb:cor:code}), the seed lemma (\cref{cdc:nb:lem:seed}) and the code-length clause of \cref{cdc:nb:cor:nosize}. New in manuscript~16, and absent here, are the single cubic and its compact form, the canonical radius, the two-site example with a $10^{100}$-scale input and the exact eventual periods. Where manuscript~19 states a result of manuscript~16, a bracket before it names the result; manuscript~19's proof is kept as a second route, never with a novelty claim.

\paragraph{\wtag{} Relation to the other Parts.} Besides manuscript~16, three relations matter. The least-action lemma is Fey, Levine and Peres's \cite{fey-levine-peres}, whose routing form is \cref{cdc:rt:lem:least}, and support burning is Dhar's burning test \cite{dhar1990} restricted to the proposed support. The borrowed firings that the certificate excludes are the obstruction that Part~XVIII meets in FIFO queues, where a proposed run borrows its own future output (\cref{cdc:cq:sec:semantics}); there a resource threshold excludes it, here support burning. The single-fold boundary is Part~IX's: \cref{cdc:nb:cor:mrdp} gives ordinary existence only, and \cref{cdc:sp:thm:singlefold} and \cref{cdc:bd:thm:universal} state what single-foldness would be equivalent to. With manuscript~16, manuscript~19 is a second route to Part~XIV's question on infinite-background abelian computation (see the note after it in \cref{cdc:rt:sec:research}).

\paragraph{\wtag{} Setting and hypotheses.} Finite loopless undirected multigraphs with an absorbing sink; components need not meet the sink except for termination. Inputs and witnesses range over $\N$: the quartic has a false integer root once negative helpers are allowed (\cref{cdc:nb:sec:examples}). Directed toppling matrices are excluded and the directed counterexample shows why. The lattice statements concern $\Z^d$ with a stable periodic background given by a finite table and finitely many positive additions; global halting means finitely many topplings in total. The 47 fields are not 47 integer witnesses: no uniqueness-preserving conversion from finite-deviation fields to a fixed-arity integer polynomial is claimed. Cairns's simulation theorem \cite{cairns} and MRDP are imported; no Turing-machine-to-sandpile loader is constructed. No fixed-47-integer-witness, single-fold MRDP, arithmetic-operation optimality or Lean claim is made.

\section{Sandpiles, legal stabilization, and least action\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:least}
\srcnote{\wtag{} [Manuscript~19's Section~2 sets up the finite sink graphs of \cref{cdc:sp:sec:finite} in its own letters (\cref{cdc:conv:b79-nb}), with one weaker hypothesis: it does not require every component to meet the sink, and assumes this only where termination is needed (\cref{cdc:nb:lem:dissipative}).]}


Throughout, $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. All polynomial equations have integer
coefficients and ordinary signed subtraction; all witnesses, unless stated
otherwise, range over $\N$.

\subsection{Finite graphs and conventions}

Let $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, where $n\ge1$. Let
\[
 a_{vw}=a_{wv}\in\N,\qquad a_{vv}=0,\qquad b_v\in\N,
 \qquad d_v=b_v+\sum_{w\in V}a_{vw}\ge1.
\]
Here $a_{vw}$ is the number of undirected edges between two nonsink
vertices, and $b_v$ counts edges from $v$ to an absorbing sink. There is
no requirement that every connected component meet the sink. Set
\[
 L=D-A,\qquad (Lf)_v=d_vf_v-\sum_w a_{vw}f_w.
\]
The parameter $E$ counts \emph{distinct unordered adjacent pairs}
$\{v,w\}$ with $a_{vw}>0$, not the sum of their multiplicities.

A configuration is a vector $c\in\N^V$. Vertex $v$ is unstable when
$c_v\ge d_v$. A \emph{legal firing} at $v$ subtracts $d_v$ chips there,
adds $a_{vw}$ at each $w$, and loses $b_v$ chips to the sink. After firing
$v$ a total of $u_v$ times, the final balance is
\begin{equation}
 s=c-Lu.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:balance}
\end{equation}
A configuration is stable if $0\le s_v<d_v$ for every $v$. A finite legal
sequence that ends stable is a stabilization. Its firing-count vector is
called the odometer and denoted $u^*$.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same false odometer as in manuscript~16's subsection ``Why this is more than conservation'', after \cref{cdc:sp:thm:support}: the input and the false odometer are $(1,1)$, the stable endpoint is $(0,0)$.]}
\begin{example}[Balance without legal computation]
\label{cdc:nb:ex:phantom}
Take two nonsink vertices, one edge between them, and one edge from each
to the sink. Then
\[
 L=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The input $c=(1,1)$ is already stable, so its legal odometer is $(0,0)$.
Nevertheless $u=(1,1)$ gives $c-Lu=(0,0)$, also stable. Each proposed
firing needs a chip that only the other proposed firing would supply.
There is no legal first move.
\end{example}

\subsection{Upper stabilizers cap every legal run}

\srcnote{\wtag{} [\Cref{cdc:sp:lem:leastaction} of manuscript~16, the least-action principle of Fey, Levine and Peres \cite{fey-levine-peres}, here in an upper-stabilizer form that asks no lower bound on $c-Lv$ and no connection to the sink. Manuscript~19's first-excess proof is kept as a second route, because the subtraction in the proof of \cref{cdc:nb:thm:burning} needs this form.]}
\begin{lemma}[Least action in the form needed here]
\label{cdc:nb:lem:least}
Suppose $v\in\N^V$ satisfies
\[
 (c-Lv)_x<d_x\quad\text{for every }x\in V.
\]
No lower bound on $c-Lv$ is required. Every finite legal firing sequence
has count vector at most $v$ coordinatewise. Consequently a legal
stabilization exists, and its odometer $u^*$ is unique and satisfies
$u^*\le v$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose a legal sequence first exceeds $v$ at vertex $x$. Immediately
before that firing, its counts $w$ satisfy $w_x=v_x$ and $w_y\le v_y$
for all $y$. The number of chips at $x$ is therefore
\[
 c_x-d_xw_x+\sum_y a_{xy}w_y
 \le c_x-d_xv_x+\sum_y a_{xy}v_y<d_x,
\]
contradicting legality. Thus every legal sequence has at most
$\sum_xv_x$ firings. Repeatedly firing any available unstable vertex must
terminate. Its final state is stable and remains nonnegative because
all moves were legal. If two stabilizations had counts $u$ and $u'$,
apply the first assertion with each count vector as the upper stabilizer
for the other run. It follows that $u\le u'$ and $u'\le u$.
\end{proof}

This elementary proof will also justify a subtraction of a forbidden
subset that temporarily produces negative final balances. Those balances
need only be \emph{upper} stabilizers; incorrectly requiring them to be
nonnegative would obscure the argument.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The termination half of \cref{cdc:sp:lem:leastaction}, with the positivity of $L^{-1}\one$ from \cref{cdc:sp:lem:inverse}; manuscript~19 scales it to an integer potential. Second route.]}
\begin{lemma}[Finite dissipative graphs terminate]
\label{cdc:nb:lem:dissipative}
If every connected component meets the sink, every finite natural input
has a legal stabilization.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $x\in\R^V$,
\[
 x^{\mathsf T}Lx=
 \sum_{\{v,w\}}a_{vw}(x_v-x_w)^2+\sum_v b_vx_v^2.
\]
The right side vanishes only for $x=0$, since a zero-energy vector is
constant on each component and zero at every sink-adjacent vertex.
Thus $L$ is invertible. The vector $h=L^{-1}\one$ is rational and
strictly positive: at a vertex with minimum value $h_v\le0$, the identity
\[
 (Lh)_v=b_vh_v+\sum_w a_{vw}(h_v-h_w)
\]
would give $(Lh)_v\le0$, contradicting $(Lh)_v=1$. Multiplying $h$ by
a common denominator gives a positive integer vector $H$ with
$LH=C\one$ for a positive integer $C$. Every legal firing decreases
the nonnegative potential $H\cdot c$ by exactly $C$. Hence no infinite
legal sequence is possible.
\end{proof}

This also explains why an ordinary fixed finite sink graph is not the
source of undecidable halting in our application. Universality enters
through an unbounded spatial support in an infinite, effectively specified
background.

\section{The support-burning characterization\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:burning}

For $S\subseteq V$, write
\[
 \degS_S(v)=\sum_{w\in S}a_{vw}.
\]
A nonempty $S$ is forbidden for a stable configuration $s$ if
$s_v<\degS_S(v)$ for every $v\in S$. The relevant subsets will lie in
$\supp(u)=\{v:u_v>0\}$, not necessarily in the whole graph.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same theorem as \cref{cdc:sp:thm:support} of manuscript~16, with the parallel-removal form~(iii) that manuscript~16 states before \cref{cdc:sp:thm:ranks}; the burning test is Dhar's \cite{dhar1990}. The sufficiency proofs are the same maximum-layer argument. For necessity manuscript~16 uses the earliest last toppling, which manuscript~19 gives below as the remark ``A last-firing interpretation'', while manuscript~19's proof subtracts the indicator of a forbidden set and applies \cref{cdc:nb:lem:least}. Kept as a second route.]}
\begin{theorem}[Exact odometer from support burning]
\label{cdc:nb:thm:burning}
Let $u\in\N^V$ and suppose $s=c-Lu$ is stable. Put $F=\supp(u)$.
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $u$ is the legal odometer $u^*$.
\item For every nonempty $S\subseteq F$, some $v\in S$ satisfies
      $s_v\ge\degS_S(v)$.
\item Starting with $F$, repeatedly remove all vertices $v$ with
      $s_v$ at least the number of incident edges to the remaining set;
      eventually the remaining set is empty.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The equivalence of (ii) and (iii) is immediate but worth making precise.
If removal stops at a nonempty set $S$, then $S$ is forbidden. Conversely,
if a forbidden set $S$ exists, no vertex of $S$ can be the first member
of $S$ removed: at that moment all edges within $S$ are still present.
Thus complete removal is impossible.

Suppose (i) holds and let $S\subseteq F$ be forbidden. Define
$v=u-\one_S\in\N^V$. If $x\in S$, then
\[
 (c-Lv)_x=s_x+d_x-\degS_S(x)<d_x.
\]
If $x\notin S$, then
\[
 (c-Lv)_x=s_x-\degS_S(x)<d_x.
\]
So $v$ is an upper stabilizer, and Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:least} implies
$u^*\le v$. This contradicts $u^*=u$ at every vertex of $S$.

Now suppose (ii) holds. Since $u$ leaves a stable final state,
Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:least} gives an actual odometer $u^*\le u$. If
$h=u-u^*\ne0$, let
\[
 M=\max_v h_v\ge1,\qquad S=\{v:h_v=M\}.
\]
The set $S$ is nonempty and contained in $F$. For $v\in S$,
\begin{align*}
 (Lh)_v
 &=b_vM+\sum_{w\notin S}a_{vw}(M-h_w)\\
 &\ge b_v+\sum_{w\notin S}a_{vw}
   =d_v-\degS_S(v).
\end{align*}
The inequality uses integrality: $M-h_w\ge1$ outside $S$.
The true final state is $s^*=c-Lu^*=s+Lh$, so its stability gives
\[
 s_v\le s_v^*-(d_v-\degS_S(v))<\degS_S(v)
 \qquad(v\in S).
\]
Thus $S$ is forbidden, contradicting (ii). Therefore $u=u^*$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the support restriction is indispensable]
If $c=(0,0)$ in Example~\ref{cdc:nb:ex:phantom}, the correct odometer is zero
and its support is empty. The full two-vertex set is nevertheless a
forbidden subconfiguration of the final state. A recurrence test on
\emph{all} vertices would reject this legitimate no-fire computation.
The theorem asks a legality question about already proposed firings,
not whether an arbitrary final configuration is globally recurrent.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[A last-firing interpretation]
Necessity has a second, useful explanation. In a real finite run, choose,
among the vertices of a nonempty fired subset $S$, the vertex $v$ whose
\emph{last} firing occurs earliest. Each of its neighbors in $S$ fires
at least once after that event, so the final number of chips at $v$ is
at least $\degS_S(v)$. Thus the support test is related to last-event
arguments, but it requires no last-event timestamps in the certificate.
The maximum-layer proof supplies the converse.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Where undirectedness enters]
The proof uses that the diagonal degree dominates the sum of the incoming
edge multiplicities in each row of $L$. Symmetry ensures this from the
usual sandpile convention that outgoing chips determine the threshold.
One can formulate extensions under other row-dominance assumptions, but
an arbitrary directed sandpile is not covered. Section~\ref{cdc:nb:sec:directed}
gives an explicit false positive for the naive directed extension.
\end{remark}

\section{Two local inequalities force canonical burning rounds\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:ranks}

A certificate containing an arbitrary valid elimination order is generally
not unique. We instead encode the round of \emph{parallel} elimination:
at every round, remove every currently eligible vertex. Let $r_v=0$ for
$v\notin F$, and let $r_v\ge1$ be the round in which $v\in F$ is removed.
For a proposed rank vector $r$, define
\begin{equation}
 K_v(r)=\sum_w a_{vw}\one_{r_w\ge r_v},\qquad
 H_v(r)=\sum_w a_{vw}\one_{r_w\ge r_v-1}.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:KH}
\end{equation}
The first quantity is relevant only when $r_v>0$, and the second only
when $r_v>1$. In those cases inactive rank-zero neighbors are not counted.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same theorem as \cref{cdc:sp:thm:ranks}: manuscript~19's $K_v,H_v$ of \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:KH} are manuscript~16's $A_v,B_v$ of \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:AB} (the conditions $r_w\ge r_v-1$ and $r_w+1\ge r_v$ coincide), and both bound the ranks by the size of the support. Manuscript~19's converse runs the induction on rounds directly, without manuscript~16's separate minimum-rank step. Kept as a second route.]}
\begin{theorem}[Canonical local rank test]
\label{cdc:nb:thm:ranks}
Fix a stable $s$ and a support set $F$. There exists a vector $r\in\N^V$
with
\begin{align}
 r_v>0&\ \Longleftrightarrow\ v\in F, \label{cdc:nb:eq:r-support}\\
 r_v>0&\ \Longrightarrow\ s_v\ge K_v(r), \label{cdc:nb:eq:r-now}\\
 r_v>1&\ \Longrightarrow\ s_v<H_v(r) \label{cdc:nb:eq:r-before}
\end{align}
if and only if the support-burning algorithm empties $F$. When it
exists, $r$ is unique: it is exactly the parallel burning-round vector.
In particular, $\max r_v\le |F|$ when $F\ne\varnothing$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the actual parallel rounds, the remaining set at the start of round
$j$ is $\{w:r_w\ge j\}$. Eligibility at round $r_v$ gives
\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:r-now}. If $r_v>1$, the vertex was ineligible at round $r_v-1$;
this gives \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:r-before}.

Conversely, suppose the three conditions hold. We show inductively that
the parallel algorithm removes exactly $\{v:r_v=j\}$ at round $j$.
Assume smaller ranks have already been removed, so the remaining set is
$S_j=\{v:r_v\ge j\}$. A vertex with $r_v=j$ is eligible by
\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:r-now}. If $r_v>j$, then $r_v>1$ and
\[
 \{w:r_w\ge r_v-1\}\subseteq S_j.
\]
Consequently \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:r-before} gives
$s_v< H_v(r)\le\degS_{S_j}(v)$: it is not yet eligible.
Thus precisely the rank-$j$ vertices are removed.

There cannot be a gap followed by a positive rank: after an empty removal
round, the remaining set and its eligibility do not change, whereas the
induction would later require a nonempty removal. Since $V$ is finite,
all positive ranks have finite maximum and all members of $F$ are
removed. The algorithm is deterministic, which proves uniqueness.
Every nonempty round removes at least one vertex, giving the bound.
\end{proof}

The second inequality is not cosmetic. A single active vertex joined
only to a sink satisfies \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:r-now} with \emph{every} positive rank.
For ranks above one, however, $H_v=0$, so \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:r-before} is impossible.
Its unique rank is one. No externally chosen rank bound or big-$M$
constant is required anywhere in the compiler.

\section{Canonical arithmetic gadgets over the natural numbers\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:gadgets}
\srcnote{\wtag{} [Manuscript~16 makes the same unique comparison with complementary selectors and weighted squares of total degree three (\cref{cdc:sp:lem:compare}), and its gated gap \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:gated} plays the role of the mask \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:mask}. Manuscript~19's $\GE$ uses one Boolean, two inactive-branch products and quadratic residuals, so its sum of squares is a quartic; the forced remainders of the two comparison gadgets are the same, $x-y$ or $y-x-1$.]}


We need branch tests with \emph{unique} helper tuples. Standard existential
inequality encodings often leave inactive branch slacks arbitrary. That
would preserve satisfiability but destroy the promised one-point zero set.

\subsection{A unique positivity indicator}

For $x,z,a\in\N$, define $\NZ(x;z,a)$ by three residuals:
\begin{equation}
 z(z-1)=0,\qquad x-z(a+1)=0,\qquad (1-z)a=0.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:nz}
\end{equation}
\begin{lemma}
\label{cdc:nb:lem:nz}
For each fixed $x\in\N$, the unique solution of \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:nz} is
\[
 z=\one_{x>0},\qquad a=\max(x-1,0).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first equation gives $z\in\{0,1\}$. If $z=0$, the second forces
$x=0$ and the third forces $a=0$. If $z=1$, the second gives $x=a+1>0$.
These two cases are disjoint and exhaustive.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A comparison with unique branch remainders}

For integer-valued expressions $x,y$ and natural helpers $B,p,q$, define
$\GE(x,y;B,p,q)$ by four residuals:
\begin{align}
 B(B-1)&=0,\nonumber\\
 x-y-Bp+(1-B)(q+1)&=0,\label{cdc:nb:eq:ge}\\
 (1-B)p&=0,\nonumber\\
 Bq&=0.\nonumber
\end{align}
\begin{lemma}
\label{cdc:nb:lem:ge}
For fixed integers $x,y$, there is exactly one natural helper triple:
\[
 (B,p,q)=
 \begin{cases}
 (1,x-y,0),&x\ge y,\\
 (0,0,y-x-1),&x<y.
 \end{cases}
\]
When $x,y$ are linear expressions, all four residuals are quadratic or
linear in the full set of variables.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $B=1$, the equations reduce to $x-y=p\ge0$ and $q=0$.
If $B=0$, they reduce to $x-y=-(q+1)<0$ and $p=0$.
The Boolean equation excludes all other branches.
\end{proof}

Allowing $y$ to be a signed expression matters: the compiler compares a
neighboring rank with $r_v-1$, which is $-1$ at an inactive vertex. The
helpers still range over $\N$, and Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:ge} still applies.

\subsection{Masked inequalities without unused freedom}

If $g\in\{0,1\}$ is already certified and $F$ is an integer linear
expression, a natural helper $\lambda$ with
\begin{equation}
 \lambda-gF=0
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:mask}
\end{equation}
expresses $g=1\Rightarrow F\ge0$. It sets $\lambda=F$ on the active
branch and $\lambda=0$ on the inactive branch. Thus its helper is unique.
The product $gF$ has degree at most two.

\section{The complete finite-graph quartic compiler\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:compiler}

The following is an explicit equation schema. There are no hidden calls
to a halting predicate, a transitive closure, a permutation test, or a
bounded history verifier.

\subsection{Variables and equations}

For every vertex $v$ introduce exactly eleven natural variables:
\begin{equation}
 u_v,s_v,\sigma_v,z_v,\alpha_v,r_v,k_v,e_v,\beta_v,\lambda_v,\mu_v.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:vertexvars}
\end{equation}
For each \emph{ordered} internal adjacent pair $(v,w)$, introduce the
six helpers in the two comparisons
\begin{align}
 \GE(r_w,r_v;A_{vw},p_{vw},q_{vw}),\label{cdc:nb:eq:edgege1}\\
 \GE(r_w,r_v-1;B_{vw},P_{vw},Q_{vw}).\label{cdc:nb:eq:edgege2}
\end{align}
Define the linear expressions
\begin{equation}
 K_v=\sum_w a_{vw}A_{vw},\qquad H_v=\sum_w a_{vw}B_{vw}.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:linearKH}
\end{equation}
At every vertex impose the following twelve quadratic or linear residuals:
\begin{align}
 s_v-c_v+d_vu_v-\sum_w a_{vw}u_w&=0,
       &&\text{balance},\label{cdc:nb:eq:allbalance}\\
 s_v+\sigma_v-(d_v-1)&=0,
       &&\text{stability},\label{cdc:nb:eq:allstable}\\
 z_v(z_v-1)&=0,\nonumber\\
 u_v-z_v(\alpha_v+1)&=0,\label{cdc:nb:eq:allu}\\
 (1-z_v)\alpha_v&=0,\nonumber\\
 r_v-z_v-k_v&=0,\label{cdc:nb:eq:allrank}\\
 (1-z_v)k_v&=0,\nonumber\\
 e_v(e_v-1)&=0,\nonumber\\
 k_v-e_v(\beta_v+1)&=0,\label{cdc:nb:eq:alllater}\\
 (1-e_v)\beta_v&=0,\nonumber\\
 \lambda_v-z_v(s_v-K_v)&=0,
       &&\text{burn now},\label{cdc:nb:eq:allnow}\\
 \mu_v-e_v(H_v-s_v-1)&=0,
       &&\text{not before}.\label{cdc:nb:eq:allbefore}
\end{align}
Each invocation of $\GE$ in \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:edgege1}--\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:edgege2}
means the four displayed residuals \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:ge}. The relations
\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:allu} and \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:alllater} include their adjacent Boolean
and inactive-slack equations.

\subsection{Exact zero-set theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Canonical quartic certificate]
\label{cdc:nb:thm:finitecompiler}
Let $G$ satisfy the assumptions of Section~\ref{cdc:nb:sec:least}, and let
$c\in\N^V$. The preceding system has
\begin{equation}
 N=11n+12E\quad\text{natural witnesses},\qquad
 \mathcal R=12n+16E\quad\text{quadratic residuals}.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:counts}
\end{equation}
If its residual polynomials are $f_1,\ldots,f_{\mathcal R}$, then
\begin{equation}
 Q_{G,c}(\mathbf y)=\sum_{j=1}^{\mathcal R} f_j(\mathbf y)^2
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:quartic}
\end{equation}
is an explicit integer polynomial of degree four, and
\[
 \#\{\mathbf y\in\N^N:Q_{G,c}(\mathbf y)=0\}
 =\begin{cases}
 1,&\text{a finite legal stabilization of $c$ exists},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The $u$-coordinates of its unique zero, when present, are precisely $u^*$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since the variables $s_v,\sigma_v$ are natural, \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:allstable}
forces $0\le s_v<d_v$. Together with \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:allbalance}, this is the
stable balance equation. Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:nz} makes $z_v$ the positivity
indicator of $u_v$. If $z_v=0$, \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:allrank} and its inactive
equation give $k_v=r_v=0$. If $z_v=1$, they give $r_v=1+k_v>0$.
The second $\NZ$ instance makes $e_v=1$ exactly when $k_v>0$, which is
exactly when $r_v>1$.

Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:ge} identifies $A_{vw}$ and $B_{vw}$ with the rank
comparisons in \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:KH}. Nonnegativity of $\lambda_v$ imposes
\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:r-now}, and nonnegativity of $\mu_v$ imposes the strict integer
inequality \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:r-before}. Hence Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:ranks} gives a
successful support burning, and Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:burning} gives $u=u^*$.
This proves soundness.

Conversely, take a legal stabilization. Use its odometer and final
configuration for $u,s$, its parallel burning ranks for $r$, and set
$\sigma_v=d_v-1-s_v$. The gadgets supply $z_v,\alpha_v$, put
$k_v=r_v-z_v$, supply $e_v,\beta_v$, and supply the six comparison helpers
on each ordered pair. Finally put
\[
 \lambda_v=z_v(s_v-K_v),\qquad
 \mu_v=e_v(H_v-s_v-1).
\]
The rank inequalities make both values natural. This yields a zero of
every residual and proves completeness.

For uniqueness, first $u$ is uniquely determined by legality; then $s$
is fixed by balance, and $r$ is fixed by Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:ranks}.
The positivity gadgets, rank offset, stability slack, comparisons, and
masked slacks are each uniquely determined in turn. Thus the entire
witness tuple is unique, not merely its projection onto $u$.

There are eleven variables and twelve residuals per vertex. There are
$2E$ ordered pairs, each contributing six variables and eight residuals.
This gives \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:counts}. Every residual has degree at most two, so
\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:quartic} has degree at most four. Its degree is exactly four:
the degree-four homogeneous part is a sum of squares of quadratic
homogeneous parts and is not the zero polynomial, since at least one
Boolean residual has a nonzero quadratic part. Finally, a sum of squares
of integer values is zero exactly when each value is zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Integral rejection gap]
\label{cdc:nb:cor:gap}
At every natural tuple other than the unique valid one, if it exists,
$Q_{G,c}(\mathbf y)\ge1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The polynomial is a sum of squares of integers. A nonzero residual has
absolute value at least one.
\end{proof}

This is a discrete gap only. We make no numerical-conditioning assertion
for real-valued optimization near the zero.

\subsection{The meaning of the size bound}

The residual description has $O(n+E)$ monomial occurrences: its long
linear sums run once over incident neighbors. For bounded degree, the
fully expanded quartic also has $O(n+E)$ monomial occurrences before
collection. For unbounded degree, expansion of squared neighbor sums
can produce $O(\sum_v\deg_{\mathrm{adj}}(v)^2)$ occurrences; the linear-size
claim is therefore a \emph{residual or shared-expression} claim in that
case. Coefficient bit lengths also depend on the edge multiplicities,
sink multiplicities, and input chip counts. None of these counts is
claimed optimal.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The delivered source breaks this subscript (a line break stands where \texttt{\textbackslash rm} was meant, so that its PDF prints the subscript as the italic letters $madj$); it is printed as $\deg_{\mathrm{adj}}(v)$, the degree of $v$ in the internal graph.]}


Over strictly positive witnesses, substitute $y_i=x_i-1$ with
$x_i\in\{1,2,\ldots\}$. This preserves degree and gives a bijection
of zero sets. Replacing each natural witness by a sum of four integer
squares preserves existence over all integers but generally introduces
many sign and representation choices. It does not preserve our
single-witness conclusion.

\paragraph{\wtag{} Comparison with manuscript~16's cubics.} Batch~79, 2 October 2026. In this report's letters ($E$ nonzero undirected adjacencies, $m=2E$ ordered ones), manuscript~19's system has $11n+12E$ natural witnesses and $12n+16E$ quadratic residuals, and its sum of squares is a quartic that is nonnegative on all of $\Z^N$. Manuscript~16's baseline cubic has $13n+6m=13n+12E$ coordinates (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:compiler}) and its compact cubic $10n+6E$ (\cref{cdc:sp:thm:compact}); both are single polynomials of degree three, nonnegative on the real orthant, where manuscript~19 has a system of degree-two equations. The compact cubic always has fewer coordinates than this system; the research tree's projection of it (the next paragraph), with $8n+12E$ witnesses, has fewer than the compact cubic exactly when $E<n/3$. For the two-vertex graph ($n=2$, $E=1$) the counts are 34 (projected 28) against 38 and 26; for $n=10$, $E=15$ they are 290 (260) against 310 and 190. Neither construction improves the other: they trade degree and form (residual degree two and a quartic, against one cubic) for coordinates. Part~XI's classification makes every fixed member of manuscript~16's cubic family semilinear (the note in \cref{cdc:sp:sec:mrdp}); manuscript~19's quartic has degree four and is outside \cref{cdc:of:cor:no-cubic-universal}, but each fixed member concerns one finite graph, and the field normal form of \cref{cdc:nb:sec:fields} is not a fixed-arity scalar polynomial, so no universal fixed-arity statement follows from either.

\paragraph{\wtag{} The research tree's review.} Batch~79, 2 October 2026. ProveIt's Hilbert's-tenth-problem research tree, maintained separately, reviewed this archive on the day it arrived \cite{repo-bsrev}. It confirms the support-burning converse, the rank argument, the natural-domain signs of $\NZ$, $\GE$ and the masks (including comparisons with $r_v-1=-1$), the counts and the exact degree four, the halo and the normalized field verifier; it finds no semantic or domain defect and supplies no patch. Its helper also checks a projection of the emitted compiler: substituting $u_v=z_v+\alpha_v$, $k_v=e_v+\beta_v$ and $r_v=z_v+e_v+\beta_v$ and deleting three residuals per vertex leaves $8n+12E$ witnesses and $9n+16E$ quadratic residuals, of degree at most two, with a bijection between complete natural zero sets; the analogous field schema has 44 fields and 57 local residuals in dimension three. On arbitrary tuples the parent sum of squares exceeds the new one by $\sum_v[((1-z_v)\alpha_v)^2+((1-e_v)\beta_v)^2]$, so the projection is an equivalence of zero sets, not a polynomial identity. The review claims no saving of arithmetic operations (without $u$ and $r$, neighbouring field expressions read more fields) and no improvement of the project's operation bounds. It answers manuscript~19's first question in part (\cref{cdc:nb:q:smaller}).


\section{Worked examples and a directed obstruction\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:examples}

\subsection{A complete 34-variable example}
\srcnote{\wtag{} [Manuscript~16's worked example is a two-site graph too, with $L=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and an input that needs $10^{100}+6$ topplings (\cref{cdc:sp:prop:twosite}); this one certifies the input $(3,1)$.]}


Return to the two-vertex graph of Example~\ref{cdc:nb:ex:phantom}, now with input
$c=(3,1)$. A legal firing sequence is $1,2,1$:
\[
 (3,1)\longrightarrow(1,2)\longrightarrow(2,0)
 \longrightarrow(0,1).
\]
Thus $u=(2,1)$ and $s=(0,1)$. In the support-burning test, vertex 2 burns
first because $s_2=1$ meets its one remaining internal edge; vertex 1
then burns. Hence $r=(2,1)$.

\node[above=3mm of b,align=center] {$c_2=1,\ u_2=1$\\$s_2=1,\ r_2=1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

All eleven vertex fields are displayed below; this is the complete
vertex part of the unique witness.
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}crrrrrrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$v$ & $u$ &$s$ &$\sigma$ &$z$ &$\alpha$ &$r$ &$k$ &$e$ &$\beta$ &$\lambda$ &$\mu$\\
\midrule

The remaining twelve helpers are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
(v,w)&(A_{vw},p_{vw},q_{vw})&(B_{vw},P_{vw},Q_{vw})\\\hline
(1,2)&(0,0,0)&(1,0,0)\\
