Here $n=2,E=1$, so the compiler has 34 natural witnesses and 40 residuals.
The supplied coefficient-level expansion has exactly 201 distinct
nonzero monomials after collection, and degree four. The machine-readable
file \path{data/19-no-borrowed-firings-two_vertex_certificate.json} contains the variable
order, every residual, and the complete expanded quartic. Its companion
witness file uses zero-based vertex indices; the article uses one-based
indices. No coefficients are suppressed in the JSON artifact.

Changing only the input to $(1,1)$ demonstrates rejection of the borrowed
firing profile $(1,1)$. Its stable final state $(0,0)$ has a forbidden
support, so \emph{no} assignment of the rank and comparison helpers can
extend that profile to a zero. This is stronger than rejecting one
arbitrarily chosen rank assignment.

\subsection{The natural domain cannot be dropped}
The borrowed profile in Example~\ref{cdc:nb:ex:phantom} actually gives an
integer zero of the same quartic if negative helpers are allowed.
Take $u=(1,1)$, $s=(0,0)$, $r=(1,1)$, the canonical nonnegative Boolean
and comparison helpers, and $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=-1$.
Both burn-now residuals vanish because $K_1=K_2=1$; the second masked
conditions are inactive. Every other residual vanishes as well.
This is a false root over $\Z$, excluded exactly by the specified
natural witness domain. The implementation tests this example and
rejects it through its domain-validating certificate interface.

\subsection{Why this is not a directed compiler}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:directed}
\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same example as \cref{cdc:sp:sec:directed}: the toppling matrix, the input $(0,2)$, the false odometer $(2,1)$, the endpoint $(0,1)$ and the accepted ranks $(2,1)$ coincide. Printed as delivered; manuscript~19 adds Dhar's caveat on nonsymmetric matrices \cite{dhar1998}.]}


Consider a directed graph with one edge from $a$ to $b$, two edges from
$b$ to $a$, and one edge from $b$ to the sink. The outgoing degrees are
$(1,3)$, and the column-firing balance matrix is
\[
 L=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Input $c=(0,2)$ is stable and cannot legally fire. Nevertheless
\[
 u=(2,1),\qquad Lu=(0,1),\qquad s=c-Lu=(0,1)
\]
gives a stable balance. A naive burning rule that uses the incoming
matrix accepts it: $b$ has one incoming edge from the remaining $a$ and
$s_b=1$, so $b$ burns first; $a$ burns next. The ranks $(2,1)$ also satisfy
the two naive local rank inequalities.

Thus neither replacing undirected neighbors by incoming neighbors nor
assuming that every vertex can reach a sink repairs the compiler. The
row for $a$ has incoming multiplicity two but threshold one, which breaks
the maximum-layer inequality in Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:burning}. The Python
constructor checks symmetry and rejects this graph before compiling it.
Dhar discusses the broader need for script tests in nonsymmetric systems
\cite{dhar1998}; a canonical low-degree script compiler is a meaningful
extension problem rather than a theorem silently assumed here.

\section{Infinite lattices: finite support and the boundary halo\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:lattice}

\subsection{Effective inputs and the exact halting notion}

Fix $d\ge1$. Every vertex of $\Z^d$ has $2d$ nearest neighbors, and a
firing sends one chip to each neighbor. The input is
\begin{equation}
 \eta=b+\delta,
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:periodicinput}
\end{equation}
where $b:\Z^d\to\{0,\ldots,2d-1\}$ is specified by a complete finite
period table with positive periods, and $\delta:\Z^d\to\N$ has finite
support and is specified by a finite list. In particular, the periodic
background is stable and is \emph{effectively} given.

\begin{definition}
The input \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:periodicinput} \emph{globally finitely stabilizes} if
there is a finite legal sequence of firings after which every lattice
site is stable. Equivalently, its legal complete odometer has finite
total sum. Such an odometer has finite support and a finite natural
value at each site.
\end{definition}

This is not the same as local stabilization, where every site can fire
finitely often while infinitely many different sites fire. It is also
not the question whether one designated site ever fires. Our certificates
address \emph{finite total activity} only.

Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:least} extends to this setting whenever its upper
stabilizer has finite support: the same first-excess argument applies,
and the finite sum of the upper stabilizer bounds the total number of
legal firings. At any finite stage there are only finitely many unstable
sites, because the background was stable and only finitely many sites
have been affected. A greedy legal run must therefore end globally stable.

\subsection{A finite cube must not silently discard escaping chips}

Let
\[
 B_R=\{-R,\ldots,R\}^d,\qquad
 \partial^+B_R=\{y\notin B_R:y\sim x\text{ for some }x\in B_R\}.
\]
Choose $R\ge0$ containing $\supp(\delta)$. On the induced finite cube,
retain threshold $2d$ at each vertex, treating every edge leaving the
cube as a sink edge. Compile the finite graph as in
Section~\ref{cdc:nb:sec:compiler}. At every exterior neighbor $y\in\partial^+B_R$
add a natural slack $\tau_y$ and the linear residual
\begin{equation}
 \tau_y+\eta(y)+\sum_{\substack{x\in B_R\\x\sim y}}u_x-(2d-1)=0.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:halo}
\end{equation}
This is a \emph{no-firing halo}: it requires the chips sent outside the
cube to leave every exterior recipient stable.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same theorem as \cref{cdc:sp:thm:collar}: the halo slack $\tau_y$ is manuscript~16's collar gap $\lambda_x$ of \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:collar}, and both proofs replay the finite stabilization on the lattice without toppling an exterior site. Manuscript~16 then chooses a canonical radius (\cref{cdc:sp:cor:radius}); manuscript~19 removes the radius by passing to fields (\cref{cdc:nb:sec:fields}). Kept as a second route.]}
\begin{theorem}[Exact finite-window certificate]
\label{cdc:nb:thm:halo}
Under the preceding input and containment assumptions, the augmented
system has exactly one natural zero if the infinite-lattice odometer
is finite and supported in $B_R$, and has no natural zero otherwise.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A zero of the finite graph part certifies its legal stabilization. Replay
that same sequence on the whole lattice while never firing an exterior
site. At an interior site the evolution is identical to the finite
sink-graph evolution, because exterior sites send nothing back. Thus
the replay is legal and leaves every interior site stable.
Equation~\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:halo} leaves the immediate exterior sites stable as
well. Every other site is unchanged from the stable periodic background,
because all input additions lie in $B_R$. The replay is therefore a
global finite stabilization. Its odometer is supported in $B_R$.

Conversely, if a global finite stabilization has odometer supported in
$B_R$, its firing sequence uses only interior sites and is legal on the
finite cube. Its exterior final values are exactly the values in
\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:halo} without $\tau_y$, so stable halo slacks exist. The graph
witness is unique by Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:finitecompiler}; every halo slack
is then fixed by its equation. This proves uniqueness of the extension.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[The smallest leaking boundary]
\label{cdc:nb:ex:halo}
In $\Z^3$, put five chips at every site and add one at the origin. On the
radius-zero sink cube, the origin topples once and ends with zero chips.
A certificate that discarded outgoing chips would accept this as a
complete stabilization. In the actual lattice, each of its six neighbors
now has six chips and is unstable. All six halo slacks would have to be
$-1$, so \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:halo} correctly rejects this cube. The example only
needs this finite calculation; no assertion about its eventual infinite
dynamics is needed for the counterexample.
\end{example}

\subsection{Exact lattice counts}

Put $\ell=2R+1$. The cube has
\[
 n=\ell^d,\qquad E=d(\ell-1)\ell^{d-1},\qquad
 h=|\partial^+B_R|=2d\ell^{d-1}.
\]
The halo adds one witness and one residual per site. Therefore the
complete scalar certificate has
\begin{align}
 N_R&=(11+12d)\ell^d-10d\ell^{d-1},\label{cdc:nb:eq:cubeN}\\
 \mathcal R_R&=(12+16d)\ell^d-14d\ell^{d-1}.\label{cdc:nb:eq:cubeE}
\end{align}
In dimension three these are
\begin{equation}
 N_R=47\ell^3-30\ell^2,\qquad
 \mathcal R_R=60\ell^3-42\ell^2.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:3dcounts}
\end{equation}

\srcnote{\wtag{} [Here $E=d(\ell-1)\ell^{d-1}=2dR(2R+1)^{d-1}$ is half of manuscript~16's $m_R$. Manuscript~16's counts for the same box, which include its canonical-radius gap, are \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:spatialarity} and, for the compact cubic, \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:compactspatialvars}.]}

There is no time horizon in these formulas. The externally chosen
parameter measures space, not the number of individual topplings.

Increasing $R$ after it contains the true support yields different-sized
scalar tuples representing the \emph{same} odometer. The next section
removes this representational padding by taking the fields themselves,
not a chosen box, as the mathematical witnesses.

\section{A fixed 47-field quasi-Diophantine normal form\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:fields}

\subsection{The domain is part of the theorem}

For a specified periodic tail $t:\Z^d\to\N$, define
\begin{equation}
 \FS_t=\{f:\Z^d\to\N:\{x:f(x)\ne t(x)\}\text{ is finite}\}.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:fielddomain}
\end{equation}
We use pointwise addition and multiplication, signed polynomial
expressions, and the nearest-neighbor shifts
\[
 (\shift_\epsilon f)(x)=f(x+\epsilon),
 \qquad \epsilon\in\{\pm e_1,\ldots,\pm e_d\}.
\]
A pointwise polynomial identity means equality as functions on the
whole lattice. In this article a \emph{finite-deviation quasi-Diophantine
representation} means an existential formula over the specified domains
\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:fielddomain}, using polynomial identities with finitely many
shifts. This is an explicitly defined difference-algebraic setting. It
is not ordinary polynomial arithmetic on finitely many natural numbers.

An element of $\FS_t$ has a finite effective representation: a finite
list of its exceptional sites and their actual nonnegative values,
with the periodic tail understood. There is no claim that an arbitrary
non-effectively-described eventual periodicity is adequate.

\subsection{The fixed local expression}

Place the eleven fields in \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:vertexvars} at every site. For each
of the $2d$ directions $\epsilon$, add six fields
\[
 A_\epsilon,p_\epsilon,q_\epsilon,
 B_\epsilon,P_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon.
\]
At site $x$ use the comparisons
\begin{align}
 \GE((\shift_\epsilon r)(x),r(x);
             A_\epsilon(x),p_\epsilon(x),q_\epsilon(x)),\label{cdc:nb:eq:fieldge1}\\
 \GE((\shift_\epsilon r)(x),r(x)-1;
             B_\epsilon(x),P_\epsilon(x),Q_\epsilon(x)).\label{cdc:nb:eq:fieldge2}
\end{align}
Use the twelve vertex residuals
\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:allbalance}--\eqref{cdc:nb:eq:allbefore}, with
\[
 c_v\rightsquigarrow\eta(x),\quad d_v\rightsquigarrow2d,\quad
 \sum_w a_{vw}u_w\rightsquigarrow\sum_\epsilon(\shift_\epsilon u)(x),
 \quad K=\sum_\epsilon A_\epsilon,\quad H=\sum_\epsilon B_\epsilon.
\]
These are $12+16d$ local residuals in $11+12d$ field witnesses. Denote
the sum of their squares by $\mathscr Q_d$. It is one fixed degree-four
difference-polynomial expression of radius one. Its coefficients and
stencil depend only on $d$; the input $\eta$ is a parameter field.

The domains are prescribed by the following tails:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{.49\textwidth}c@{}}
\toprule
Field or field group & Required periodic tail\\
\midrule
$u,z,\alpha,r,k,e,\beta,\lambda,\mu$ & $0$\\
$s$ & $b$\\
$\sigma$ & $2d-1-b$\\
$(A_\epsilon,p_\epsilon,q_\epsilon)$ for each $\epsilon$ & $(1,0,0)$\\
$(B_\epsilon,P_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)$ for each $\epsilon$ & $(1,1,0)$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The remainder $P_\epsilon=1$ in the last row is necessary: in the tail
we are comparing $0$ with $-1$. All these tail assignments satisfy the
local equations whenever $\eta=b$.

\begin{theorem}[Unique finite-deviation field witness]
\label{cdc:nb:thm:fields}
For the effective input $\eta=b+\delta$, the identity
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr Q_d(\eta;\mathbf f)=0
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:fieldquartic}
\end{equation}
has a solution in the prescribed field domains if and only if $\eta$
globally finitely stabilizes. When a solution exists, the complete
$(11+12d)$-field tuple is unique. In dimension three this is a fixed
47-field representation with 60 quadratic residuals.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose a field solution exists. Its $u$-field has finite support, and
its stable balance $s=\eta-Lu$ is forced pointwise by the equations.
The finite-support version of Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:least} gives a global
finite legal odometer $u^*\le u$.

The positivity gadgets force $r$ to have exactly the same support as $u$.
The comparison and masked equations give the two canonical rank
inequalities on that finite support, with exterior ranks zero. The
proof of Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:ranks} therefore applies unchanged. The proof
of Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:burning} also applies: any nonempty maximum layer of
$u-u^*$ is finite, and the same row identity counts edges leaving that
layer. Hence $u=u^*$. All remaining fields are now uniquely determined
by the same sequence of arguments as in
Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:finitecompiler}.

Conversely, suppose a global finite legal stabilization exists. Its
odometer has finite support. Use its final state and support-burning
ranks, and define all helpers by the canonical formulas. The equations
hold at every site. The fields $u,r$ and their positivity and masked
helpers vanish off a finite set. The final state $s$ differs from $b$
only at the input defects, fired sites, and neighbors of fired sites;
$\sigma$ has the corresponding complementary tail. A comparison helper
can differ from its stated tail only when its site or the neighboring
site has nonzero rank. Thus all prescribed tail conditions hold, and
we obtain a finite-deviation solution.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What 47 counts]
The number 47 counts \emph{global unknown fields}. The local stencil in
dimension three reads their 47 values at the central site and additionally
reads the $u$ and $r$ fields at each of six neighbors. Thus the displayed
local polynomial uses 59 scalar witness slots, plus the input value
$\eta(x)$, but those slots are tied together at neighboring sites by the
field interpretation. Neither 47 nor 59 is asserted to be the number of
ordinary natural witnesses of a universal integer polynomial.
\end{remark}

\wtag{} Batch~79, 2 October 2026: the research tree's review \cite{repo-bsrev} reduces the schema to 44 fields and 57 local residuals in dimension three by the projection described after \cref{cdc:nb:cor:gap}, an equivalence of zero sets that claims no saving of operations. Nothing of this section is in manuscript~16, which removes the padding of the radius differently, by a canonical radius (\cref{cdc:sp:cor:radius}).


\subsection{From unique fields to unique finite codes}

Fix the periodic input description. Encode a witness tuple by the sorted
list of sites where at least one of its fields differs from its prescribed
tail, with the vector of actual values at each such site. Reject duplicate
sites, entries equal to the entire tail vector, out-of-order lists, and
malformed numbers. Any fixed injective coding of such normalized finite
lists gives a unique natural code for each field tuple. No independently
supplied box radius is part of this normalized code.

Verification is decidable. Check the finitely many listed values and
the local equations on the union of the exception set, its nearest
neighbors, and the input-defect set. Outside that union every local
window has the known tails and $\eta=b$, so the equations hold
identically. One may include an extra neighboring shell around this
whole union for a simpler implementation; it remains finite.

\begin{corollary}[A recursive unique-code verifier]
\label{cdc:nb:cor:code}
There is a decidable relation $C(p,w)$, where $p$ is an effective input
code, such that a globally finitely stabilizing input has exactly one
code $w$ satisfying $C(p,w)$, and every other input has none.
\end{corollary}

The fact that this verifier is recursive is not itself a new substitute
for MRDP. Its value here is the particular history-free geometric
witness and explicit local quartic expression. Applying ordinary MRDP
to $C$ may add many auxiliary arithmetic witnesses. The theorem about
unique \emph{field codes} says nothing that forces those new witnesses
to be unique.

\section{Universality and the uncomputable spatial frontier\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:universality}

\subsection{The imported universality theorem and its consequence}

Cairns constructs effective periodic-plus-finite sandpiles on $\Z^3$
that globally finitely stabilize exactly when a simulated Turing machine
halts; the global-halting argument uses a lazy automaton to avoid
infinitely much initialization work \cite[Section 6, Theorem 3]{cairns}.
The construction uses stable background circuitry with finite added input
chips, so it lies in the class \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:periodicinput}. This simulation
theorem is an external dependency, not reproved or numerically instantiated
in the present package.

Let $\mathcal H_{\rm sp}$ be the set of finite descriptions of such
inputs that globally finitely stabilize. Malformed descriptions may,
by convention, be rejected.

\begin{theorem}[Completeness and the fixed-field normal form]
\label{cdc:nb:thm:complete}
The set $\mathcal H_{\rm sp}$ is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete under computable
many-one reductions. Consequently the fixed expression
$\mathscr Q_3$, with its prescribed finite-deviation witness domains,
defines a $\Sigma^0_1$-complete input relation with a unique witness tuple.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For enumerability, enumerate radii $R$ containing the finitely many input
defects. Stabilize the finite sink cube, which terminates by
Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:dissipative}, and test its finite halo. Accept if the halo
is stable. Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:halo} shows that this procedure accepts
exactly the globally finitely stabilizing inputs. Alternatively, enumerate
and verify the finite codes in Corollary~\ref{cdc:nb:cor:code}.

The cited simulation supplies a computable reduction from Turing halting
to membership in $\mathcal H_{\rm sp}$, with the same yes/no orientation.
Together with enumerability this proves $\Sigma^0_1$-completeness.
The final assertion follows from Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:fields}.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} The first assertion is the first assertion of \cref{cdc:sp:thm:nobound}, from the same enumeration and Cairns's reduction \cite{cairns}; the second, a unique witness tuple for one fixed field expression, is manuscript~19's.


\srcnote{\wtag{} [Existence only. Manuscript~16's \cref{cdc:sp:thm:singlefold}, an instance of \cref{cdc:bd:thm:universal}, says what single-foldness of such a polynomial would be equivalent to.]}
\begin{corollary}[Ordinary Diophantine existence, without uniqueness]
\label{cdc:nb:cor:mrdp}
For any fixed effective natural coding of these inputs, there is an
integer polynomial $P(p,w_1,\ldots,w_k)$, with fixed finite $k$, such that
\[
 p\in\mathcal H_{\rm sp}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists\mathbf w\in\N^k\ P(p,\mathbf w)=0.
\]
Its witness uniqueness and numerical arity are not conclusions of this
article.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply MRDP to the enumerable set in Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:complete}. This is
precisely the type of interface described by the repository's
\code{Diophantine.mrdp} guide \cite{repo-mrdp}.
\end{proof}

Since $\mathcal H_{\rm sp}$ is an undecidable enumerable set, its
complement is not enumerable and hence is not definable by a purely
existential ordinary Diophantine equation over natural witnesses.
This is a consequence of the established halting reduction, not an
independent solution of a number-theoretic conjecture.

\subsection{No computable input-only radius bound}

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same theorem as \cref{cdc:sp:thm:nobound}, whose finite search is the argument of \cref{cdc:bd:prop:nobound}. Manuscript~19 bounds the radius of the support, manuscript~16 its canonical radius $R_*\ge R_0$; the two bounds differ by at most the computable radius of the input modifications. Kept as a second route.]}
\begin{theorem}[Uncomputable support radius]
\label{cdc:nb:thm:noradius}
There is no total computable function $B$ on valid finite input
descriptions such that every globally finitely stabilizing input has
odometer support contained in $B_{B(p)}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose such a $B$ existed. Given $p$, compute
\[
 R=\max\{B(p),R_\delta\},
\]
where $R_\delta$ is the maximum absolute coordinate of an input-defect
site, with value zero for an empty defect set. Stabilize the finite cube
$B_R$ and check the halo. Both are terminating finite computations.

If $p$ globally finitely stabilizes, the promised bound puts its odometer
inside $B_R$, so the halo passes by Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:halo}. If the halo
passes, that theorem itself proves global finite stabilization, without
any promise. We have obtained a decision procedure for
$\mathcal H_{\rm sp}$, contradicting Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:complete}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Support cardinality and code length}

\begin{lemma}[A fired component must have an input seed]
\label{cdc:nb:lem:seed}
Every connected component of the finite fired support intersects
$\supp(\delta)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $S$ be one component and consider the first legal firing at a vertex
of $S$. Before it, no vertex of $S$ has fired. No fired vertex outside
$S$ can be adjacent to a member of $S$, by the definition of a connected
component of the fired support. If $S$ contained no input defect, its
first proposed vertex would therefore still have its stable background
value. That firing could not be legal.
\end{proof}

\srcnote{\wtag{} [Its first assertion is \cref{cdc:sp:cor:sites}, proved there by following first topplings back to the initial defects instead of by \cref{cdc:nb:lem:seed}; its second, on the length of a canonical field code, is new. Kept as a second route.]}
\begin{corollary}[No computable cardinality or certificate-length cap]
\label{cdc:nb:cor:nosize}
There is no total computable input-only upper bound on the number of
fired sites for all globally finitely stabilizing inputs. Nor is there
such a bound on the bit length of a valid canonical field code.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If the fired support has $N$ sites, every site can be joined within its
component to an input seed by a simple path of length at most $N-1$.
Hence its support radius is at most $R_\delta+N$; the empty support is
harmless. A computable cardinality bound would thus contradict
Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:noradius}.

If canonical valid codes had computably bounded length, enumerate all
codes up to the given length and run the decidable verifier. Acceptance
of one code would decide membership in $\mathcal H_{\rm sp}$, again a
contradiction.
\end{proof}

These statements rule out \emph{computable majorants}. They do not
assert that any chosen radius-growth function eventually dominates
every computable function. They also should not be confused with a
lower bound on the number of times each individual site must fire:
spatial support and local height are different resources.

\section{Once space is supplied, witness heights are controlled\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:height}

Undecidable support growth is compatible with strong, explicit bounds
conditional on a containing cube. Let
\[
 M=\max_{x\in\Z^d}\eta(x),
\]
which is finite and computable from a period table and finite additions.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same inequality as \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:heightbound} in \cref{cdc:sp:thm:height}. Manuscript~16 compares with a Dirichlet barrier on the box, manuscript~19 with the same quadratic on the box and its halo. Kept as a second route.]}
\begin{theorem}[A quadratic odometer-height bound]
\label{cdc:nb:thm:height}
Suppose a global finite odometer $u$ is supported in $B_R$. Then
\begin{equation}
 0\le u(x)\le \frac{M}{2}\bigl((R+1)^2-x_1^2\bigr)
 \le \frac{M}{2}(R+1)^2\qquad(x\in B_R).
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:heightbound}
\end{equation}
In particular, its integer values are at most
$\lfloor M(R+1)^2/2\rfloor$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On the cube and its exterior neighbor halo put
\[
 \phi(x)=\frac M2\bigl((R+1)^2-x_1^2\bigr).
\]
For an interior site, using the full $2d$-neighbor lattice Laplacian,
$(L\phi)(x)=M$: the two neighbors in direction $e_1$ contribute the
second difference of $-Mx_1^2/2$, and every other direction contributes
zero. Also $\phi\ge0$ on the exterior halo. Since the final configuration
$s=\eta-Lu$ is nonnegative,
\[
 Lu=\eta-s\le M=L\phi\quad\text{on }B_R.
\]
Extend $u$ by zero onto the halo. If $u-\phi$ had a positive maximum in
the cube, the inequality $L(u-\phi)\le0$ would force every neighboring
value to equal that maximum. Propagating through the connected cube
would reach its halo, where $u-\phi\le0$, a contradiction. Thus
$u\le\phi$. Integrality gives the stated floor bound.
\end{proof}

The barrier is deliberately simple and not claimed sharp. Its lack of
explicit dimension dependence comes from using only one coordinate.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The bound \eqref{cdc:nb:eq:helperbound} is manuscript~16's \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:allheight}; the statement about the support of every field is added here.]}
\begin{corollary}[Bounds for the complete field witness]
\label{cdc:nb:cor:allheight}
Let $n_R=(2R+1)^d$. Every scalar value occurring in the canonical witness
or its needed exterior comparisons is bounded by
\begin{equation}
 H_R=\max\left\{\left\lceil\frac{M(R+1)^2}{2}\right\rceil,
                    n_R+1,2d\right\}.
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:helperbound}
\end{equation}
All deviations from the prescribed tails lie in $B_{R+1}$, provided
$B_R$ also contains the input defects.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The odometer is covered by Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:height}. The ranks are at most
the size of the fired support, hence at most $n_R$. The positivity and
rank-offset helpers are bounded by the corresponding odometer or rank.
Stable heights and stability slacks are at most $2d-1$. In either
comparison, the two rank expressions range between $-1$ and $n_R$, so
all nonnegative remainders are at most $n_R+1$.

For an active first inequality, $0\le\lambda=s-K\le2d-1$.
For an active second inequality,
$0\le\mu=H-s-1\le2d-1$, since $H\le2d$. Inactive masked helpers are
zero. Halo slacks are also at most $2d-1$.

The odometer and ranks vanish outside $B_R$. Their comparison helpers
can change only one step away. Final heights differ from the background
only at input defects, fired sites, or their neighbors. This proves the
support statement for every field.
\end{proof}

For fixed $d$, a dense box encoding of the entire witness therefore uses
\begin{equation}
 O_d\!\left((R+1)^d\bigl[\log(M+2)+\log(R+2)\bigr]\right)
 \label{cdc:nb:eq:bits}
\end{equation}
bits, apart from the input description itself and fixed format overhead.
This is a geometric bound, not a polynomial bound in the input length:
Theorem~\ref{cdc:nb:thm:noradius} forbids replacing $R$ by a computable universal
input-only upper bound on all halting instances.

\section{Implementation, validation, and proof obligations\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:implementation}
\srcnote{\wtag{} [The programs are shipped as \path{code/19-no-borrowed-firings-sandpile_certificates.py} and \path{code/19-no-borrowed-firings-verify.py}, the examples as \path{data/19-no-borrowed-firings-two_vertex_certificate.json}, \path{data/19-no-borrowed-firings-two_vertex_witness.json}, \path{data/19-no-borrowed-firings-three_dimensional_avalanche.json} and \path{data/19-no-borrowed-firings-three_dimensional_field_certificate.json}, and the records as \path{data/19-no-borrowed-firings-results.json} and \path{data/19-no-borrowed-firings-results.txt}; \path{data/19-no-borrowed-firings-pdf_preflight.json} records the delivered PDF. The listings below keep the delivered layout, in which \path{verify.py} imports \path{sandpile_certificates} by name and rewrites \path{examples/} and \path{verification/}; this report's README gives a recipe on a copy. The research tree's review \cite{repo-bsrev} reran both entry points and reproduced every count of the table below; only the Python version and the elapsed time differ in the regenerated records.]}


\subsection{What the package actually implements}

The file \path{code/19-no-borrowed-firings-sandpile_certificates.py} uses only the Python standard
library. Its polynomial class stores integer coefficients against sorted
monomials in variable indices. Addition and multiplication construct
actual coefficient-level polynomials. The graph compiler emits every
quadratic residual, and \code{Certificate.quartic()} expands their sum
of squares into one polynomial. Thus the example is not merely an
interpreter for the mathematical predicate ``is a legal run.''

The graph interface checks nonnegative integral multiplicities, positive
degrees, a zero diagonal, and symmetry. It defensively copies caller
inputs before retaining them. The graph data structure itself uses a
dense adjacency matrix for clarity; the residual polynomials are sparse.
No memory-optimal sparse-graph implementation is claimed.

\code{PeriodicInput} validates positive periods, the complete stable
period table, and a finite list of distinct sites with positive additions.
\code{compile_periodic_cube} also checks that the supplied cube contains
all additions. A lower-level \code{compile_cube} interface accepts an
arbitrary callback; its documentation explicitly puts the stable-tail
and defect-containment obligations on the caller. That lower-level
interface alone is not a validator of an arbitrary infinite background.

There are two separate finite-witness paths. The scalar compiler returns
an augmented cube quartic and its ordered natural tuple. The field path
returns a normalized exception table with 47 entries per exceptional
site in dimension three; its independent local verifier evaluates all
60 residuals on the finite relevant neighborhood. The field verifier
does not simulate a firing sequence. Its reader rejects duplicate or
out-of-order sites, nonnatural values, incorrect field order, and
redundant whole-tail rows. The package's JSON is a readable serialization
of the canonical mathematical table; arbitrary JSON whitespace is not
being treated as a unique arithmetic code.

A safety budget limits the supplied greedy simulator by default. Budget
exhaustion raises an explicit ``termination status unknown'' error. It is
never interpreted as a proof of divergence. The mathematical finite-cube
decider in Section~\ref{cdc:nb:sec:universality} refers to the terminating
unbounded-budget process justified by Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:dissipative}.

\subsection{Reproducing the concrete example}

From the extracted package directory, run
\srcnote{\wtag{} [The delivered layout: run in a copy in which the shipped files carry their delivered names (this report's README). The manuscript's \path{article.tex} is not shipped.]}
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
python verify.py
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{lstlisting}
The test program regenerates the example JSON files and the verification
reports. Python 3.10 or newer is sufficient for the supplied type syntax.
The recorded run used Python 3.13.5. PDF building needs a conventional
LaTeX installation with the packages declared in the preamble; no font
files are bundled.

A direct use of the finite graph compiler is
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
from sandpile_certificates import (
    Graph, compile_graph, graph_assignment,
)
graph = Graph(((0, 1), (1, 0)), (1, 1))
certificate = compile_graph(graph, (3, 1))
values = certificate.vector(graph_assignment(graph, (3, 1)))
assert all(f == 0 for f in certificate.evaluate(values))
quartic = certificate.quartic()
assert quartic.degree == 4
assert quartic.evaluate(values) == 0
\end{lstlisting}
A field witness can be generated and checked without retaining a box in
its final representation:
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
from sandpile_certificates import (
    PeriodicInput, field_witness_from_cube, verify_field_witness,
)
data = PeriodicInput((1, 1, 1), (0,), (((0, 0, 0), 100),))
witness = field_witness_from_cube(data, 2)
assert witness == field_witness_from_cube(data, 3)
assert verify_field_witness(data, witness)
\end{lstlisting}
For this input, exactly 19 sites fire, the total number of topplings is
49, the largest odometer value is 19, and the largest burning rank is
2. The normalized full field witness has 57 exceptional sites, because
final-state and comparison fields can change next to the fired support.
These are exact computations for this example, not asymptotic estimates.

\subsection{What was checked}

The reproducible test report records the following finite checks.
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{.70\textwidth}r@{}}
\toprule
Check & Count\\
\midrule
Simple dissipative graphs, with 1--3 nonsink vertices & 43\\
Initial configurations, coordinates in $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ & 4,855\\
Candidate odometers, coordinates in $\{0,1,2,3\}$ & 305,620\\
Candidates satisfying stable balance, checked against all fired subsets & 3,839\\
Compiled valid graph witnesses evaluated coefficient by coefficient & 290\\
Bounded rank assignments checked on 147 valid instances & 6,865\\
Additional multigraph inputs & 3\\
Positivity-gadget input cases & 21\\
Comparison-gadget input pairs, including negative expressions & 81\\
Random evaluations comparing the expanded quartic with residual squares & 250\\
Single-coordinate natural mutations of the 34-variable example rejected & 50\\
Cube dimension/radius count checks with zero witnesses & 9\\
Field-coordinate mutations rejected & 50\\
Field exception-row deletions rejected & 10\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The graph enumeration uses simple internal edges and sink multiplicities
in $\{0,1\}$, retaining only graphs whose components meet a sink. The
candidate test independently enumerates forbidden subsets; it does not
call the burning-round routine to decide whether a candidate should be
accepted. Rank searches include ranks through $n+1$, so they explicitly
probe delayed-rank errors in that finite range. The general exclusion
of arbitrary larger ranks is a proof, not an inference from these tests.

Adversarial tests include the borrowed firing profile, the necessity of
restricting burning to fired support, the negative-slack integer false
root, a circulating chip on a closed graph, the directed false positive,
mutable-constructor input protection, and the leaking radius-zero halo.
Field serialization tests check equality across two containing cubes,
a read/write round trip, duplicate-site rejection, redundant-tail-row
rejection, and an empty witness on a nonconstant stable periodic input.

All recorded checks passed. Their role is to expose mistakes in equation
signs, branch conventions, allocation counts, encoding, and implementation.
They do not replace any of the infinite or universally quantified proofs
in this article, and they do not constitute independent peer review.

\subsection{Recovering a run and formalization priorities}

A valid certificate can be decoded into a genuine legal run: greedily
fire available unstable sites. Its supplied $u$ is an upper stabilizer,
so Lemma~\ref{cdc:nb:lem:least} prevents overshooting it and bounds the number
of firings by $\sum_vu_v$. At termination the unique odometer must equal
the supplied one. This recovery does not require any ordering data in
the certificate. It may still take time proportional to the expanded
run; a compressed certificate is not automatically a faster simulation.

A Lean development can be divided along the actual dependency boundary.
First formalize the finite graph conventions and first-excess lemma;
then the support subtraction and maximum-layer arguments; then parallel
rank uniqueness; then the two unique gadgets and the compiler's
projection/restoration equivalence. The countable-lattice theorem only
needs finite support, so its combinatorial proofs can reduce to finite
sets plus an exterior boundary. Finally, the repository's MRDP interface
can be used for the ordinary existence corollary. The externally cited
universal sandpile simulation would need a separate formalization before
the completeness theorem could be advertised as Lean-checked.

No Lean proof is included in this package. The mathematical text supplies
full arguments, while the Python artifacts supply executable exact finite
checks and concrete polynomial data. These are distinct forms of evidence.

\section{Further research questions and next targets\srctag{19}}
\label{cdc:nb:sec:questions}

The following questions are precise continuations of the construction.
The two questions explicitly attributed to Cairns are questions raised
in that source; this limited source review does not certify their
worldwide status as of October 2026.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [Manuscript~19's nine questions are printed as delivered and labelled here. A \wtag{} line after six of them names the overlapping question of manuscript~16 (\cref{cdc:sp:sec:questions}), of Part~XIV or of \cref{cdc:sec:questions}; the questions are not merged.]}


\begin{question}[Smaller canonical field compilers; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:smaller}
Can the 47 field witnesses and 60 residuals in dimension three be
substantially reduced while preserving the complete natural zero-set
bijection? A useful result should count every comparison remainder and
inactive branch and give an explicit restoration map. The two comparison
families differ by one in their threshold, suggesting opportunities for
shared remainders. Such sharing needs a proof at the boundary cases
$r_v=0,1$ and at equal neighboring ranks. An operation-count comparison
with the existing repository compilers should use a separately specified
arithmetic-circuit model, not infer an operation count from the number
of residuals.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~16's question ``Fewer witnesses without losing uniqueness'' (\cref{cdc:sp:sec:questions}). Batch~79, 2 October 2026: answered in part. The research tree's review \cite{repo-bsrev} removes three witnesses and three residuals per vertex, giving 44 fields and 57 local residuals in dimension three with an exact bijection of natural zero sets (the paragraph after \cref{cdc:nb:cor:gap}); it shares no comparison remainder and claims no operation count, so the question stays open beyond that projection.


\begin{question}[Directed graphs and weighted scripts; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:digraphs}
Which directed toppling matrices admit a canonical local-rank certificate
with polynomially many quadratic residuals? A natural starting point is
a positive integer script or a diagonal weighting that restores a
suitable maximum principle. The counterexample in
Section~\ref{cdc:nb:sec:directed} is a mandatory regression test. In addition to
soundness, the script itself must be normalized or canonically determined
if the goal is a one-point natural zero set.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:sp:q:digraphs}, manuscript~16's question on the same counterexample.


\begin{question}[Witness-preserving scalar compression; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:scalar}
What explicit arithmetic extension suffices to encode the canonical
finite-deviation field tuple in a fixed number of scalar witnesses
\emph{without} creating multiplicity? One may first allow exponentiation,
bit extraction, finite-list primitives, or a bounded universal arithmetic
schema, but every extension should be declared. The interesting endpoint
is a uniqueness-preserving ordinary polynomial compilation; the present
field theorem does not supply it. Even a sharp intermediate theorem
identifying the exact source of helper multiplicity would improve the
repository's compiler interfaces.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~16's question ``Fixed-arity compression with controlled multiplicity'' (\cref{cdc:sp:sec:questions}) and \cref{cdc:q:compression}.


\begin{question}[Sparse support rather than a dense box; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:sparse}
Can one compile only a canonical finite support and its neighbor halo,
with size linear in the number of listed sites and logarithmic dependence
on coordinate magnitude? A sparse certificate must prove that its
adjacency is the actual lattice adjacency, that no necessary neighbor
was omitted, and that duplicate sites are absent. These obligations are
not paid for by merely writing a coordinate list. A unique canonical
ordering or a uniquely verified dictionary is needed to avoid permutation
multiplicity.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~16's question ``Local certificates on adaptive support geometry'' (\cref{cdc:sp:sec:questions}).


\begin{question}[Sharper geometry and parameterized bounds; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:geometry}
For inputs with support known to lie in a region $D$, which explicit
barrier gives the best odometer and total-toppling bound in terms of
$D$, the defect mass, and the periodic background? The one-coordinate
quadratic barrier is convenient but often very loose. A Green-function
or effective-resistance bound could strengthen verification budgets on
restricted families without contradicting the uncomputable support
frontier. The natural target is a fully stated parameterized result,
not an input-only bound for the universal class.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The exact complexity of local infinite activity; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:local}
Cairns distinguishes global halting from the problem of whether a
specified site topples infinitely often and discusses an upper
arithmetical-hierarchy bound for the latter
\cite[end of Section 7]{cairns}. Can local activity be given an equally explicit
alternating arithmetic or field normal form, with a matching completeness
theorem for the stated input class? The finite-support witness here
cannot decide that question: its negation includes both genuinely
infinite local activity and infinite activity distributed over sites
with finite local counts.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The planar periodic-plus-finite problem; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:planar}
Cairns raises the planar periodic-plus-finite halting problem in connection
with the difficulty of crossing monotone wires \cite[Section 2.5]{cairns}.
Our certificate works on $\Z^2$ with 35 fields and 44 local residuals,
but that arithmetic upper representation does not establish a planar
universality theorem or a decision algorithm. A successful extension
must address the planar computational substrate itself, not reuse the
three-dimensional crossing construction without justification.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~16's question ``Planar geometry and decidable radius bounds'' (\cref{cdc:sp:sec:questions}).


\begin{question}[Other abelian computational substrates; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:abelian}
For abelian networks with multiple message types, can the odometer
minimality condition be replaced by a similarly local finite-rank
criterion? A productive distinction is between systems where last-event
or least-action structure already provides a canonical certificate and
systems where componentwise balance misses a genuinely higher-dimensional
obstruction. Rotor routing, communicating processors, and monotone fuse
systems suggest candidates, but their state and routing constraints
must be represented separately rather than assumed identical to
undirected sandpiles.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare Part~XIV's question ``Explicit preperiods and more general abelian processors'' (\cref{cdc:rt:sec:research}), answered in part by Part~XVI for undirected sandpiles.


\begin{question}[Formal proof and universal-input end-to-end testing; source 19]\label{cdc:nb:q:formal}
Can the support-burning compiler and its field extension be formalized
with a small trusted boundary, then connected to a fully instantiated
universal periodic sandpile construction? Such a project should separately
check the input loader, the stable background, gate isolation, finite
versus local halting, field normalization, and the polynomial evaluator.
A complete universal example would materially strengthen the present
package, whose computational tests cover finite graphs and explicit
finite avalanches, not a full Turing-machine-to-sandpile compiler.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~16's question ``A verified universal periodic input loader'' (\cref{cdc:sp:sec:questions}) and \cref{cdc:q:verified}.


\section{Conclusion\srctag{19}}\label{cdc:nb:sec:conclusion}

The main obstacle was not expressing conservation of chips; it was
preventing a purported computation from using chips supplied only by
other unperformed moves. Support burning removes that circularity.
Canonical parallel ranks then remove the nonuniqueness of an arbitrary
elimination order. The resulting compiler has a completely accounted
natural witness tuple and one explicit quartic zero exactly when the
finite computation legally stabilizes.

The same local equations extend beyond an externally bounded time trace.
On an infinite periodic-plus-finite lattice, 47 finite-deviation fields
suffice in dimension three. Their unique solution has no arbitrary
padding radius, yet its support cannot be bounded by any total
computable function of the input over the established universal class.
Once a containing radius is supplied, elementary potential theory bounds
the scalar heights. This separates three resources that are easily
conflated: arithmetic degree, spatial support, and auxiliary-witness
multiplicity.

The article therefore supplies a concrete, proved compiler and a precise
representation boundary. The remaining scalar single-fold compression,
directed extensions, and end-to-end formal universal simulation are
research targets, not conclusions smuggled into the use of MRDP.

\section{Certificate coordinate dictionary\srctag{16}}
\label{cdc:sp:app:dictionary}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~A of manuscript~16.}

The following table specifies every coordinate at the unique zero.
\begin{longtable}{p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.71\linewidth}}
\toprule
Coordinate & Meaning at a zero\\
\midrule
\endhead
$u_v$ & Exact number of legal topplings at $v$.\\
$z_v$ & Final stable height $\eta_v-(Lu)_v$.\\
$\ell_v$ & Stability gap $d_v-1-z_v$.\\
$r_v$ & Canonical parallel burning round on the support, zero off support.\\
$e_v,f_v$ & Complementary indicators of $u_v\ge1$ and $u_v=0$.\\
$\alpha_v$ & $u_v-1$ on the support, zero off support.\\
$\beta_v$ & $r_v-1$ on the support, zero off support.\\
$c_v,\bar c_v$ & Complementary indicators of $r_v\ge2$ and $r_v\le1$.\\
$\gamma_v$ & $r_v-2$ when $r_v\ge2$; $1-r_v$ otherwise.\\
$g_v$ & $z_v-A_v$ when $e_v=1$; zero otherwise.\\
$h_v$ & $B_v-z_v-1$ when $c_v=1$; zero otherwise.\\
$p_{vw},\bar p_{vw},s_{vw}$ & Unique comparison data for $r_w\ge r_v$.\\
$q_{vw},\bar q_{vw},t_{vw}$ & Unique comparison data for $r_w+1\ge r_v$.\\
$\lambda_x$ & Exterior collar gap to height $2d-1$, when the collar is used.\\
$\rho$ & Zero at the minimum permitted radius; otherwise one less than the
number of active outer-boundary vertices.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

The inactive values are part of the theorem. Allowing, for example, an
arbitrary $g_v$ when $e_v=0$ would preserve existence but destroy
single-foldness. Similarly, arbitrary toppling schedules cannot be substituted
for the canonical ranks without changing the multiplicity statement.

In the compact compiler, $k_v$ is the indicator of rank one, $f_v$ of
rank zero, and $c_v$ of rank at least two. Its $\beta_v$ is the nonnegative
gap from rank two in the last case, and zero otherwise. The support indicator
and rank are derived by \eqref{cdc:sp:eq:derivedrank}. The six edge coordinates and
their forced values are specified in Lemma~\ref{cdc:sp:lem:fiveway}.

\section{Provenance and exact scope of the source audit\srctag{16}}
\label{cdc:sp:app:provenance}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~B of manuscript~16. Its machine-friendly ledger is shipped as \path{16-sandpile-SOURCES.md}; the GitHub connector it names is the delivery's reading tool, and the files it read are \cite{repo-h10}, \cite{repo-mrdp} and \cite{repo-rtsources} at \texttt{928ea9701}.}

The repository was read through the GitHub connector at the pinned revision
in Section~\ref{cdc:sp:sec:scope}. Relevant files were the Hilbert-tenth README,
its MRDP specification, and the canonical-routing source ledger. A sandpile
keyword search located the neighboring routing material; it was not an
exhaustive semantic search of every report in the repository.

For primary literature, we inspected Cairns's arXiv version 2, including the
definitions of local and global halting and the global-halting reduction in
Sections 5--6. We inspected J\'arai's survey, especially the finite graph
and burning sections, and its rendered title page to confirm version
information. The comparison with single-fold representation uses
Matiyasevich's own 2010 discussion. The formalization context is supported by
the repository's public specification and the separate 2025 work of Bayer
and David \cite{bayer-david}; their formalization is not a verification of
this report.

No source claims that either exact compiler construction is new worldwide. The
manuscript presents it as a proposed explicit construction with proofs and
reproducible tests. Absence of a search result for the precise compiler is
not proof of novelty. The package's \path{16-sandpile-SOURCES.md} records the same source
boundary in a machine-friendly form.

\clearpage
\part{Exponential trajectories: positive-spectrum sign charts and the order-two power boundary}\label{cdc:part:exp}

\paragraph{Source and scope.} \wtag{} This Part merges two manuscripts delivered together in batch~79 of ProveIt's incoming reports (arrival commit \texttt{060e08a07}), both dated 2 October 2026 and both pinned at \texttt{e58b724c2}, when Parts~I--XIV of this report had been written. Manuscript~17 is ``Beyond Polynomial Trajectories: Canonical Exponential-Diophantine Certificates for Computation'' (batch~79, manuscript~02; archive \path{Positive_Spectrum_Diophantine.zip}; shipped files prefixed \path{17-positive-spectrum-}; labels \texttt{cdc:ps:}). Manuscript~18 is ``Spectral Guards Without Time Expansion: Canonical Diophantine certificates for exponentially long linear computation'' (batch~79, manuscript~03; \path{Spectral_Guards_Without_Time_Expansion.zip}; \path{18-spectral-guards-}; \texttt{cdc:sg:}). They prove one theorem by one method in independently written texts: the complete discrete sign chart of a positive-base exponential polynomial $\sum_b P_b(n)b^n$ is certified, uniquely and with a number of coordinates independent of the horizon, by the maximal sign runs of the ladder $f_{j+1}=(E-a_j)f_j$, checked only at endpoints through the identity $f_j(n+1)/a_j^{n+1}-f_j(n)/a_j^n=f_{j+1}(n)/a_j^{n+1}$, with at most $2d-1$ runs in a row of declared order $d$ and $D^2+1$ slots in all. Manuscript~17 is the base, because its scope is wider (the infinite horizon inside the verifier, size $O(D^3)$, the minimum and least minimizer, affine, triangular and fixed-phase applications, and the order-two power boundary); its Sections 2--12 are printed first (\cref{cdc:ps:sec:definitions} to \cref{cdc:ps:sec:validation}). Manuscript~18 follows as the second route, its Sections 2--12 (\cref{cdc:sg:sec:domains} to \cref{cdc:sg:sec:validation}): the bases are inputs, the size is $O(D^4)$ with an exact pair count, the power atoms are removed for every externally fixed exponent bit bound, an explicit tail threshold handles all times, and the oscillation obstruction holds on every residue class. Where manuscript~18 proves a result of manuscript~17 again, a bracket before it names the result and says why its proof is kept. A written section compares the two interfaces (\cref{cdc:sec:b79-routes}); then come the research questions of both manuscripts, with one merged pair (\cref{cdc:ps:sec:agenda,cdc:sg:sec:questions}), their conclusions and, as the last four sections of the Part, their appendices. Their title pages, abstracts, status statements and introductions are \cref{cdc:sec:ms17,cdc:sec:ms18}; the conventions of this Part are \cref{cdc:conv:b79-XVII}.

\paragraph{Relation to the other Parts.} \wtag{} Both manuscripts read this report's README, not its article, and name Part~IV as their starting point. Five relations matter.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Part~IV is the case of base~$1$.} For the shape $B=\{1\}$ the operator $E-1$ is the forward difference and the ladder is Part~IV's difference tower: the run bound $2m-1$ for declared order $m=d+1$ is \cref{cdc:pt:lem:runs}, the lifted child interval is Part~IV's closed interval $[c,e]$, and the finite verifier and its compiler are \cref{cdc:pt:lem:propagation,cdc:pt:thm:tower,cdc:pt:thm:main} (base~$1$ needs no power atom). These specializations are pointers, and no novelty is claimed for them; notes after \cref{cdc:ps:prop:runs,cdc:ps:thm:local,cdc:ps:thm:compiler} say so.
\item \emph{Generalized statements of Part~IV.} The affine theorem (\cref{cdc:ps:thm:affine}) generalizes unipotent acceleration (\cref{cdc:pt:prop:unipotent}) to split positive spectrum, the triangular theorem (\cref{cdc:ps:thm:triangular}) generalizes unitriangular substrates (\cref{cdc:pt:thm:triangular}) to positive diagonals, and the first-failure and fixed-phase statements stand beside \cref{cdc:pt:cor:first-exit,cdc:pt:prop:composition}. Part~IV's certificates are ordinary quartics; these keep fixed-base power atoms.
\item \emph{Part~IX.} The single-fold implication of manuscript~17's power-graph lemma (\cref{cdc:ps:lem:powerbottleneck}) is \cref{cdc:pt:prop:exponential-boundary}, proved by the same argument. The lemma's converse and the order-two theorem \cref{cdc:ps:thm:powbarrier} sharpen that proposition: the complete sign-chart graph of $2^n-y$ has a single-fold (finite-fold) ordinary representation exactly when every c.e.\ set has one, while order one needs no exponentiation. This is the pattern of \cref{cdc:bd:thm:universal}, and its classical input is formalized in ProveIt (\cref{cdc:bd:rem:sfu}). Dated notes after the proposition and at Source~02 of \cref{cdc:q:compression}, which this Part answers in part, say how far.
\item \emph{Parts~XII--XIV.} Fixed-phase schedules with the counts as inputs (\cref{cdc:ps:thm:phases}) are the exponential counterpart of Part~XII's flat schedules (\cref{cdc:pf:cor:flat}). Part~XIII's least-reservoir relation (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:FF}) and Part~XIV's rank function (\cref{cdc:rt:thm:bottleneck}) are further single relations equivalent to $\FF$ or $\SF$, beside the chart graph of $2^n-y$.
\item \emph{Ordinary quartics.} Manuscript~18's bounded-bit quartics (\cref{cdc:sg:thm:quartic}) are ordinary single-fold quartics, one for each externally fixed exponent bit bound $B$ and valid for horizons $T<2^B$. They do not conflict with \cref{cdc:ps:thm:powbarrier}, which concerns one polynomial uniform in the horizon.
\end{itemize}
The Hilbert's-tenth-problem research tree, maintained separately, reviewed both archives on the day they arrived \cite{repo-sprev}. It finds the mathematics sound and reproduces executable defects of the delivered programs, with two tested patches that are not applied to the shipped programs; the review paragraphs at the end of \cref{cdc:ps:sec:validation,cdc:sg:sec:validation} give the details.

\paragraph{Setting and hypotheses.} \wtag{} The bases are fixed positive integers in manuscript~17 (fixed positive rationals after clearing denominators) and ordered positive integers supplied as inputs in manuscript~18; the shape, that is the degree bounds, is fixed in both, and the signed integer coefficients are encoded by canonical natural pairs. Every witness ranges over $\N$. Manuscript~17's systems and manuscript~18's \cref{cdc:sg:thm:quasi} are \emph{power-assisted}: quadratic residuals conjoined with exact power atoms $u=b^v$, so their sums of squares are not complete ordinary Diophantine equations. Manuscript~18's ordinary quartics fix an exponent bit bound $B$ before the polynomial is written. The coordinate counts bound neither bit lengths nor expanded monomials. Negative and zero eigenvalues enter only through fixed residue splitting of a split rational spectrum (\cref{cdc:ps:cor:rationalspectrum}); irrational rotations defeat bounded sign charts (\cref{cdc:ps:thm:rotation,cdc:sg:thm:oscillation}). Repetition counts of fixed phases are inputs; unbounded branching is not compressed. The order-two boundary is an equivalence between open statements, not a proof of either.

\section{Definitions and arithmetic conventions\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:definitions}

Throughout, $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. Every arithmetic witness in a compiled
certificate ranges over $\N$. Polynomial residuals have integer coefficients.
Their values may be signed even though their coordinates are natural.

\begin{definition}[Fixed shape and order]
A shape is a nonempty finite set $B\subset\N_{>0}$ together with integers
$d_b\geq0$ for $b\in B$. Its order is $D=\sum_b(d_b+1)$. An input coefficient
array $c=(c_{b,k})$ determines
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:ep}
 f_c(n)=\sum_{b\in B}P_b(n)b^n,
 \qquad P_b(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{d_b}c_{b,k}n^k.
\end{equation}
Leading coefficients, entire $P_b$, and even $f_c$ may vanish. All size bounds
use the declared shape, not the numerically reduced one.
\end{definition}

A horizon is either $T\in\N$ or the symbol $\infty$. Write
$I_T=\{0,\ldots,T\}$ and $I_\infty=\N$. A run is a nonempty interval of
consecutive indices on which the sign is one of $-1,0,+1$. In the infinite
case its upper endpoint may be $\infty$.

\begin{definition}[Canonical sign profile]
The canonical sign profile of $f$ on $I_H$ is its ordered partition into
maximal constant-sign runs. Its first run starts at $0$, consecutive runs
are adjacent, consecutive signs differ, and its last run ends at $H$.
Profiles are stored in a fixed number of slots with active slots first;
inactive slot descriptors are all zero. An infinite last endpoint is stored
as a tail flag, not as a natural number denoting infinity.
\end{definition}

Our core certificates contain charts for several related sequences, not only
$f$. The top chart is the output; the remaining charts and arithmetic wires
are auxiliary witnesses. Every one of them is canonically determined.

\begin{definition}[Power-assisted quadratic certificate]
A power-assisted quadratic certificate is a conjunction
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:system}
 R_1(x,w)=\cdots=R_s(x,w)=0,
 \qquad u_\ell=b_\ell^{v_\ell}\quad(1\leq\ell\leq p),
\end{equation}
where $\deg R_i\leq2$, $b_\ell$ are fixed positive integers, and all variables
range over $\N$. The power atoms are graphs of exact functions, not
uninterpreted predicates. The arithmetic part is equivalently
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:sos}
 Q(x,w):=\sum_{i=1}^s R_i(x,w)^2=0,
 \qquad \deg Q\leq4.
\end{equation}
Equation \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:sos} must still be conjoined with every power atom.
\end{definition}

This is an explicit form of exponential-Diophantine representation and a
precise interpretation of ``quasi-Diophantine'' in this manuscript. We do not
use bounded universal quantifiers as primitive arithmetic predicates.

A relation $A(x)$ has a single-fold representation if there is a fixed finite
witness tuple $w$ with exactly one solution for each true input and none for
each false input. Finite-fold means finitely many solutions for each input,
with at least one exactly when the input belongs to $A$. For a graph
$A(x,y)$, the output $y$ is counted as an input to this definition; when it
is subsequently existentially projected away, its uniqueness must be
proved separately.

\section{Annihilation and the number of sign intervals\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:chain}

Let $E$ denote the shift operator, $(Ef)(n)=f(n+1)$. Choose once and for all
an ordered list $a_0,\ldots,a_{D-1}$ containing each base $b$ exactly $d_b+1$
times. The implementation uses ascending base order. Define
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:chain}
 f_0=f,\qquad f_{j+1}=(E-a_j)f_j\quad(0\leq j<D).
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Dimension drops at every step]\label{cdc:ps:lem:annihilate}
We have $f_D=0$. After $j$ factors, $f_j$ belongs to a positive-base
exponential-polynomial space of dimension at most $D-j$ determined by the
remaining multiplicities.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For one summand,
\[
 (E-a)\big(P(n)b^n\big)=\big(bP(n+1)-aP(n)\big)b^n.
\]
If $a=b$, the degree of $P$ decreases by at least one, with a constant
polynomial annihilated. If $a\ne b$, the degree does not increase. The
operators commute because they are polynomials in $E$. Thus the total number
of available polynomial coefficients decreases by one whenever a listed
factor is consumed, and all summands are eventually annihilated. The
argument permits zero coefficients throughout.
\end{proof}

No symbolic differentiation or logarithm is required by the eventual
arithmetic verifier. The next lemma uses real analysis only to prove a
uniform bound on the finite object that will be certified.

\begin{lemma}[Real zero bound]\label{cdc:ps:lem:zeros}
Let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s$ be distinct real numbers, and let
\[
 F(t)=\sum_{i=1}^s p_i(t)e^{\lambda_i t}
\]
be nonzero, with declared order $m=\sum_i(\deg_{\rm allowed}p_i+1)$. Then
$F$ has at most $m-1$ distinct real zeros.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induct on $m$. The assertion is immediate for $m=1$. Choose one exponent
$\lambda$ whose declared multiplicity is positive and put
$G(t)=e^{-\lambda t}F(t)$. Differentiating $G$ lowers the degree of the
polynomial associated with exponent $0$ by one and leaves the allowed
degrees at all other exponents unchanged. Thus $G'$ has declared order
$m-1$.

If $G'=0$, then $G$ is constant; because $F\ne0$, this constant is nonzero,
so $F$ has no zeros. Otherwise, by induction, $G'$ has at most $m-2$
distinct real zeros. Any $r$ distinct real zeros of $G$ would give at least
$r-1$ distinct zeros of $G'$ by Rolle's theorem. Hence $r\leq m-1$.
The same argument rules out infinitely many zeros, since an arbitrarily
large finite subset would already contradict the bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharp discrete run bound]\label{cdc:ps:prop:runs}
A nonzero positive-base exponential polynomial of declared order $m$ has at
most $2m-1$ maximal sign runs on $I_T$ or $I_\infty$. The zero sequence has
one run. Consequently the full chain \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:chain} fits in
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:slots}
 B_j=2(D-j)-1\quad(0\leq j<D),\qquad B_D=1,
 \qquad \sum_{j=0}^D B_j=D^2+1
\end{equation}
slots. The bound $2m-1$ for one level is attained for every $m\geq1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Extend the sequence to a real function using $b^t=e^{t\log b}$. Every
transition between adjacent nonzero signs without an intervening zero
sample forces a real zero in the corresponding open unit interval. Each
maximal block of zero samples has at most two neighboring transitions and
contains a real zero. These zeros for distinct blocks or distinct
open-unit-interval transitions are distinct. Charging at most two
transitions to each zero and using \cref{cdc:ps:lem:zeros} gives at most
$2(m-1)$ transitions, hence $2m-1$ runs. This proof also applies to an
infinite domain because the real zero bound is global.

For sharpness take
\[
 F_m(n)=2^n\prod_{r=1}^{m-1}(n-2r).
\]
Each of its $m-1$ zeros is a singleton integer run, and the $m$ intervening
nonzero intervals alternate in sign. On $I_T$ with $T\geq2m$ there are
$2m-1$ runs. Finally apply the bound with $m=D-j$ to each chain level and
sum the odd integers in \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:slots}.
\end{proof}

The sum $D^2+1$ is a convenient universal allocation. We do not claim that
all levels simultaneously attain their separate bounds.

\wtag{} [For the shape $B=\{1\}$, of declared order $m=d+1$, this is Part~IV's \cref{cdc:pt:lem:runs}: a polynomial of degree at most $d$ has at most $2d+1=2m-1$ sign runs. Manuscript~18 proves the same bound, sharp by the same product, as \cref{cdc:sg:prop:capacity}. The zero bound \cref{cdc:ps:lem:zeros} is the classical one for real exponential polynomials; both manuscripts call it standard and prove it in full.]


\begin{lemma}[Eventual sign]\label{cdc:ps:lem:eventual}
For a nonzero $f$ of the form \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:ep}, choose the largest base $b_*$
with nonzero $P_{b_*}$, and then its largest degree $k_*$ with nonzero
coefficient. For all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
 \sgn f(n)=\sgn c_{b_*,k_*}.
\]
The eventual sign is zero exactly when all coefficients vanish.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Divide by $b_*^n n^{k_*}$ for positive $n$. Terms at smaller bases tend to
zero, even after multiplication by any fixed polynomial; lower-degree
terms at the same base also tend to zero. The quotient tends to the
nonzero leading coefficient. The all-zero case is immediate.
\end{proof}

\section{A local verifier for finite and infinite profiles\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:verifier}

\subsection{The normalized monotonicity identity}
The purpose of the entire chain is the identity
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:normalized}
 \frac{f_j(n+1)}{a_j^{n+1}}-\frac{f_j(n)}{a_j^n}
 =\frac{f_{j+1}(n)}{a_j^{n+1}}.
\end{equation}
Because $a_j>0$, a constant sign for $f_{j+1}$ gives monotonicity of
$f_j(n)/a_j^n$, with the same pointwise signs as $f_j$.

If a child run is $[L,R]$, its \emph{lift} is the node interval
$[L,R+1]$. At a finite horizon it is clipped to
$[L,\min(R+1,T)]$. The last infinite child run $[L,\infty)$ lifts to
$[L,\infty)$. Child lifts cover the parent domain and can overlap at their
endpoints. This one-step lift matters: a sign at time $n$ of a difference
controls the edge from $n$ to $n+1$.

\subsection{The verification conditions}
Suppose that profiles $\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_D$ are supplied, with
the capacities in \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:slots}. The verifier makes the following checks.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{V\arabic*.},leftmargin=2.6em]
\item Each profile is an adjacent cover of the required domain, starts at
zero, has nonempty active runs, and has different signs on adjacent active
runs. Its unused slots have zero descriptors.
\item The bottom profile is the single zero run on the whole domain.
\item For each run of $\mathcal C_j$, $j<D$, the sign of $f_j$ at its
left endpoint equals its label. The same is true at its right endpoint
when that endpoint is finite.
\item For every finite endpoint of every lifted child run, evaluate $f_j$
there and compare its sign with the label of each parent run containing
that index. Only actual finite endpoints of active child lifts are used.
\item In infinite mode, the label of the last run of $\mathcal C_j$ equals
the eventual sign computed from the coefficients of $f_j$ by
\cref{cdc:ps:lem:eventual}.
\end{enumerate}
All checks concern finitely many named indices and comparisons. No check
asks directly whether a sign condition holds at every point of an interval.

\begin{lemma}[Monotone interval test]\label{cdc:ps:lem:monotone}
Let $h$ be a monotone real sequence on a finite integer interval. If both
endpoints have sign $s\in\{-1,0,1\}$, every point has sign $s$. On an
infinite interval, the same holds if the first point has sign $s$ and
$h$ eventually has sign $s$. In the application to $h=f_j/a_j^n$, an
eventual zero sign means $f_j$ is identically zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On a finite interval, each value lies between the two endpoint values.
On an infinite interval, a point of a different sign would, by
monotonicity, contradict either the sign at the first point or the
permanent sign of all sufficiently late points. The final assertion follows
from \cref{cdc:ps:lem:eventual} and positivity of the normalizing factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact local verification]\label{cdc:ps:thm:local}
For every fixed shape, coefficient array, and finite or infinite horizon,
conditions V1--V5 accept exactly one tuple of padded profiles: the actual
maximal sign profiles of the chain \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:chain}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Completeness.} The actual profiles exist and fit the capacities by
\cref{cdc:ps:prop:runs}. They satisfy the cover and maximality conditions, and the
bottom sequence is zero. Every tested endpoint has its true sign.
\Cref{cdc:ps:lem:eventual} gives V5. Padding is uniquely specified.

\emph{Soundness.} Induct downward from $j=D$. The bottom profile is correct
by V2 and \cref{cdc:ps:lem:annihilate}. Assume the child profile at level $j+1$
is correct. Fix a parent run $J$ with claimed sign $s$, and intersect $J$
with each child lift $K$. On every nonempty intersection, the normalized
parent $h(n)=f_j(n)/a_j^n$ is monotone by \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:normalized}.

Every finite endpoint of $J\cap K$ is either an endpoint of $J$ or a
finite endpoint of $K$. Conditions V3 and V4 therefore give the claimed
sign at each such endpoint. If $J\cap K$ is finite, apply
\cref{cdc:ps:lem:monotone}. If it is infinite, $J$ is the last parent run; V5
provides its true eventual sign, and the infinite part of
\cref{cdc:ps:lem:monotone} applies. Thus $f_j$ has sign $s$ at every point of
$J\cap K$. The lifts cover the domain, so the whole run $J$ has the
claimed sign. This establishes the induction.

\emph{Uniqueness.} Any accepted row is now a correct constant-sign
partition. Adjacent labels differ, so its runs are maximal. A sequence has
only one ordered maximal constant-sign partition. Inactive descriptors are
zero, and the infinite-tail convention is fixed. Thus every row is unique.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} [The finite case with $B=\{1\}$ is Part~IV's sign tower: there $E-1$ is the forward difference, the lift $[L,R+1]$ is the closed interval $[c,e]$ of \eqref{cdc:pt:eq:intersection}, the cover and maximality conditions V1 correspond to \eqref{cdc:pt:eq:shape-order}--\eqref{cdc:pt:eq:shape-maximal} and the endpoint conditions V3--V4 to \eqref{cdc:pt:eq:endpoint-condition}, the soundness induction is \cref{cdc:pt:lem:propagation}, and the uniqueness argument is that of \cref{cdc:pt:thm:tower}. Part~IV's tower stops at the constant row $q_d$, whose tag it tests directly, while the ladder here continues to the zero row, so the slot count is $D^2+1$ against Part~IV's $(d+1)^2=D^2$. No novelty is claimed for that case. Manuscript~18 proves the finite-horizon theorem again with the bases as inputs (\cref{cdc:sg:thm:endpoint}); the infinite mode, condition V5, is manuscript~17's alone.]


\subsection{Why the infinite case does not hide a cutoff}
A common way to certify positivity is to guess $N$ after which a dominant
term wins and then verify the prefix through $N$. Such a proof either leaves
$N$ noncanonical or needs another argument establishing that the selected
cutoff is minimal. Here the last run itself is an exact part of the output,
and its tail sign is fixed by a finite coefficient test. Monotonicity from
the child profile bridges the gap between the run's first point and its
asymptotic sign. No auxiliary domination threshold is guessed.

For instance, if the normalized parent is decreasing to zero from above,
a positive eventual sign is still the correct test. We never infer the
sign of a tail from the sign of its limit, which in this example is zero.
The test is the eventual \emph{sign of the sequence}, not its limit.

\subsection{Constructing the unique profile}\label{cdc:ps:sec:construct}
The proof is also algorithmic. Start with the bottom zero row and build
upward. On a child lift, multiply the sign of $f_j$ by the child label
$\varepsilon\in\{-1,+1\}$. For a nonzero child label this transformed
sign is nondecreasing in the order $-1<0<+1$. Locate its first nonnegative
and first positive index by binary search. A zero child label makes the
normalized parent constant, so one evaluation suffices.

In infinite mode, \cref{cdc:ps:lem:eventual} determines whether each threshold is
ever reached. If it is reached but its location is unknown, doubling the
search interval followed by binary search finds it. If it is not reached,
no unbounded search is started. Merge adjacent pieces with equal signs,
including consistent overlapping endpoints of child lifts.

This algorithm terminates. It uses exact integer evaluations; it does not
assume an oracle for real roots. Its number of evaluations can depend on
the bit lengths of boundary locations. The \emph{certificate size}, by
contrast, depends only on the shape.

\section{From the verifier to canonical arithmetic\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:compiler}

\subsection{Canonical elementary gadgets}
Every signed integer $z$ is represented by its disjoint natural parts:
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:parts}
 z=z^+-z^-,\qquad z^+z^-=0,\qquad z^+,z^-\in\N.
\end{equation}
For a known signed polynomial expression $r$, the equations
$z^+-z^--r=0$ and $z^+z^-=0$ force a unique pair whenever $r$ has a
specified value. We do not use arbitrary differences of two naturals,
which would introduce infinitely many witnesses.

For a natural wire $v$ (introduce a computed coordinate if necessary),
its zero flag $e$ and unique slack $k$ are
specified by
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:zero}
 e(e-1)=0,\qquad ev=0,\qquad(1-e)(v-1-k)=0,\qquad ek=0.
\end{equation}
If $v=0$, these force $e=1,k=0$. If $v>0$, they force $e=0,k=v-1$.
In particular, the inactive branch slack is fixed rather than left free.
A comparison $x\leq y$ is the zero test on the positive part of $x-y$.

Boolean conjunction is $h=ef$, and disjunction is $h=e+f-ef$. For a
signed value with parts $p,n$, let $e_p,e_n$ be their zero flags. Its
one-hot sign vector, ordered negative, zero, positive, is
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:signvec}
 (1-e_n,\ e_pe_n,\ 1-e_p).
\end{equation}
The middle product is assigned its own wire. Given a Boolean gate $g$,
matching two sign vectors amounts to the three quadratic residuals
$g(s_i-t_i)=0$.

These gadgets have two properties we need: their residuals have degree at
most two after assigning multiplication outputs to wires, and every
intermediate coordinate is uniquely determined. Conditional constraints
must never be implemented by leaving a disabled subcomputation arbitrary.
We evaluate all arithmetic wires and gate only the final assertions.

\subsection{Fixed-capacity profile descriptors}
A row has $B_j$ slots. Slot $k$ has natural coordinates
\[
 (a_k,L_k,R_k,s_k^-,s_k^0,s_k^+),
\]
where $a_k$ is an activity bit and
$s_k^-+s_k^0+s_k^+=a_k$. Because these coordinates are natural, this
single equation and $a_k\in\{0,1\}$ already make the active sign vector
one-hot. Put $a_{B_j}=0$ as a constant. Impose
\begin{align}
 &a_0=1,\quad L_0=0,\quad a_k(1-a_{k-1})=0 \quad(k>0),\label{cdc:ps:eq:pad1}\\
 &(1-a_k)L_k=(1-a_k)R_k=0,\label{cdc:ps:eq:pad2}\\
 &a_k(L_k-R_{k-1}-1)=0 \quad(k>0),\label{cdc:ps:eq:pad3}\\
 &s_{k-1}^-s_k^-+s_{k-1}^0s_k^0+s_{k-1}^+s_k^+=0\quad(k>0).
 \label{cdc:ps:eq:pad4}
\end{align}
For a finite horizon, also impose active $L_k\leq R_k\leq T$ and
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:lastfinite}
 (a_k-a_{k+1})(R_k-T)=0.
\end{equation}
All conditional inequalities use the comparison gadgets above.

For an infinite horizon, the finite-run bit is $a_{k+1}$ and the tail bit
is $a_k-a_{k+1}$. Impose
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:infinitepad}
 (1-a_{k+1})R_k=0,
 \qquad a_{k+1}=1\Longrightarrow L_k\leq R_k.
\end{equation}
Thus only the last active run is infinite; its stored $R_k$ is zero.
Activity is a prefix, so these expressions are Boolean where required.
The next active run forces adjacency through \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:pad3}. The bottom
row is pinned to its unique all-domain zero descriptor.

\subsection{Evaluating the chain and its endpoints}
For $P_b(n)=\sum_kc_{b,k}n^k$, one step $E-a$ transforms coefficients by
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:coefficient}
 c'_{b,k}=b\sum_{h=k}^{d_b}\binom hk c_{b,h}-a c_{b,k}.
\end{equation}
These are fixed linear combinations of the input coefficients. We compute
and share their canonical signed parts once, instead of duplicating their
expressions at every endpoint.

At an index $n$, Horner evaluation computes each polynomial $P_b(n)$
using signed canonical wires. A power atom supplies $u_b=b^n$; for
$b=1$, use the constant $1$ without an atom. Multiplication by $u_b$ and
summation give canonical parts for $f_j(n)$, and \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:signvec}
gives its sign. All multiplication equations are quadratic in their
natural coordinates.

A finite child lift has upper endpoint $\min(R+1,T)$. Its value is
computed canonically by a comparison bit and one selected linear
expression. For a lifted endpoint $x$, its membership in a parent run is
the conjunction of activity, child-endpoint validity, $L\leq x$, and
$x\leq R$; in infinite mode the upper test is replaced by
``tail or $x\leq R$''. Compare signs only under that gate. A fixed
number of natural wires implements every such operation.

Finally, the eventual-sign vector is obtained by examining transformed
coefficients in descending base and degree order. A running prefix-zero
bit selects the first nonzero coefficient. If every coefficient is zero,
the zero component is selected. This is a fixed Boolean/arithmetic circuit,
not a comparison involving real logarithms.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical power-assisted compilation]\label{cdc:ps:thm:compiler}
For each fixed shape of order $D\geq1$, one can effectively construct a
finite-horizon system and an infinite-horizon system of the form
\eqref{cdc:ps:eq:system} with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The coefficient array, given by canonical signed natural pairs, and
in finite mode $T$, are the only numeric inputs. The bases, multiplicities,
and choice of finite or infinite mode determine the system's structure.
\item For every valid input there is exactly one complete natural witness
tuple. Its profile coordinates are the actual maximal profiles of all
levels of \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:chain}.
\item There are $D^2+1$ profile slots and $O(D^3)$ witnesses, quadratic
residuals, fixed-base power atoms, and straight-line arithmetic operations.
These counts are independent of $T$ and, in infinite mode, cover all of
$\N$.
\item The arithmetic residuals can be combined into an explicit polynomial
of degree at most four. The power atoms are retained as separate conjuncts.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:pad1}--\eqref{cdc:ps:eq:infinitepad} for V1 and V2, the endpoint
evaluation circuits for V3 and V4, and the leading-coefficient circuit
for V5. This is an effective finite construction involving no quantified
interval condition.

Given an actual input, \cref{cdc:ps:thm:local} determines the profile coordinates
uniquely. All coefficient, comparison, sign, Horner, power, membership, and
selection wires are then uniquely forced in dependency order by
\eqref{cdc:ps:eq:parts}, \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:zero}, Boolean gate equations, and the exact
power graphs. This remains true for disabled assertions: their data paths
are still evaluated. Thus the complete tuple is unique. Conversely, any
solution gives true endpoint evaluations and all of V1--V5, so
\cref{cdc:ps:thm:local} forces those same profiles and then the same wires.

For the size bound put $m=D-j$. A level has $O(m)$ parent slots and
$O(m)$ child endpoints. There are $O(m^2)$ membership/sign-match tests.
The values at parent and child endpoints are shared, requiring $O(m)$
evaluations, each with $O(m)$ arithmetic wires. Coefficient transforms
