across the whole chain have $O(D^2)$ scalar outputs and at most $O(D^3)$
linear arithmetic work under a literal sparse evaluation. Summing
$O(m^2)$ from $m=1$ to $D$ gives $O(D^3)$. All constants depend only on
the declared shape and circuit conventions, not on input values.

Every residual has degree at most two after introduction of its computed
wires. Over the integers a sum of their squares vanishes exactly when
all residuals vanish, proving (iv).
\end{proof}

\wtag{} [For $B=\{1\}$ the compiler needs no power atom, because base~$1$ uses the constant~$1$ (\cref{cdc:ps:sec:compiler}); the system is then an ordinary single-fold quartic with $O(D^3)$ witnesses, Part~IV's \cref{cdc:pt:thm:main} with $D=d+1$. Manuscript~18's \cref{cdc:sg:thm:quasi} is the second route, with the bases as inputs and size $O(D^4)$, and its \cref{cdc:sg:thm:quartic} removes the power atoms for every externally fixed exponent bit bound; \cref{cdc:sec:b79-routes} compares the two interfaces.]


\begin{remark}[What the size bound does not say]
The bounds count scalar coordinates, equations, atoms, and straight-line
operations. They do not bound coefficient bit lengths independently of the
bases, do not bound the number of monomials after expanding the whole
quartic by $O(D^3)$, and do not claim polynomial bit complexity in $\log T$.
Already $2^T$ has $T+1$ binary digits. Powers evaluated at inactive padded
indices may equal $1$; it is the unused \emph{profile descriptors}, not
every derived wire, that are forced to zero.
\end{remark}

\section{Safety, first failure, and exact optimization\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:consequences}

The full-chart relation always has one witness. Properties of the sequence
are obtained by adding tests on its uniquely determined output. This avoids
having to invent a new interval certificate for each property.

\begin{corollary}[Finite and perpetual sign conditions]\label{cdc:ps:cor:safety}
For fixed shape, each of
\[
 \forall n\in I_T\ f_c(n)\geq0,
 \qquad
 \forall n\in\N\ f_c(n)\geq0
\]
has a single-fold power-assisted quadratic certificate of size $O(D^3)$.
The same holds for positivity, nonpositivity, negativity, identically zero,
and avoidance of zero on the selected domain.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Append the full-chart compiler and exclude the disallowed sign labels in
its top row. For nonnegativity this means $s_k^-=0$ for every slot.
The full chart is unique, so adding a filter either retains its unique
witness or removes it. All filters are linear equations on existing bits.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Canonical first failure]\label{cdc:ps:cor:first}
The first negative index of $f_c$, together with a Boolean flag indicating
whether one exists, has a unique-witness certificate of size $O(D^3)$, both
on $I_T$ and on all of $\N$. The no-failure index is canonically taken to
be $T+1$ in finite mode and $0$ in infinite mode.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first negative index, if any, is the left endpoint of the first
negative top-level run. A prefix Boolean circuit selects that run. Its
activity flag and endpoint therefore determine the answer uniquely. When
no negative run exists, pin the index to the stated sentinel. The index
$0$ in infinite mode is unambiguous because it is paired with the
existence flag. The additional circuit has $O(D)$ size and unique wires.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} [Compare Part~IV's first-exit statements (\cref{cdc:pt:cor:first-exit}), which are ordinary quartics for polynomially iterable updates. Here the observable may grow exponentially, and the certificate keeps its fixed-base power atoms. Manuscript~18 reads the same first index from its certificate (\cref{cdc:sg:cor:predicates}).]


Explicitly, if $s_k^-$ are the top-row negative flags, set
\[
 p_0=1,\quad e_k=p_k s_k^-,\quad
 p_{k+1}=p_k(1-s_k^-),\quad b=\sum_k e_k.
\]
Then $b$ is the failure flag and the finite first-failure output is
$\sum_k e_kL_k+(1-b)(T+1)$. In infinite mode omit the sentinel term.
Introducing the products as wires keeps every defining residual quadratic.

For a conjunction of finitely many polynomial guards, compute each first
failure and take the earliest index, with a fixed guard order to break
simultaneous ties. Every comparison and selection is canonical. At a
finite horizon, counts of negative, zero, or positive indices are also
obtained by summing the lengths $R-L+1$ of the appropriate runs. In
infinite mode a sign occurs infinitely often exactly when it is the label
of the final run; all its other occurrences form a finite set with the
same finite-length formula.

\begin{theorem}[Exact minimum and least minimizer]\label{cdc:ps:thm:min}
For a fixed shape of order $D$, the graph
\[
 m=\min_{0\leq n\leq T}f_c(n),\qquad
 k=\min\{n\in I_T:f_c(n)=m\}
\]
has a single-fold power-assisted quadratic representation using
$O((D+1)^3)$ witnesses and residuals. The signed value $m$ is represented
canonically. The same construction represents the minimum and least
minimizer on all of $\N$ whenever a minimum exists.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Enlarge the shape by the constant function $1^n$ if necessary. Its order
increases by at most one. Apply the full-chart compiler to
$h(n)=f_c(n)-m$. Require that its top row contain no negative run and at
least one zero run, and set $k$ to the left endpoint of its first zero
run. These conditions say exactly that $m$ is an attained lower bound and
$k$ its least attainment. On the finite nonempty domain such a pair
always exists. On the infinite domain the conditions hold exactly when a
minimum is attained.

The value $m$ is unique, the least minimizer is unique even when the
minimum is attained many times, and the chart and its arithmetic
extension are unique. Thus existentially introducing $m$ and $k$ does not
create extra witnesses when the input is only $(c,T)$, or only $c$ in
infinite mode.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[When the infinite minimum exists]\label{cdc:ps:prop:boundedbelow}
For integer bases $b\geq1$, a sequence \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:ep} has a minimum on
$\N$ exactly in the following cases: it is constant, or its dominant
nonconstant term has positive coefficient. Otherwise it tends to
$-\infty$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
After combining equal bases, a nonconstant sequence has either a largest
nonzero base greater than $1$, or base $1$ with positive polynomial degree.
The dominant monomial then has magnitude tending to infinity, and the
ratio of all other terms to it tends to zero. Its coefficient determines
divergence to $+\infty$ or $-\infty$. In the former case a minimum is
attained on some finite prefix. A constant sequence attains its minimum
already at zero.
\end{proof}

This proposition gives a finite coefficient test for whether the infinite
minimum relation has an output. One may make the output total by adding
a bounded-below flag and assigning default values $m=k=0$ in the
unbounded-below case. Canonically evaluate the otherwise unused chart
there too, and gate only the minimum assertions.

\subsection{Positive rational bases}
There is a sign-preserving extension to fixed positive rational bases and
fixed-denominator rational coefficients. Choose a fixed positive integer
$q$ making every $qb$ integral, and a fixed positive denominator $K$ for
the coefficients. Then
\[
 \widetilde f(n)=Kq^n f(n)=\sum_b \widetilde P_b(n)(qb)^n
\]
has integer coefficients and positive integer bases, with exactly the
same signs and sign boundaries. This transfers finite and infinite sign
certificates and first-failure certificates.

A necessary qualification concerns optimization: minimizing
$Kq^n f(n)$ is generally \emph{not} the same as minimizing $f(n)$.
To certify an original threshold $m$, scale $f(n)-m$, not $f(n)$
by itself. For an integer-valued original trajectory, this still gives
the attained-minimum certificate of \cref{cdc:ps:thm:min}, with an added base
$q$ for the scaled constant threshold. We make no claim that a
rational-valued sequence tending to a positive infimum must attain it.

\section{Affine computation with polynomial guards\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:affine}

\subsection{Split positive spectrum}
Let $F(x)=Ax+b$ on $\Z^d$, with $A$ and $b$ integral. Homogenize the
update by
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:homogeneous}
 z=\binom{x}{1},\qquad
 M=\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \binom{F^n(x)}1=M^n z.
\end{equation}
Assume first that the characteristic polynomial of $M$ splits over
$\Q$ and all its eigenvalues are positive. Because $M$ is integral,
these rational eigenvalues are positive integers. Diagonalizability is
not assumed.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform closed forms]\label{cdc:ps:lem:matrix}
Every scalar linear observation of $M^n z$ has a positive-base
exponential-polynomial form of order at most $d+1$. Its coefficients are
rational linear functions of $z$, with a common positive denominator
depending only on $M$ and the observation.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Over $\Q$, decompose into generalized eigenspaces. On a Jordan block
$\lambda I+N$ with $N^s=0$ and $\lambda>0$,
\[
 (\lambda I+N)^n
 =\sum_{k=0}^{s-1}\binom nk\lambda^{n-k}N^k.
\]
For fixed $k$, $\binom nk$ is a rational polynomial in $n$, and
$\lambda^{-k}$ is a fixed rational number. The basis change and all
coefficient denominators are fixed independently of $z$ and $n$.
A block of size $s$ needs degree at most $s-1$ at its base. Using the
largest block at each eigenvalue gives order no larger than $d+1$.
\end{proof}

Polynomial guards can be handled without expanding every substituted
closed form separately. Homogenize a guard of degree at most $r$ to a
linear form in homogeneous monomials of degree $r$ in the $d+1$
coordinates of $z$. There are
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:symdimension}
 N_r=\binom{d+r}{r}
\end{equation}
such monomials. Substitution by $M$ acts linearly on this space through
its symmetric-power representation. After triangularizing $M$, this
lift is triangular with diagonal entries products of $r$ eigenvalues,
so they are again positive integers.

\begin{theorem}[Affine guarded trajectories]\label{cdc:ps:thm:affine}
Fix an integer affine map whose augmented matrix has split positive
rational spectrum, and fix finitely many polynomial guards. There are
horizon-independent single-fold power-assisted quadratic certificates
for the entire guard-sign profiles, for satisfaction of all guards up
to a supplied horizon, for perpetual satisfaction, and for first guard
failure on a specified input. A guard of degree at most $r$ may use a
shape of order at most $N_r$ from \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:symdimension}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the symmetric-power lift and \cref{cdc:ps:lem:matrix} to obtain fixed-shape
exponential-polynomial observations. Compute the initial monomials and
coefficient arrays by canonical arithmetic circuits, and multiply by
fixed positive denominators. The sign is unchanged. Apply
\cref{cdc:ps:thm:compiler,cdc:ps:cor:safety,cdc:ps:cor:first}. All preprocessing outputs are
unique functions of the input, so they preserve the single-fold property.
Their size is fixed by the map and guards, not by the time horizon.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} [This generalizes Part~IV's unipotent acceleration (\cref{cdc:pt:prop:unipotent}, every eigenvalue $1$) to split positive spectrum, at the price of fixed-base power atoms. Part~IV's eventually quasi-polynomial theorem (\cref{cdc:pt:thm:quasi}) covers the eigenvalues $0$ and roots of unity with ordinary quartics; for an integer matrix with split rational spectrum the two overlap exactly when every eigenvalue lies in $\{0,1,-1\}$, a case that \cref{cdc:ps:cor:rationalspectrum} below also treats. Manuscript~18 proves the affine-guard case with the bases as inputs (\cref{cdc:sg:prop:affine,cdc:sg:cor:macro}).]


The theorem is about a specified initial point and a certified complete
sign history for its fixed update. It is not a statement that arbitrary
linear recurrence positivity has been settled. In particular, positive
\emph{algebraic irrational} eigenvalues are not automatically within this
natural-number fixed-base encoding.

\subsection{Negative and zero rational eigenvalues}
For an integral augmented matrix with arbitrary split rational spectrum,
all eigenvalues are integers, but some may be negative or zero. Choose a
fixed $\tau\leq d+1$ at least as large as the largest nilpotent Jordan
block at zero. Inspect the prefix $0\leq n<\tau$ directly. On the tail
write
\[
 n=\tau+2m+\varepsilon,
 \qquad m\in\N,\quad\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}.
\]
The zero-eigenvalue contribution has vanished. Each remaining term
$P(n)\lambda^n$ becomes a polynomial in $m$ times the positive integer
base $(\lambda^2)^m$, with a fixed signed coefficient depending on
$\varepsilon$. Equal squared bases are combined.

For a finite horizon, the residue class is present exactly when
$T\geq\tau+\varepsilon$, and its horizon is
$\lfloor(T-\tau-\varepsilon)/2\rfloor$. Division by two is represented
by its unique quotient and remainder. For an absent residue class, pin
its dummy horizon to zero and evaluate a canonical dummy chart, gating
off only the requested safety assertions. For infinite time both tail
charts are used. A polynomial guard can either be lifted first or
substituted into the residue-wise closed forms; both give finitely many
positive integer bases.

\begin{corollary}[Split rational spectrum]\label{cdc:ps:cor:rationalspectrum}
The conclusion of \cref{cdc:ps:thm:affine} extends to integer affine maps whose
augmented characteristic polynomial splits over $\Q$, including negative
and zero eigenvalues, by a fixed prefix and two residue-wise charts.
The unique witness now contains these residue charts rather than one
bounded ordinary sign-run chart on consecutive times.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The preceding decomposition is exact for every index. Each prefix value,
residue horizon, coefficient array, chart, and merged first-failure
selection is canonical. Apply the positive-base compiler separately to
the residue sequences. The number of scalar pieces is fixed independently
of $T$.
\end{proof}

The last distinction matters: $(-1)^n$ has a sign change at every step,
but it has constant signs on the two parity classes. The residue-wise
certificate is compact even though the ordinary consecutive-time sign
profile is not.

\section{Triangular polynomial register computation\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:triangular}

The scope is not restricted to affine updates. Consider fixed integer
polynomial maps of the form
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:triangular}
 F_i(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=a_i x_i+p_i(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1}),
 \qquad a_i\in\N_{>0},\quad p_i\in\Z[x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1}].
\end{equation}
For $i=1$, $p_1$ is constant. This is the positive-diagonal triangular
weakly nonlinear setting, with the variable order reversed relative to
some of the literature. The class, its linearization, and its loop
analysis have substantial precedents \cite{hfg2024}; here we use a direct
weighted construction to transfer the canonical certificate theorem.

\begin{lemma}[Finite invariant monomial space]\label{cdc:ps:lem:weights}
Choose positive integer weights recursively so that
\[
 w_i\geq\max\{1,\wt(p_i)\},
 \qquad \wt(x^\alpha)=\sum_iw_i\alpha_i.
\]
For any fixed $W$, the space spanned by monomials of weight at most $W$
is invariant under $q\mapsto q\circ F$. On that finite space, substitution
has an integral triangular matrix with diagonal entries
\[
 a^\alpha:=\prod_i a_i^{\alpha_i}>0.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By construction, each $F_i$ has weighted degree at most $w_i$. Thus
substituting $F$ into a monomial of weight at most $W$ cannot increase
its weight beyond $W$. There are only finitely many such monomials because
all weights are positive integers.

Order exponent vectors lexicographically starting with the highest-index
variable $x_d$, then $x_{d-1}$, and so on. In expanding
$\prod_i(a_i x_i+p_i)^{\alpha_i}$, the term obtained by choosing $a_i x_i$
every time is $a^\alpha x^\alpha$. Any different term first decreases
the exponent at its largest index where a $p_i$ was chosen; variables
introduced by that $p_i$ have smaller indices and cannot undo this
first decrease. Hence all other terms are earlier in the order.
The substitution matrix is triangular with the stated positive diagonal.
\end{proof}

Let
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:weightedN}
 N(W,w)=\#\{\alpha\in\N^d:\textstyle\sum_i w_i\alpha_i\leq W\}.
\end{equation}
Choose $W$ large enough to contain every guard polynomial and every
coordinate needed for an endpoint output.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical certificates for triangular nonlinear loops]
\label{cdc:ps:thm:triangular}
For every fixed map \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:triangular} and fixed polynomial guards,
finite and infinite exact guard-sign profiles, finite and perpetual
safety, first failure, and finite-horizon endpoint states admit
single-fold power-assisted quadratic certificates. Their size depends
on the fixed map and guards but not on the number of iterations. Each
scalar observation can use declared order at most $N(W,w)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Collect the monomials in \cref{cdc:ps:lem:weights} into a vector $v(x)$.
There is a fixed integral matrix $L$ with
$v(F(x))=Lv(x)$, so $v(F^n(x))=L^n v(x)$. The spectrum of $L$ consists
of its positive integer diagonal entries. Every guard and requested
coordinate is a fixed linear observation of this lifted vector.
Apply \cref{cdc:ps:lem:matrix,cdc:ps:thm:compiler}. Initial monomials are unique
polynomial functions of the original input and are computed by
canonical signed arithmetic. For an endpoint state, evaluate its closed
form at the supplied repetition count, again with unique arithmetic
wires and power outputs.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} [This generalizes Part~IV's nonlinear unitriangular substrates (\cref{cdc:pt:thm:triangular}: all $a_i=1$, polynomially iterable, certified by ordinary quartics) to positive diagonal coefficients $a_i$; the price is the fixed-base power atoms.]


\begin{example}[A nonlinear update with an interior guard failure]
Take
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:nonlinearexample}
 F(x,y)=(2x,\ y+x^2),\qquad (x_0,y_0)=(1,0),
 \qquad g(x,y)=3y-20x+65.
\end{equation}
Induction gives
\[
 x_n=2^n,\qquad y_n=\frac{4^n-1}{3},
 \qquad g(x_n,y_n)=4^n-20\,2^n+64.
\]
Thus the scalar example \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:example} is an actual guard observation
of a nonlinear integer register update. Its first negative value occurs
at time $3$, even though the guard is positive again later. Weights
$w_x=1,w_y=2$ make $\{1,x,x^2,y\}$ an invariant space. Its substitution
matrix in that order is
\[
 L=\begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0&0\\
 0&2&0&0\\
 0&0&4&0\\
 0&0&1&1
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The observation uses only the three scalar modes $1,2,4$, so its actual
shape order is $3$, smaller than the invariant-space dimension $4$.
\end{example}

\subsection{Closure under fixed instruction words}
Unlike arbitrary positive-spectrum matrices, maps \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:triangular}
with the same variable order are closed under composition. Indeed,
if $F_i=a_i x_i+p_i(x_{<i})$ and
$G_i=b_i x_i+q_i(x_{<i})$, then
\[
 (G\circ F)_i=b_i a_i x_i+b_i p_i(x_{<i})
                 +q_i(F_1(x),\ldots,F_{i-1}(x)),
\]
whose second part still depends only on earlier variables and whose
own-variable coefficient is positive. Consequently every fixed word
in such instructions admits the same kind of acceleration. Weights
may be recomputed for the word; they need not be the weights used for
one constituent instruction.

\section{Embedding the certificates in a Turing-complete substrate\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:universal}

\subsection{The register language}
Consider a finite-control language with integer registers and commands
consisting of a polynomial sign guard, an update of the form
\eqref{cdc:ps:eq:triangular}, and a next control label. Include disjoint zero
and positive branches when operating on natural counters. This language
contains the standard counter instructions: increment, a guarded
nonzero decrement, and a zero-test branch with identity update. Each
uses diagonal coefficients $a_i=1$ and a constant $p_i$.

Counter machines are Turing complete; the repository's classical
register-machine bridge explicitly compiles three-counter programs and
relates their acceptance to the exponential representation
\cite{repo-dpr,jm1984}. Thus the language containing our supported
nonlinear instructions is Turing complete. The theorem below concerns
structured execution schedules in that language, not arbitrary
unbounded control traces.

\subsection{Repeated words}
Fix a finite control-compatible instruction word
$w=e_0e_1\cdots e_{\ell-1}$. Let $F_w$ be its composite update, and let
$F_{<s}$ be the prefix before instruction $s$. Pull its guard back to
the word's entry state:
\[
 h_s=g_s\circ F_{<s}.
\]
If $w$ is a repeatable control cycle, executing $w^t$ from $x$ is valid
exactly when
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:wordguards}
 h_s(F_w^n(x))\ \hbox{satisfies the selected sign condition}
 \quad(0\leq n<t,\ 0\leq s<\ell).
\end{equation}
These are finitely many scalar observations of one fixed composite map.
Their degree can grow under prefix substitution, but it is fixed when
$w$ is fixed.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical fixed-phase compilation]\label{cdc:ps:thm:phases}
Fix a finite schedule template
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:phases}
 w_1^{t_1}w_2^{t_2}\cdots w_k^{t_k},
\end{equation}
where $k$ and the words are fixed and control-compatible. Every
variable-count word is a control cycle; fixed noncyclic connecting words
may be inserted as additional phases with count exactly one. Suppose all
updates are positive-diagonal triangular polynomial maps with a common
variable order. Then validity of the schedule and its final state have
single-fold power-assisted quadratic certificates whose arity is
independent of $t_1+\cdots+t_k$. The initial state and all repetition
counts are numeric inputs.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By composition closure and \cref{cdc:ps:thm:triangular}, each $F_{w_i}$ has a
finite-dimensional positive-spectrum lift for all pulled-back guards
and endpoint coordinates. For $t_i>0$, use the finite-horizon compiler
at horizon $t_i-1$ for \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:wordguards}, and evaluate the endpoint
$F_{w_i}^{t_i}$ at time $t_i$. Feed that endpoint into the next phase.

For $t_i=0$, the phase has no guard obligations and its output equals
its input. To retain one fixed arithmetic system, use the canonical
dummy horizon $\max(t_i-1,0)$ and still evaluate its chart, but enable
the guard filters only when $t_i>0$. The endpoint closed form at time
zero is the identity. All these comparisons, selections, and
subcomputations have unique natural witnesses.

Induction over the fixed number of phases gives the actual unique
boundary state at every phase. Each guard chart and every internal
arithmetic wire is then unique. If any scheduled guard fails, no
complete satisfying witness exists. The number of phases, words,
guards, and lifted dimensions is fixed, proving the arity assertion.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} [Part~IV composes deterministic phases in the same way (\cref{cdc:pt:prop:composition}). As in Part~XII's flat schedules (\cref{cdc:pf:cor:flat}), the repetition counts are inputs; with the counts existentially quantified, uniqueness can fail, as the next subsection says.]


A repeated word on an infinite tail is handled by the infinite versions
of its pulled-back guard charts. Its first failing instruction, if any,
occurs at the least index $\ell n+s$ among the corresponding guard
failures. This converts iteration counts into exact machine-step
counts without unrolling the cycle.

\subsection{What is not being compressed}
The number of phases in \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:phases} is not a numeric input to a
fixed-arity certificate. A universal program may alternate among
branches in an arbitrarily complicated way. The existence of compact
certificates for each fixed repeated word does not provide a compact
certificate for an arbitrary word of unbounded length.

Likewise, if repetition counts are existentially quantified instead of
supplied as inputs, many count tuples may describe accepted executions,
and stuttering may give infinitely many. Our single-fold theorem fixes
the schedule counts. A canonical control-history decomposition would be
an additional theorem, not a consequence of phasewise uniqueness.

This is the intended computational payoff: a universal register
language can contain large fragments whose arithmetic proofs scale
with algebraic structure rather than elapsed time. It is not an
unrestricted, fixed-arity single-fold halting representation.

\section{An order-two boundary for eliminating exponentiation\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:boundary}

The core construction leaves the graphs $u=b^v$. Ordinary MRDP permits
these graphs to be replaced by polynomial equations, but says nothing
about preserving the number of auxiliary solutions. The distinction
is fundamental, not just an implementation nuisance.

Let $\SF$ denote the assertion that every computably enumerable subset
of $\N$ has an ordinary single-fold Diophantine representation over
$\N$. Let $\FF$ be the corresponding finite-fold assertion. These are
the familiar multiplicity questions described by Matiyasevich
\cite{mat-scholarpedia}. We use the classical strengthened exponential
representation theorem in the following form.

\begin{theorem}[Classical unary exponential representation]
\label{cdc:ps:thm:classical}
Every computably enumerable set has a single-fold representation by an
equation between terms built using natural constants, variables,
addition, multiplication, and the unary operation $v\mapsto2^v$.
\end{theorem}

This is the Jones--Matiyasevich single-fold exponential framework
\cite{jm1984}; the exact unary formulation is also present in the
inspected repository source as \texttt{re\_single\_equation}
\cite{repo-dpr}. It is a cited input here, not reproved from scratch.
Ordinary polynomial replacement of powers with arbitrary multiplicity
uses MRDP, not the stronger conjectures.

\wtag{} [The theorem is formalized in ProveIt as \path{JM1984.RM.re_sfu} and \path{JM1984.RM.re_single_equation} (\cref{cdc:bd:rem:sfu}); Part~IX uses the same input in \cref{cdc:pt:prop:exponential-boundary}.]


\srcnote{\wtag{} The single-fold implication from $\Pow_2$ to $\SF$ is Part~IX's \cref{cdc:pt:prop:exponential-boundary}, proved there by the same substitution into the single-fold exponential normal form. Manuscript~17's proof is kept because the lemma adds the finite-fold implication and the converse, which the theorem below uses. Part~XIII proves the analogous equivalence for a least-reservoir relation (\cref{cdc:rx:thm:FF}), and Part~XIV for the graph of a polynomial-time rank function (\cref{cdc:rt:thm:bottleneck}), neither through the exponential normal form.}

\begin{lemma}[The power graph bottleneck]\label{cdc:ps:lem:powerbottleneck}
The graph $\Pow_2=\{(t,y)\in\N^2:y=2^t\}$ has an ordinary single-fold
Diophantine representation if and only if $\SF$ holds. Its finite-fold
representability is equivalent to $\FF$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Assume a single-fold polynomial representation of $\Pow_2$. Start with
\cref{cdc:ps:thm:classical} for an arbitrary computably enumerable set.
Introduce one output wire for every subterm in its fixed finite
expression tree, and replace every $2^v$ occurrence by the assumed
power-graph representation. The original accepting exponential witness
is unique. Once it is fixed, all arithmetic subterm values are unique,
and every power occurrence has exactly one internal polynomial witness.
Thus the complete polynomial witness is unique. Combine the finitely
many equations by a sum of squares. This proves $\SF$.

With a finite-fold power graph, the original exponential witness and
its subterm values are still unique. Each of finitely many power
occurrences has finitely many internal choices; their product is finite.
This proves $\FF$.

Conversely, $\Pow_2$ is a computable relation, so its appropriately
paired code is a computably enumerable set. An injective natural
polynomial pairing may be used, for example
$\pi(x,y)=(x+y)^2+x$. If two pairs have different sums, their image
intervals $[s^2,s^2+s]$ are disjoint; within a fixed sum the first
coordinate determines the pair. Computing this code introduces no
choice of auxiliary witnesses. Thus $\SF$ or $\FF$ implies the
corresponding representation for the power graph.
\end{proof}

Define $C_2(T,y,C)$ to mean that $C$ is the padded maximal sign profile
of
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:order2}
 f_y(n)=2^n-y\qquad(0\leq n\leq T),
\end{equation}
using three top-row slots and the finite conventions from
\cref{cdc:ps:sec:compiler}. The output $C$ consists only of finitely many
natural descriptor coordinates; it is unique for every $T,y$. It need
not include the difference-chain rows.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp order-one/order-two distinction]\label{cdc:ps:thm:powbarrier}
The following assertions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $C_2$ has an ordinary single-fold Diophantine representation.
\item $\Pow_2$ has an ordinary single-fold Diophantine representation.
\item Every computably enumerable set has an ordinary single-fold
Diophantine representation.
\end{enumerate}
The same three-way equivalence holds with ``finite-fold'' throughout.
In contrast, the complete chart graph for every fixed order-one shape
$f(n)=c b^n$ has an unconditional ordinary single-fold representation,
in finite and infinite modes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For (a)$\Rightarrow$(b), existentially introduce $C$ and require that
its last active run be labeled zero. Since the profile includes its
rightmost index $T$, this is equivalent to $f_y(T)=0$, hence to
$y=2^T$. The last-run condition is a finite polynomial Boolean condition
on the descriptor coordinates. For every $T,y$ there is only one
possible $C$. Thus projecting $C$ away preserves single-foldness;
in the finite-fold case it leaves only the finite number of internal
witnesses for that one $C$.

Equivalence of (b) and (c) is \cref{cdc:ps:lem:powerbottleneck}. For
(c)$\Rightarrow$(a), the graph $C_2$ is computable: evaluating the
finitely many terms through $T$ and forming their maximal runs is an
algorithm. Encode its fixed-arity tuples by iterated injective pairing
and apply (c). This direction is about existence of a representation,
not an efficient implementation. Alternatively, for this particular
shape the explicit compiler uses only base-two power atoms, so one
can replace them directly under (b).

For order one, $b^n>0$ for every $n$, so the sign is simply $\sgn c$.
The unique chart is the single run $[0,T]$ or $[0,\infty)$ with that
label. Its sign bits and canonical signed parts are defined by the
ordinary quadratic gadgets of \cref{cdc:ps:sec:compiler}; no power evaluation
is necessary. Their sum of squares gives an ordinary quartic.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The exact meaning of the boundary]
The theorem is not a lower bound saying that every order-two shape is
hard: the polynomial shape $\{1,n\}$ is already covered by ordinary
polynomial methods. It identifies one fixed order-two family whose
\emph{full chart graph}, with variable $y$ and $T$, carries the entire
multiplicity problem. Nor is the theorem a new proof of the classical
power-graph equivalence itself. The contribution is its localization
inside a minimal nonconstant exponential sign-chart interface.
\end{remark}

\wtag{} [This sharpens \cref{cdc:pt:prop:exponential-boundary} from an implication about a hypothetical accelerator to an equivalence for one explicit order-two chart graph, in the pattern of \cref{cdc:bd:thm:universal}: a single computable relation whose single-fold (finite-fold) representability is equivalent to the general principle. It answers in part Source~02 of \cref{cdc:q:compression} (see the dated note there). The research tree's review checked the argument, including the last-run criterion $y=2^T$ (\cite{repo-sprev}).]


\begin{corollary}[Ordinary representability without multiplicity control]
Every chart and safety relation constructed in this manuscript is
ordinarily Diophantine over $\N$. The present explicit constructions do
not give unconditional finite-fold or single-fold \emph{ordinary}
representations for them.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Replace each fixed-base power graph by an ordinary Diophantine
representation and combine all polynomial equations. This preserves
existence. The chart coordinates remain a unique semantic projection,
but the newly introduced witnesses need not be finite in number.
\end{proof}

\section{Oscillation and failure of spectral closure\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:oscillation}

\subsection{A linearly growing sign diagram}
Positive real bases are responsible for the global bound on the number of
runs. Once genuine rotations are allowed, even a two-dimensional linear
system can violate that bound maximally in its dependence on time.

\begin{theorem}[A rational rotation defeats bounded raw profiles]
\label{cdc:ps:thm:rotation}
Let
\[
 R=\frac15\begin{pmatrix}3&-4\\4&3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \theta=\arg(3+4i)\in(0,\pi/2).
\]
The first coordinate of $R^n(1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ is $\cos(n\theta)$ and
is never zero. Its number of sign changes on $0,\ldots,T$ is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:rotationcount}
 \left\lfloor\frac{T\theta}{\pi}+\frac12\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
The same sign sequence is obtained from the integral matrix $5R$.
Consequently no bound depending only on dimension can bound the number
of ordinary consecutive-time sign runs for arbitrary rational or
integer linear recurrences.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $\zeta=(3+4i)/5=e^{i\theta}$. If $\zeta$ were a root of unity,
then $\zeta+\zeta^{-1}=6/5$ would be a rational algebraic integer and
hence an integer, a contradiction. Thus $\theta/\pi$ is irrational.
If $\cos(n\theta)=0$ for $n>0$, then $\zeta^{2n}=-1$, again forcing
$\zeta$ to be a root of unity. The value at $n=0$ is $1$.

As the unwrapped angle moves from $n\theta$ to $(n+1)\theta$, it
traverses an interval of length less than $\pi$, so it crosses at most
one zero of cosine. It changes sign exactly when it crosses one.
The positive zeros of cosine before $T\theta$ are
$\pi/2,3\pi/2,\ldots$, and none equals $T\theta$. Their number is
\eqref{cdc:ps:eq:rotationcount}. Multiplication by the positive factor $5^n$
does not change signs, so the integral recurrence has the same count.
\end{proof}

This is a limitation of \emph{bounded raw sign-run certificates}, not
a theorem that the recurrence has no other short arithmetic description.
The matrix itself is already such a description, and ordinary
Diophantine representations exist by general methods. The missing issue
is a compact, complete, canonical way to certify all guard signs without
using a number of run descriptors linear in time.

Fixed residue splitting removes phases that are roots of unity. It
cannot turn the rotation above into positive real modes: $\zeta^h$ is
not a root of unity for any positive integer $h$. Indeed each residue
subsequence still has an irrational rotation; density of an irrational
circle rotation implies infinitely many samples in both sign
half-circles, so no residue has an eventually constant sign. This last
observation is not needed for the exact lower bound
\eqref{cdc:ps:eq:rotationcount}, but explains why parity alone is not a general
repair.

\wtag{} [Manuscript~18 proves this observation quantitatively, for the same sequence $5^n\cos(n\theta)=\operatorname{Re}((3+4i)^n)$: on every residue class the sign changes have asymptotic density $\delta_q/\pi>0$, so the maximal charts grow linearly along each class (\cref{cdc:sg:thm:oscillation}). Its irrationality argument is the one above.]


\subsection{Good individual instructions need not give a good word}
The positive split-spectrum condition for affine maps is not closed
under arbitrary composition. An entirely integral example is
\[
 U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 V=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 UV=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Each factor has eigenvalues $1,2$. The product has characteristic
polynomial $X^2-3X+4$ and eigenvalues $(3\pm i\sqrt7)/2$.
Their normalized unit-modulus factors have sum $3/2$, so they cannot
be roots of unity by the algebraic-integer argument used above.

Therefore an affine fixed-word compiler must inspect the composite
word's spectrum, not merely those of its instructions. The common-order
triangular polynomial class in \cref{cdc:ps:sec:triangular} avoids this problem
because it is closed under composition. That closure is one reason to
use it as the main accelerated fragment of the register language.

\section{Worked certificates and executable validation\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:validation}

\subsection{A full finite and infinite example}
For \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:example}, use the annihilator list $(1,2,4)$. The chain is
\begin{align*}
 f_0(n)&=4^n-20\,2^n+64,\\
 f_1(n)&=3\,4^n-20\,2^n,\\
 f_2(n)&=6\,4^n,\\
 f_3(n)&=0.
\end{align*}
Its finite profiles through $T=6$ are as follows.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cl}
\toprule
Level & Maximal sign runs \\
\midrule
$0$ & $[0,1]:+$, $[2,2]:0$, $[3,3]:-$, $[4,4]:0$, $[5,6]:+$ \\
$1$ & $[0,2]:-$, $[3,6]:+$ \\
$2$ & $[0,6]:+$ \\
$3$ & $[0,6]:0$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
There are nine active runs in ten allocated slots. The infinite
profiles replace the last right endpoint in each row by $\infty$ and
leave the other boundaries unchanged. Direct values in the top row
are
\[
 45,\ 28,\ 0,\ -32,\ 0,\ 448,\ 2880.
\]
The first failure of nonnegativity is $3$. Both the finite and infinite
minimum are $-32$, attained first and only at $3$. The minimum assertion
was separately checked by applying the infinite profile verifier to
$f_0+32$, whose only zero run is $[3,3]$ and which has no negative run.

The two JSON exports use this example as a \emph{sample assignment},
not as a specialization of their coefficients. Their inputs are the
six canonical natural coordinates for three signed coefficients, plus
$T$ in finite mode. All other values are quantified witness coordinates.
Thus the same exported residual/power system applies to every signed
coefficient triple for the shape $\{1,2,4\}$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Actual exported systems for declared order $D=3$. Counts are
unoptimized and exclude no listed arithmetic witnesses.}
\label{cdc:ps:tab:counts}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Quantity & Finite mode & Infinite mode \\
\midrule
Natural input coordinates & 7 & 6 \\
Natural witness coordinates & 1,231 & 1,297 \\
Quadratic residuals & 1,703 & 1,767 \\
Fixed-base power atoms & 52 & 52 \\
Expanded arithmetic quartic monomials & 7,502 & 8,256 \\
Maximum arithmetic residual degree & 2 & 2 \\
Expanded arithmetic polynomial degree & 4 & 4 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

These are not small universal-polynomial operation records. They are
complete, inspectable outputs of a deliberately direct compiler.
The exported quartic includes the arithmetic residuals, but not an
ordinary-polynomial replacement for its 52 power atoms. The input and
witness roles are explicitly marked in the JSON data.

\subsection{An isolated defect at a large horizon}
Set $K=50{,}000$, $T=100{,}000$, and
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:ps:eq:large}
 f(n)=2^n\big((n-K)^2-1\big).
\end{equation}
This order-three shape has exactly one negative integer sample, at
$n=K$, and zero samples at $K-1$ and $K+1$. The construction stores
nine active runs across all four chain levels. With the included
memoized implementation, constructing its profiles used 54 distinct
exact sequence evaluations; checking them afterward increased the
total to 55. These counts do not include individual integer
multiplications inside evaluation, and they are not bit-operation
counts. The value $2^T$ itself has 100,001 bits.

This experiment illustrates the intended compression: a very narrow
failure far into the execution is not missed, yet the certificate's
shape is unchanged. It does not claim that manipulating exponentially
large exact integers has constant cost. The large-horizon experiment
tests the profile generator and verifier; the fully expanded compiler
exports use the small example from the preceding subsection.

\subsection{Tests that were actually run}
All computational checks use Python's exact integers or exact rational
arithmetic and require only its standard library. The reproducible seed
for randomized tests is \texttt{20261002}. The delivered results record:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item 1,134 randomized fixed shapes of order at most seven, with bases
from $1$ through $6$, repeated roots, signed coefficients, and horizons
including zero. Finite charts and restrictions of infinite charts were
compared with direct enumeration at every chain level.
\item For the order-three example, all 1,419 top-level sign profiles
arising from sign assignments on $0,\ldots,6$ with at most five runs
were tested against the correct child charts. Exactly one was
accepted. A separate infinite test extended the final assigned sign
forever; again exactly one of those 1,419 candidates was accepted.
This is exhaustive over those candidate top rows, not over arbitrary
infinite boundaries or all arithmetic witnesses.
\item Twelve compiler instances with different coefficients and
horizons had the same structural signatures in each mode. The tests
include the identically zero sequence. Sixteen additional compiled
instances exercise repeated-root shapes.
\item Increasing each witness coordinate individually by one in the
two example assignments produced 2,528 rejected mutations. This
checks that these particular coordinates are constrained; it is not
an exhaustive uniqueness proof.
\item Sharp run-bound examples of orders one through seven attained
$1,3,5,7,9,11,13$ top-level runs. The rational-rotation sign sequence
was evaluated using the integer recurrence for $(3+4i)^n$; it had 295
sign changes through time 1,000.
\item Application checks verified 735 nonlinear-state and invariant-lift
instances for \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:nonlinearexample} with varied initial values,
82 parity identities for a negative-base example, the global-minimum
example, and the integer matrix nonclosure example.
\end{enumerate}
The mathematical uniqueness claim rests on \cref{cdc:ps:thm:local,cdc:ps:thm:compiler},
not on the finite tests.

\subsection{Independent checking and artifact interfaces}
The program \path{code/17-positive-spectrum-check_export.py} does not invoke the chart compiler.
It reads the exported polynomial terms, evaluates every residual and
power atom on the stored sample assignment, and checks the expanded
quartic. It additionally compares the quartic with the sum of squared
residuals at a deterministic off-zero vector, an independent check of
the expansion identity rather than only its vanishing at one root.

\wtag{} [Editorial note: a comparison at two points is not a polynomial-identity check. The ProveIt review of this archive (\cite{repo-sprev}, finding~3) adds $(x_0-64)(x_0-3)$ to the delivered finite quartic; both tested points are unchanged, and the delivered checker prints PASS. The review replaces the test by full sparse coefficient equality and confirms the delivered expansions (7,502 and 8,256 monomials). The shipped \path{code/17-positive-spectrum-check_export.py} is the delivered program, without that repair.]


Each polynomial is a list of pairs consisting of an integer coefficient
and a sorted list of variable indices forming its monomial. A power
atom records a fixed base and the indices of its exponent and result.
The JSON documents declare the domain to be the nonnegative integers
and state the conjunction semantics explicitly. The code does not
serialize symbolic predicates that have been left without a verifier.

The implementation covers scalar fixed-shape exponential polynomials
and their arithmetic certificates. The affine and general triangular
front ends are proved mathematically and illustrated by exact
application tests; a general Jordan-decomposition or invariant-monomial
front-end compiler is not included. This division is important when
assessing which components are executable today.

\paragraph{\wtag{} The research tree's review.} ProveIt's Hilbert's-tenth-problem research tree, maintained separately, reviewed this archive and manuscript~18's on the day they arrived (\cite{repo-sprev}). It finds the endpoint argument, the eventual-sign test, the triangular transfer and the order-two boundary sound, and reproduces three defects of the delivered programs, none of them a counterexample to a theorem: (1)~the public constructor and verifier of \path{code/17-positive-spectrum-profiles.py} accept a supplied chain without checking that it is the annihilator chain, so the chain $[f,0]$ with the rows $[0,6]:+$ and $[0,6]:0$ passes for $f=4^n-20\cdot2^n+64$ although $f(3)=-32$ (the compiler's own path builds the chain itself; the batch-79 intake reproduced this case); (2)~cached coefficients are mutable, so a changed coefficient leaves stale cached endpoint values and an old chart still verifies; (3)~the two-point expansion check above. Its tested patch \path{positive_boundaries.patch}, in \path{Computability/HilbertTenthProblem/Papers/research-wip/native-stream-queue/spectral_repairs_060e08a07/}, authenticates every ladder step, freezes the coefficients and checks full coefficient equality; it changes no residual, arity or recorded export. It is not applied: the shipped programs are the delivered bytes.

% ---- manuscript 18, lines 191-1171 ----
\section{Data, domains, and representation conventions\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:domains}
We use $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. An interval $[a,b]$ in a sign chart always means
$[a,b]\cap\Z$ and is inclusive at both ends. Coefficients may be negative;
all quantified coordinates in the arithmetic representations are natural
numbers.

\begin{definition}[A fixed shape]
A shape is a tuple $\boldsymbol m=(m_1,\ldots,m_s)$ of positive integers. Its
dimension is $D=\sum_i m_i$. Input data of this shape are ordered positive
integer bases $b_1<\cdots<b_s$, integer coefficients $c_{ij}$ for
$0\le j<m_i$, and a horizon $T\in\N$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:sequence}
 P_i(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{m_i-1}c_{ij}X^j,
 \qquad F(n)=\sum_{i=1}^s P_i(n)b_i^n.
\end{equation}
Zero polynomials and zero declared leading coefficients are permitted. The
shape is not reduced according to the numerical coefficients.
\end{definition}

Keeping the shape fixed is important. Otherwise deleting a zero leading
coefficient can accidentally make the polynomial syntax depend on input data.
Our compiler's syntax depends only on $\boldsymbol m$, the optional bit bound,
and the selected output predicate. Numerical coefficients, bases, and the
horizon are polynomial parameters.

\begin{definition}[Single-fold and exponential arithmetic]
A representation $R(\boldsymbol a)\iff\exists\boldsymbol w\in\N^k\,
P(\boldsymbol a,\boldsymbol w)=0$ is \emph{single-fold} when every true input has
exactly one witness tuple. A \emph{quasi-Diophantine} representation in this
article means a finite existential conjunction of polynomial equations and
atoms
\[
 \Pow(b,n,y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=b^n,
 \qquad b\ge1,\ n,y\in\N.
\]
This is also called exponential arithmetic here. An equation containing
$\Pow$ is \emph{not} being called an ordinary polynomial equation.
\end{definition}

A signed integer $x$ is represented canonically by $(x^+,x^-)\in\N^2$ with
$x=x^+-x^-$ and $x^+x^-=0$. The latter condition is indispensable: omitting it
would introduce infinitely many encodings of the same integer. Input
coefficient pairs obey this convention too. Single-fold assertions are
relative to valid, canonically encoded inputs; invalid base ordering or
noncanonical input pairs have no solution in the compiled system.

Positive rational bases cause no conceptual difficulty at the sequence level.
For $\lambda_i\in\Q_{>0}$ and rational coefficients, choose positive integers
$Q,C$ clearing respectively the bases and coefficients. Multiplication by
$CQ^n$ transforms the sequence to one with integer positive bases $Q\lambda_i$
and integer coefficients, without changing any sign. A fixed input format must
specify these denominators or compute them canonically; arbitrary denominator
witnesses would not preserve uniqueness.

\section{The root-removing difference ladder\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:ladder}
Let $E$ denote the forward-shift operator, $(EG)(n)=G(n+1)$. List the bases in
order with their declared multiplicities:
\[
 (\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_{D-1})
 = (\underbrace{b_1,\ldots,b_1}_{m_1},\ldots,
    \underbrace{b_s,\ldots,b_s}_{m_s}).
\]
Define $F_0=F$ and
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:ladder}
 F_{r+1}=(E-\beta_r)F_r\qquad(0\le r<D).
\end{equation}

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same as manuscript~17's \cref{cdc:ps:lem:annihilate}, with the coefficient transform \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:coefficient}. Manuscript~18's statement and proof are kept as a second route, because its bases are inputs and its ladder order is fixed by their input order.]}

\begin{lemma}[Dimension decreases deterministically]\label{cdc:sg:lem:ladder}
The sequence $F_r$ has a prescribed polynomial-exponential shape of dimension
$D-r$, and $F_D=0$. Its coefficients are obtained from the input by a fixed
integer arithmetic circuit.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On one mode,
\[
 (E-\beta)(P(n)b^n)
   =\bigl(bP(n+1)-\beta P(n)\bigr)b^n.
\]
If $b=\beta$, the top coefficient cancels, lowering the declared degree by one;
a declared constant mode is deleted. Other modes keep their declared degrees.
We always remove from the first remaining base, so this rule is independent of
whether any numerical coefficient vanishes. More explicitly, if
$P(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}c_kX^k$, the coefficient of $X^j$ in the new polynomial is
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:coeff}
 c'_j=b\sum_{k=j}^{m-1}\binom{k}{j}c_k-\beta c_j.
\end{equation}
For the removed mode its identically zero top coefficient is not stored.
After $D$ steps no modes remain. Formula~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:coeff} is a fixed arithmetic
circuit, with binomial coefficients determined by the shape.
\end{proof}

The analytic fact needed for verification is much simpler than solving for
real zeros.
\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same identity as manuscript~17's \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:normalized}, which manuscript~17 uses without stating it as a lemma; kept as a second route.]}

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity transfer]\label{cdc:sg:lem:monotone}
Fix $r<D$ and set $H_r(n)=F_r(n)/\beta_r^n$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:normalized}
 H_r(n+1)-H_r(n)=\frac{F_{r+1}(n)}{\beta_r^{n+1}}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $F_{r+1}$ has constant sign $\tau$ on $[a,b]$, then $H_r$ is
increasing, constant, or decreasing on $[a,b+1]$ according as $\tau$ is
positive, zero, or negative. Moreover, $H_r$ and $F_r$ have the same sign.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Subtract the two normalized values and use~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:ladder}. The denominator
is strictly positive. The successive differences therefore have exactly the
claimed signs.
\end{proof}

There is no need to introduce rational values $H_r(n)$ into a certificate.
Only the integer values $F_r(n)$ and their signs are evaluated. The
normalization is a proof device, not an extra arithmetic primitive.

\subsection{A classical zero bound, with proof}
The following is the relevant elementary Chebyshev-system phenomenon. We
include its proof so that the certificate size does not depend on an external
root-isolation theorem.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same as manuscript~17's \cref{cdc:ps:lem:zeros}, proved by the same Rolle induction; kept as a second route.]}

\begin{lemma}[Real zero bound]\label{cdc:sg:lem:zeros}
Let $\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_s$ be real, and let $P_i$ have declared degrees
less than $m_i$. A nonzero function
$G(x)=\sum_iP_i(x)e^{\lambda_i x}$ has at most $D-1$ distinct real zeros,
where $D=\sum_i m_i$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induct on $D$. For $D=1$, a nonzero constant multiple of an exponential has no
zeros. Divide $G$ by $e^{\lambda_1x}$ and differentiate. The first polynomial
loses one declared degree; every other mode retains its degree and has
exponent $\lambda_i-\lambda_1$. Thus the derivative belongs to a shape of
dimension $D-1$.

If this derivative is zero everywhere, $G/e^{\lambda_1x}$ is a nonzero
constant and there are no zeros. Otherwise the induction hypothesis bounds
the derivative's distinct zeros by $D-2$. Any $k$ distinct zeros of
$G/e^{\lambda_1x}$ give at least $k-1$ distinct zeros of its derivative by
Rolle's theorem. Hence $k\le D-1$. If there were infinitely many zeros, apply
this argument to an arbitrary finite selection of $D$ of them, obtaining the
same contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Maximal discrete sign chart]
The maximal sign chart of $G$ on $[0,T]$ is the ordered partition into nonempty
integer intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_k$ on each of which $\sgn G$ is constant, with
adjacent labels different. A zero interval has label $0$, not an omitted
label. The identically zero sequence has the one-block chart $[0,T]:0$.
\end{definition}

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same as manuscript~17's \cref{cdc:ps:prop:runs}, sharp by the same product; kept as a second route. For base~$1$ alone it is Part~IV's \cref{cdc:pt:lem:runs}.]}

\begin{proposition}[Sharp capacity for a single row]\label{cdc:sg:prop:capacity}
For a polynomial-exponential sequence of declared dimension $d\ge1$ with
positive bases, a maximal sign chart has at most $2d-1$ blocks, uniformly in
$T$. The bound is sharp, already for a single base equal to $1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If the function is nonzero, Lemma~\ref{cdc:sg:lem:zeros}, with $\lambda_i=\log b_i$,
gives at most $z=d-1$ distinct real zeros. Along the integer samples, each real
zero can account for at most two sign-label changes: entering and leaving a
sampled zero. A zero lying strictly between successive samples accounts for
at most one change. One can make this count formal by subdividing the real
line at its zeros; on every remaining open interval the sign is constant.
Sampling and merging cannot produce more than $2z+1$ blocks. The identically
zero case has one block.

For sharpness use $\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}(n-2j)$ on $[0,2d]$. Each of its $d-1$
zeros is an isolated sampled zero, separated from the next by nonzero samples;
there are exactly $2d-1$ maximal blocks. For $d=1$, any nonzero constant gives
the bound one.
\end{proof}

The use of a \emph{real} zero bound here is only combinatorial. We do not
replace nonnegativity at integer times with nonnegativity throughout a real
interval. Section~\ref{cdc:sg:sec:examples} gives an example where those properties
differ.

\section{The canonical endpoint certificate\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:certificate}
For row $F_r$, $0\le r<D$, allocate
\[
 M_r=2(D-r)-1
\]
slots. Allocate $M_D=1$ slot for the bottom zero row. An actual chart occupies
a nonempty prefix; all remaining chart slots have a specified inactive encoding.
Thus the number of allocated slots is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:slots}
 \sum_{r=0}^{D}M_r=1+\sum_{d=1}^D(2d-1)=D^2+1.
\end{equation}

For the moment we describe the certificate mathematically; the polynomial
encoding of every condition follows in Section~\ref{cdc:sg:sec:compiler}. Every row
is a partition of $[0,T]$ into nonempty intervals with labels in $\{-1,0,1\}$
and distinct adjacent labels. The bottom row is $[0,T]:0$.

Take an upper-row block $I=[\ell,u]$ with claimed sign $\sigma$, and a
lower-row block $J=[a,b]$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:intersection}
 K(I,J)=[\ell,u]\cap[a,\min(b+1,T)].
\end{equation}
When $K(I,J)$ is nonempty, require only
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:endpointchecks}
 \sgn F_r(\min K(I,J))=\sigma,
 \qquad \sgn F_r(\max K(I,J))=\sigma.
\end{equation}
No other samples are required.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The finite-horizon case of manuscript~17's \cref{cdc:ps:thm:local}, with the bases as inputs: the clipped interval $[a,\min(b+1,T)]$ is manuscript~17's lift, and the two checks \eqref{cdc:sg:eq:endpointchecks} on each nonempty intersection amount to its conditions V3 and V4, because every end of an intersection is an end of the parent block or of the lifted child block. New here is the exact count $Q_D$ of slot pairs. Manuscript~18's proof is kept as a second route; for base~$1$ the theorem is Part~IV's \cref{cdc:pt:thm:tower}.]}

\begin{theorem}[Exact endpoint verification and uniqueness]\label{cdc:sg:thm:endpoint}
The conditions just stated hold if and only if each row is the true maximal
sign chart of its $F_r$ on $[0,T]$. Consequently there is exactly one chart
certificate for every valid input. Its number of upper/lower slot pairs is
\begin{align}\label{cdc:sg:eq:pairs}
 Q_D&=1+\sum_{d=2}^D(2d-1)(2d-3)\\
 &=\frac{4D^3-6D^2-D+6}{3},\nonumber
\end{align}
so at most $2Q_D$ endpoint evaluations suffice, before sharing repeated
arguments. The assertion includes $T=0$ and every possible vanishing pattern
of the coefficients.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For soundness, induct upward from the bottom row, whose correctness follows
from Lemma~\ref{cdc:sg:lem:ladder}. Suppose the lower chart is correct. On the
expanded interval $[a,b+1]$, the normalized upper row is monotone or constant
by Lemma~\ref{cdc:sg:lem:monotone}. On a nonempty intersection $K$, every value of
this normalized row lies between its two endpoint values. If both endpoints
are positive, all intermediate values are positive; if both are negative,
all are negative; if both are zero, all are zero. Since normalization is
positive,~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:endpointchecks} certifies the entire upper block within
$K$.

The expanded lower blocks cover all integer vertices in $[0,T]$. Thus every
point of every upper block receives the asserted sign. The partition and
adjacent-different conditions now imply that the upper chart is maximal.
This completes the induction.

For completeness take the actual maximal charts. They fit the allocated
capacities by Proposition~\ref{cdc:sg:prop:capacity}, and their endpoint signs are
correct by definition. A function on a finite ordered set has exactly one
maximal constant-label partition; hence uniqueness follows. For $T=0$ the
same argument uses singleton intersections and one-block actual charts.
The row-pair count is $\sum_{r<D}M_rM_{r+1}$; summing the displayed quadratic
terms gives~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:pairs}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why both levels of structure matter}
The sign-chart capacity alone would not suffice: a guessed partition could
mislabel a long interval. Conversely, monotonicity regions alone need not
select a unique certificate: their arbitrary refinement would give many
witnesses. The lower-row certificate establishes the monotonicity needed for
soundness, while maximality eliminates refinements and supplies uniqueness.
Zero blocks must be retained to make both arguments exact.

\begin{corollary}[Canonical predicates]\label{cdc:sg:cor:predicates}
For valid input data, each of the following can be read from the unique
certificate without additional choice: nonnegativity at every $0\le n\le T$;
strict positivity at every such $n$; the existence of a zero or a negative
value; and the first index with sign $0$ or $-1$, whenever it exists.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Inspect the labels of the top row. The first occurrence of a selected label
has the left endpoint of the first block carrying it. A fixed scan of the
bounded slot list can use a unique ``found'' bit and a value defaulting to
zero when absent. This does not existentially choose one of several violating
indices.
\end{proof}

\section{A single-fold arithmetic compiler\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:compiler}
We next translate the certificate to arithmetic while preserving the
uniqueness of \emph{all} auxiliary coordinates. Merely encoding the same
truth value would be insufficient.

\subsection{Functional quadratic gadgets}
An arithmetic circuit is evaluated in its fixed topological order. To store a
signed output of a polynomial expression $E$ of degree at most two, introduce
$z^+,z^-\in\N$ and require
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:signedgate}
 z^+-z^--E=0,\qquad z^+z^-=0.
\end{equation}
These determine one and only one pair. Products of signed values remain
quadratic after replacing each signed value by the difference of its two
coordinates.

For a known signed value $X$, its three sign bits $p,z,n$ and positive/negative
slacks $a,b$ are specified by
\begin{align}\label{cdc:sg:eq:signgate}
 p+z+n&=1,& X&=p(1+a)-n(1+b),\\
 (1-p)a&=0,&(1-n)b&=0.\nonumber
\end{align}
All variables are natural. Thus $(p,z,n)$ is automatically one-hot. If $X>0$,
only $p=1$ is possible and $a=X-1$, $b=0$; the negative and zero cases are
similar. The slacks in inactive cases are pinned, not left arbitrary.

To compare naturals $u,v$, apply~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:signgate} to $v-u$. The bit
$c=p+z$ is uniquely $1$ exactly when $u\le v$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:minmax}
 \min(u,v)=cu+(1-c)v,\qquad
 \max(u,v)=cv+(1-c)u
\end{equation}
are functional quadratic gates, with an explicit tie convention. Finite
Boolean circuits can similarly be represented by quadratic equations; for
example conjunction is multiplication and complement is $1-c$.

Each row coefficient is computed with~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:coeff} and normalized
by~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:signedgate}. Evaluate a polynomial by Horner's rule, multiply by a
functional power value, sum the modes, and apply~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:signgate}. An
evaluation costs $O(D)$ signed arithmetic gates and at most $D$ power atoms.
All equations are quadratic or linear once intermediate values are named.

\subsection{Chart slots and the inactive-branch problem}
A slot has an activity bit $A$, endpoints $\ell,u$, and sign indicators
$p,z,n$ with $p+z+n=A$. Require
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:slot}
 A(A-1)=0,\quad (1-A)\ell=(1-A)u=0,\quad
 u-\ell=L,\quad u+V=T,
\end{equation}
where $L,V\in\N$ are unique slacks. The first slot has $A=1$ and $\ell=0$.
For consecutive slots with next activity $A'$ and next left endpoint $\ell'$,
require
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:adjacent}
 A'(1-A)=0,\qquad A'(\ell'-u-1)=0,
 \qquad pp'+zz'+nn'=0.
\end{equation}
Put $A'=0$ after the last allocated slot and require at every slot
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:last}
 (A-A')(u-T)=0.
\end{equation}
The activity prefix, contiguity, last endpoint, and different adjacent labels
are now enforced. Inactive endpoints and labels are zero. Their bound slack
is $T$, not an arbitrary padding coordinate. The bottom slot is anchored to
label zero.

For every allocated upper/lower pair, compute both endpoints of the formal
intersection~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:intersection} with min/max gates. If the pair is
inactive or the intersection empty, its endpoint constraints must not become
spurious requirements. On the other hand, simply multiplying every internal
residual by a guard bit would leave inactive auxiliary variables free and
could raise the degree.

We instead \emph{evaluate all internal circuits unconditionally}. All
candidate endpoints are in $[0,T]$, even for inactive slots: left endpoints
are nonnegative and at most $T$; upper endpoints are clipped by $T$. Compute
their powers, values, and sign bits uniquely. Then use the conjunction of
the two activity bits and the nonempty-intersection comparison to gate only
the final sign-bit equalities. Such a gated equality has degree at most two.
This is a direct way to avoid the uniqueness hazard for inactive branches
discussed in the single-fold literature \cite{cco2024}.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The same theorem as manuscript~17's \cref{cdc:ps:thm:compiler} in finite mode, for a different interface: the bases are inputs (ordered by positive slacks), every allocated slot pair is tested, and the size is $O(D^4)$, against $O(D^3)$ there, where the endpoint evaluations of a level are shared. Both keep the power atoms. Kept as a second route.]}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform single-fold exponential certificate]\label{cdc:sg:thm:quasi}
For every fixed shape $\boldsymbol m$ of dimension $D$, one can effectively
construct a finite existential system over $\N$ with the following properties.
It consists of degree-at-most-two polynomial equations and functional power
atoms, with $O(D^4)$ variables, equations, and atoms. Its syntax is independent
of the numerical values of the bases, coefficients, and horizon. For every
valid input it has exactly one solution, encoding the full ladder sign chart.
Adding the condition that no active top-row label is negative gives exactly
one solution if
\[
 F(n)\ge0\quad\hbox{for every }0\le n\le T,
\]
and no solution otherwise. Analogous single-fold systems represent the
predicates and canonical indices in Corollary~\ref{cdc:sg:cor:predicates}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the fixed ladder circuit, the allocated slots, and the endpoint circuits
above. Every arithmetic gate and power atom is functional. The input domain
is enforced by positive ordering slacks for the bases and canonical
coefficient pairs. The slot constraints express precisely the chart
conditions of Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:endpoint}. That theorem supplies exactly one
possible chart; the functional circuit supplies exactly one extension to all
remaining coordinates. Conversely, evaluating the true chart gives a
solution. Adding a prescribed predicate merely selects this unique solution
or rejects it.

There are $D^2+1$ chart slots and $Q_D=O(D^3)$ slot pairs. At most two
$O(D)$-size endpoint evaluations per pair give $O(D^4)$ gates and power atoms.
The fixed ladder has no greater size. The scan for a first occurrence has
size $O(D)$. No loop over the numerical horizon is used to generate the
system.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A certificate, not an equation solver]
The accompanying compiler emits a fixed-shape system and an assignment from
a candidate chart. It does not search for natural roots. Existence,
soundness, and uniqueness are mathematical claims proved above. The separate
chart generator is an effective way to construct the correct assignment.
\end{remark}

\section{Ordinary quartics with a fixed exponent bit bound\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:quartic}
Fix $B\ge1$ as part of the representation's syntax. Restrict inputs to
$T<2^B$. Since every exponent in an endpoint evaluation lies in $[0,T]$, it
suffices to eliminate powers with exponent less than $2^B$.

\begin{lemma}[Single-fold binary powering]\label{cdc:sg:lem:power}
For fixed $B$, the relation $y=b^n$ on $b\ge1$, $0\le n<2^B$ has a functional
quadratic-residual encoding with $O(B)$ natural coordinates.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Introduce bits $\varepsilon_0,\ldots,\varepsilon_{B-1}$ and enforce
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:binary}
 \varepsilon_j(\varepsilon_j-1)=0,\qquad
 n=\sum_{j=0}^{B-1}2^j\varepsilon_j.
\end{equation}
These bits are unique. Starting with $q_0=b$, define
$q_{j+1}=q_j^2$ for $0\le j<B-1$. Set $v_0=1$ and, for $0\le j<B$, require
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:powergadget}
 w_j=1+\varepsilon_j(q_j-1),\qquad v_{j+1}=v_jw_j,
 \qquad y=v_B.
\end{equation}
All values are uniquely determined, all residuals have degree at most two,
and $v_B=\prod_j b^{2^j\varepsilon_j}=b^n$.
\end{proof}

Squaring tables may be shared among all evaluations of the same base, and bit
decompositions may be shared for the same endpoint variable. Such sharing
changes constants but not the proof or asymptotic bound.

\begin{theorem}[Single-fold bounded-bit quartics]\label{cdc:sg:thm:quartic}
For each fixed shape $\boldsymbol m$ and fixed $B\ge1$, there is an explicitly
constructible polynomial with integer coefficients, of degree at most four,
whose natural zeros are in bijection with the valid sign-chart certificates
for inputs $T<2^B$. It has $O(D^4(B+1))$ witness coordinates. In particular,
one obtains a single-fold quartic representation of bounded nonnegativity,
strict positivity, and the other canonical sign predicates.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Add the natural slack equation $T+v=2^B-1$ to constrain the horizon. Replace
each power atom in Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:quasi} by
Lemma~\ref{cdc:sg:lem:power}. Call the resulting quadratic residuals
$R_1,\ldots,R_L$. Over the natural numbers,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:quartic}
 \mathcal P_{\boldsymbol m,B}(\boldsymbol a,\boldsymbol w)
       =\sum_{j=1}^L R_j(\boldsymbol a,\boldsymbol w)^2=0
\end{equation}
is equivalent to the simultaneous vanishing of all residuals. Its degree is
at most four, and no power atoms remain. The replacement introduces at most
$O(B)$ coordinates per former power atom and preserves the uniqueness of
every auxiliary value. The claimed count follows.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exactly where the bit bound lives}
The integer $B$ is fixed before the polynomial is written. Changing it gives
a different polynomial and generally a different number of variables. It is
not a quantified coordinate inside one fixed-arity polynomial. Similarly,
$D$ specifies a family of representations, not a single certificate size for
arbitrarily large recurrence order.

Thus Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:quartic} does not eliminate arbitrary exponentiation
single-fold in fixed arity. Classical Diophantineness of exponentiation can
supply ordinary existential representations, but substituting one does not
supply the required uniqueness or explicit witness count. This is precisely
the distinction relevant to the broader finite-fold and single-fold
questions \cite{mat2010,cco2024}.

\subsection{Witness height is not certificate arity}
Suppose the input coefficient magnitudes are at most $C$ and all bases at most
$M\ge1$. Formula~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:coeff} gives the crude coefficient-height bound
\[
 C'\le\max(1,C)\bigl(2^{D+1}M\bigr)^D
\]
for the ladder. Indeed, the binomial shift of a coefficient is bounded by a
factor $2^D$, and each ladder step adds at most another factor $2M$.
At an endpoint $n\le T$, a value is bounded in magnitude by
\[
 D C'(T+1)^{D-1}M^T.
\]
Consequently its bit length is at most
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:height}
 O\bigl(\log(C+1)+D^2+D\log(M+1)
       +D\log(T+1)+T\log(M+1)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The binary-powering squaring table can contain values with $O(2^B\log(M+1))$
bits, even when a loose bit bound greatly exceeds the actual horizon.
Arithmetic-coordinate bounds should therefore not be advertised as
polynomial-time verification in the binary input size, or as polynomial-bit
NP certificates. The representation compresses the number of stored time
positions; it need not compress the bit length of the values stored there.

\section{Constructing the charts without scanning time\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:algorithm}
The proof of Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:endpoint} also yields a constructive algorithm.
The bottom chart is known. Suppose a lower chart has been constructed.
On each expanded lower block, $H_r$ is monotone and has the same sign as
$F_r$. If it is increasing, two binary searches find the first nonnegative
and the first positive value. These cut the interval into at most three
pieces, labelled negative, zero, and positive. If it is decreasing, apply
those searches to the reversed sign order. If it is constant, one evaluation
suffices.

Expanded lower intervals overlap in at most a boundary vertex. Process them
left to right, skip vertices already covered, and merge adjacent pieces with
the same sign. The result is the maximal upper chart, not a possibly
noncanonical refinement.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The construction of manuscript~17's \cref{cdc:ps:sec:construct}, with an explicit bound on the number of evaluations; kept as a second route.]}

\begin{theorem}[Non-expanding chart construction]\label{cdc:sg:thm:algorithm}
The full certificate can be constructed with
$O(D^2\log(T+2))$ exact evaluations of ladder sequences, in addition to fixed
shape-dependent arithmetic. The algorithm does not enumerate $0,1,\ldots,T$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are $\sum_{r=1}^{D}M_r=O(D^2)$ lower-row blocks to process over the entire
ladder. Each uses at most two binary searches of an interval of length at
most $T+1$, and possibly a constant number of boundary evaluations. Each
search costs $O(\log(T+2))$ sign evaluations. The monotonicity precondition is
proved by Lemma~\ref{cdc:sg:lem:monotone}; merging gives the unique maximal chart.
\end{proof}

\begin{lstlisting}[caption={Conceptual chart constructor; exact integer arithmetic only.}]
charts[D] = [(0, T, zero)]
for r = D-1, ..., 0:
    pieces = []
    next_vertex = 0
    for (a, b, direction) in charts[r+1]:
        left  = max(a, next_vertex)
        right = min(b+1, T)
        if left <= right:
            split [left, right] by two monotone sign searches
            append pieces, merging equal adjacent signs
            next_vertex = right+1
    charts[r] = pieces
\end{lstlisting}

The independent verifier does not rerun these searches. It checks the
partition conditions and the $O(D^3)$ endpoint tests of
Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:endpoint}. Construction and verification therefore rely on
separate control logic. Exact arithmetic is required: a floating-point sign
near a zero is not an admissible substitute.

\section{An explicit tail threshold and all-time guards\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:tail}
A finite chart handles a given horizon. An elementary dominance bound also
lets us handle the entire nonnegative time axis for this spectral class.
The point is an explicit, arithmetically specifiable threshold, not a new
general theorem on recurrence positivity.

Delete zero leading coefficients and zero modes for this subsection only.
This reduction is deterministic; at a fixed shape it is a finite decision
procedure on coefficient signs. If all modes vanish, the sequence is zero
and we set $(T_0,\sigma_\infty)=(0,0)$. Otherwise let the largest remaining base
be $B_*$, with polynomial
\[
 P_*(X)=aX^m+\sum_{j<m}a_jX^j,\qquad a\ne0,
 \qquad A_0=\sum_{j<m}|a_j|.
\]
If there are no smaller modes, set
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:tail-one}
 T_0=\max(1,2A_0+1).
\end{equation}
If smaller modes exist, let $b_*$ be their largest base, let $C_0$ be the sum
of absolute values of all their coefficients, let $M_0$ be their greatest
polynomial degree, and put $K=\max(0,M_0-m)$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:tail-bound}
 \begin{split}
 T_0=\max\bigl\{&1,\ 2(K+1),\ 2A_0+1,\\
               &2^{K+2}(K+1)!\,b_*^{K+1}C_0+1\bigr\}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}

\srcnote{\wtag{} [Manuscript~17 certifies the infinite horizon inside its verifier, by the eventual-sign test of \cref{cdc:ps:lem:eventual} and condition V5, without any threshold. The explicit threshold below is manuscript~18's alone; \cref{cdc:sec:b79-routes} compares the two routes to all-time guards.]}

\begin{theorem}[Elementary permanent-sign threshold]\label{cdc:sg:thm:tail}
For nonzero input data, $F(n)$ is nonzero and has sign $\sgn(a)$ for every
integer $n\ge T_0$, with $T_0$ given above.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $n\ge1$, the lower-degree part of $P_*$ has absolute value at most
$A_0n^{m-1}$ when $m\ge1$; for $m=0$ that part is absent. Since $n>2A_0$ and
$|a|\ge1$, we have
\[
 \sgn P_*(n)=\sgn a,\qquad
 |P_*(n)|\ge\tfrac12|a|n^m.
\]
This proves the assertion if there are no smaller modes.

Otherwise their combined absolute contribution is at most
$C_0n^{M_0}b_*^n$. Distinct integer bases imply
$B_*/b_*\ge1+1/b_*$. Since $n\ge2(K+1)$,
\begin{align*}
 \left(\frac{B_*}{b_*}\right)^n
 &\ge \binom{n}{K+1}b_*^{-(K+1)}\\
 &\ge \frac{n^{K+1}}{2^{K+1}(K+1)!b_*^{K+1}}
 > 2C_0n^K
 \ge \frac{2C_0}{|a|}n^{M_0-m}.
\end{align*}
The strict inequality uses the last term in~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:tail-bound}. The final
comparison uses $K\ge M_0-m$ and $n\ge1$. Multiplying through shows
\[
 \tfrac12|a|n^m B_*^n > C_0n^{M_0}b_*^n.
\]
The largest-base contribution therefore strictly dominates the sum of all
smaller modes, with sign $\sgn a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A finite certificate for all-time nonnegativity]
\label{cdc:sg:cor:global}
For a nonzero sequence of the stated class, all-time nonnegativity is
equivalent to $a>0$ and nonnegativity at all integer times $0\le n\le T_0$.
This gives an effective fixed-shape single-fold exponential-arithmetic
representation of all-time nonnegativity and of its complement.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The equivalence follows directly from Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:tail}. The zero
sequence is handled separately and is nonnegative everywhere. At fixed shape,
the choice of active modes, degrees, and leading coefficient is determined by
a bounded number of canonical sign tests. The numbers $K$, $m$, and $M_0$
range over a fixed finite set; hence powers such as $b_*^{K+1}$ in the
threshold can be computed by fixed arithmetic circuits selected with
canonical Boolean logic. No unbounded search is required to specify $T_0$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:quasi} at this uniquely determined horizon and inspect
the top chart and tail sign. The same unique data decide the complement;
there is no need to guess an arbitrary counterexample index.
\end{proof}

The threshold is deliberately conservative. It gives up sharpness to avoid
logarithms, transcendental comparisons, and root isolation. The implementation
includes its exact scalar computation and sample checks; it does \emph{not}
yet export a separate global-positivity polynomial frontend. Corollary
\ref{cdc:sg:cor:global} is established by the explicit composition argument above.

\section{Guarded affine computation and universal substrates\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:loops}
\subsection{Positive-spectrum affine phases}
Consider an integer affine update and a conjunction of integer affine guards,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:loop}
 x\leftarrow Ax+c,\qquad
 g_j(x)=u_j^{\mathsf T}x+v_j\ge0\quad(1\le j\le h),
\end{equation}
with $x\in\Z^d$. The update is executed only when all guards hold. Define
\[
 z=\binom{x}{1},\qquad
 H=\begin{pmatrix}A&c\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then $z_n=H^nz_0$. An affine guard becomes a linear form in $z_n$.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [Manuscript~17 proves the same reduction, for polynomial guards as well, in \cref{cdc:ps:lem:matrix,cdc:ps:thm:affine}; for unipotent updates it is Part~IV's \cref{cdc:pt:prop:unipotent}.]}

\begin{proposition}[Spectral form of every affine guard]\label{cdc:sg:prop:affine}
Assume that all eigenvalues of $H$ are positive rational numbers. Every guard
sequence $g_j(x_n)$ has a representation of the form~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:sequence}
after multiplication by a fixed positive integer, with declared dimension at
most $d+1$. Coefficients depend rational-linearly on the initial state before
denominators are cleared. The data are effectively computable from fixed
$A,c,u_j,v_j$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Since the characteristic polynomial of the integer matrix $H$ is monic, every
rational eigenvalue is in fact an integer. The polynomial splits over $\Q$,
so a rational change of basis puts $H$ in Jordan normal form. On a block
$J=bI+N$ of size $m$, with $N^m=0$ and $b>0$,
\[
 J^n=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\binom{n}{k}b^{n-k}N^k.
\]
Each summand is $b^n$ times a polynomial in $n$ with rational coefficients.
For a repeated base, combine the blocks and use the greatest block size as
its declared polynomial multiplicity. The sum of these sizes is at most
$d+1$ (indeed, it is the degree of the minimal polynomial). Applying the guard
linear form and clearing fixed positive denominators yields the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact macro certificates]\label{cdc:sg:cor:macro}
For a fixed phase satisfying Proposition~\ref{cdc:sg:prop:affine}, the relation
``execute exactly $N$ enabled updates from $x_0$ and finish at $x_N$'' has a
single-fold exponential-arithmetic certificate with size independent of the
numerical value of $N$. With an externally fixed bit bound on $N$, it has an
