ordinary single-fold quartic family of size linear in that bit bound up to
shape-dependent constants. The same holds for the exact first-exit relation.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $N>0$, apply Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:quasi} to every guard on $[0,N-1]$, and
compute the endpoint from the same Jordan formulas at $N$. The $N=0$ case
uses a deterministic branch requiring $x_N=x_0$ and no guard checks. For
first exit, also require that some guard fails at $N$; either use the Boolean
disjunction of the computed sign bits or canonically choose the least failed
guard. Do not introduce a freely chosen failed-guard index. Every chart,
endpoint, and Boolean gate is uniquely determined. Lemma~\ref{cdc:sg:lem:power}
eliminates powers for a fixed exponent bit bound and the sum of squares
produces a quartic.
\end{proof}

A fixed finite sequence of phases can be composed by sharing their endpoint
states. The counts for the phases are parameters; they may be enormous.
The total certificate size is the sum of the phase sizes. If phase counts
are instead existential choices in a nondeterministic schedule, distinct
choices represent distinct executions; single-foldness must then be stated
relative to the specified schedule or established by a separate canonical
scheduling theorem.

\subsection{Where Turing completeness enters, and where it does not}
The branching language containing affine counter increments and conditional
zero-test/decrement instructions can simulate counter machines. This is a
universal computational substrate, and the counter-machine route is already
central in formal work on Hilbert's tenth problem \cite{lf2022}. Our certificates
accelerate specified affine phases inside such a substrate, including
non-unipotent phases with true exponential growth.

It would be incorrect to infer that one positive-spectrum affine loop is
itself universal, or that an arbitrary computation has a bounded number of
these phases. General branching can cause an unbounded sequence of phase
changes. We compress repetition inside a specified phase, not the entire
control history of an arbitrary Turing computation. This distinction is why
the result does not provide a uniform solution to an undecidable halting
problem.

\subsection{Extensions that follow from the same proof}
A fixed polynomial guard can be substituted into polynomial-exponential state
coordinates. Products of modes have positive bases, and sums can be regrouped
by equal bases. This again gives a positive-base polynomial-exponential
sequence, possibly of much greater dimension. For a fixed matrix and guard
syntax this regrouping is computable in advance. We make no claim that the
resulting dimension is small for high-degree guards.

Negative rational eigenvalues can be treated by two residue classes. On
$n=2k+\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$, a mode
$P(n)(-b)^n$ becomes
$(-b)^\varepsilon P(2k+\varepsilon)(b^2)^k$, with positive base $b^2$.
Coincident squared bases are combined. Zero eigenvalue Jordan blocks vanish
after a fixed nilpotent prefix, which can be checked directly. Thus fixed
rational real spectra reduce to a bounded prefix and positive-base charts on
even and odd times. Empty residue domains at small horizons require the same
canonical case treatment as the $N=0$ loop branch.

For rational, rather than integer, update matrices, additional semantic care
is needed. Multiplying a guard sequence by a positive denominator preserves
its sign, but does not prove that intermediate states are integers. Our
integer-state loop theorem assumes integer $A,c$. Rational-state semantics,
or an extra integrality certificate, is required for a rational-update
variant. An automatic matrix/Jordan frontend is a future implementation task,
not part of the supplied scalar compiler.

\section{Worked examples and actual certificate sizes\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:examples}
\subsection{Positive endpoints conceal an interior violation}
Let
\[
 F_0(n)=4^n-10\cdot2^n+16,\qquad 0\le n\le4.
\]
Use bases $(1,2,4)$ with multiplicities $(1,1,1)$, so $D=3$. The ladder is
\begin{align*}
 F_1(n)&=3\cdot4^n-10\cdot2^n,\\
 F_2(n)&=6\cdot4^n,\\
 F_3(n)&=0.
\end{align*}
The values of $F_0$ are $7,0,-8,0,112$. The exact charts are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cl}
\toprule
Row & Maximal sign blocks\\
\midrule
$F_0$ & $[0,0]:+,\ [1,1]:0,\ [2,2]:-,\ [3,3]:0,\ [4,4]:+$\\
$F_1$ & $[0,1]:-,\ [2,4]:+$\\
$F_2$ & $[0,4]:+$\\
$F_3$ & $[0,4]:0$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Nine slots are occupied out of the ten allocated. A full-chart certificate
correctly exists: its purpose is to describe signs, including a negative
one. Adding top-row nonnegativity rejects this input. This distinction is
important when reading the exported examples.

The actual uncompacted compiler output is as follows. ``Witnesses'' excludes
input parameters. Quadratic residuals are stored sparsely; their sum of
squares is the authoritative exact representation of the ordinary quartic.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
 & Power-atom system & Ordinary quartic, $B=3$\\
\midrule
Input natural coordinates & 10 & 10\\
Witness natural coordinates & 1,294 & 1,935\\
Quadratic residuals & 1,212 & 1,995\\
Functional power atoms & 104 & 0\\
Maximum residual degree & 2 & 2\\
Maximum final polynomial degree & not applicable & 4\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The corresponding concrete loop starts at $(x,y)=(1,1)$ and repeatedly
updates $(x,y)\leftarrow(2x,4y)$ while $y-10x+16\ge0$.
Its first exit is after two enabled updates, at $(x,y)=(4,16)$.
The later positive value at time four belongs to the unguarded affine orbit;
it cannot justify a four-step enabled execution.

These counts are not claimed optimal. The implementation prioritizes
transparent, functional gates over aggressive common-subexpression
elimination. The 10 input coordinates are $T$, three bases, and six natural
coordinates for three signed coefficients.

\subsection{Discrete positivity is not continuous positivity}
Consider
\[
 G(n)=4^n-6\cdot2^n+8=(2^n-2)(2^n-4).
\]
For every integer $n\ge0$, $G(n)\ge0$: the zeros are $n=1,2$, and all other
integer values are positive. But
\[
 G(3/2)=16-12\sqrt2<0.
\]
A method that demanded real-interval positivity would incorrectly reject
this valid integer-time guard. The certificate above accepts it because the
zero-bound argument limits chart size without changing the domain of the
predicate.

A repeated-root example is $J(n)=(n-2)(n-5)2^n$. Its declared shape has one
base and multiplicity three. The $E-2$ ladder removes the polynomial factor
one degree at a time. The supplied example includes its exact chart on
$[0,8]$, exercising both negative blocks and a genuine Jordan-type factor.
Another example declares a two-dimensional mode with all coefficients zero,
testing that unused shape dimensions do not introduce nonunique witnesses.

\subsection{A million-horizon guard without a million-row trace}
Take
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:million}
 F(n)=(2^n-2^{400})(2^n-2^{600}),\qquad T=1{,}000{,}000.
\end{equation}
In the three-mode representation this has coefficients
$2^{1000}$, $-(2^{400}+2^{600})$, and $1$ at bases $1,2,4$. Its top chart is
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 \text{interval}&[0,399]&[400,400]&[401,599]&[600,600]&[601,T]\\
 \hline
 \text{sign}&+&0&-&0&+
 \end{array}
\]
and the entire ladder again has only nine occupied blocks, out of ten
allocated. This chart covers \emph{1,000,001} integer time points.

The supplied generator produced it using 75 exact evaluations of ladder
sequences. Its largest evaluated absolute value had 1,000,602 bits. These
statistics describe chart construction, not the largest value an independent
checker might evaluate at an endpoint such as $T$, and not the cost of
exporting every arithmetic witness. The package stores the compact chart,
not a huge bounded-bit quartic assignment for this example.

The example demonstrates the intended separation: time-index storage can be
small even when exact integer arithmetic is expensive. It is not evidence of
unit-cost evaluation of million-bit numbers.

\section{A rigorous boundary: oscillatory spectra\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:obstruction}
Positive bases were used twice: to obtain a uniformly bounded number of sign
blocks and to preserve signs under normalization. A negative real base can
already force alternating signs, although parity splitting repairs that
case. An irrational complex phase gives a stronger obstruction that no fixed
residue splitting repairs.

\srcnote{\wtag{} [The residue-class strengthening of manuscript~17's \cref{cdc:ps:thm:rotation}, for the same sequence: manuscript~17 counts the sign changes exactly and remarks that no residue class has an eventually constant sign; here every residue class has a positive density $\delta_q/\pi$ of sign changes.]}

\begin{theorem}[A fixed order-two obstruction]\label{cdc:sg:thm:oscillation}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:oscillatory}
 u_0=1,\quad u_1=3,\quad u_{n+2}=6u_{n+1}-25u_n.
\end{equation}
For every fixed $q\ge1$ and $r\ge0$, the sequence $(u_{qk+r})_{k\ge0}$ has
no zeros and changes sign with a positive asymptotic density. More precisely,
write $e^{i\theta}=(3+4i)/5$ and
$\delta_q=\arccos(\cos(q\theta))\in(0,\pi)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:sg:eq:density}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \#\{0\le k<N:\sgn u_{q(k+1)+r}\ne\sgn u_{qk+r}\}
       =\frac{\delta_q}{\pi}>0.
\end{equation}
In particular, maximal sign-chart size is $\Theta(N)$ along each such
residue class, despite recurrence order two.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The characteristic roots are $3\pm4i$, so the initial conditions give
\[
 u_n=\Repart((3+4i)^n)=5^n\cos(n\theta).
\]
If $e^{i\theta}$ were a root of unity, then
$e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}=6/5$ would be an algebraic integer. A rational
algebraic integer is an integer, contradiction. For completeness, the latter
fact follows by clearing denominators in a monic integer polynomial for a
reduced fraction: its denominator must divide its numerator. Hence
$\theta/\pi$ is irrational. A zero $\cos(n\theta)=0$ for $n\ge1$ would make
$\theta/\pi$ rational; $u_0=1$ is also nonzero.

For fixed $q,r$, the angles $qk\theta+r\theta$ are equidistributed modulo
$2\pi$. One standard elementary proof first observes that for every nonzero
integer $m$ the average
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e^{im(qk\theta+r\theta)}
\]
tends to zero by the finite geometric-sum formula, since
$e^{imq\theta}\ne1$. Trigonometric-polynomial approximation then proves the
averaging formula for continuous periodic functions. Approximating interval
indicators from above and below extends it to sets whose boundary is finite.

The positive-sign set of cosine is a semicircle. Its symmetric difference
with a shift by $q\theta$ has angular measure $2\delta_q$, where
$0<\delta_q<\pi$ by irrationality. Thus the proportion of angles for which
$\cos x$ and $\cos(x+q\theta)$ have different signs is
$2\delta_q/(2\pi)=\delta_q/\pi$. Applying equidistribution to this finite union
of intervals proves~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:density}. With no zeros, each sign change adds
one block, proving the linear chart growth.
\end{proof}

This is a limitation of \emph{explicit maximal sign-chart compression} and
its fixed-residue variants. It is not a proof that this recurrence, its
positivity predicate, or any other oscillatory system lacks a different
Diophantine certificate. In particular, it establishes no undecidability
result for general linear recurrence positivity. The broader landscape has
substantially different arithmetic obstructions \cite{bkl-survey}.

\section{Executable artifacts, validation, and trust boundaries\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:validation}
\subsection{What the implementation actually does}
The package uses Python's exact integers and standard library. No
floating-point sign computations or external computer algebra system are
required. Its three main source files separate responsibilities:
\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=0pt,labelsep=0pt]
\item[\code{code/18-spectral-guards-spectral_guards.py}]
Polynomial-exponential sequences, exact $E-b$ ladders, non-expanding chart
construction, independent endpoint verification, canonical first-negative
extraction, and the scalar eventual-sign threshold.
\item[\code{code/18-spectral-guards-quartic_compiler.py}]
Natural-coordinate arithmetic gates, sparse quadratic residuals, either
functional power atoms or bounded-bit binary powering, and serialization of
the resulting system and assignment. The function \texttt{verify\_export}
reevaluates the serialized residuals without using the emitter's polynomial
evaluator.

\wtag{} [On well-formed exports. The ProveIt review (\cite{repo-sprev}, finding~5) shows that the delivered checker accepts a Boolean coordinate, a float coefficient and a negative variable index that aliases a legal coordinate, and that the emitter accepts \texttt{True} as a bit width; its patch \path{spectral_boundaries.patch} adds exact type and schema checks. The shipped \path{code/18-spectral-guards-quartic_compiler.py} is the delivered program, without that patch.]

\item[\code{code/18-spectral-guards-run_tests.py}]
Deterministic exhaustive and randomized tests, malformed-sign tests,
coordinate perturbations, shape-uniformity comparisons, and generation of
all bundled examples and validation records.
\end{description}

The compiler supports the scalar sequence frontend. It does not compute a
Jordan decomposition of an input matrix, compile a complete branching
program, export the global-threshold frontend, or produce a Lean proof term.
Those are distinct implementation layers.

\subsection{The executed test record}
The test seed is 20261002. The actual completed run reported the following;
these are categories of checks, not a count of formally proved theorems.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\toprule
Check category & Count\\
\midrule
Exhaustive chart instances compared with direct sampling & 3,087\\
Additional randomized chart instances & 700\\
Root-removing ladder identity checks & 8,097\\
Forged chart sign claims rejected & 704\\
Permanent-tail sample sign checks & 480\\
Compiled assignments checked & 12\\
Single-coordinate witness perturbations rejected & 3,134\\
Independent serialized-system checks & 2\\

All listed checks passed. Mutation testing is useful for catching forgotten

provide those assertions.

The output format lists integer coefficients and monomials for every
quadratic residual. In ordinary mode, the unexpanded sum of their squares is
an exact, finite specification of the polynomial, not a numerical hash or
probabilistic identity test. The exported witness makes direct checking
possible without solving any equation.

\subsection{Repository integration and formalization plan}
The audit used the fixed commit printed on the title page. The inspected
Lean module contains the named results \texttt{boundedForall\_dioph},
\texttt{exactIter\_dioph}, and \texttt{existsExactIter\_dioph}
\cite{repo-trace}. The existing research report's polynomial-trajectory
construction is the closest conceptual predecessor within the inspected
repository \cite{repo-cdc}. We have not rebuilt the repository,
audited all of its axioms, or checked all its research reports for overlap.

\srcnote{\wtag{} Batch~79, 2 October 2026. The research report is this one, and its polynomial-trajectory construction is Part~IV. Manuscript~17, written from the same pin on the same day and printed first in Part~XVII, is a closer relative still; manuscript~18 did not know it.}


A suitable Lean development would separate a pure finite-certificate layer
from arithmetic representability. First formalize finite integer intervals,
maximal labelled partitions, the normalized-difference lemma, and endpoint
soundness. These need not depend on MRDP. Next formalize the root-removing
coefficient transform and the chart capacity theorem; the latter can use a
real-function Rolle argument or a discrete alternative. Finally formalize a
functional-circuit compiler and its unique-extension theorem, then instantiate
binary powering and the sum-of-squares construction. The key invariant is
that every named intermediate coordinate is a function of the inputs and
chart, including all inactive cases.

A connection to the existing Diophantine interfaces can then establish
ordinary existence where appropriate. A separate theorem should carry the
single-fold assertion. Conflating these two contracts would erase the main
content of this manuscript.

It is not applied: the shipped programs are the delivered bytes. With and without the patch, all nine regenerated examples and records equal the delivered ones.

\paragraph{Neither interface contains the other.} Manuscript~17's systems need fixed bases: they compute the coefficient transform \eqref{cdc:ps:eq:coefficient} with the bases as constants and evaluate $b^n$ by atoms of fixed base. Manuscript~18's systems take the bases as inputs and pay for it with a variable-base atom and the all-pairs test. Manuscript~17 certifies an infinite tail by a coefficient test, so its infinite system has no threshold and evaluates nothing at a large index; manuscript~18's all-time certificate evaluates a finite chart up to the explicit threshold $T_0$, which can be large. Only manuscript~18 removes the power atoms, and only for an externally fixed bit bound. That is consistent with manuscript~17's order-two boundary, which concerns one ordinary polynomial uniform in the horizon: already for the shape $(1,1)$ with bases $1<2$, a fixed-arity single-fold ordinary system without the bound $B$ would represent the chart graph of $2^n-y$ and so prove $\SF$.

\paragraph{The size question.} Manuscript~18 asks for an $O(D^3)$ arithmetic bound through a canonical merge of adjacent rows. Manuscript~17's verifier attains $O(D^3)$ in its fixed-base interface by sharing the endpoint evaluations of a level, without a merge circuit, and asks in turn for $O(D^2)$. The review in the research tree confirms both counts \cite{repo-sprev}. The two questions are printed together (\cref{cdc:ps:q:1}).

\paragraph{What the polynomial case adds.} For base~$1$ both theorems reduce to Part~IV's sign tower, which manuscript~17 extends by a zero row and an infinite mode and manuscript~18 by input bases. In Part~IV's language the result is an ordinary quartic with $O((d+1)^3)$ coordinates (\cref{cdc:pt:thm:main}), the case $D=d+1$ of manuscript~17's count.

\section{Research questions and integration priorities\srctag{17}}
\label{cdc:ps:sec:agenda}

The following questions separate direct engineering improvements from
new mathematical extensions and from genuinely strong multiplicity
conjectures.

\srcnote{\wtag{} Manuscript~17 posed its ten questions as a numbered list Q1--Q10 with bold headings; each is one \texttt{question} environment here, titled by its number and heading, and the text is unchanged. Q1 is merged with manuscript~18's first question, which asks for the same saving one level lower; that question's text is printed in it. A \wtag{} line after a question names the questions of this report or of manuscript~18 that it overlaps; those are not merged.}

\begin{question}[Q1. Can the cubic checker be made quadratic?; sources 17, 18]\label{cdc:ps:q:1}
\emph{Source 17 (Q1).}
The current construction compares every parent run with every child
endpoint, producing $O(D^3)$ work after summing over levels. Since both
lists are ordered, their true overlap relation has only linear size per
level. Construct a \emph{canonical arithmetic merge certificate} whose
unique routing witnesses avoid all-pairs comparisons. The target is
$O(D^2)$ arithmetic size for full-chain verification, while accounting
honestly for the shared endpoint-evaluation cost. Reducing overlap
checks alone does not automatically reduce Horner evaluation cost.

\emph{Source 18 (Reduce the endpoint-pair overhead).}
The transparent compiler tests every allocated upper/lower slot pair,
producing $O(D^3)$ intersections and an $O(D^4)$ total arithmetic bound. Actual
partitions on a line have only a linear number of nonempty overlay intervals.
Can one compile their canonical merge in $O(D^2)$ total pair operations over
the ladder, without a guessed permutation, variable-length output, or
nonunique inactive witnesses? A functional merge circuit with a proved
unique trace would be a concrete route to an $O(D^3)$ arithmetic bound.
The challenge is to preserve the external fixed shape while avoiding a
quadratic all-pairs comparison inside each pair of rows.
\end{question}

\wtag{} The two sources ask for one improvement at two levels. Manuscript~17's verifier already shares the parent and child endpoint evaluations of a level, and so reaches $O(D^3)$ in its fixed-base interface (\cref{cdc:ps:thm:compiler}), the total that manuscript~18 asks for, by sharing evaluations rather than by a merge circuit; the research tree's review confirms both counts (\cite{repo-sprev}). For input bases, as in \cref{cdc:sg:thm:quasi}, neither manuscript proves an $O(D^3)$ bound, and the canonical merge certificate that both describe, with linearly many pair operations for each pair of rows, is open in both interfaces.

\begin{question}[Q2. Can endpoint evaluations be shared across levels?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:2}
The same index often occurs in several charts, and neighboring levels
are linked by $f_{j+1}(n)=f_j(n+1)-a_j f_j(n)$. Determine whether a
canonical evaluation DAG can reduce repeated power atoms and Horner
wires without introducing free choices of a DAG or silently adding
many shifted evaluation indices.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Q3. What is the best annihilator order?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:3}
All orders give correct certificates, but they can produce quite
different intermediate sign profiles and coefficient sizes. Find
criteria for choosing an order that minimizes actual active runs,
coefficient height, or evaluation cost. If the order becomes a witness
rather than a compile-time choice, impose a canonical minimization or
lexicographic convention and account for its verification cost.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Q4. Can positive algebraic irrational bases be supported without losing canonical arithmetic witnesses?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:4}
A real zero-count and monotonicity argument still applies, but an
integer encoding must represent algebraic powers, comparison signs,
and the chosen real embedding. A complete solution needs more than
naming a minimal polynomial: conjugate roots must not be confused,
and sign-certifying auxiliaries must be uniquely determined. A useful
first target is one fixed real quadratic field with two positive
embeddings and explicitly tracked coordinates.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Manuscript~18 asks the same question (\cref{cdc:sg:q:algebraic}).

\begin{question}[Q5. Can residue splitting be made fully algebraic and automatic?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:5}
Extend the negative-root treatment to spectra whose phases have a
fixed finite order. Determine the required residue modulus from the
fixed matrix, strip nilpotent prefixes, and compile all tails with
canonical input loaders. The rational-rotation obstruction shows why
this route cannot handle arbitrary complex phases.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~18's questions on a verified matrix frontend and on complex phases (\cref{cdc:sg:q:frontend,cdc:sg:q:complex}); its \cref{cdc:sg:thm:oscillation} shows that no fixed residue splitting handles the rotation of \cref{cdc:ps:thm:rotation}.

\begin{question}[Q6. How far can exact phase compression extend beyond triangular maps?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:6}
For a fixed polynomial update, search for a finite invariant space of
observables that contains the guards and state outputs. A successful
space provides a lifted recurrence; the next issue is its spectrum.
Design a verified sparse-space discovery procedure and certify both
invariance and the claimed spectral factorization rather than trusting
a computer-algebra heuristic.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~18's question on a verified matrix frontend (\cref{cdc:sg:q:frontend}).

\begin{question}[Q7. Can ordinary witness multiplicity be controlled on useful restricted power interfaces?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:7}
The full variable-$T$, variable-$y$ chart of $2^n-y$ is already
equivalent to $\SF$ or $\FF$. Less expressive interfaces may avoid
this barrier: fixed horizon, coefficient restrictions preventing
zero tests at an arbitrary endpoint, or purely qualitative sign
questions. Classify which interfaces still recover the power graph.
Any positive result must state the restrictions explicitly.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Answered in part by manuscript~18 for one restricted interface: its bounded-bit quartics (\cref{cdc:sg:thm:quartic}) are ordinary and single-fold for horizons below an externally fixed $2^B$, one polynomial for each $B$. Compare Source~02 of \cref{cdc:q:compression}, \cref{cdc:q:ffprimitives}, and manuscript~18's question on separating bounded-bit optimization from unrestricted elimination (\cref{cdc:sg:q:bounded}).

\begin{question}[Q8. Can structured control histories have canonical bounded phase decompositions?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:8}
For an identified subclass of universal-language programs, bound the
number of repeated-word phases by program structure rather than runtime.
Alternatively, prove a lower-bound family showing that every such
decomposition requires unboundedly many phases. Do not infer this
property from the fact that each individual loop has a compact
certificate.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:restricted} and manuscript~18's question on composition across branching phases (\cref{cdc:sg:q:branching}).

\begin{question}[Q9. Can the arithmetic backend be integrated with ProveIt's verified expression infrastructure?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:9}
Formalize the coefficient transform, chain annihilation, slot
semantics, monotonicity lemma, endpoint verifier, and unique-extension
gadgets as separate interfaces. The natural-number domain is essential.
A first milestone is a kernel-checked theorem that the exported
degree-two residual system plus its exact power graphs has precisely
the stated full-witness relation. Ordinary power elimination should
remain a separate theorem with its actual multiplicity guarantees.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:verified}.

\begin{question}[Q10. Can bit complexity be improved without weakening exactness?; source 17]\label{cdc:ps:q:10}
The coordinate bound does not prevent large powers. Investigate
canonical sign certificates based on exact interval bounds or modular
reconstruction that avoid storing every full endpoint value. Such a
method must certify separation from zero, handle exact zero samples,
and fix any precision or reconstruction choices uniquely. Merely
using floating-point evaluation is not a sound replacement.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~18's question on smaller exact sign witnesses (\cref{cdc:sg:q:values}).

The most immediate deliverables are a verified local checker, a general
triangular front end, and a smaller canonical merge circuit. The
multiplicity-preserving elimination problem in Q7 is a different level
of difficulty: \cref{cdc:ps:thm:powbarrier} proves that an unrestricted solution
would settle the corresponding general conjecture.

\section{Further research questions and concrete next targets\srctag{18}}
\label{cdc:sg:sec:questions}

\srcnote{\wtag{} Manuscript~18 posed its nine questions as unnumbered subsections; their headings are the titles here, and the text is unchanged. The first, \emph{Reduce the endpoint-pair overhead}, is printed with manuscript~17's Q1 in \cref{cdc:ps:q:1}. A \wtag{} line after a question names the question of manuscript~17 or of this report that it overlaps.}

\begin{question}[Find sharper purely discrete capacity invariants; source 18]\label{cdc:sg:q:capacity}
The bound $2d-1$ is sharp for a single row, but the sum $D^2+1$ is an allocated
capacity, not a proved minimum for simultaneous ladder certificates. Which
sign-block patterns can occur together across an $E-b$ ladder? A sharp
joint-capacity theorem could improve constants or even the total order.
A second objective is a fully discrete proof of the needed variation bound,
removing logarithms and Rolle's theorem from a Lean formalization while
retaining the same fixed-size certificate.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Replace large values by smaller exact sign witnesses; source 18]\label{cdc:sg:q:values}
The million-horizon example exposes a real cost: few sampled values can still
have millions of bits. Could a canonical sign verifier use separated
mantissa/exponent bounds, dominant-term intervals, or verified comparison
certificates instead of storing every complete integer power? Any proposed
scheme must handle exact cancellation and isolated zeros, not merely
well-separated generic inputs. The meaningful target is an explicit bit-size
bound under stated separation assumptions, together with exact fallback
certificates outside those assumptions.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~17's Q10 (\cref{cdc:ps:q:10}).

\begin{question}[Positive algebraic eigenvalues; source 18]\label{cdc:sg:q:algebraic}
The proof of the sign-chart bound works for arbitrary positive real bases,
but the natural-number compiler uses integer power values. For positive
algebraic bases, one could work in an explicitly represented number field,
store powers in a rational basis, and certify the sign of the selected real
embedding. The missing ingredient is a compact canonical sign certificate
for field elements that composes with the ladder and has transparent witness
height. This is more than changing a datatype: embedding selection and
separation bounds must be represented without introducing arbitrary choices.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Manuscript~17's Q4 asks the same question (\cref{cdc:ps:q:4}).

\begin{question}[A verified matrix-to-certificate frontend; source 18]\label{cdc:sg:q:frontend}
For fixed rational-split matrices, automate the reduction in
Proposition~\ref{cdc:sg:prop:affine}, including denominator clearing, repeated roots,
zero-mode prefixes, and parity splitting. Instead of trusting a numerical
Jordan decomposition, output rational similarity identities or a minimal
polynomial/closed-form certificate checked by exact arithmetic. A useful first
milestone is a frontend for upper-triangular integer matrices with positive
diagonal, followed by a proof that the scalar guard coefficients are correct
for every initial state.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~17's Q5 and Q6 (\cref{cdc:ps:q:5,cdc:ps:q:6}).

\begin{question}[Canonical composition across branching phases; source 18]\label{cdc:sg:q:branching}
A fixed phase word is easy to compose; arbitrary branch changes are not.
Identify program classes with a canonically bounded number of spectral phases,
or a canonical compressed phase grammar. The question is structural, not
merely algebraic: why should one phase summary determine the next without
storing an unbounded branch history? A result for flat control-flow graphs,
with explicit conditions excluding ambiguous cycle decompositions, would be
a useful intermediate target. No general bounded-phase theorem for universal
programs should be expected from the present argument.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~17's Q8 (\cref{cdc:ps:q:8}) and \cref{cdc:q:restricted}.

\begin{question}[Improve the arithmetic tail threshold; source 18]\label{cdc:sg:q:tail}
The threshold in~\eqref{cdc:sg:eq:tail-bound} uses only one binomial term and discards
the actual base gap beyond its being at least one. Derive substantially
smaller canonical bounds that exploit $B_*-b_*$, actual leading coefficient
size, and individual lower-mode degrees. An attractive target is a
piecewise-polynomial or exponential-arithmetic threshold with a formal proof
and a quantified comparison to the elementary bound. Better thresholds matter
both for the global certificate and for the size of values computed by its
checker.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Manuscript~17's infinite verifier needs no threshold (condition V5 and \cref{cdc:ps:lem:eventual}); the threshold matters for manuscript~18's finite-chart route to all-time guards (\cref{cdc:sg:cor:global}).

\begin{question}[Beyond sign charts for complex phases; source 18]\label{cdc:sg:q:complex}
Theorem~\ref{cdc:sg:thm:oscillation} rules out fixed-capacity interval charts for a
simple oscillatory example, even after fixed residue splitting. It suggests
looking for a different certificate language: phase cells on a torus,
trigonometric algebraic identities, or dominant oscillatory components with
certified exceptional times. Such a language must distinguish infinite sign
oscillation from the much subtler questions about zeros and nonnegativity of
sums of several modes. A first target is an exact certificate for a single
conjugate pair plus a strictly dominant positive real mode.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~17's Q5 (\cref{cdc:ps:q:5}).

\begin{question}[Separate bounded-bit optimization from unrestricted elimination; source 18]\label{cdc:sg:q:bounded}
There are two very different projects: optimize the ordinary quartic family
at fixed $B$, and eliminate the $B$-dependence while retaining fixed arity and
unique witnesses. The former admits concrete compiler benchmarks, sharing
optimizations, and lower-bound questions. The latter touches the substantive
single-fold representation issue, not a routine exponentiation gadget.
Any proposed improvement should state explicitly which project it addresses.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare manuscript~17's Q7 (\cref{cdc:ps:q:7}). A fixed-arity single-fold ordinary version without the bound $B$, already for the shape $(1,1)$ with bases $1<2$, would give one for the chart graph of $2^n-y$ and hence $\SF$ (\cref{cdc:ps:thm:powbarrier}); a finite-fold version would give $\FF$.

\section{Conclusions\srctag{17}}\label{cdc:ps:sec:conclusions}

The main result replaces a time-indexed execution tableau by a finite
hierarchy of maximal sign intervals. Positive-base exponential
polynomials have a bounded number of such intervals, and the
annihilating chain turns this geometric fact into a local endpoint
verifier. Canonical padding, exact coefficient signs, and unique
arithmetic gadgets then produce a complete natural-number witness,
not just an existential outline.

The construction handles an entire infinite trajectory without a guessed
asymptotic cutoff. It applies to exponential growth, repeated roots,
polynomial guards, and nonlinear triangular register updates. It
composes across fixed repeated-word phases inside a Turing-complete
language. At the same time, it exposes rather than hides the two main
obstacles: oscillatory sign complexity and multiplicity-preserving
power elimination.

The complete sign-chart interface for $2^n-y$ provides a particularly
small test case for the latter obstacle. Its order is only two, yet an
ordinary single-fold or finite-fold implementation would entail the
corresponding general Diophantine multiplicity assertion. This gives a
precise boundary between the constructive power-assisted result proved
here and a much stronger theorem that has not been established.

% ---- manuscript 18, lines 1263-1279 ----
\section{Conclusion\srctag{18}}\label{cdc:sg:sec:conclusion}
The main construction replaces a time-expanded guard tableau by a canonical
ladder of discrete sign intervals. Positive-root differences supply the exact
monotonicity needed to verify each interval at endpoints, and a classical
zero bound supplies a fixed capacity. The result is a unique certificate with
$D^2+1$ allocated chart slots and an explicit fixed-shape exponential-arithmetic
compiler. Externally bounded exponent bit width then yields ordinary
single-fold quartics.

The contribution is deliberately separated from broader claims. It extends
the repository's polynomial-trajectory method to exponential growth and
Jordan factors, gives reproducible arithmetic witnesses, and exposes both a
bit-height limitation and an oscillatory-spectrum limitation. These are
concrete advances in certificate design, with complete proofs and a tested
scalar implementation. They do not substitute a new name for MRDP, claim
universal fixed-history compression, or establish historical novelty beyond
the source comparison actually performed.

From its root directory, run:

Python 3.10 or later is required. No external Python package is needed.
The PDF build uses pdfLaTeX with the packages named in the source.

A minimal scalar use is:
\par\noindent
\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
from profiles import ExpPoly, make_chain, build_profiles, verify_profiles

shape = {1: 0, 2: 0, 4: 0}
f = ExpPoly({1: [64], 2: [-20], 4: [1]})
chain, factors = make_chain(f, shape)
finite = build_profiles(chain, 6)
infinite = build_profiles(chain, None)
assert verify_profiles(chain, finite, 6)
assert verify_profiles(chain, infinite, None)
\end{lstlisting}
\end{minipage}
\par
Run this from the \texttt{code} directory or add that directory to
\texttt{PYTHONPATH}. Coefficient lists are in ascending degree order.
A value of \texttt{None} for the horizon denotes all nonnegative
integers. A supplied shape reserves every declared coefficient even
when it is numerically zero.

The exported arithmetic systems are intentionally verbose. They make
witness roles, comparison slacks, disabled-branch computations, and the
power predicates visible for inspection. A smaller encoding is a
reasonable optimization target, but one should compare complete
systems rather than omitting auxiliary constraints from the ledger.

\section{Formalization and provenance checklist\srctag{17}}\label{cdc:ps:app:checklist}

\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~B of manuscript~17. Its \path{SOURCE_AUDIT.md} is shipped as \path{17-positive-spectrum-SOURCE_AUDIT.md}.}


No new theorem in this manuscript is presented as already checked by
Lean or Rocq. The following dependency order would keep a future
formalization auditable.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Prove the symbolic $E-a$ coefficient transform and its annihilation
in a fixed finite exponential-polynomial space.
\item Prove the real zero bound, discrete run bound, and finite-profile
existence, treating the identically zero case separately.
\item Prove the eventual-sign theorem and infinite-profile existence.
The asymptotic theorem is used only for a coefficient-determined sign,
not for a real-valued witness.
\item Define the padded natural descriptor relation and prove its
bijection with maximal interval partitions.
\item Prove the local-verifier theorem, including the lifted endpoint
$R+1$, finite clipping, singleton intersections, and the infinite-tail
case.
\item Prove each arithmetic gadget has exactly one extension on valid
inputs and that compilation preserves this property under composition.
\item Export a checked correspondence between the residual/power system
and the semantic profile relation. Only after this should one discuss
ordinary Diophantine replacement of power atoms.
\end{enumerate}

The repository audit was targeted, not exhaustive. Its main files were
the Hilbert-tenth-problem README, the canonical-certificate report
README, and the relevant declarations in \path{Paper1984/DPR.lean}.
The exact pin is printed on the title page and recorded in
\path{17-positive-spectrum-SOURCE_AUDIT.md}. No repository writes, commits, or pull
requests were made. No third-party article PDFs or font files are
redistributed in the archive.

\section{Reproduction and the exact export format\srctag{18}}\label{cdc:sg:app:format}

\srcnote{\wtag{} Appendix~A of manuscript~18. The listings keep the delivered layout (\path{code/}, \path{examples/}, \path{validation/}); the programs are shipped as \path{code/18-spectral-guards-*}, and the examples and validation records as \path{data/18-spectral-guards-*}. The manuscript's \path{article.tex}, \path{article.pdf}, \path{README.md} and \path{SHA256SUMS.txt} and the console copy \path{validation/test_output.txt} (the same bytes as \path{results.json}) are not shipped. The README of this report gives a recipe on a copy.}

The package requires Python 3.10 or later and a standard LaTeX installation.
From the package directory:
\begin{lstlisting}
python3 code/run_tests.py
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{lstlisting}
The Python command regenerates the example and validation JSON files. A
minimal scalar invocation is:
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "code")
from spectral_guards import Mode, Sequence, build_certificate
from spectral_guards import verify_certificate, first_negative
from quartic_compiler import compile_certificate, verify_export

f = Sequence((Mode(1, (16,)), Mode(2, (-10,)), Mode(4, (1,))))
certificate = build_certificate(f, 4)
assert verify_certificate(certificate)
assert first_negative(certificate) == 2
system = compile_certificate(certificate, bits=3)
assert not system.failed_residuals()
system.export("example_quartic.json")
assert verify_export("example_quartic.json")
\end{lstlisting}

Each exported residual is a list of terms $[c,[i_1,\ldots,i_k]]$, denoting
$c\,w_{i_1}\cdots w_{i_k}$. The empty index list denotes a constant and
repeated indices denote repeated factors. Degree is at most two. The arrays
\texttt{names}, \texttt{values}, and \texttt{inputs} identify all coordinates,
the proposed natural assignment, and which coordinates are parameters.
A \texttt{power\_atoms} triple $[i,j,k]$ means $w_k=w_i^{w_j}$; this list is
empty in the bounded-bit quartic exports. Thus a reader can independently
reconstruct and verify every equation from the JSON, including the distinction
between quasi-Diophantine and ordinary-polynomial mode.

\part{Compressed queue traces: grammar-size quartics, exact macro repetition and infinite-loop certificates}\label{cdc:part:cqueue}

\paragraph{Source and scope.} \wtag{} This Part is manuscript~20, ``Compressed Queue Computation: Grammar-size quartic certificates, exact periodic acceleration, and certified infinite loops'' (batch~79, manuscript~11; archive \path{Compressed_Queue_Diophantine_Research.zip}, inner directory \path{Compressed_Queue_Diophantine}; arrival commit \texttt{ef2fc7990}; pinned at \texttt{44983ed7e}; placed by \texttt{bbaf322e5}; shipped files prefixed \path{20-compressed-queue-}; labels \texttt{cdc:cq:}). It prints the manuscript's Sections 2--15 and its two appendices in their own order: reliable FIFO actions and the obstruction of borrowed output (\cref{cdc:cq:sec:semantics}); the length-resource algebra and the causal endpoint theorem (\cref{cdc:cq:lem:resourcecomposition,cdc:cq:thm:endpoint}) with its content-sensitive saturation (\cref{cdc:cq:prop:saturation}); radix pairs and a unique minimum gadget (\cref{cdc:cq:sec:arith}); the grammar-size quartic with exactly $6g+3c+1$ natural witnesses and $6l+9c+3$ residuals (\cref{cdc:cq:thm:compiler}) and a doubling example of $2^{16}$ steps (\cref{cdc:cq:sec:examples}); the exact number of copies of a closed macro, a finite conjugacy criterion for infinite repetition and a Fine--Wilf pumping threshold (\cref{cdc:cq:thm:maxrepeat,cdc:cq:thm:conjugacy,cdc:cq:thm:pump}); an ordinary unique-witness quartic for a supplied infinite loop (\cref{cdc:cq:thm:infinitequartic}); powered schemas with explicit power predicates (\cref{cdc:cq:thm:powered}); deletion-tag systems and several channels (\cref{cdc:cq:thm:multiqueue}); polynomial-time decision of supplied grammars through an external compressed-word algorithm, and two impossibility theorems (\cref{cdc:cq:cor:compresseddecision,cdc:cq:thm:nobound,cdc:cq:thm:nolassocomplete}); the validation record, a formalization path, ten research questions, the conclusion and two appendices. Its title page, abstract, status statement and Section~1 are \cref{cdc:sec:ms20}; the conventions of this Part are \cref{cdc:conv:b79-XVIII}.

\paragraph{Relation to the other Parts.} \wtag{} Manuscript~20 inspected ProveIt at \texttt{44983ed7e}, when Parts~I--XV of this report had been written; it read this report's README and manuscript~07's integration note, not the article, which it could not retrieve. About a quarter of its text therefore proves again, in one coordinate, results printed above; brackets at those places say so, and no novelty is claimed for them.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Part~I.} The resource pair and its composition (\cref{cdc:cq:lem:resourcecomposition}), the prefix-deficit formula, the power formula (\cref{cdc:cq:prop:resourcepower}) and the minimum gadget are manuscript~06's resource-summary algebra in one coordinate (\cref{cdc:cs:lem:resourceproduct}, \eqref{cdc:cs:eq:prefixformula}, \cref{cdc:cs:thm:power,cdc:cs:lem:min}).
\item \emph{Part~VI.} The endpoint theorem (\cref{cdc:cq:thm:endpoint}) is the one-queue case of manuscript~07's network reconstruction (\cref{cdc:qc:thm:network-causality}), with its first-failure product (\cref{cdc:qc:thm:first-failure}) replaced by an equivalent threshold that composes along a grammar. Part~VI's certificates have one coordinate per consumed symbol (its local quartic has $3T-2$, \cref{cdc:qc:thm:quartic}); here the size is that of a supplied grammar, and no comparison of constants for uncompressed traces is made.
\item \emph{Parts~VIII and~IX.} The six-coordinate word summary makes reliable FIFO actions satisfy manuscript~06's unique-summary contract (\cref{cdc:cs:prop:abstract}) under concatenation; for variable powers the predicates of \cref{cdc:cq:thm:powered} remain, the obstruction Part~IX's exponentiation boundary describes (\cref{cdc:pt:prop:exponential-boundary}). The Part answers the queue clause of \cref{cdc:q:storage} and bears on \cref{cdc:q:acceleration,cdc:q:readcounts}; see the dated notes there.
\item \emph{Parts~XII and~XIV.} The repetition count, the conjugacy criterion and the pumping threshold are queue counterparts of Part~XII's capacity, infinite tails and sharp pumping bound (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:capacity,cdc:pf:thm:infinite,cdc:pf:thm:pumping}); the grammar-size bound fails for the reason of \cref{cdc:bd:prop:nobound}, and for priority FRACTRAN Part~XII proves more than the lasso incompleteness here (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:ep}). Part~XIV also compiles straight-line grammars (\cref{cdc:rt:thm:grammar}), but there the loads are inputs; here the whole trace is compiler data.
\item \emph{Manuscript~19.} A proposed queue run that ``borrows its own future output'' is the FIFO form of the borrowed firings that manuscript~19 excludes in sandpiles (\cref{cdc:nb:ex:phantom}, inside Part~XVI).
\end{itemize}
ProveIt's Hilbert's-tenth-problem research tree, maintained separately, reviewed this archive on the day it arrived \cite{repo-cqrev}: it finds no theorem-level defect, reproduces two defects of the low-level constructors with a tested patch that is not applied to the shipped programs, and verifies a projection of the finite compiler to $6c+1$ coordinates and $6c+3$ residuals; the notes after \cref{cdc:cq:thm:compiler} and at the end of \cref{cdc:cq:sec:validation} give the details.

\paragraph{Setting and hypotheses.} \wtag{} Reliable FIFO queues over a finite alphabet; an action reads a whole fixed word and then appends a fixed word; control compatibility is checked statically. The whole trace grammar, not only a horizon, is compiler data, and the queue endpoints are actual words: every witness is determined bottom-up by $(G,q,r)$, so the polynomial checks a supplied compressed run and quantifies no computational choice. Contrast Part~VI, whose witnesses are the consumed symbols, and Part~XIV, whose loads are inputs. Witnesses range over $\N$; no uniqueness over $\Z$ is claimed. The theorems bound numbers of variables and residuals and the degree, not the bit lengths of the witnesses, which can be exponential in the grammar size. Macros and lassos are supplied, never inferred; schedule synthesis is not addressed. Powered schemas are quasi-Diophantine, with explicit power predicates. Nothing here is a universal fixed-arity equation, a single-fold or finite-fold MRDP theorem, an improvement of the project's 75- and 87-operation bounds, or a Lean development.
